docs.title: HQL
docs.text:
HQL, the Hyper Query Language, is a strongly typed expression and query language. It combines functional expressions with pipelines over files, streams, structured data and HyperMarkDown documents, and checks a program's types before it evaluates it.

type Book { title : String, year : Int, rating : Int }

books = [
    Book(title = "Dune", year = 1965, rating = 5),
    Book(title = "Emma", year = 1815, rating = 3),
    Book(title = "Beloved", year = 1987, rating = 4),
]

books
| filter(b => b.rating >= 4)
| sort(b => b.title)
| map(b => b.title)

["Beloved", "Dune"]

source reads the documents a file holds, and target writes a value to one:

source(file("sightings.jsonl"), Json)
| filter(s => s.seen == "morning")
| target(file("morning.json"))
  • Install — a release binary or cargo install hql.
  • Learn HQL — the book in three parts, the language, data flows, and knowledge and AI, one runnable program at a time.
  • Reference — the grammar, the command line, and reporting.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The example corpus is where HQL's features are designed: an example is written first, and the implementation is held to it. Each query file declares its expected type and result in a header, and the test suite runs every one.

Corpus What it shows tutorial The reading-club vault the HQL book runs against: books, authors, their links, a relation card, an agent card and an embedding index for the questions the book asks notebook A reading list whose cells share values by id, built with hql render, and a meeting note whose cells run an agent over the draft, written as design birds Linked cards with runnable collection queries: repeated sightings, distinct species, keyed counts, ordered routes and sorted keys — plus intentional errors for duplicate keys and non-orderable sorted-map keys mapreduce Book cards filtered, grouped and reduced, read as a chain of steps functions Declared, generic and aliased functions, partial application, and intentional errors streams Generators with yield, an unbounded stream ended by take, and the lazy steps

docs.title: Reading a query header
docs.text:
// status: valid-now
// feature: Bird cards filtered and sorted by name
// implementation: implemented
// vault: birds/wiki
// expected-type: Seq<String>
// expected: ["Barn owl", "Common raven", "European robin"]

A header may instead say status: proposed with implementation: pending and a proposal: naming the record that specifies it. Such a case is a design input, pinned before it runs, and the suite asserts that it does not check yet — the day it does, it has to be promoted.

docs.title: Running one
docs.text:
From a clone, after cargo build --locked:

target/debug/hql --vault examples/birds/wiki run examples/birds/queries/catalog.hql

docs.title: From a release
docs.text:
Each release ships a binary for every supported target, with a checksum beside it. Download the pair from the releases page, check it, and put hql somewhere on your PATH:

shasum -a 256 -c hql-<version>-<target>.tar.gz.sha256   # sha256sum -c on Linux
tar -xzf hql-<version>-<target>.tar.gz

The targets are x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, aarch64-apple-darwin and x86_64-apple-darwin. Verify the archive against the published SHA-256 checksum before extracting it.

docs.title: With Cargo
docs.text:
With Rust 1.95 or newer from rustup:

cargo install hql --locked                                   # the last release
cargo install --git https://github.com/ewiger/hql --locked   # the latest commit
cargo install --path . --locked                              # from a clone

docs.title: Check it works
docs.text:
hql eval '40 + 2'

42

hql builtins lists every step a pipeline may use, grouped by the extension that provides it.

Versions

While the major version is 0, a minor release may change the language incompatibly. The changelog lists each such change by release.

docs.title: Learn HQL
docs.text:
This is a book about HQL, read from the first page to the last. It starts with a number and ends with a web of vaults, and every chapter builds on the ones before it. Every program in it prints what the book shows. Chapter 18 and chapters 25 to 27 describe APIs and object stores, the ai module and the direction beyond one vault, which are design and not in the current release, as do the marked sections of chapters 14, 15 and 19. Chapter 14's companion on planning separates the local backend from future execution strategies. The programs of chapters 16, 17, 19 and 20 that reach a server are checked in the book and run in the hql-demo repository.

HQL is a strongly typed language for querying, transforming, connecting and computing over data, knowledge and AI workflows. A program is checked before it runs, and values flow through pipelines of typed steps: over records and lists, as jq works over JSON; over tables, as SQL does; over files, standard input and streams that do not end; over a vault of Markdown documents, their links and their meaning; and through the context, prompts and runs of a language model.

The book is in four parts. The language is the steps, the values they pass and the types that join them, from the first expression to the type system and the boundary where data from outside becomes typed. Data flows is the pipeline those steps form: what | does, when a program is checked, where it runs, and the systems a pipeline connects. Knowledge and AI is a vault of documents as a namespace, its graph, retrieval by meaning, documents that compute themselves, agents whose runs are values, documents that run them, and the web they point at. The standard library is the modules a program imports for work that is neither a type nor I/O: statistics, random values, digests and encodings, and cryptography.

docs.title: Following along
docs.text:
Install hql, clone the repository for the tutorial vault, and run each program with hql eval:

git clone https://github.com/ewiger/hql && cd hql
hql --vault examples/tutorial eval 'cards | size'

The tutorial vault, examples/tutorial/, is a small reading club: seven books, five authors, the links between them, one claim about which book inspired which, and a librarian.

docs.title: Part I: The language
docs.text:
1. Hello world — the first program, running it, and the check before a program runs.
  2. Data types — Int, Float, String and Bool in the REPL, Bytes, Data and its JSON-shaped trees, Option for a value that may be missing, and how sets, Data and maps differ.
  3. Collections — lists, sets and maps, and the steps they share.
  4. Functions — lambdas, declared functions, the two body forms = expr and { … }, generic functions, aliases, and partial application.
  5. Modules — modules of your own, imports, receiver modules, public and private declarations, and how a name resolves.
  6. SQL-like Queries — where, order by, group by and the aggregates.
  7. Streams that do not end — generators, laziness, and batches.
  8. Writing results out — presentation formats and who chooses them.
  9. I/O — sources and targets: endpoints, source, tap, target and sink, finite or live, formats, endpoints by id and the schema boundary, channels, logging, the network, files and folders, the environment and arguments, and hql as a command-line data tool.
  10. The type system — records, unions and match, results, subtypes and narrowing, generics, receiver calls, operators and traits.
  11. Advanced data typing — the type boundary where loose data becomes typed, open and closed types, TypeContract and DataContract, validators, validation as a value, and what a contract states that a schema cannot.
  12. Errors — failures kept as data, diagnostics and the run's diagnostic channel, strict and collect.
  13. Working with hql — the commands, the reports, and what to do when something is wrong.

docs.title: Part II: Data flows
docs.text:
1. ETL pipelines — the wiring as a program: | and ., the three phases, logical steps and effects, hql in a shell pipe, the shop whose orders the rest of Part II follows, and partitioning, schedules and backends. Its companion, Logical steps and physical plans, follows a checked program into local execution and the design direction for parallel workers, SQL translation and distributed execution.
  2. Endpoints — one model for every system: a file by path or by id, source, tap, target and sink, the kind that states the type, secrets in the environment, and transports.
  3. Tables and topics — the shop's orders in a SQLite table, a PostgreSQL table and a Kafka topic, what a write promises, and a topic whose messages are not all orders.
  4. Subjects and the lakehouse — core NATS notifications, a JetStream log and a durable consumer, and bronze, silver and gold Delta tables.
  5. APIs, webhooks and stores — a paginated REST API, a GraphQL catalogue, a webhook, an archive in object storage, and the systems the transport families reserve.
  6. OLTP — the shop's transactional side: its whole day in one checked file, where its mistakes are found, a replay as the same file, and streams against tables.
  7. OLAP — the history those transactions leave: bronze, silver and gold, the grain of a row and its keys, deduplication, a table kept up to date by key, and incremental loads.

docs.title: Part III: Knowledge and AI
docs.text:
1. A vault of documents — cards, their metadata, a reading list nobody maintains, and the vault as a namespace.
  2. Links and graphs — following links, building graphs, drawing them.
  3. Finding cards by meaning — rankings, hits, and the evidence behind a score.
  4. Queries inside documents — cells, documents built from them, and cells that maintain a vault.
  5. Agents and runs — agents as cards, context and prompts, tools, and runs kept as values.
  6. Agents inside documents — a document whose cells retrieve evidence, run an agent over the draft they sit in, and remember the answer.
  7. The hyper web — namespaces beyond one tree, providers, retrieval and agents across them, and a reader who asks.

docs.title: Part IV: The standard library
docs.text:
1. Statistics — means, spread, quantiles, the mode and correlation, over a list and over a query's column.
  2. Random values — sampling, shuffling, choice, numbers and UUIDs, and a seed that makes them reproducible.
  3. Digests and encodings — digests of text and bytes, the fingerprint of a Data tree, and hex, base64 and the other text encodings.
  4. Keys and cryptography — keys and their formats, secrets that print redacted, signatures, MACs and password hashes, and the encryption and key vault that are design.

docs.title: 1. Hello world
docs.text: HQL is a strongly typed expression and query language. A program is an expression, or a few statements ending in one; hql checks its type, then evaluates it, and writes the value. This chapter is about that loop.

docs.title: Hello, world
docs.text:
The smallest program that says hello is the text itself:

"Hello, world!"

"Hello, world!"

A program is an expression, and its value is what hql writes. fmt writes values into a template, one {} each:

fmt("Hello, {}!", "world")

"Hello, world!"

docs.title: Running a program
docs.text:
hql eval takes a program as an argument:

hql eval '"Hello, world!"'

Every program in this book runs that way. Most of them run against the tutorial vault, a small reading club in examples/tutorial/, so the commands in later chapters start with hql --vault examples/tutorial eval. The book shows each program in an hql block and what hql writes in the block after it.

1 + 2

3

docs.title: Values and their types
docs.text:
Every value has a type: 1 + 2 is an Int, "Hello" a String. hql check writes a program's type without evaluating it:

$ hql check - <<< '7 / 2'
Int

Chapter 2 meets the types one by one.

docs.title: Checked before it runs
docs.text:
A program is checked as a whole before anything is evaluated. A type error names the expression it found and points at it:

1 + "two"

check error[type-mismatch]: addition requires two Int, two Float or two Decimal operands
 --> <expression>:1:5
  |
1 | 1 + "two"
  |     ^^^^^

Nothing ran: there is no value, only the report, and the exit status is 1. The same holds for a name nobody bound:

pages + 1

check error[unknown-name]: `pages` is not bound
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | pages + 1
  | ^^^^^

docs.title: Bindings
docs.text:
name = expression binds a value to a name for the statements after it. The program's value is its last expression.

pages = 280
chapters = 24
pages / chapters

11

A binding may state its type, and the checker holds the value to it:

rating : Int = 5
rating

5

docs.title: Choosing a value
docs.text:
a given condition otherwise b is a when the condition holds, and b otherwise. It is an expression, so it has a type: both branches have one.

pages = 412
"long" given pages > 300 otherwise "short"

"long"

match compares one value against patterns, in order, and the first that fits gives the result:

status = "reading"
match status {
    "done" => "finished",
    "reading" => "on the nightstand",
    _ => "on the shelf",
}

"on the nightstand"

The checker rejects a match that does not cover every case before it runs; _ is the pattern that fits anything.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 2 meets the data types: Int, Float, String and Bool, tried in the REPL, and Data, the records and lists that JSON and YAML are made of.

docs.title: 3. Collections
docs.text: A Data list holds trees. Most collections in HQL hold values of one known type, and say what they promise about order and repetition. This chapter meets them, and the steps every collection shares.

docs.title: Lists, sets and maps
docs.text:
A list keeps every element at its position, duplicates included:

[412, 280, 310, 145]

[412, 280, 310, 145]

A set keeps each distinct value once and promises no order. Braces around values, rather than fields, write one:

{"novel", "essay", "novel", "poetry"}

{"novel", "essay", "poetry"}

A value prints as the literal that writes it, so a set prints in braces and a string inside a collection keeps its quotes. hql check writes a program's type without running it:

{"novel", "essay", "novel", "poetry"}

Set<String>

A map pairs each key with one value. Map(keys, values) builds one, and get looks a key up — an Option, since the key may be missing:

pages = Map(["Dune", "Frankenstein"], [412, 280])
get(pages, "Dune")

412

docs.title: A step keeps its input's shape
docs.text:
Steps work on any collection, and each returns the kind of collection it was given wherever it can: a list stays a list, a set stays a set.

[412, 280, 310, 145] | sort | take(2)

[145, 280]

[412, 280, 310, 145] | drop(1)

[280, 310, 145]

A set has no order of its own, so sort gives it one and the result is a list. And because a set keeps each value once, mapping it can make it smaller:

{3, 1, 2} | map(n => n * 0)

{0}

[3, 1, 2] | map(n => n * 0)

[0, 0, 0]

size, count and contains ask about a whole collection:

genres = ["novel", "essay", "novel"]
[genres | size, genres | count("novel")]

[3, 2]

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
sort orders by a value's own order. sort(by = key) orders by a key, and a function of two values that returns an Ordering orders by comparison:

[412, 280, 310] | sort((a, b) => compare(b, a))

[412, 310, 280]

min and max find the least and greatest value. Over an empty list there is none, and the type says so: the result is an Option.

[412, 280, 310] | min

280

[] | List<Int> | min

none

[] | List<Int> is a constructor written as a step: x | T is T(x). A constructor builds a value of its type — Set(xs), List(xs), Map(keys, values) — and the pipeline form reads left to right:

["novel", "essay", "novel", "poetry"] | Set | size

3

docs.title: Positions are promises
docs.text:
A list, a ranking and a sequence of cards have positions; a set does not. The checker rejects a set given to a step that needs positions, and says what to write instead:

{3, 1, 2} | drop(1)

check error[type-mismatch]: `drop` needs values in a stable order, and Set<Int> has none; sort it first
 --> <expression>:1:13
  |
1 | {3, 1, 2} | drop(1)
  |             ^^^^^^^

Whether a collection has a stable order is part of its type: Set<Int> has none and drop requires one, so the program is refused when it is checked, before it is evaluated, not after a wrong answer.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Steps take functions — n => n * 0, (a, b) => compare(b, a). Chapter 4 is about functions themselves: naming them, passing them, and making them generic.

docs.title: 6. SQL-like Queries
docs.text:
SQL asks a table questions: which rows, in what order, how many, grouped by what. HQL asks the same questions with pipeline steps. This chapter works through them over one table — the reading club's shelf, written as a list of records.

These examples run locally in hql. Translating their logical steps into SQL for a database engine is a future backend capability, described in Logical steps and physical plans.

docs.title: The table
docs.text:
shelf = [
    {title: "Frankenstein", author: "Mary Shelley", year: 1818, genre: "novel", pages: 280, status: "done", rating: 5},
    {title: "Dune", author: "Frank Herbert", year: 1965, genre: "novel", pages: 412, status: "reading"},
    {title: "The Hobbit", author: "J. R. R. Tolkien", year: 1937, genre: "novel", pages: 310, status: "todo"},
    {title: "Leaves of Grass", author: "Walt Whitman", year: 1855, genre: "poetry", pages: 145, status: "todo"},
    {title: "A Room of One's Own", author: "Virginia Woolf", year: 1929, genre: "essay", pages: 112, status: "done", rating: 4},
    {title: "The Common Reader", author: "Virginia Woolf", year: 1925, genre: "essay", pages: 304, status: "todo"},
    {title: "Mrs Dalloway", author: "Virginia Woolf", year: 1925, genre: "novel", pages: 194, status: "reading"},
]
shelf | size

7

Every program in this chapter begins with these lines; the book shows them once.

docs.title: Select and where
docs.text:
map is SQL's SELECT: it says what to keep of each row. filter is WHERE:

shelf
| filter(b => b.status == "todo")
| map(b => b.title)

["The Hobbit", "Leaves of Grass", "The Common Reader"]

shelf
| filter(b => b.author == "Virginia Woolf")
| map(b => {title: b.title, year: b.year})

[{title: "A Room of One's Own", year: 1929}, {title: "The Common Reader", year: 1925}, {title: "Mrs Dalloway", year: 1925}]

docs.title: Typed views of a record
docs.text:
ORDER BY pages needs pages to be numbers, and a record's leaves have no type of their own. A small function gives a record a typed view — one field, as the type the program means it to be, with what to do when it is missing:

fn title(b: Data) : String = match b.title { some(String t) => t, _ => "" }
fn pages(b: Data) : Int = match b.pages { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 }
fn year(b: Data) : Int = match b.year { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 }

From here on, the programs begin with the table and these views.

docs.title: Order by and limit
docs.text:
sort(by = key) is ORDER BY, and take(n) is LIMIT. A comparison orders the other way:

shelf
| sort(by = year)
| take(3)
| map(title)

["Frankenstein", "Leaves of Grass", "The Common Reader"]

shelf
| sort((a, b) => compare(pages(b), pages(a)))
| take(2)
| map(b => {title: title(b), pages: pages(b)})

[{pages: 412, title: "Dune"}, {pages: 310, title: "The Hobbit"}]

docs.title: Distinct
docs.text:
A set keeps each value once, so SELECT DISTINCT is the Set constructor:

shelf | map(b => b.genre) | Set

{"novel", "poetry", "essay"}

docs.title: Aggregates
docs.text:
size counts rows. sum, average, min and max work over numbers, so the pages are read through their view first:

lengths = shelf | map(pages)
{books: lengths | size, pages: lengths | sum, longest: lengths | max, average: lengths | average}

{average: 251.0, books: 7, longest: 412, pages: 1757}

Every aggregate is a fold: reduce with a starting value and a way to combine two values. sum is reduce(0, +). max is reduce(max), which starts from the first value and so is an Option: an empty list has none.

lengths = shelf | map(pages)
{total: lengths | reduce(0, +), longest: lengths | reduce(max)}

{longest: 412, total: 1757}

docs.title: Group by
docs.text:
group(by = key) partitions the rows by a key. Each group holds its key and its items, and a map over the groups computes one row per group — SQL's GROUP BY with its aggregates:

shelf
| group(by = b => b.genre)
| map(g => {genre: g.key, books: g.items | size, pages: g.items | map(pages) | sum})

{{books: 4, genre: "novel", pages: 1196}, {books: 1, genre: "poetry", pages: 145}, {books: 2, genre: "essay", pages: 416}}

HAVING is a filter after the group:

shelf
| group(by = b => b.author)
| filter(g => size(g.items) > 1)
| map(g => g.key)

{"Virginia Woolf"}

docs.title: Several answers in one pass
docs.text:
tee names a side branch of a pipeline. The branch reads the same rows, its result is bound to a name, and the main pipeline goes on unchanged. A branch of several steps continues on lines indented past the | before tee:

reading = shelf
| tee unread =
    filter(b => b.status == "todo")
    | size
| tee read =
    filter(b => b.status == "done")
    | size
| filter(b => b.status == "reading")
| map(title)
{unread: unread, read: read, reading: reading}

{read: 2, reading: ["Dune", "Mrs Dalloway"], unread: 3}

docs.title: From SQL to HQL
docs.text: SQL HQL SELECT title map(b => b.title) WHERE status = 'todo' filter(b => b.status == "todo") ORDER BY year sort(by = year) LIMIT 3 take(3) OFFSET 3 drop(3) SELECT DISTINCT genre map(b => b.genre) \| Set COUNT(*), SUM(pages) size, map(pages) \| sum GROUP BY genre group(by = b => b.genre) HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 filter(g => size(g.items) > 1)

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: The shelf was written by hand. In chapter 21 the same books are documents in a vault, and the same questions are asked of the documents themselves.

docs.title: 7. Streams that do not end
docs.text: Every collection so far had an end: a size, a last element. A stream is a succession of values whose production need not end — a log, a feed, the natural numbers. HQL types the difference, so a program cannot ask an endless stream a question that needs its end.

docs.title: A function that yields
docs.text:
A fn whose body is a block, in braces, produces its values with yield, in the order each yield is reached. Its result type says whether production ends: Seq<T> promises an end, Stream<T> does not. These are the natural numbers:

fn naturals(from: Int) : Stream<Int> {
    yield from
    for n in naturals(from + 1) {
        yield n
    }
}
naturals(1) | take(5)

[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

for name in collection { … } runs its block once per value. A block that yields is an iterating block: it holds yield, for and bindings, one per line (function bodies).

Calling naturals(1) evaluates nothing. Its value is a recipe for the numbers, and take(5) asks for five of them and then stops asking — which is what makes an endless producer usable.

docs.title: One value at a time
docs.text:
map, filter and drop take a stream and give a stream. Each value passes through the whole pipeline before the next is produced, so only as many are made as the end of the pipeline asks for:

naturals(1)
| filter(n => n % 7 == 0)
| map(n => n * n)
| take(3)

[49, 196, 441]

docs.title: Questions that need the end
docs.text:
sum, size, sort, group and the other whole-input steps need the last value before they can answer. Over a stream there may be none, and the checker says so before anything runs:

fn naturals(from: Int) : Stream<Int> {
    yield from
    for n in naturals(from + 1) {
        yield n
    }
}
naturals(1) | sum

check error[type-mismatch]: `sum` needs a finite input, and Stream<Int> may not end; bound it first with `take(n)`, or batch it with `collect(n)`
 --> <expression>:7:15
  |
7 | naturals(1) | sum
  |               ^^^

A stream becomes finite through take(n), or is answered in pieces through collect(n), which gathers consecutive values into batches of n:

naturals(1)
| collect(3)
| map(batch => batch | sum)
| take(3)

[6, 15, 24]

emit is the inverse of collect: it passes on every member of every batch, in order. flat_map(f) is map(f) | emit.

[[1, 2], [3]] | emit

[1, 2, 3]

docs.title: A sequence over the shelf
docs.text:
A generator that promises an end is a Seq. This one yields the title of each book on the shelf of chapter 6, in title order — a sequence the shelf produces on demand:

shelf = [
    {title: "Frankenstein", pages: 280},
    {title: "Dune", pages: 412},
    {title: "The Hobbit", pages: 310},
    {title: "Leaves of Grass", pages: 145},
    {title: "A Room of One's Own", pages: 112},
    {title: "The Common Reader", pages: 304},
    {title: "Mrs Dalloway", pages: 194},
]
fn title(b: Data) : String = match b.title { some(String t) => t, _ => "" }

fn titles() : Seq<String> {
    for b in shelf | sort(by = title) {
        yield title(b)
    }
}
titles() | take(3)

["A Room of One's Own", "Dune", "Frankenstein"]

A list is such a sequence already. So are the documents of a file read with source, in chapter 9, produced as each one is read.

docs.title: Writing a stream
docs.text:
Formatting an endless stream writes it piece by piece as it arrives: a line of text, a JSON value per line, a CSV row. hql flushes each piece, and a reader that stops reading ends the stream:

naturals(1) | map(n => n * n) | json

$ hql eval '…naturals… | map(n => n * n) | json' | head -3
1
4
9

A diagram format describes a whole, so | mermaid over a stream is a type error until take(n) bounds it.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 8 is about every format a value can be written in, and who chooses it.

docs.title: 8. Writing results out
docs.text:
A program's value is computed first, and written second. How it is written is a presentation format — plain text, HQL, Markdown, JSON, YAML, CSV, or a diagram — and each format is a value of type Format. A step that formats a value returns a String that also carries the format it was encoded in.

The programs of this chapter read the shelf of chapter 6, with its typed views, and the book shows these lines once:

shelf = [
    {title: "Frankenstein", author: "Mary Shelley", year: 1818, genre: "novel", pages: 280, status: "done"},
    {title: "Dune", author: "Frank Herbert", year: 1965, genre: "novel", pages: 412, status: "reading"},
    {title: "The Hobbit", author: "J. R. R. Tolkien", year: 1937, genre: "novel", pages: 310, status: "todo"},
    {title: "Leaves of Grass", author: "Walt Whitman", year: 1855, genre: "poetry", pages: 145, status: "todo"},
    {title: "A Room of One's Own", author: "Virginia Woolf", year: 1929, genre: "essay", pages: 112, status: "done"},
    {title: "The Common Reader", author: "Virginia Woolf", year: 1925, genre: "essay", pages: 304, status: "todo"},
    {title: "Mrs Dalloway", author: "Virginia Woolf", year: 1925, genre: "novel", pages: 194, status: "reading"},
]
fn title(b: Data) : String = match b.title { some(String t) => t, _ => "" }
fn pages(b: Data) : Int = match b.pages { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 }

docs.title: Formats are a category of their own
docs.text:
Each format is a Format: Text, Lines, Hql, Markdown, Hmd, Json, JsonLines, Yaml, Csv, D2 and Mermaid. A format describes how values are written, not the text itself: a step named for a format encodes any value in it, and what comes out is a String:

shelf | filter(b => b.status == "todo") | map(title) | markdown

- The Hobbit
- Leaves of Grass
- The Common Reader

shelf | filter(b => b.status == "todo") | map(title) | markdown

String

A formatted value is a String that carries its format, and a host writes its text unchanged instead of encoding it again. A later step may read it, and comparing it with a string compares the text:

([1, 2] | json) == "[\n  1,\n  2\n]"

true

docs.title: The longhand, format
docs.text:
markdown is the shorthand for format(Markdown). The longhand takes two options. limit keeps the first n elements and says how many were cut:

shelf
| map(title)
| format(Text, limit = 3)

["Frankenstein", "Dune", "The Hobbit"]
… 4 more not shown

A list of records in Markdown is a bullet list. A table is a value of its own type, Table: Table(xs, columns = [...]) takes one row per record and the columns in the order written, and every format writes it as a table, a pipe table in Markdown:

shelf
| map(b => {title: title(b), pages: pages(b)})
| Table(columns = ["title", "pages"])
| markdown

| title               | pages |
| ------------------- | ----- |
| Frankenstein        | 280   |
| Dune                | 412   |
| The Hobbit          | 310   |
| Leaves of Grass     | 145   |
| A Room of One's Own | 112   |
| The Common Reader   | 304   |
| Mrs Dalloway        | 194   |

The same table in Csv is a header row and one row per record, in Json an array of objects with their keys in column order, and in Text space-aligned columns. renderer names one of a format's encoders for a shape over the project's choice, format(Markdown, renderer = "mermaid") for a graph; a table renderer, such as pipe, writes only a Table.

A format that cannot write a value is a type error, reported before the program runs:

1 | d2

check error[type-mismatch]: no renderer writes Int as D2
 --> <expression>:1:5
  |
1 | 1 | d2
  |     ^^

docs.title: Choosing the format from outside
docs.text:
A program that does not format its result is written as HQL — the literal you would type to get the value back, a string in quotes. --to text writes a string bare instead, and --to names any other format without changing the program:

shelf | filter(b => b.status == "todo") | map(title)

- The Hobbit
- Leaves of Grass
- The Common Reader

--to none evaluates the program and writes nothing. --envelope json wraps the answer for another program to read: the type, the value, and every diagnostic the run wrote:

shelf | filter(b => b.status == "todo") | size

{
  "diagnostics": [],
  "origin": "<expression>",
  "type": "Int",
  "value": 3
}

The order is fixed: a format step in the program wins, then --to, then the host's own — Markdown for a document, HQL for a terminal.

docs.title: A project chooses its renderers
docs.text:
Which renderer writes a type in a format is a project's choice, in the hql.toml of the vault a program runs in (chapter 21), over the built-in defaults. A graph in Markdown is a D2 diagram unless the file says otherwise:

[format.Graph]
markdown = "mermaid"

A renderer or format the binary does not have fails loading the vault, so the mistake is reported before any query runs.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Every value so far was written to the terminal. Chapter 9 reads files, standard input and the network, and writes files and standard output, without leaving the language.

docs.title: 13. Working with hql
docs.text: The language is half of what you use; the other half is the command and what it says back. This chapter is about the tools: the commands, the diagnostics, and the messages hql writes when a program is wrong.

docs.title: The commands
docs.text:
Command What it does hql eval <program> check and evaluate a program given as an argument hql run <file> check and evaluate a program in a file; - reads standard input hql check <file> write the program's type, and the signature of every alias, without evaluating hql repl read, evaluate and print, keeping bindings between lines hql render <file> build a document from its cells (chapter 24) hql builtins list every step, by the provider that implements it, with its signature hql config the settings in force, and where each came from hql context [file] the execution context: the mode, the workspace, the configuration files and module roots, and where each came from hql doctor check the semantic-search chain and name the first missing part

--vault <dir> names the vault, --to <format> the output format, and --envelope json wraps the answer for another program. --workspace <dir>, --bare and --context <name> set the execution context, below.

docs.title: The REPL
docs.text:
hql repl keeps its bindings from one input to the next. The arrow keys edit a line and recall earlier inputs, from a history kept between sessions. An input goes on over several lines while a bracket is open, or while the next line opens with |, so every program in this book can be pasted in as it is written. :type asks for the type of an expression, or, given a function's name, prints the standard library's declarations of it, one per overload. :quit leaves, as do quit, exit and Ctrl-D:

$ hql repl
hql 0.5.1. `:help` for commands, `:quit` to leave.
hql> shelf = [412, 280]
()
hql> shelf | sum
692
hql> :type shelf
List<Int>
hql> :type range
fn range(start: Int, end: Int, step: Int = 1) : List<Int>    // std/seq
hql> :quit

docs.title: What a step takes
docs.text:
hql builtins lists every step with its signature, one line per form:

$ hql builtins
core 0.5.0 (always available)
  size
    Collection<T> | size<T>() -> Int
    Count all element occurrences.
  contains
    Collection<T> | contains<T>(value: T (positional)) -> Bool
    Whether a value occurs in the collection.
  …

A function of a module that the program has not imported is listed too, so the import it needs can be looked up. import lexical makes a module visible; lexical.lexical(…) names a function with its module, when two visible modules declare one name and the input does not tell them apart. The modules of lib/std/prelude.hql, string, seq, math, option, result, graph, format and io among them, are visible in every program unless the vault's hql.toml says prelude = false.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
A run produces a value and the diagnostics its phases wrote: warnings that change nothing, errors that make a result wrong, failures that make one impossible. Each is headed by the phase that wrote it, its severity and its kind, and names where it points, by line and column. Chapter 12 is the whole error model.

By default hql stops at the first error. --report collect reports every error it can find:

$ hql --report collect eval 'a = nosuchthing
b = alsomissing'
check error[unknown-name]: `nosuchthing` is not bound
 --> <expression>:1:5
  |
1 | a = nosuchthing
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^

check error[unknown-name]: `alsomissing` is not bound
 --> <expression>:2:5
  |
2 | b = alsomissing
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^

2 diagnostics: 0 failure, 2 error, 0 warning

A misspelled step suggests the nearest one, and a retired name says what replaced it, on a help line under the caret:

$ hql eval '[1, 2] | mapp(n => n)'
check error[unknown-step]: `mapp` is not a pipeline step
 --> <expression>:1:10
  |
1 | [1, 2] | mapp(n => n)
  |          ^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = help: did you mean `map`?

A warning never changes the exit status. Names have one casing per kind — snake_case for bindings, functions and fields, PascalCase for types — and a name off its kind's convention is a warning where it is written:

$ hql eval 'bookCount = 7
bookCount'
7
check warning[naming-convention]: `bookCount` is a binding, written in snake_case
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | bookCount = 7
  | ^^^^^^^^^
  = help: write it `book_count`

--envelope json carries every diagnostic, whatever the level, as data, and --diagnostics-format json writes each one to standard error as one JSON document per line. A program that wants to report on itself, apart from its result, writes to a logger: the logging page of chapter 9.

docs.title: The execution context
docs.text: Every invocation runs in an execution context: a mode, a workspace or none, and the configuration gathered for it. The same program text checks and evaluates the same way in every mode; the context determines the documents, module roots and settings it is given.

docs.title: Modes and workspace discovery
docs.text:
The anchor is the directory discovery starts from: the directory of the program's file for hql run, check, plan, boundary and context <file>, and the working directory for an expression or standard input. hql walks from the anchor upward and stops at the first directory holding .hmd/ or hql.toml; that directory is the workspace. The mode follows from what it holds:

Mode Workspace Vault bare none none workspace the directory holding hql.toml none vault the directory holding .hmd/, with or without hql.toml the workspace

The walk stops at the nearest boundary: a hql.toml inside a vault is a workspace of its own, and the outer vault's configuration does not reach it. The working directory is not consulted when a file is the anchor, so a program finds its workspace wherever hql is run from. A workspace marked by hql.toml alone still loads its documents as cards.

--workspace <dir> (or --vault <dir>) names the workspace and replaces the walk; the directory must hold .hmd/ or hql.toml. --bare runs with no workspace whatever the filesystem holds, and an operation that needs a vault fails with needs a vault rather than reading the working directory as one. --bare with --workspace is a usage error. hql render discovers a workspace for each document from that document's directory, and under --bare renders none.

hql context writes the context, each part with the layer it came from:

$ cd ~/tmp
$ hql context ../notes/scripts/report.hql
mode:      vault
context:   work (user configuration)
workspace: /home/ada/notes (discovered from the anchor)
vault:     /home/ada/notes
anchor:    /home/ada/notes/scripts
cwd:       /home/ada/tmp
hql-home:  /home/ada/.hql (the default)
prelude:   on (the default)
config:
  /etc/hql/config.toml (system configuration, absent)
  /home/ada/.hql/config.toml (user configuration)
  /home/ada/notes/hql.toml (the workspace's hql.toml, absent)
module roots:
  /home/ada/.hql/lib (user configuration)
imports:
  none

--envelope json writes the same as one JSON document.

docs.title: Configuration layers
docs.text:
Bare means no workspace, not no configuration. These layers contribute in every mode, each read in turn:

Layer Where system /etc/hql/config.toml on Unix, %ProgramData%\hql\config.toml on Windows; $HQL_SYSTEM_CONFIG names another file user config.toml in the HQL home, ~/.hql/; $HQL_HOME names another directory named context the selected [context.<name>] table of the system or user file HQL home modules ~/.hql/modules/, a module root when it exists workspace the workspace's hql.toml $HQL_PATH further module roots, separated as $PATH is command line --modules <dir>

The system and user files take the keys a workspace's hql.toml takes: [modules] roots, [extensions] import and prelude, [report] mode and level, and [execution] backend. A relative path is read against the directory of the file that declares it, never the working directory. A system or user file that does not parse fails every run, naming the file.

Module roots and extension imports gather across the layers, each once. A gathered root is a place to look, not a priority: a module that two roots provide is still an error. prelude is the last layer's that states it. The HQL home is the user's environment, not a workspace, and never a vault.

docs.title: Named contexts
docs.text:
A named context is a [context.<name>] table of the system or user file: settings grouped under a name and reused across workspaces. It takes the keys above, and workspace, which binds a workspace, read against the directory of the declaring file. A user file's definition of a name replaces the system file's; a workspace's hql.toml defines no context.

current-context = "work"

[modules]
roots = ["lib"]

[context.work.report]
level = "info"

[context.archive]
workspace = "../archive"

One context is selected: --context <name>, else $HQL_CONTEXT, else current-context, else a context named default when one is defined. A selected name that no file defines fails every run, naming the layer that selected it. A context that binds a workspace replaces the walk; a context without one leaves discovery as it is. A context selected by --context or $HQL_CONTEXT that binds a workspace, together with --bare or a --workspace naming another directory, is an error; under a context selected by current-context, the command line wins.

hql config lists and changes the selection; use-context writes current-context into the user file and keeps every other line of it:

$ hql config get-contexts
CURRENT  NAME     WORKSPACE          DEFINED IN
         archive  /home/ada/archive  /home/ada/.hql/config.toml
*        work     -                  /home/ada/.hql/config.toml
$ hql --context archive context
mode:      vault
context:   archive (--context)
workspace: /home/ada/archive (context `archive`)
…
$ hql --context nope eval 1
hql: no context is named `nope`, which --context selects; the defined contexts are `archive`, `work`

hql config current-context writes the persistent current-context, which --context and $HQL_CONTEXT leave unchanged, hql config use-context <name> sets it, and hql config view writes the system and user files merged, a table key by key and any other value from the user file.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
The report mode and level come from the command line, then the vault's hql.toml, then the environment ($HQL_REPORT, $HQL_REPORT_LEVEL), then the selected context, the user file and the system file, then the defaults. The backend follows the same order with --backend, [execution] backend and $HQL_BACKEND. hql config says which applies, and why:

$ hql config
report mode: strict (from the default)
report level: warning (from the default)
backend: localhost (from the default)
vault: none

backend selects the execution strategy described in Logical steps and physical plans, and localhost is the only one. Run inside a vault, or with --vault, the last line names it and counts its cards.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Every chapter so far was about a step. Chapter 14 is about the pipeline the steps form: what | does, when a program is checked, where it runs, and the systems a pipeline will connect.

docs.title: 14. ETL pipelines
docs.text:
Every data platform has a language for the wiring. Data Factory wires activities in JSON, PySpark in a DataFrame API, ksqlDB in SQL over topics, Kafka Streams in Java, dbt in SQL models with a dependency graph around them. Each describes the same four things: where data comes from, what is done to it, where it goes, and when. They differ in where a mistake is found: in a validator before deployment, in a cluster at run time, or in a dashboard the next morning.

HQL's claim is that the wiring is a program like any other in this book. A pipeline is one .hql file. What it reads and writes are endpoint ids that configuration binds to systems. Its types are checked before anything connects. And the same text runs over a subject that never ends and over the archive of what the subject once carried.

Part I was about the steps: what each one takes, what it gives, and the type that joins them. This part is about the pipeline the steps form, and the systems a pipeline connects. This chapter is the frame: what a pipeline is, when it is checked, what a step may and may not do, and what stays outside the file. The five after it follow one shop's orders through every kind of system a pipeline reaches, and chapters 19 and 20 are the shop's two sides, the transactions as they happen and the history they leave.

docs.title: A pipeline language
docs.text:
An HQL program is values flowing through typed steps. | is the operator that forms a step: the value on its left becomes the input of the operation on its right, and the result is the input of the next. A step invokes exactly one operation, filter, sort, map, or one presentation, json, markdown:

[3, 1, 2] | filter(n => n > 1) | sort | map(n => n * 10)

[20, 30]

A dot selects a field or calls a function on a value. s.trim() is a receiver call, and b.title a field read. Inside a pipeline step, these expressions compute the values that its operation uses:

["Dune ", " Emma"] | map(s => s.trim().upper())

["DUNE", "EMMA"]

The pipes describe the logical steps and their data dependencies. The dots express computations within those steps. A planner uses that checked program to choose physical execution stages; several steps may share a stage. The companion Logical steps and physical plans follows this distinction through local, parallel and SQL execution.

docs.title: Three phases
docs.text:
A program is parsed, then checked, then executed, and a diagnostic is headed by the phase that wrote it: parse failure and check error before anything runs, execute failure after (chapter 12). Checking resolves every name, import and module, infers and checks every type, and verifies every trait implementation; a program the checker rejects has no meaning, and no step of it executes. hql check runs the first two phases alone and prints the type the third would produce:

[3, 1, 2] | filter(n => n > 1) | sort | map(n => n * 10)

List<Int>

Execution is a strategy a backend chooses. localhost, the one backend the current release has, evaluates the checked program in process. Finite collections pass through each step in turn; streams produce values on demand. A future backend that compiles a program or runs it over many machines receives the same checked program. For the work it supports, it must compute the value localhost computes, at the same type, with the same failure where localhost fails. Unsupported work is a planning refusal before execution. Backend selection belongs to configuration, and hql config reports it.

docs.title: Logical steps and effects
docs.text:
A step is a logical unit of computation, established before planning. Its operation defines the transformation from input to result. Physical planning chooses how to perform that transformation, subject to its data dependencies, shape and effects.

An effectful operation interacts with state outside the evaluation: source reads, target and sink write, and a logger's info emits a record. Planning preserves the order of effects that the program orders and the scope of each transaction. Repeating an effect requires a delivery or transaction guarantee that permits the repeat. A backend that cannot honor the program's contract refuses it before execution.

A pure step may be rewritten as its shape and dependencies permit, while preserving results, sequence order and failures. A step that processes each value alone, filter, map, may run over separate parts of the input; a step such as sort, group, sum or size needs coordination to produce its complete result. The reading list of chapter 21 has three steps: filter tests each card, sort orders the retained cards, and map turns each card into its title. MapReduce is one possible execution strategy for suitable steps: work on parts, then combine the results. The planner chooses traversals and intermediate storage while preserving the pipeline's result. collect(n) and emit change the shape of what flows, batches of values or their members, and tee branches a pipeline without ending it; each of them is a step like any other, and the type says what the next step may ask.

docs.title: The command line
docs.text: The smallest pipeline is a shell pipe. hql '<program>' reads standard input with source(stdin, Json), writes its result as jq or awk would, and names no input or output of its own: input is source or tap in the program, output is target or sink in the program, or the result, presented by --to. The command-line page of chapter 9 shows each flag; one program there reads a log as it is written, appends its errors to a file and prints every message, with no orchestration around it. The shell connects the processes, and each hql process evaluates its program with the localhost backend.

docs.title: Streaming and batching
docs.text:
A platform's second vocabulary is about how a pipeline runs. A batch job reads an input that is all there, computes over the whole of it, and writes a result; it ends. A streaming job reads values as they arrive, computes over each, and writes as it goes; it does not end. The same transformation is often wanted both ways, and most platforms have two engines, two APIs or two deployment modes for it.

In HQL the difference is the type of the input, and the four steps of chapter 9 carry it. source gives a Seq, which ends; tap gives a Stream, which may not. target writes one completed value; sink writes each value as it arrives. A transformation written over a Seq is a batch job, and over a Stream the same text is a streaming job, and the checker says which steps each allows. The revenue of the shop's orders, over a table that ends:

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

orders : Seq<Event> = source("ledger")
orders | filter(o => o.kind == "order_placed") | map(o => o.amount) | sum

185.74

and over a topic that does not:

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

events : Stream<Event> = tap("order_events")
events | filter(o => o.kind == "order_placed") | map(o => o.amount) | sum

check error[type-mismatch]: `sum` needs a finite input, and Stream<Decimal> may not end; bound it first with `take(n)`, or batch it with `collect(n)`
  --> <expression>:10:71
   |
10 | events | filter(o => o.kind == "order_placed") | map(o => o.amount) | sum
   |                                                                       ^^^

A sum over a stream has no moment to be complete, so it is refused before the program runs, and the error names the two ways out. take(n) bounds the stream and makes a batch of its first n values. collect(n) keeps the stream and makes it a stream of batches, which is the micro-batch of Spark Structured Streaming: inside each batch every whole-input step applies, and the result is one value per batch, written as each closes:

events : Stream<Event> = tap("events")
events
| collect(4)
| map(batch => batch | filter(o => o.kind == "order_placed") | map(o => o.amount) | sum)
| sink(stdout, Json)

170.49
15.25

tap over the events file gives the six orders as a stream that ends after the last, so this program is the streaming job run against recorded input. That is the other half of the rule: an input that ends can be read either way, source as a batch or tap as a stream, and a program written for the stream is tested over a file and replayed over an archive with no change but the id it reads, which chapter 19 relies on.

The two vocabularies are independent. Streaming and batching say how a pipeline runs, one value at a time or all of them at once. OLTP and OLAP, chapters 19 and 20, say what the data is for, the transactions as they happen or the history they leave. A transactional pipeline is usually streaming and an analytical one usually batch, and the exceptions are everyday: an analytical table filled as events arrive, a transactional table backfilled from an archive. The types let a program say which it is without the platform having a word for the combination.

docs.title: The shop
docs.text:
A small shop sells to three customers, ada, grace and linus. Each thing that happens to an order is an event: placed, shipped, or a payment that failed. On the first day the events are one JSON file, and the shop's whole data platform is a pipeline over it:

source("events")
| filter(e => e.kind == "order_placed")
| map(e => e.customer)
| distinct

["ada", "grace", "linus"]

source("events") names no file. The shop's hql.toml, in examples/pipelines/shop/, declares events as a json endpoint, and the program names the id. That one indirection is what lets the rest of Part II happen without the program changing shape: as the shop grows, the events move into a table, then onto a topic, then onto a subject a stream keeps, then into a lakehouse, and at each move the configuration names the new system and the pipeline keeps its steps.

Chapter The shop's events are in Read by Written by 15. Endpoints anywhere: the model every system shares source, tap target, sink 16. Tables and topics a SQLite table, a PostgreSQL table, a Kafka topic source for a table, tap for a topic target, sink 17. Subjects and the lakehouse NATS subjects, a JetStream stream, Delta tables tap for a subject, source for a table sink, target 18. APIs, webhooks and stores a REST API, a webhook, an object store, as design source, tap target, sink 19. OLTP the transactions as they happen, all of the above in one file tap sink 20. OLAP the history they leave: bronze, silver and gold tables source target

Every system in chapters 16, 17, 19 and 20 is in the current release. The programs that reach a server are checked in this book, against the shop's configuration and with no connection made, and run against real servers in the hql-demo repository, whose output is the output the book shows. A checked program is shown with what hql check prints, the type its result would have, and a pipeline that ends in target or sink has the type Step: its result is nothing, because its work is the writing.

A job is one run of a program's plan. An .hql file defines the program; each invocation starts another run, which may include several pipelines. Its steps describe transformations, reads and writes. Configuration names the environment variables that supply credentials and selects the backend. The schedule determines when the program runs. hql check reads the configuration without connecting to endpoints, so a deployment can check the program before running it.

A job's own settings, the customer a report is for or the day it covers, come from the invocation that runs it. hql --arg customer=ada run report.hql passes one, and the program reads it with env.arg from import io.env, as text, with a default where it is not passed (environment and arguments):

import io.env

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

customer = env.arg("customer") | unwrap_or("grace")
orders : Seq<Event> = source("ledger")
orders
| filter(o => o.kind == "order_placed" and o.customer == customer)
| map(o => o.amount)
| sum

135.75

docs.title: Partitions, schedules and backends
docs.text:
The program can declare logical partitioning. Scheduling and backend selection are configuration around it.

A partition is the logical unit of ownership. partition(by = e => e.customer) is in the current release: it states that the orders of one customer belong together, keeps every value and its type, and on localhost changes nothing else. It names no worker and no Kafka partition. A backend reads it as the statement that a per-customer group may run on separate parts without the parts having to meet.

Design only

The rest of this section describes functionality that is not in the current release. The configuration examples illustrate design direction; names and keys may change before it ships.

A schedule is configuration beside the endpoints, [jobs.report] run = "report.hql" with an at, or a trigger that is itself a source: a subject whose messages each start a run. The program declares no schedule; when it runs is configuration.

A backend supplies an execution strategy for the checked program. Future backends could use parallel workers in one process, translate a supported computation into SQL, or distribute it across a cluster. Each must preserve the result, types, sequence order, failures and effects of local evaluation. The companion Logical steps and physical plans explains the planning handoff, including Spark SQL and CTEs on Databricks.

[execution]
backend = "spark"

This illustrates future execution configuration. The spark endpoint kind in chapter 17 already identifies a table the program reads and writes. Backend selection would additionally choose where pipeline computation runs, while keeping the checked program's meaning.

docs.title: What each of them wires
docs.text:
Sources and sinks Transformations Where a mistake is found Data Factory linked services and datasets, in JSON activities, each a box at validation of the JSON, or in the run's monitor PySpark readers and writers, in code DataFrame operations when the job runs, at the operation that fails ksqlDB topics as streams and tables SQL over them when the statement is submitted, or in the records it skips dbt models over a warehouse SQL, with tests after when the model builds, or when its tests run HQL ids bound in hql.toml the steps of this book when the file is checked, before anything connects

The columns are the same four things. What HQL adds is a type for each arrow: stream against table, finite against live, a declared record against a configured boundary, a contract against what a producer actually sent, each checked where the file is written, so that the file that passed is the file that runs.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 15 looks at what "events" names: an endpoint, the one model behind a file, a table, a topic and a webhook.

docs.title: Logical steps and physical plans
docs.text:
An HQL program describes a computation before choosing how to execute it. Its types, operations, data dependencies and ordered effects form the logical program. Planning turns that checked program into work for a particular backend. The physical plan describes how that work will run: which operations share a traversal, where data moves, and which work can run in parallel.

The same HQL expression should be able to run locally, be pushed down into SQL, or become a distributed Spark plan while keeping the meaning of |. This is the design contract for alternative backends.

Current implementation and design direction

localhost is the only execution backend in the current release. Checking, local planning and hql plan work today. Parallel execution, HQL-to-SQL translation and distributed backends are design direction. Their examples below explain the intended separation; they are not commands for selecting an available backend.

docs.title: Logical steps come before planning
docs.text:
Consider two steps over a list:

[3, 1, 2] | filter(n => n > 1) | map(n => n * 10)

[30, 20]

The head supplies three integers. The filter step retains 3 and 2; the map step multiplies each retained value by ten. The checker establishes the operations and their types before planning begins. The result has type List<Int> and preserves the order of the retained elements.

Each | composes the value on its left with the operation on its right. These two logical steps remain the explanation of the result under every execution strategy. Their source positions identify computation; the planner chooses where that computation runs and how much work to combine.

Term Meaning Established by Step One operation or presentation at one position in a pipeline The program, resolved by the checker Stage A region of planned work with an execution strategy The planner Task One scheduled attempt to execute a stage, over a partition where applicable The backend's scheduler Job One run of the whole program's plan The runtime

The stage belongs to physical planning. The task and job describe execution of the plan. The task and job vocabulary here describes the intended model; the current CLI exposes stage annotations through hql plan.

docs.title: From the checked program to execution
docs.text:
Planning resolves execution choices as far as the selected backend allows. For a local evaluator, it can select in-process evaluation directly. For a SQL backend, it can select a query to submit and delegate the remaining physical decisions to the database engine.

HQL program
    -> checking: typed steps, data dependencies, effects
    -> backend planning and translation
        -> localhost: in-process evaluation
        -> parallel backend: work divided among local workers
        -> SQL backend: SQL -> engine planning -> physical execution
        -> distributed backend: stages -> scheduled tasks on workers

SQL pushdown and distributed execution can be parts of the same route: a Databricks backend could translate HQL to Spark SQL, then let the engine plan and distribute the work. A backend may also refine a plan during a run. The logical program supplies the contract throughout those decisions.

docs.title: Local, parallel and distributed execution
docs.text:
Today, localhost puts all steps of each pipeline in stage 0, marked in process. For the finite list above, it evaluates the filter and then the map. hql plan shows the chosen stages without running the program. For streams, values are consumed on demand, as described in chapter 7.

An alternative parallel backend could divide the list into parts and apply both operations in one traversal of each part. It would assemble the retained results in their original order. A distributed backend could do the same work on several machines, often where the input already resides. Parallel execution describes work that runs concurrently; distributed execution adds placement and communication across machines.

More demanding operations need other plans. A reduction may combine partial results from several workers; grouping may move values so that equal keys reach the same worker. Several logical steps can share a stage, and the work of one logical step may span several stages. Those choices depend on the operation's contract, the data and the backend's capabilities.

docs.title: SQL translation and CTEs
docs.text:
Design direction. A backend for Databricks could translate a supported region of HQL into Spark SQL. A chain of common table expressions (CTEs) is one way to express the intermediate relations in a single SQL statement. For the small expression above, a possible translation is:

WITH input(pos, n) AS (
    VALUES (0, CAST(3 AS BIGINT)),
           (1, CAST(1 AS BIGINT)),
           (2, CAST(2 AS BIGINT))
), filtered AS (
    SELECT pos, n FROM input WHERE n > 1
), mapped AS (
    SELECT pos, n * 10 AS value FROM filtered
)
SELECT value FROM mapped ORDER BY pos;

This is an illustrative translation, written by hand. HQL does not generate it today. The backend would decode the returned column as List<Int>. The explicit position column and final ordering preserve the HQL list's order, producing 30 followed by 20.

A CTE names a result within a SQL statement. CTE dependencies express how the relations build on one another; their number does not prescribe the number of physical stages or tasks. Spark plans the submitted SQL and chooses its physical operators. Its EXPLAIN EXTENDED shows the logical plans and the physical plan separately.

Generating SQL therefore completes HQL's translation for that region while leaving physical planning to the engine. A single submitted statement can involve many scheduled tasks. HQL's job describes the whole program run; the engine may organize that work into its own jobs and stages. The backend integration will need to relate those identities when reporting progress.

docs.title: What every plan must preserve
docs.text:
The reference behavior is localhost's result, including its type, sequence positions and failures. Planning also preserves the order of observable effects and the scope of transactions. Reading, writing and logging carry those constraints into the plan.

Pure operations give a planner room to combine or distribute work when their contracts permit it. Data dependencies and failure behavior still apply: changing the order of two pure functions can change the result. A retry of an effectful task also needs the endpoint's delivery guarantees or a transaction protocol that makes the retry valid.

For SQL translation, matching operation names is only a starting point. The backend must preserve HQL's treatment of missing values, numeric precision, ordering and diagnostics. It must reject unsupported work before execution. Which expressions can be translated, and how SQL and local work could share a plan, remain decisions for a future backend specification.

docs.title: An endpoint and an execution backend
docs.text:
The current spark endpoint connects HQL to a table on Databricks or a Spark Thrift Server. It sends the SQL needed for endpoint operations; the HQL pipeline's filter, map and grouping still run in hql.

A future Spark execution backend would also run translated pipeline computation on the engine. Endpoint configuration identifies the data; execution configuration selects where the checked computation runs. Chapter 17 uses the existing endpoint, and chapter 15 explains how endpoints are configured.

docs.title: 15. Endpoints
docs.text: Every system in Part II is reached the same way. A file, a table, a topic, a subject and a webhook differ in where their data is and whether it ends; to a program each is an endpoint, and four steps read and write all of them. This chapter is that model, told over the shop of chapter 14. The programs run with --vault examples/pipelines/shop.

docs.title: One file, two spellings
docs.text:
An endpoint is a value that states where documents are. Constructing one performs no I/O, and a program can reach the shop's events by writing the endpoint itself, file(path):

source(file("examples/pipelines/shop/data/events.json")) | size

1

or by naming the id the shop's hql.toml declares it under:

[endpoint.events]
kind = "json"
path = "data/events.json"

source("events") | size

6

The two answers differ because the two spellings say different things. A .json file read by file is one JSON document, the whole array, so the Seq holds one value. The json kind is a file whose one document is an array of records, and it gives the array's elements. A constructed endpoint states where the bytes are and leaves the rest to the program; a configured endpoint states the system, its documents, and, on the schema boundary, the names and types that system uses.

The rest of Part II uses ids, for the reason the second spelling exists: a program that names an id is not tied to one machine's paths, one server's address, or one system. Moving the events from a file into a table is a change to hql.toml, not to the pipeline.

docs.title: Four steps
docs.text:
Two questions sort every read and write. Does the endpoint end, and does the step take the data whole or one value at a time?

Whole One at a time Read source(e): a Seq, every document, from an endpoint that ends tap(e): a Stream, one document held at a time Write target(e): one completed value, written once sink(e): one document per value, written as each arrives

A table ends, so source reads it. A topic does not, so it is read by tap; source of one is a check error, because a Seq is a value that ends and a topic has no last message:

source("order_events")

check error[type-mismatch]: `order_events` is a `kafka` endpoint, read by `tap` as a `Stream`, not by `source` as a `Seq`
 --> <expression>:1:8
  |
1 | source("order_events")
  |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The writing side is the mirror. A stream has no last value for target to wait for, so a stream is written with sink:

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

events : Stream<Event> = tap("order_events")
events | target("orders")

check error[type-mismatch]: `target("orders")` writes a Table or a sequence of a declared record, not Stream<Event>
  --> <expression>:10:10
   |
10 | events | target("orders")
   |          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

events : Stream<Event> = tap("order_events")
events | sink("orders")

Step

tap reads an endpoint that ends as well: tap("ledger") gives the table's rows one at a time, which is how a table larger than memory is read. The type of each step is fixed before the program runs, so a pipeline that would wait forever, tap("order_events") | size, is a check error and not a process that hangs (finite or live).

docs.title: The kind states the type
docs.text:
source("orders") is a PostgreSQL table, and the program above was checked without a database. Checking reads hql.toml, finds kind = "postgres", and types orders from the kind alone: it ends, source reads it as a Seq of rows, and target writes it in one transaction or sink row by row. No connection is made until the program runs, and hql check never runs it:

source("customer_revenue")

Seq<Data>

customer_revenue is a Delta table in a lakehouse; the shop's configuration names it, and that is all the checker needs. The kinds in the current release, and the chapter each is told in:

Kind What one endpoint is Ends Chapter csv, json, json_lines, yaml a file in that format yes 9 vault a folder of documents yes 20 sqlite one table of a database file yes 16 postgres one table of a PostgreSQL database yes 16 kafka one Kafka topic no 16 nats one core NATS subject no 17 nats_jetstream one subject of a JetStream stream no 17 spark one table of a lakehouse, over Spark SQL yes 17

The id is a literal. A computed id, a connection string in place of an id, and an id the configuration does not declare are each refused at checking, on the endpoints-by-id page of chapter 9.

docs.title: Secrets live in the environment
docs.text:
The shop's hql.toml holds no password. An endpoint whose address may carry a secret names the environment variable that holds it, dsn_env for a database, brokers_env for Kafka, url_env for NATS and the lakehouse, and token_env for a token:

[endpoint.orders]
kind = "postgres"
dsn_env = "SHOP_DSN"
table = "orders"
order = ["id"]

An address with credentials written into the configuration refuses the whole vault, before any program is read:

$ hql --vault shop eval '1'
hql: shop: `[endpoint.x]`: `url` holds credentials; name the environment variable that holds the address, `url_env = "VARIABLE"`

A variable that is not set is found when the endpoint is first read, and the failure names the endpoint and the variable, never its value:

$ hql --vault examples/pipelines/shop eval 'source("orders")'
execute failure[io-failure]: endpoint `orders`: the environment variable `SHOP_DSN`, which `dsn_env` names, is not set
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | source("orders")

Every failure past checking has that form: the endpoint by its id, then the system's own words, then the row or message by its position. A row that does not decode stops the evaluation there; chapter 16 routes such rows instead of stopping.

docs.title: Transports
docs.text:
An endpoint that reaches outside the evaluation is a transport. Two properties of a transport matter to a program and to whoever runs it:

  • its locality: Direct, on this machine, such as a file or standard input, or Network, another process over a connection;
  • its carriage: what one read moves, bytes that a format splits into documents, a framed message that is one document, or a row of named columns that needs no format at all.

Sqlite and the two NATS transports are declared with both today. Each is a module of its own, imported by its full path, and its constructor takes the keys its kind takes, so a program reaches a subject without any configuration:

import io.msg.nats_jetstream

tap(nats_jetstream("orders.raw", stream = "ORDERS", url_env = "NATS_URL", idle_ms = 2000))

Stream<Data>

A message is one document, so no format is named, and it is Json unless one is. A table is rows of named columns, so it takes no format at all, and naming one is a check error:

import io.db.sqlite

source(sqlite("data/shop.db", table = "orders", order = ["id"]))

Seq<Data>

A constructor takes no secret, only the name of the variable that holds one; and a constructed transport has no schema boundary, which only configuration states. A row is read as Data, or as the record an annotation names, each column decoded as its type holds it, and a record is written to a constructed table a column per field, replacing the rows it held. A database file is written whole, by target; sink writes rows to a server's table, not to a file's.

Design only

The rest of this section describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: names and types may change before it ships.

Every kind is a transport with a constructor of its name, and every transport states its locality and carriage:

Transport Locality Carriage File, Stdin, Stdout Direct bytes Sqlite Direct rows Http, Tcp Network bytes WebSocket, Kafka, Nats, NatsJetStream, Rest, Graphql, Webhook Network messages Postgres, Spark Network rows

The carriage settles whether a step takes a format: a byte transport needs one, a message transport may name one and is Json without, and a row transport takes none, so source(postgres(dsn_env = "SHOP_DSN", table = "orders"), Json) is a check error. The locality is what a host grants: a document being rendered reaches no Network transport, constructed or configured, and the check reads that from the type, not from a list of names (effects and what a host allows).

The transports are grouped into modules by the system they reach:

io                     file, stdin, stdout, stderr, source, tap, target, sink
├── net                http, websocket, tcp, rest, graphql, webhook
├── db                 sqlite, postgres, spark, and further databases
├── msg                kafka, nats, nats_jetstream, and further brokers
└── store              s3, azure_blob, gcs, sftp, hdfs

import io.db.postgres brings postgres(...) into scope, as import io.db.sqlite brings sqlite(...) and import io.msg.nats brings nats(...) today. A configured id needs no import: the configuration names the kind, and the kind names its module. A program that constructs a network transport names its module in its first lines, so what a program may reach is visible before reading it. Chapter 18 is the net and store transports the shop reaches next.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 16 moves the shop's events out of a file: into a SQLite table, then a PostgreSQL table, then onto a Kafka topic and back.

docs.title: 16. Tables and topics
docs.text:
The shop's events outgrow a file. This chapter moves them three times: into a SQLite table on this machine, into a PostgreSQL table on a server, and onto a Kafka topic that the checkout writes to as orders happen. At each move the configuration changes and the pipeline does not. The last section is the move every real pipeline makes sooner or later: a topic carrying messages that are not what the type says.

Every event in the shop is an Event, declared once for the chapter:

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

docs.title: A table on this machine
docs.text:
A sqlite endpoint is one table in a database file. The shop's ledger is the table orders in data/shop.db:

[endpoint.ledger]
kind = "sqlite"
path = "data/shop.db"
table = "orders"
order = ["id"]

order names the columns the rows are read in, so two reads give the rows in the same order. Filling the table is a target: the events are read as Events, and each field becomes a column. The program is shown checked rather than run, so that the book's tests do not rewrite the table, and Step is the type of a program whose result is what it wrote:

events : Seq<Event> = source("events")
events | target("ledger")

Step

A table ends, so source reads it whole, as a Seq, and every step of chapter 6 applies. The revenue per customer is a group and a sum, and an amount keeps its digits as a Decimal on the way in and on the way out:

orders : Seq<Event> = source("ledger")
orders
| filter(o => o.kind == "order_placed")
| group(by = o => o.customer)
| map(g => {customer: g.key, total: g.items | map(o => o.amount) | sum})

{{customer: "ada", total: 135.75}, {customer: "grace", total: 42.00}, {customer: "linus", total: 7.99}}

tap("ledger") gives the same rows one at a time, a Stream that ends after the last row, and holds one row in memory:

tap("ledger") | take(2) | map(o => o.id)

[1, 2]

docs.title: The same table on a server
docs.text:
The shop hires a second clerk, and the ledger moves to PostgreSQL, where both can reach it. The configuration names the database by the variable holding its connection string; the table and its order are the same:

[endpoint.orders]
kind = "postgres"
dsn_env = "SHOP_DSN"
table = "orders"
order = ["id"]

The revenue report is the program above with "ledger" replaced by "orders". It checks without a database:

orders : Seq<Event> = source("orders")
orders
| filter(o => o.kind == "order_placed")
| group(by = o => o.customer)
| map(g => {customer: g.key, total: g.items | map(o => o.amount) | sum})

Set<Data>

and run against one, it prints what the SQLite table printed. What changes is what happens at the edges. The table's columns are read before the first row and compared with Event through the schema boundary, so a column Event does not declare, or one of the wrong type, fails before any row is decoded. Only the columns Event reads are selected. A numeric column is a Decimal with its digits, jsonb the tree it holds, and NULL an absent field.

docs.title: A topic
docs.text:
The shop opens a web store. The checkout does not write to the ledger: it publishes each event to a Kafka topic, order_events, and whatever needs to know about orders reads the topic.

[endpoint.order_events]
kind = "kafka"
brokers_env = "KAFKA_BROKERS"
topic = "order_events"
idle_ms = 2000

A topic is a log that does not end. tap("order_events") is a Stream, one JSON document per message, decoded as the element type; the stream starts at the earliest message the topic keeps, or at the next one published under from = "latest":

events : Stream<Event> = tap("order_events")
events
| filter(e => e.kind == "order_placed")
| map(e => {id: e.id, customer: e.customer, amount: e.amount})

{amount: 120.50, customer: "ada", id: 1}
{amount: 42.00, customer: "grace", id: 2}
{amount: 7.99, customer: "linus", id: 4}
{amount: 15.25, customer: "ada", id: 6}

The four lines appear as the messages arrive, and the program ends two seconds after the last one: idle_ms bounds how long the stream waits for the next message. Without it the stream waits without end, which is what a service that reads a topic does.

Moving data between the two is a pipeline of two steps each way. A table's rows onto the topic, one message per row, in the table's order:

orders : Seq<Event> = source("orders")
orders | sink("order_events")

Step

and the topic's messages into the table, one row per message, committed as each arrives:

events : Stream<Event> = tap("order_events")
events | sink("orders")

Step

These are the first two programs of the kafka-postgres case of hql-demo, which seeds the table, moves its rows through the topic into a second table, and compares the second with the first.

docs.title: What a write promises
docs.text:
The four steps say what is written. The kind says when it is safe.

target sink a sqlite or postgres table every row in one transaction: all of them or none each row committed as it arrives a kafka topic one message per element of a completed collection one message per value, as each arrives

mode in the configuration states what a write does with what the table already holds: create refuses an existing table, append adds after its rows, and replace, the default, empties it and keeps its definition, indexes and grants. A table that does not exist is created with a column per field. A topic that does not exist is an evaluation failure: creating a topic is the cluster's business.

A write replaces or extends what a table holds. Changing rows it holds, in place, and several such changes as one transaction, are the statements of chapter 19's transfer page.

Every message one program writes goes to the topic's first partition, so a reader is given them in the order they were written.
