A read records no position: each run of a program starts where from says, so reading a topic twice gives its messages twice. A reader that resumes where it stopped is a JetStream consumer, in chapter 17.

docs.title: A topic that lies
docs.text:
Not every message on a topic is an Event. The web store has a bug that sends "free" as an amount, an old client leaves out the customer, a refund is negative, and a new service publishes order_cancelled, a kind nobody has agreed on. Reading the topic as Stream<Event> is strict: the first such message stops the evaluation, naming the endpoint and the message.

A pipeline that must keep running reads the messages as Data, so none fails to decode, and states what an order is as a contract (validation as a value):

type EventData : DataContract = {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String

    require amount >= 0 as non_negative
    require ["order_placed", "order_shipped", "payment_failed"] | contains(kind) as known_kind
}

validate(EventData) gives one Result per message: the order, or the message as it arrived with every rule it broke. fork gives every branch the same input, and oks() and errs() keep each side. The producer's eight events are in a file as well, so the policy can be tried on this machine before it meets the topic:

source("raw_events")
| validate(EventData)
| fork {
    clean    = oks()  | map(e => e.id),
    rejected = errs() | map(e => {id: e.value.id, rules: e.violations | map(v => v.rule)}),
}

{clean: [1, 2, 4, 6], rejected: [{id: 3, rules: ["EventData.amount.type"]}, {id: 5, rules: ["EventData.customer.missing"]}, {id: 7, rules: ["EventData.non_negative"]}, {id: 8, rules: ["EventData.known_kind"]}]}

The production pipeline is the same shape over the topic, with each branch ending in a table. The clean side is read into a closed Event, since a table is written from a declared record; the rejected side keeps the message as the producer sent it, so it can be repaired and sent again:

type Rejected {
    id      : Int
    message : Data
    rules   : List<String>
}

tap("order_events_raw")
| validate(EventData)
| fork {
    clean =
        oks()
        | map(e => Event(id = e.id, kind = e.kind, customer = e.customer, amount = e.amount, at = e.at))
        | sink("order_clean"),
    quarantine =
        errs()
        | map(e => Rejected(
            id = match e.value.id { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 },
            message = e.value,
            rules = e.violations | map(v => v.rule)))
        | sink("order_quarantine"),
}

{clean: Step, quarantine: Step}

Each message goes to exactly one branch, in the order the topic holds them, and neither branch ends the other. After a run, the quarantine table holds:

rejected : Seq<Rejected> = source("order_quarantine")
rejected | map(r => {id: r.id, rules: r.rules})

[{id: 3, rules: ["EventData.amount.type"]}, {id: 5, rules: ["EventData.customer.missing"]}, {id: 7, rules: ["EventData.non_negative"]}, {id: 8, rules: ["EventData.known_kind"]}]

Each row's message is the tree the producer sent, {amount: "free", …} for the first, so a repaired message is the same tree with one field changed.

The contract is the policy: what an order is. The shape of the pipeline is what happens to a message that is not one. Changing either is a change to one declaration, and the checker checks both before a message is read.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 17 gives the shop a message bus that keeps its place, and a lakehouse whose tables are files in object storage: the same pipeline, with a subject in place of the topic and Delta tables in place of PostgreSQL.

docs.title: 17. Subjects and the lakehouse
docs.text:
The shop's Kafka topic of chapter 16 carries every order, and three needs have grown around it. The warehouse wants to hear about each shipment as it happens and does not care about the ones it missed. Billing wants every order exactly where it left off yesterday. And the owner wants reports over all of history without anyone's pipeline slowing down to produce them.

This chapter meets the three with NATS and a lakehouse. NATS is two kinds: nats, a subject whose messages nobody keeps, and nats_jetstream, a subject of a stream the server keeps. A lakehouse is tables kept as files in object storage, reached by kind = "spark". Each key of each kind is on the subjects and lakehouse tables page of chapter 9; this chapter is what the shop does with them.

The programs need servers. They are checked here against the shop's configuration, and run in the hql-demo repository, whose nats-core, nats and nats-lakehouse cases start NATS, MinIO and a Spark Thrift Server with Docker Compose. The outputs shown are theirs.

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

docs.title: Notifications nobody keeps
docs.text:
Core NATS delivers a message to whoever is subscribed to its subject when it is published, and keeps nothing. That is what a notification is: the warehouse screen shows what is happening now, and an event from before the screen was switched on is not news.

The shop publishes each event to a subject named for its kind, orders.order_placed, orders.payment_failed, orders.order_shipped. The subject is computed, so the program writes the transport itself, with the constructor of io.msg.nats:

import io.msg.nats

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

events : Seq<Event> = source("events")

for_kind = (kind: String) => events | filter(e => e.kind == kind)
subject = (kind: String) => nats("orders." + kind, url_env = "NATS_URL")

for_kind("order_placed") | sink(subject("order_placed"))
for_kind("payment_failed") | sink(subject("payment_failed"))
for_kind("order_shipped") | sink(subject("order_shipped"))

Step

A reader names one subject or a family of them. A subject may hold the wildcards *, one token, and >, every token that follows, so the shop's notifications endpoint reads all three:

[endpoint.notifications]
kind = "nats"
url_env = "NATS_URL"
subject = "orders.>"
idle_ms = 3000

events : Stream<Event> = tap("notifications")
events
| filter(e => e.kind == "order_placed")
| map(e => {id: e.id, customer: e.customer, amount: e.amount})

{amount: 120.50, customer: "ada", id: 1}
{amount: 42.00, customer: "grace", id: 2}
{amount: 7.99, customer: "linus", id: 4}
{amount: 15.25, customer: "ada", id: 6}

The subscription starts when the stream is first traversed, so the nats-core case starts this program before the publisher, and a message published before it would not be there to be given. Nothing confirms a core message: sink ends once the server has the messages, whether or not anyone was listening. A wildcard endpoint is read only, since a message is published to one subject.

docs.title: A log the server keeps
docs.text:
Billing cannot miss an order. JetStream is the part of the NATS server that keeps messages: a stream stores every message published to its subjects, in order, and a nats_jetstream endpoint names the stream and one subject in it. The shop's checkout publishes raw orders to orders.raw, in the stream ORDERS:

[endpoint.orders_raw]
kind = "nats_jetstream"
url_env = "NATS_URL"
stream = "ORDERS"
subject = "orders.raw"
idle_ms = 2000

source("raw_events") | sink("orders_raw")

Step

A message is written once the stream answers that it stored it, so a program that ends without a failure has lost nothing. A subject no stream stores is an evaluation failure rather than a message that disappears.

tap("orders_raw") reads the stream's messages under that subject in the order the stream holds them, from the earliest it keeps, or from the next one published under from = "latest". Like a Kafka read, it records no position: two runs give the same messages twice.

docs.title: Billing's place
docs.text:
A consumer is the server's record of how far one reader has come in a stream, and a durable consumer is one the server keeps under a name. Billing's endpoint is the same subject with a consumer named:

[endpoint.billing]
kind = "nats_jetstream"
url_env = "NATS_URL"
stream = "ORDERS"
subject = "orders.raw"
consumer = "billing"
idle_ms = 2000

The first run through billing reads every message the stream keeps. The next run reads only what was published since; a run with nothing new prints nothing. Another endpoint with another consumer keeps its own place over the same messages, so the warehouse's reports and billing's invoices never move each other's position.

A message is acknowledged once the program asks for the one after it, and the last one when the stream ends. A message is therefore delivered at least once: a program that fails while it holds a message, or stops early, is given that message again by its next run.

tap("billing") | take(2) | map(e => e.id)

[1, 2]

take(2) asked for no third message, so 2 was never acknowledged, and the next run of this program starts with 2. A program that writes what it reads, an invoice per order, writes it so that writing it twice does no harm.

docs.title: The lakehouse
docs.text:
The owner's reports need history, and a broker is not where history is queried. A lakehouse keeps tables as files in object storage, with a transaction log beside them, and answers SQL over them. Databricks is one; Apache Spark with Delta Lake over an S3 bucket is another, built from open-source parts, and the spark kind reaches either, by the URL of a Databricks SQL warehouse or of a Spark Thrift Server:

[endpoint.orders_silver]
kind = "spark"
url_env = "LAKEHOUSE_URL"
table = "default.orders_silver"
order = ["id"]
mode = "append"

[endpoint.orders_silver.fields.amount]
type = "DECIMAL(12,2)"

A lakehouse table ends, so it sits on the table side of the line: read by source through the schema boundary, written by target in commits of up to 500 rows, or by sink as rows arrive. A DECIMAL column states how many digits it holds, so the boundary names the type each amount is written as. The valid orders of the subject above land in this table by the quarantine of chapter 16 with the ids changed, a subject in place of the topic and this table in place of the clean one:

type EventData : DataContract = {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String

    require amount >= 0 as non_negative
    require ["order_placed", "order_shipped", "payment_failed"] | contains(kind) as known_kind
}

type Rejected {
    id      : Int
    message : Data
    rules   : List<String>
}

tap("orders_raw")
| validate(EventData)
| fork {
    silver =
        oks()
        | map(e => Event(id = e.id, kind = e.kind, customer = e.customer, amount = e.amount, at = e.at))
        | sink("orders_silver"),
    rejected =
        errs()
        | map(e => Rejected(
            id = match e.value.id { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 },
            message = e.value,
            rules = e.violations | map(v => v.rule)))
        | sink("orders_rejected"),
}

{silver: Step, rejected: Step}

That table is the shop's first analytical one, and what it is for, the layers a lakehouse is organized in, and what a report built over it needs from it are chapter 20. This chapter's business with it ends at the transport: a subject in, a table out, and what each promises.

docs.title: Where the work runs
docs.text:
The filter and the grouping above run where hql runs. The spark endpoint reaches a table over Spark SQL and sends the statements needed to read or write it. The surrounding HQL pipeline is evaluated locally.

A future Spark execution backend could translate supported pipeline steps into SQL and let the engine plan their execution on the cluster. The companion Logical steps and physical plans explains that handoff and the requirement to preserve the meaning of |.

What the current release does not do: several programs sharing one consumer to divide its messages, NATS credential files, a lakehouse column holding a list or a record, and a Databricks token other than a personal access token.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 18 is where the shop's data comes from outside: a payment provider calling a webhook, a carrier's REST API, and an archive in object storage. It is design, not yet in the release.

docs.title: 18. APIs, webhooks and stores
docs.text:
Design only

This chapter describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: apart from http, websocket and tcp, which the network page of chapter 9 shows running, these programs do not run against the current binary, and names, keys, types and outputs may change before they ship.

Everything the shop has read so far, it wrote first: its own files, tables, topics and subjects. A business also reads what others publish. The payment provider calls the shop when a payment settles. The carrier answers questions about parcels, a page of answers at a time. The supplier's catalogue is a GraphQL API. And the auditor wants every order kept for seven years, somewhere cheaper than a lakehouse.

Each of those is one more transport, and the model of chapter 15 does not change for any of them: an endpoint by id or by constructor, read by source if it ends and by tap if it does not, written by target or sink, its type known from configuration before anything connects.

docs.title: Three transports over HTTP
docs.text:
http(url) in the current release reads one resource as bytes, with a format to say what the bytes are. Most APIs are more than one resource: a collection split into pages, a query posted to one address, or a server that calls back. Three transports of io.net name those shapes, and each gives messages, one item per document, Json unless a format is named:

Transport What one read is Ends Read by rest(url, items, next) the items of a collection, every page in turn yes source graphql(url, query, variables, items) the nodes one query returns yes source webhook(port, path) the body of each request the host receives no tap

The shapes are the same two as before. A paginated collection and a query result are finite, read once per evaluation and replayable within it. A webhook is live: requests arrive when the sender decides, and the stream is as endless as a topic.

docs.title: The carrier's API
docs.text:
The carrier lists parcels at https://api.carrier.example/parcels. Each response holds a page of them under results, and the Link header names the next page. The shop configures it once, with the token in the environment:

[endpoint.parcels]
kind = "rest"
url = "https://api.carrier.example/parcels"
items = "results"
next = "link"
token_env = "CARRIER_TOKEN"

type Parcel {
    order   : Int
    status  : String
    updated : String
}

parcels : Seq<Parcel> = source("parcels")
parcels
| filter(p => p.status == "delivered")
| map(p => p.order)

source sends a GET for each page in turn until none is named, and gives every item in page order. items is a field path into each response body, "data.results" for one nested deeper; next is "link" for the rel="next" target of the Link header, or a field path to a URL in the body. The token is sent as Authorization: Bearer, and the pages are fetched once per evaluation, so a program that reads parcels twice asks the carrier once.

The parcels are now one more table to the shop. Joining them to the silver orders of chapter 17, each an Event of chapter 16, is a join of two Seqs, which chapter 6 already showed:

orders : Seq<Event> = source("orders_silver")

orders
| filter(o => o.kind == "order_placed")
| left_join(parcels, left = o => o.id, right = p => p.order,
            into = (o, p) => {id: o.id, customer: o.customer, status: p.map(x => x.status).unwrap_or("not sent")})

A rest endpoint is read only. Creating something on the carrier's side is a request by another method, which is a write to an http endpoint.

docs.title: The supplier's catalogue
docs.text:
The supplier answers GraphQL. A graphql endpoint is one query: one POST of the query and its variables, and the items are the array at items below the response's data:

[endpoint.catalogue]
kind = "graphql"
url = "https://supplier.example/graphql"
query = "{ products(inStock: true) { sku name price } }"
items = "products"
token_env = "SUPPLIER_TOKEN"

type Product {
    sku   : String
    name  : String
    price : Decimal
}

products : Seq<Product> = source("catalogue")
products | filter(p => p.price < 50.00) | map(p => p.name)

A response whose errors is not empty is an evaluation failure naming the URL and the first error's message: a GraphQL server answers 200 for a query it could not run, and the endpoint does not mistake that for an empty catalogue.

docs.title: The payment provider's webhook
docs.text:
The payment provider does not wait to be asked. When a payment settles or fails, it sends a POST to an address the shop gave it. A webhook endpoint is that address, and tap over it is a Stream of request bodies:

[endpoint.payments]
kind = "webhook"
port = 8080
path = "/payments"
token_env = "PAYMENTS_TOKEN"

type Payment {
    order  : Int
    status : String
    amount : Decimal
}

payments : Stream<Payment> = tap("payments")
payments
| filter(p => p.status == "failed")
| map(p => {id: p.order, kind: "payment_failed", amount: p.amount})
| sink("orders_raw")

The program listens from the first traversal until it ends, and each accepted body is one value. The sender is answered as HTTP has it: 202 once the body is read and decoded, 400 for a body that does not decode, 401 for a request without the token, 404 for another path. A body that does not decode is answered and dropped; the stream goes on, because the sender, not the shop, made the mistake.

A webhook listens on the loopback address unless host says otherwise, so a program on a developer's machine is not reachable from outside by accident. It is the one transport that accepts connections, and like every Network transport it is refused in a document being rendered.

The failed payments go onto the shop's own raw subject, where the bronze pipeline of chapter 17 validates them with every other order. The webhook is an edge; what comes through it joins the flow the shop already has.

docs.title: The archive
docs.text:
The auditor wants every raw order kept for seven years, as files, in object storage. An object store is a transport whose documents are objects under keys, and its module is in the io.store family: s3, which also reaches MinIO and Ceph, azure_blob, adls, gcs, sftp and hdfs.

[endpoint.archive]
kind = "s3"
bucket = "shop-archive"
prefix = "orders/raw/"
region = "eu-central-1"
format = "json_lines"
credentials_env = "ARCHIVE_CREDENTIALS"

tap("orders_raw") | collect(1000) | sink("archive")

collect(1000) turns the stream into batches, and sink writes each batch as one object under the prefix, so the archive is files of a thousand orders each rather than a million files of one. Read back, the prefix is a finite set of objects, and source("archive") is a Seq of every order in it: a replay of last year is a pipeline over the archive instead of over the subject, as chapter 19 shows.

A format says what the bytes of one object are. Beside the text formats of chapter 9, binary formats decode bytes to values with a schema of their own: Parquet for columns of a table, Avro and Protobuf for records on a wire. An archive written as Parquet is smaller and is read by every analytics tool there is:

import io.store.s3

orders : Seq<Event> = source("orders_silver")
orders | target(s3("shop-archive", key = "orders/2026.parquet", credentials_env = "ARCHIVE_CREDENTIALS"), Parquet)

A table format is one level up: Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg keep a table as Parquet objects and a transaction log in a store. Where the spark kind of chapter 17 asks a SQL server for a table's rows, a delta or iceberg kind reads the log and the objects itself, through the store's transport, so a table in a bucket is readable with no server running at all.

docs.title: Further brokers and databases
docs.text:
The families have room for the systems a shop meets next, each a module named for its system, each a transport with a constructor and a kind:

Family Systems io.msg rabbitmq, pulsar, mqtt, redis_streams, sqs, azure_service_bus, artemis, rocketmq, nsq, zeromq io.db duckdb, clickhouse, mongodb, couchdb, cassandra, opensearch, redis, neo4j io.net grpc, feed io.store s3, azure_blob, adls, gcs, sftp, hdfs

A queue such as RabbitMQ or SQS is a tap and a sink, as a topic is; a document database is a source and a target, as a table is. Whether a new system ends is the one fact about it a program depends on, and the kind states it.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 19 puts every system of Part II into one file: the shop's whole day as a pipeline, checked before it runs, and where that pipeline may run.

docs.title: 21. A vault of documents
docs.text: The shelf of chapter 6 was a list written by hand. Here the same books are documents in a folder, and HQL reads the folder. This part of the book is about knowledge: documents, the links between them, their meaning, and the agents that read them.

docs.title: A vault is a folder
docs.text:
A vault is a directory of Markdown and HyperMarkDown documents. The tutorial vault looks like this:

examples/tutorial/
├── authors/
│   ├── frank-herbert.hmd
│   ├── jrr-tolkien.hmd
│   ├── mary-shelley.hmd
│   ├── virginia-woolf.hmd
│   └── walt-whitman.hmd
├── books/
│   ├── a-room-of-ones-own.hmd
│   ├── dune.hmd
│   ├── frankenstein.hmd
│   ├── leaves-of-grass.hmd
│   ├── mrs-dalloway.hmd
│   ├── the-common-reader.hmd
│   └── the-hobbit.hmd
├── club.hmd
├── frankenstein-inspires-dune.hmd
├── librarian.hmd
└── hql.toml

Each document is a card. A card has a header of metadata and a body someone wrote:

---
title: Dune
metadata:
  category: book
  author: Frank Herbert
  year: 1965
  genre: novel
  pages: 412
  status: reading
---
# Dune

A novel by [[frank-herbert]]. A desert planet, a spice, and a family that inherits both.

A program run inside a vault runs against it: hql takes the nearest directory at or above the program's file that holds .hmd/ or hql.toml, or at or above the working directory for an expression or standard input. --vault <directory> names one instead, and --bare runs with none:

hql --vault examples/tutorial eval 'cards | size'

cards | size

15

docs.title: cards
docs.text:
cards is every card of the vault, as a sequence. Its order is the order a sorted walk of the folder reaches each document — the entries of each directory by name, depth first — so a program answers the same on every machine:

cards | take(4) | map(c => c.name)

["frank-herbert", "jrr-tolkien", "mary-shelley", "virginia-woolf"]

A card has the fields of a document: its name (the file stem), title, path, format, body, its kind, and metadata, the header's tree.

docs.title: A link is an optional card
docs.text:
@[[name]] refers to a card by name: @ followed by the link a document writes, [[name]]. A link may point at a document nobody has written yet, so its type is Option<Card>, and reading a field through it reads through the option:

@[[dune]].title

"Dune"

@[[nowhere]].title

none

docs.title: Metadata is Data
docs.text:
A card's metadata is the Data of chapter 2, so every question from chapters 2 and 6 applies. The books are the cards whose category says so:

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
| map(c => c.title)

["A Room of One's Own", "Dune", "Frankenstein", "Leaves of Grass", "Mrs Dalloway", "The Common Reader", "The Hobbit"]

docs.title: The reading list
docs.text:
The club's reading list is the books still to read, by title:

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
| sort(by = c => c.title)
| map(c => c.title)

["Leaves of Grass", "The Common Reader", "The Hobbit"]

Read it as three steps, each consuming the one before: filter decides each card on its own, sort needs every card before it can place the first, and map turns each card into its title. Nothing is stored in between, and nothing is a loop.

No one maintains this list. Mark a book status: done in its header and the next run of the query no longer lists it.

docs.title: Writing cards
docs.text:
The formats of chapter 8 apply to a card as to any value. A card written as Markdown is its body; a list of cards, a list of links:

cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "author") | markdown

- [[frank-herbert]]
- [[jrr-tolkien]]
- [[mary-shelley]]
- [[virginia-woolf]]
- [[walt-whitman]]

docs.title: Grouping cards
docs.text:
group partitions the books by a header value, as it partitioned the shelf:

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
| group(by = c => c.metadata.status)
| map(g => {status: g.key, books: g.items | map(c => c.title)})

{{books: ["A Room of One's Own", "Frankenstein"], status: "done"}, {books: ["Dune", "Mrs Dalloway"], status: "reading"}, {books: ["Leaves of Grass", "The Common Reader", "The Hobbit"], status: "todo"}}

A typed view of a card works as the views of chapter 6 did, and the pages per author are a map over each group and a sum — map, then reduce:

fn pages(c: Card) : Int = match c.metadata.pages { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 }

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
| group(by = c => c.metadata.author)
| map(g => {author: g.key, pages: g.items | map(pages) | sum})

{{author: "Virginia Woolf", pages: 610}, {author: "Frank Herbert", pages: 412}, {author: "Mary Shelley", pages: 280}, {author: "Walt Whitman", pages: 145}, {author: "J. R. R. Tolkien", pages: 310}}

docs.title: Kinds of card
docs.text:
A card whose header declares a relation between two other cards is a RelationCard; every other card is a ConceptCard. of_type keeps the cards of one kind:

cards | of_type(RelationCard) | map(c => c.title)

["Frankenstein inspires Dune"]

Chapter 22 is about what that relation means: cards and the links between them form a graph.

docs.title: The vault itself
docs.text:
cards is a binding the standard library makes, cards = vault.cards, over vault, the value the host seeds when it is given a vault:

[vault.name, vault.cards | size | text]

["tutorial", 15]

Outside every vault and without --vault there is no vault, and naming one says so:

cards | size

check error[unknown-name]: `cards` needs a vault: run inside one or pass --vault <directory>
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | cards | size
  | ^^^^^

docs.title: A vault is a namespace
docs.text:
A card is a file with a place in a vault, and the place is what makes it addressable by name: [[dune]] names a card because there is one tree to resolve the name in. That tree is a namespace, rooted at the vault's directory, and a vault is exactly one namespace. cards holds what a wikilink can reach and nothing else, and a card's path is its place in the vault, relative to the root, so the cards of one folder are a filter on the path:

cards | filter(c => c.path | starts_with("books/")) | size

7

docs.title: Other vaults
docs.text:
A second vault is a second namespace. It is reached as a configured endpoint of kind vault (endpoints by id), with its own cards and graph, and its cards are never merged into cards: a wikilink in one vault never resolves into another, and a relation between cards of two vaults is a join's result, not a link. The field station of the data sources examples configures two:

journal = source("journal")
archive = source("archive")
[journal.cards | map(c => c.name), archive.cards | map(c => c.name)]

[["kite", "owl", "wren"], ["finch", "heron"]]

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: A document that writes [[frank-herbert]] links to another. Chapter 22 follows the links, and the cards and links together are a graph.

docs.title: 22. Links and graphs
docs.text: A document that writes [[frankenstein]] links to another. The links of a vault make its cards a graph: cards are the nodes, links are the edges. This chapter follows links, builds graphs, and draws them.

docs.title: Following links
docs.text:
An edge goes from the card that wrote the link, its source, to the card it names, its target. uplinks gives the edges leaving a card, and downlinks the edges arriving at it:

@[[mrs-dalloway]] | uplinks

[mrs-dalloway -> virginia-woolf]

@[[virginia-woolf]] | downlinks | map(e => e.source)

["a-room-of-ones-own", "mrs-dalloway", "the-common-reader"]

A link in a body may carry data of its own, written after it in braces: [[bearer-tokens]] {relation: defines}. The edge holds it as e.data.

docs.title: Building a graph
docs.text:
Graph(cards) — or cards | Graph — is the graph of those cards and the links among them:

cards
| filter(c => c.name == "virginia-woolf" or c.metadata.author == "Virginia Woolf")
| Graph
| text

a-room-of-ones-own
  -> virginia-woolf
mrs-dalloway
  -> virginia-woolf
the-common-reader
  -> virginia-woolf
virginia-woolf
  -> a-room-of-ones-own
  -> mrs-dalloway
  -> the-common-reader

A graph is a value with two fields, both sets: its nodes, the cards, and its edges. The vault's whole graph is bound as graph:

{nodes: graph.nodes | size, edges: graph.edges | size}

{edges: 22, nodes: 14}

A graph can also be built from edges alone, Graph(edges), or from cards and edges together, Graph(nodes, edges). Its nodes are the cards given and every edge's endpoints:

@[[virginia-woolf]] | downlinks | Graph | text

a-room-of-ones-own
  -> virginia-woolf
mrs-dalloway
  -> virginia-woolf
the-common-reader
  -> virginia-woolf
virginia-woolf

docs.title: Growing a graph
docs.text:
expand(depth = n) starts from some cards and follows links outwards, n steps, in both directions. Every node it reaches records why it is present — which card it was reached from, and how far away:

@[[mrs-dalloway]] | expand(depth = 1) | text

club  (expanded from mrs-dalloway at depth 1)
  -> mrs-dalloway
mrs-dalloway
  -> virginia-woolf
virginia-woolf  (expanded from mrs-dalloway at depth 1)
  -> mrs-dalloway

direction = "uplinks" or "downlinks" follows links one way only. A graph of matches and their neighbours never claims that the neighbours matched: the reason travels with each node.

docs.title: A relation is an edge
docs.text:
The card frankenstein-inspires-dune declares a relation in its header:

---
title: Frankenstein inspires Dune
metadata:
  category: influence
  knowledge:
    type: Relation
    relation:
      source: frankenstein
      target: dune
---

In a graph such a card is not a node but the edge it declares, between the two cards it names:

cards | of_type(RelationCard) | Graph | text

dune  (expanded from frankenstein-inspires-dune at depth 1)
frankenstein  (expanded from frankenstein-inspires-dune at depth 1)
  -> dune

docs.title: Drawing a graph
docs.text:
A graph is written in a diagram format by the step named for it. mermaid writes a Mermaid diagram and d2 a D2 one; json writes the node-link form a graph library reads:

cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book") | Graph | mermaid

graph LR
  n0["a-room-of-ones-own"]
  n1["dune"]
  n2["frankenstein"]
  n3["leaves-of-grass"]
  n4["mrs-dalloway"]
  n5["the-common-reader"]
  n6["the-hobbit"]
  n2 --> n1

In a Markdown document — chapter 24 — a graph is written as a fenced d2 block, which documentation sites draw.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: expand grew a graph from a starting card. Chapter 23 finds the starting cards for a question in words.

docs.title: 23. Finding cards by meaning
docs.text: filter answers a question with a yes or no per card. Retrieval answers a question in words with a ranking: every card that matches, best first, each with a score. HQL has two retrievals, each an extension a program imports.

docs.title: Lexical retrieval
docs.text:
lexical matches the words of a query against the words of each card. It needs nothing built in advance:

import lexical
cards | lexical("desert spice") | take(3)

[dune (0.2928), frankenstein-inspires-dune (0.2778), frankenstein (0.2471)]

import lexical makes the extension's step available to the program. Without it, the name is not a step, and the error says which import provides it:

cards | lexical("desert spice")

check error[unknown-name]: `lexical` is provided by the `lexical` extension: write `import lexical`
 --> <expression>:1:9
  |
1 | cards | lexical("desert spice")
  |         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: A ranking holds hits
docs.text:
A ranking is a sequence of hits. A hit holds the card it retrieved, as value, and its score:

import lexical
cards
| lexical("desert spice")
| take(2)
| map(h => {card: h.value.name, score: h.score})

[{card: "dune", score: 0.2927674902397191}, {card: "frankenstein-inspires-dune", score: 0.2777641653663699}]

A score is evidence that a card is relevant to the query, not relevance itself, so every hit carries the retrieval that produced it — the model, the index, the metric, and whether the search was approximate:

import lexical
ranked = cards | lexical("desert")
{model: ranked.retrieval.model, metric: ranked.retrieval.metric, approximate: ranked.retrieval.approximate}

{approximate: false, metric: "cosine", model: "hql.hashbag.v1"}

take keeps a ranking a ranking, in the retrieval's order. Any other order is the program's own: sorting a ranking by another key makes it a plain sequence of hits.

docs.title: Retrieval, then the graph
docs.text:
A ranking is a collection of cards, so every step of the earlier chapters applies. expand grows a graph from the best hits, and the nodes it adds say they were reached, not retrieved:

import lexical
cards
| lexical("a creature and its maker")
| take(2)
| expand(depth = 1)
| text

club  (expanded from frankenstein at depth 1)
  -> dune
  -> frankenstein
  -> leaves-of-grass
dune  (expanded from frankenstein at depth 1)
frankenstein  (retrieved 0.2064)
  -> mary-shelley
  -> dune
leaves-of-grass  (expanded from walt-whitman at depth 1)
  -> walt-whitman
mary-shelley  (expanded from frankenstein at depth 1)
  -> frankenstein
walt-whitman  (retrieved 0.1261)
  -> leaves-of-grass

docs.title: Semantic retrieval
docs.text:
lexical matches spellings: a card that never uses the query's words scores nothing, and a card that uses common ones scores something. semantic scores by meaning, against embeddings a language model computed ahead of time into an index the vault names in hql.toml:

[semantics]
index = ".hql/index.sqlite"

Asked for a creature and its maker, semantic ranks Frankenstein, the relation card that names it, and Mary Shelley, though none of the three contains the word "creature":

import semantic
cards | semantic("a creature and its maker") | take(3) | map(h => h.value.title)

["Frankenstein", "Frankenstein inspires Dune", "Mary Shelley"]

The same question, by spelling, finds Frankenstein and then two cards that share only its small words:

import lexical
cards | lexical("a creature and its maker") | take(3) | map(h => h.value.title)

["Frankenstein", "Walt Whitman", "Librarian"]

A semantic ranking reports the model that embedded the cards, so two indexes built by two models are never compared by score:

import semantic
ranked = cards | semantic("a creature and its maker")
{model: ranked.retrieval.model, metric: ranked.retrieval.metric, approximate: ranked.retrieval.approximate}

{approximate: false, metric: "cosine", model: "sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2"}

The binary never loads a model: contrib/semantics/ embeds the cards and builds the index, and embeds each question the index will be asked, named at build time with --query. The tutorial vault's index holds the three questions this book asks. A question it does not hold is a diagnostic naming the build command, not a ranking of nothing:

import semantic
cards | semantic("night hunting birds") | take(1)

execute failure[invalid-argument]: the index holds no vector for `night hunting birds`, and this binary has no model to make one: rerun `hql-semantics build --query "night hunting birds"`
 --> <expression>:2:9
  |
2 | cards | semantic("night hunting birds") | take(1)
  |         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

hql doctor checks the chain — vault, configuration, index, model, query vectors — and names the first part that is missing.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: A ranking, a graph and a reading list are values a program prints. Chapter 24 writes them into the document that asks for them, and builds the document from its queries.

docs.title: 24. Queries inside documents
docs.text: A document can hold the queries that compute parts of it. hql render runs them and builds the document they describe, so a reading list, an index or a status table is a query, not a list somebody keeps up to date.

docs.title: Cells
docs.text:
A fenced block whose info string is hql — or hql#eval, or hql#query — is a cell. This is examples/notebook/reading-list.hmd:

# The club's reading list

Built from the vault with `hql --vault examples/tutorial render`.

```hql id=books hidden
cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
```

## Still to read

```hql id=todo
books
| filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
| sort(by = c => c.title)
| map(c => c.title)
```

## How far along

```hql
{books: books | size, to_read: todo | size}
```

docs.title: Building the document
docs.text:
hql render runs every cell against the vault and writes the document with each cell replaced by its output, as Markdown:

hql --vault examples/tutorial render examples/notebook/reading-list.hmd

# The club's reading list

Built from the vault with `hql --vault examples/tutorial render`.

## Still to read

- Leaves of Grass
- The Common Reader
- The Hobbit

## How far along

| key     | value |
| ------- | ----- |
| books   | 7     |
| to_read | 3     |

The source is the program; the built document is its result. --write <file> writes the build to a file instead of standard output.

docs.title: Cells share values
docs.text:
A cell's info string carries attributes after its kind:

  • id=<name> exports the cell's value to the other cells of the document, under that name. books and todo above are such names.
  • hidden runs the cell and writes nothing, for a value other cells read.
  • replace or after chooses where that one cell's output goes.

Only a cell's value leaves it: a binding inside a cell stays in that cell. The cells form a dependency graph, and run in the order their reads require, not the order they are written in. A cycle or a duplicate id is an error naming the cells, and a cell that reads a failed one is skipped, saying which cell it waited on.

The document is checked as a whole before any cell runs, so a type error in the last cell stops the build before the first one runs.

docs.title: Keeping the cells
docs.text:
--emit after keeps every cell and writes its output after it, between two comments a Markdown preview does not display:

```hql id=todo
books
| filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
| sort(by = c => c.title)
| map(c => c.title)
```
<!-- hql:output id=todo hash=9c9f41e99b94 status=ok -->
- Leaves of Grass
- The Common Reader
- The Hobbit
<!-- /hql:output -->

With --in-place that rewrites the source itself, the way a notebook saves its outputs, and the next render replaces what is between the markers. The opening marker records the cell's id, a hash of its code and of the code of every cell it reads, and its status. An output whose hash differs from the cell's current one is stale, and an editor can say so without running anything.

--cell <id> runs one cell and the cells it reads, and rewrites only its output. --envelope json prints the built document and a record per cell — its id, span, hash, type, status, output and reports — for an editor to read.

docs.title: Cells that maintain a vault
docs.text:
Design only

This section describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: these cells do not run against the current binary, and names, types and outputs may change before they ship.

A vault's upkeep is a set of questions asked of the vault itself: which cards are related to this one, what does each category hold, which card does nothing link to. Each is a cell a card carries, and the hash in its saved output says when the answer is stale, so maintenance is a render, not a chore. A card of a vault's own wiki might end with these:

## Related

```hql#eval id=related
cards | semantic(this.title) | take(3) | map(h => h.value)
```

## Index

```hql#eval id=index
cards
| group(by = c => c.metadata.category)
| map(g => {category: g.key, cards: g.items | map(c => c.name)})
```

## Health

```hql#eval id=orphans
cards | filter(c => (c | downlinks | size) == 0) | map(c => c.name)
```

this is the card the cell is written in, so the related cards are the three nearest in meaning to its title, written below its body as links. A cell marked cached would keep its output until the hash of its code and its inputs changes, so a summary a model wrote (chapter 25) is computed once and read many times. The cell kinds exist today; this, cached and a semantic over a question the index was not built for are design direction.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 25 gives a language model the cards a query selected, runs an agent over them, and keeps the run as a value.

docs.title: 25. Agents and runs
docs.text:
Design only

This chapter describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: these programs do not run against the current binary, and names, types and outputs may change before it ships.

Most of the work around a language model is not the call itself. Choosing evidence, building the context, writing the prompt, giving the model tools, continuing a conversation and keeping what came back are dataflow, and HQL writes them as dataflow. Every stage is a typed value: what reached the model, what it called and what it answered are read the way a card is read.

The constructors in this chapter are pure and need no import. The steps that reach a model need import ai, which is how a program states that it may spend money and send text to a third party.

docs.title: An agent is a card
docs.text:
An agent is behaviour and configuration, written as a card. Its body is its instructions, and its agent header table configures it. This one is the reading-club vault's librarian.hmd:

---
title: Librarian
agent:
  model: default
  tools: [books_by]
  max_turns: 4
---
# Librarian

Answer questions about the club's shelf from the cards you are given and the
tools you have. Name the books you rely on. Say so when the shelf does not
answer the question.

Agent reads one from a card:

librarian = @[[librarian]] | Agent
librarian.tools

["books_by"]

A card is an agent only by saying it is one: Agent refuses a card with no agent table, and an unknown key in it, so a misspelt max_turn does not quietly select the default. model names a key of [ai.models] in the vault's hql.toml, never a provider, so a committed card does not fix a vendor:

[ai]
recordings = ".hql/runs"

[ai.models.default]
api = "messages"
endpoint = "https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages"
model = "claude-sonnet-5-5"
max_tokens = 1024
temperature = 0

docs.title: Context and prompt
docs.text:
Context(label) turns values into what a model reads: one item per element, each written as markdown writes it, with where it came from:

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
| Context("unread")
| map(i => {label: i.label, source: i.provenance.name})

[{label: "unread", source: "leaves-of-grass"}, {label: "unread", source: "the-common-reader"}, {label: "unread", source: "the-hobbit"}]

A context is a Seq<ContextItem>, so contexts are combined with concat and narrowed with filter, like any other sequence. A ranking from chapter 23 keeps each hit's score and retrieval in its item, so cards | semantic(question) | take(10) | Context("evidence") is evidence that says how it was found.

Prompt(instructions) puts the task in front of the context. Its rendered field is the text exactly as sent:

p = cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
| Context("unread")
| Prompt("Which unread book should the club start with?")

p.rendered

Which unread book should the club start with?

## unread

Source: leaves-of-grass

# Leaves of Grass

Poems by [[walt-whitman]], revised and enlarged for the rest of his life.

Source: the-common-reader

# The Common Reader

Essays by [[virginia-woolf]] on reading, written for readers rather than critics.

Source: the-hobbit

# The Hobbit

A novel by [[jrr-tolkien]]. A hobbit is talked into an adventure and comes home changed.

docs.title: Tools are functions
docs.text:
A tool is a named HQL function. Tool records its name, a description and the JSON Schema of its parameters, derived from their types:

fn books_by(author: String) : List<String> =
    cards | filter(c => c.metadata.author == author) | map(c => c.title) | List

Tool(books_by, "The titles on the shelf by one author")

Tool {name: "books_by", description: "The titles on the shelf by one author", parameters: {"properties":{"author":{"type":"string"}},"required":["author"],"type":"object"}}

A tool is pure. While the harness evaluates one for a model, every effectful step is refused, so no path through the function reaches a file, a network or another model. The tools a run is given must be exactly those the agent's card lists: the card is where a reader learns what an agent can do.

docs.title: Running an agent
docs.text:
run(agent, tools = …) executes the agent over a context or a prompt until it stops, and returns a Run. This program is pick.hql:

import ai

fn books_by(author: String) : List<String> =
    cards | filter(c => c.metadata.author == author) | map(c => c.title) | List

librarian = @[[librarian]] | Agent

pick =
    cards
    | filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
    | Context("unread")
    | Prompt("Which unread book should the club start with?")
    | run(librarian, tools = [Tool(books_by, "The titles on the shelf by one author")])

pick.result

"Start with The Common Reader. It is the only unread book by Virginia Woolf, and the club has already read A Room of One's Own and is reading Mrs Dalloway, so it completes the club's Woolf."

The answer is one field among many. The harness never collapses a run into the text the model last wrote:

pick.calls | map(c => {tool: c.tool, status: c.status, output: c.output})

[{output: "[\"A Room of One's Own\",\"Mrs Dalloway\",\"The Common Reader\"]", status: "ok", tool: "books_by"}]

turns is the conversation, stop says why it ended — end, max_tokens, max_turns or refused — and model and usage are what the provider reported, not what configuration asked for. trace puts everything that happened in one order:

pick | trace | map(e => e.kind)

["prompt", "request", "response", "tool_call", "request", "response", "stop"]

docs.title: Continuing and delegating
docs.text:
A Run never changes. ask(message) continues its conversation with the same agent and tools, and returns a new run whose parent is the first:

why = pick | ask("What did you rely on?")
why.result

"The books_by tool listed three Woolf titles, and the card for The Common Reader is the only one marked todo."

delegate(agent, task) starts a fresh conversation for another agent, given the first run's context and its result. An agent named in a card's agents: list is offered to the model as a tool of that name, so a model may delegate by itself; each child run is kept in children, and delegation stops at depth three.

remember(name) writes a run's result, or a string, as a card in the vault's [ai.memory] dir. Memory is cards: writing it is one explicit step, and reading it is a query like any other.

docs.title: Recordings: a run that answers again
docs.text:
A program that reaches a model would answer differently on every evaluation. HQL keeps each response as a recording, keyed by the SHA-256 of the request it answers, under the vault's [ai] recordings directory. --ai chooses what may happen:

Mode What it does replay the default: answers from recordings only, and never reaches a network record sends what is not recorded yet, and records it live always sends

The mode is never read from hql.toml, so spending money is always a choice made on the command line. Record once, and the same program then evaluates offline, byte for byte:

$ hql --vault . --ai record run pick.hql
"Start with The Common Reader. …"
$ hql --vault . run pick.hql
"Start with The Common Reader. …"

A request with no recording is a diagnostic, not an empty answer:

evaluation failure: no recording for this request (5e10ae23…); run with --ai record
  --> pick.hql:13:7

hql check checks the whole program, its type is Run, and no model is reached. Committed recordings make a document that calls a model as reproducible as one that does not.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: A cell is a program, so a cell may run an agent, and the document around it is the prompt. Chapter 26 writes a document whose cells retrieve evidence, run the librarian over the draft they sit in, and save the answer where it was asked.

docs.title: 26. Agents inside documents
docs.text:
Design only

This chapter describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: these programs do not run against the current binary, and names, types and outputs may change before it ships.

Chapter 25 ran an agent from a program. This chapter runs one from inside the document that asks the question. The knowledge, the prompt, the program that assembles the prompt and the answer then sit in one file, each visible, each editable, each a value a later cell can read. The document is examples/notebook/next-meeting.hmd, rendered against the tutorial vault like the reading list of chapter 24.

docs.title: The document is the harness
docs.text:
Two bindings reach a cell from the host. cell is the cell being rendered, whose logs channel the logging page wrote to. this is the card the cell is written in, as it stands when the render starts: its header, its prose, and every output a previous render saved into it.

The prose of a cell's section, from the nearest heading above the cell down to the cell itself, is the default instructions of every Prompt the cell builds. The question is written once, as prose a reader reads, and the cell below it carries only the program that gathers the evidence.

hql render --emit after --in-place writes each cell's output back into the document, between the markers of chapter 24. The opening marker's hash covers the cell's code and the code of every cell it reads; a cell that reads this also covers the document's text, so its output is stale after every edit of the prose around it. That is the loop this chapter is about: edit the draft, render, read the answer, edit again.

docs.title: The document
docs.text:
---
title: Next meeting
---
# Next meeting

Notes for the club's next meeting, built from the shelf with
`hql --vault examples/tutorial render`.

```hql id=books hidden
cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
```

## Candidates

The books nobody has finished.

```hql id=unread
books
| filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
| sort(by = c => c.title)
| map(c => c.title)
```

## Evidence

What the shelf holds on the question the club keeps returning to.

```hql id=evidence hidden
import semantic
cards | semantic("which unread book suits a reading club") | take(3) | Context("evidence")
```

## What should we read next?

Pick one unread book for the next meeting, and say why. The candidates and
the evidence are in this draft; rely on them and on the shelf.

```hql#eval id=pick
import ai

fn books_by(author: String) : List<String> =
    cards | filter(c => c.metadata.author == author) | map(c => c.title) | List

[this]
| Context("draft")
| concat(evidence)
| run(@[[librarian]] | Agent, tools = [Tool(books_by, "The titles on the shelf by one author")])
```

## What happened

```hql#eval id=trace
pick | trace | map(e => e.kind)
```

## Remembered

```hql id=note hidden
pick | remember("next-meeting-pick")
```

```hql#eval
cards | filter(c => c.path | starts_with("memory/")) | map(c => c.title)
```

The first two cells run against the current binary; they are the reading list of chapter 24 again. The rest is the subject of this chapter.

docs.title: Evidence by meaning
docs.text:
The evidence cell is a ranking of chapter 23 turned into a context. Each hit becomes one item, and the item keeps what the hit knew: its score, and the retrieval that produced it, in its provenance. Evidence that reaches a model says how it was found:

evidence | map(i => {source: i.provenance.name, score: i.score})

[{score: 0.3127, source: "the-common-reader"}, {score: 0.2904, source: "club"}, {score: 0.2851, source: "leaves-of-grass"}]

The question is a literal because the vault's index answers the questions it was built for, as chapter 23 explains; a question the index lacks is a diagnostic naming the build command, not an empty context.

docs.title: The agent reads the draft
docs.text:
[this] | Context("draft") is a context of one item: the document as it stands, written as Markdown, with the card's name and path as its provenance. concat(evidence) appends the ranking. The run step builds the prompt from the section's prose and both contexts, and the rendered prompt opens with the question the reader just read:

Pick one unread book for the next meeting, and say why. The candidates and
the evidence are in this draft; rely on them and on the shelf.

## draft

Source: next-meeting

# Next meeting
…

## evidence

Source: the-common-reader
…

The run's result is written after the cell, and the next cell reads the run itself, not its text:

```hql#eval id=pick
…
```
<!-- hql:output id=pick hash=3b91c0e4d2a7 status=ok -->
Start with The Common Reader. It is the only unread book by Virginia Woolf,
the club has read A Room of One's Own and is reading Mrs Dalloway, and the
draft lists it among the candidates.
<!-- /hql:output -->

["prompt", "request", "response", "tool_call", "request", "response", "stop"]

Change the prose above the cell, "say why" to "say why, in one sentence", and the cell's hash no longer matches its saved output. An editor shows the answer as stale without running anything; the next render asks again, with the new instructions and the draft as it now stands, which includes the previous answer. The agent reads what it wrote last time, as a value among the others.

docs.title: Memory is cards
docs.text:
remember(name) writes a run's result as a card in the vault's [ai.memory] directory, here memory/next-meeting-pick.hmd, with the run's id in its header so the card names the run that wrote it. Memory is cards: writing it is one explicit step, and reading it is a query like any other, which is what the last cell does. On the next render, cards holds the memory card and this holds the saved pick, so the document reads what it wrote.

In replay mode, the default, remember succeeds only when the card already holds the same content, so a committed vault renders without writing. Under --ai record or --ai live it writes.

docs.title: The editor loop
docs.text:
A request a run makes can be answered by three answerers, and every answer is a recording under the hash of the request, so a document rendered later reads all three alike. A provider answers over HTTP, as chapter 25 configured. A headless session of an agent host answers when the model entry names one. And under --ai host, a request with no recording is not sent anywhere: it waits, and whoever is driving the program answers it. In an editor that is the agent the user is already chatting with.

$ hql --vault examples/tutorial --ai host render --emit after --in-place examples/notebook/next-meeting.hmd
$ hql --vault examples/tutorial ai pending
5e10ae23…  messages  next-meeting.hmd:31  pick
$ hql --vault examples/tutorial ai answer 5e10ae23… --text "Start with The Common Reader. …"
$ hql --vault examples/tutorial render examples/notebook/next-meeting.hmd

hql ai pending lists each waiting request with its key, the wire format its answer is written in, and the request itself: the agent's instructions, the conversation, and the tools offered with their schemas. hql ai answer writes the answer as a recording marked answered_by: host, so a reader of the document can tell a provider's answer from one a person's chat gave. The second render replays it. Committed recordings make the document a procedure the chat executed once and anyone can read again.

edit the draft ──► render ──► request waits ──► chat answers ──► recording
      ▲                                                             │
      └───────────────── read the saved output ◄────────────────────┘

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Every card in this chapter was in one vault. Chapter 27 asks what the same steps are over a web of them.

docs.title: 27. The hyper web
docs.text:
Design only

This chapter describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: nothing in it runs against the current binary, and names, types and outputs may change before any of it ships. It is the direction the rest of the book points in, stated so that the direction can be read, questioned and changed.

A vault is one namespace: a tree of cards, closed by construction, in which every [[name]] resolves or is reported. The chapters of Part III queried, drew, ranked and ran agents over one such tree. This chapter asks what each of those steps is over many trees, authored and served independently, and what a reader is when the trees are read by programs and agents as much as by people.

docs.title: Namespaces beyond one tree
docs.text:
A reference may name a namespace: [[club:dune]] is the card dune in the namespace bound as club. The binding lives in the vault's configuration, never in a card, so a card cannot reach a namespace by mentioning it, and removing the binding breaks every link that used it, visibly. A prefix is a permission.

[namespaces.club]
root = "../reading-club"

[namespaces.lit]
url = "https://lit.example.org/"

HQL already has the local half of this. source("club") in chapter 21 is a vault bound by configuration, with its own cards and graph, and a relation across the two is a join. A namespace bound to a URL is the same source whose provider is a server; the program is unchanged:

lit = source("lit")
lit.cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book") | size

The rule the design rests on is no silent dereference: rendering, checking and linting make no network call, and a program that reads a remote namespace does so in a step the host sees and may refuse, as it sees and may refuse source(http(…)) today.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text:
A provider is anything that returns a card for a path: the vault's own folder, another folder, a web server that speaks plain HTTP and publishes a route description so a client does not guess its layout, a database holding cards as rows. The card's name is the same whichever provider answers, so a program over cards is a program over a web of vaults, and where a card is stored stays out of every reference to it.

What arrives from another provider is untrusted. A remote card's header is Data, as every tree from outside a program is, and it becomes a typed value at a boundary of chapter 11, where the program states what it requires and the rest is refused or kept as Data. A card of a namespace carries the namespace in its provenance, and so does every value derived from it: a hit, a context item, a run.

docs.title: Retrieval over the web
docs.text:
semantic over a namespace is the provider's index answering a question it holds, with its model, metric and approximation reported in the ranking's retrieval, as chapter 23 reports them for a local index. Two namespaces are two rankings, and a program that combines them does so explicitly, by score within a retrieval or by a join across them, because a score is evidence relative to one index and means nothing against another's.

import semantic

here  = cards | semantic("a creature and its maker") | take(3)
there = source("lit").cards | semantic("a creature and its maker") | take(3)
[here, there] | emit | Context("evidence")

Each item of that context says which namespace it came from, which index ranked it and how. Knowledge semantics becomes a way to query the web: a question in words, answered with cards and the evidence for each, rather than with pages to read.

docs.title: Agents reading agents
docs.text:
An agent is a card, so a namespace can serve one, and a document in one vault can run the librarian of another. delegate across a binding is a run whose child ran elsewhere, kept in children with its provenance, and whose trace records the delegation as an event like any other. The rules of chapter 25 do not change at the boundary: a child run is bounded in depth, every request is recorded under its hash, and a tool stays pure wherever it is evaluated.

import ai

review = cards | lexical("influence") | Context("claims") | run(@[[librarian]] | Agent)
second = review | delegate(@[[lit:reviewer]] | Agent, "Check the claims against your shelf.")
second.trace | filter(e => e.kind == "delegate") | map(e => e.data.namespace)

An agent that reads another agent's run reads a value: the prompt it was given, the tools it called, the answer it gave, and where each piece came from. A conversation between agents is a tree of such values, and a program queries it with the steps of chapter 6.

docs.title: A reader who asks
docs.text:
The same card is served to a person in a browser, to a tool that lints it, and to an agent building a context, from one source and in one format. A site that is a vault answers a question the way a document of chapter 26 does: with a run whose evidence is the site's own cards, whose trace says which cards were read, and whose answer carries their names. The reader asks instead of browsing, and what comes back is not a page but a value with its provenance attached, which the reader, or the reader's agent, may query further.

None of this needs a new language. It needs bindings in configuration, providers that answer by path, and the discipline the earlier chapters already hold: every step typed, every effect explicit, every value carrying where it came from.

docs.title: Where to go from here
docs.text: You have met the whole language, in three parts. The language: values and data, collections and functions, modules, questions in the style of SQL, streams, formats, data read and written through endpoints, the types a program declares and the boundary where data becomes typed, and the tools around it. Data flows: the pipeline, its phases, its unit of execution, and the systems it will connect. Knowledge and AI: a vault that is a namespace, its graph, retrieval by meaning, documents that compute themselves, agents whose runs are values, documents that run them, and the web they point at. The reference states each shipped part precisely, and the examples are where the next part is designed.

docs.title: 28. Statistics
docs.text: This chapter is about the module stats: descriptive statistics over a collection of numbers. It covers the centre of the values (the mean, the median and the mode), their spread, their quantiles, the correlation of two columns, and what a statistic is over an input too small to define it. Each statistic applies to a list written by hand and to a column a query reads.

docs.title: The module
docs.text:
stats is not in the prelude: a program writes import stats. Without the import, a statistic is an unknown name, and the checker names the import it needs:

[1, 2, 3, 4] | mean

check error[unknown-name]: `mean` is provided by the `stats` extension: write `import stats`
 --> <expression>:1:16
  |
1 | [1, 2, 3, 4] | mean
  |                ^^^^

docs.title: The centre
docs.text:
mean is the sum divided by the count, median the middle value of the sorted values, and the mean of the two middle values where the count is even, and mode the most frequent value:

import stats
xs = [2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9]
{mean: xs | mean, median: xs | median, mode: xs | mode}

{mean: 5.0, median: 4.5, mode: 4}

A statistic of Int or Float values is a Float. A statistic of Int values is computed exactly and rounded to a Float once. A statistic of Decimal values is a Decimal, exact except where a quotient does not terminate, which is rounded half to even to 100 significant digits as Decimal / is. A literal with a decimal point is a Decimal (Decimal), so a list of prices keeps its cents:

import stats
prices = [1.10, 2.20, 3.30, 4.45, 5.05]
[prices | mean, prices | median]

[3.22, 3.30]

mode takes values of any Orderable type, not only numbers. Among equally frequent values, the mode is the least by the type's order:

import stats
[[3, 1, 3, 1, 2] | mode, ["novel", "essay", "novel", "poetry"] | mode]

[1, "novel"]

docs.title: Spread
docs.text:
variance is the sample variance, the sum of squared deviations from the mean divided by n - 1, and stdev its square root. pvariance is the population variance, the same sum divided by n, and pstdev its square root:

import stats
xs = [2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9]
[xs | stats.variance, xs | stdev, xs | pvariance, xs | pstdev]

[4.571428571428571, 2.138089935299395, 4.0, 2.0]

The prelude declares a variance too: the population variance of Int and Float values. With stats imported, a bare variance over those is ambiguous, and the checker asks for the module's name:

import stats
[1, 2, 3, 4] | variance

check error[unknown-name]: `variance` over List<Int> is declared by `core` and `stats`, so the call is ambiguous; qualify it, `core.variance(…)`
 --> <expression>:2:16
  |
2 | [1, 2, 3, 4] | variance
  |                ^^^^^^^^

stats.variance is the sample variance and core.variance the population variance. Over Decimal values only stats declares one, and a bare variance is the sample variance.

docs.title: Quantiles
docs.text:
quantile(q) is the value below which the fraction q of the sorted values lies, by linear interpolation between the two nearest values: the method R and NumPy use by default. quantiles(n) is the n - 1 cut points that divide the sorted values into n groups of equal probability, so quantiles(4) is the three quartiles and quantiles(100) the percentiles:

import stats
xs = [2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9]
{p90: xs | quantile(0.9), quartiles: xs | quantiles(4)}

{p90: 7.6, quartiles: [4.0, 4.5, 5.5]}

median is quantile(0.5). Over Int and Decimal values a quantile is computed exactly, so the 95th percentile of the prices is a Decimal:

import stats
[1.10, 2.20, 3.30, 4.45, 5.05] | quantile(0.95)

4.9300

A q outside 0.0 to 1.0, or an n below 2, is an evaluation error:

import stats
[1, 2, 3] | quantile(1.5)

execute failure[invalid-argument]: `quantile` needs a `q` from 0 to 1, and 1.5 is outside it
 --> <expression>:2:22
  |
2 | [1, 2, 3] | quantile(1.5)
  |                      ^^^

docs.title: Correlation
docs.text:
covariance and correlation take a collection of pairs: the first column in each pair's first, the second in its second. zip builds the pairs from two lists. covariance is the sample covariance, and correlation Pearson's coefficient, the covariance divided by the product of the two standard deviations, from -1.0 to 1.0:

import stats
pairs = zip([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], [2, 1, 4, 3, 7, 5])
[pairs | covariance, pairs | correlation]

[3.2, 0.7917946548886297]

docs.title: A column of a query
docs.text:
A statistic takes any collection, so it ends a pipeline as sum and size do. The books of the tutorial vault (chapter 21) carry their pages in the header, and a typed view reads them as numbers:

import stats
fn pages(c: Card) : Int = match c.metadata.pages { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 }
books = cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
lengths = books | map(pages)
{mean: lengths | mean, median: lengths | median, stdev: lengths | stdev, quartiles: lengths | quantiles(4)}

{mean: 251.0, median: 280.0, quartiles: [169.5, 280.0, 307.0], stdev: 105.56040924513319}

A statistic per group is a map over the groups, as each aggregate of chapter 6 was:

import stats
fn pages(c: Card) : Int = match c.metadata.pages { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 }
cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
| group(by = c => c.metadata.genre)
| map(g => {genre: g.key, books: g.items | size, mean: g.items | map(pages) | mean})

{{books: 2, genre: "essay", mean: 208.0}, {books: 4, genre: "novel", mean: 299.0}, {books: 1, genre: "poetry", mean: 145.0}}

Two columns of one query are a column of pairs. Whether longer books are the later ones is the correlation of the year and the pages:

import stats
fn pages(c: Card) : Int = match c.metadata.pages { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 }
fn year(c: Card) : Int = match c.metadata.year { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 }
cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
| map(b => Pair(year(b), pages(b)))
| correlation

0.33335874566223495

docs.title: An empty input
docs.text:
A statistic that is undefined over its input is none, so each statistic but quantiles is an Option. The mean, median and mode of nothing are none. The sample variance and standard deviation need two values, so of one value they are none, while the population variance of one value is 0.0. The correlation is none also where one side has no variance:

import stats
nothing = [1, 2, 3] | filter(n => n > 5)
[nothing | mean, nothing | median, [4] | stdev, [4] | pvariance, zip([1, 2, 3], [5, 5, 5]) | correlation]

[none, none, none, 0.0, none]

quantiles of nothing is an empty list. Where a program needs a number whatever the input, unwrap_or gives a default (Option); 0.0f is a Float literal:

import stats
nothing = [1, 2, 3] | filter(n => n > 5)
nothing | mean | unwrap_or(0.0f)

0.0

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: A statistic describes values a program has. Chapter 29 is about values a program draws: samples, shuffles and random numbers, and the seed that makes them repeatable.

docs.title: 29. Random values
docs.text: This chapter is about the module random: samples, shuffles, choices, random numbers and UUIDs. It covers the two forms each draw has, the seeded one and the unseeded one, and the evaluation seed that makes a program's random output repeatable.

docs.title: The module
docs.text:
random is not in the prelude: a program writes import random. Each draw has two forms. With a seed argument it is pure: its result is a function of the seed, its input and its call site, the same on every run. Without one it is effectful and draws from the evaluation seed, fixed once per evaluation.

The generator is ChaCha12. A seeded draw is predictable by design, so no draw of random is fit for a key, a token or any other secret.

docs.title: Samples, shuffles and choices
docs.text:
sample(n) is n elements drawn without replacement, in the order they have in the input:

import random
range(1, 21) | sample(5, seed = 7)

[1, 5, 9, 13, 16]

shuffle is every element in a uniformly random order, and choice one element drawn uniformly:

import random
titles = cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book") | map(c => c.title)
{shuffled: titles | shuffle(seed = 7), picked: titles | choice(seed = 7)}

{picked: "A Room of One's Own", shuffled: ["The Hobbit", "Frankenstein", "The Common Reader", "Mrs Dalloway", "Dune", "A Room of One's Own", "Leaves of Grass"]}

choice is an Option: over an empty input it is none. sample(n) with n at or above the input's size is the whole input, and a negative n is an evaluation error:

import random
nothing = [1, 2, 3] | filter(n => n > 5)
[nothing | choice(seed = 1), [1, 2, 3] | choice(seed = 1)]

[none, 1]

A collection without an order, such as a Set, is sorted by its elements before it is sampled, so the sample does not depend on how the set was built.

docs.title: A seed
docs.text:
A seeded draw is a function of its call site, its position in the program text, as well as of its seed. Two calls with one seed at two places are two draws:

import random
deck = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]
[deck | shuffle(seed = 1), deck | shuffle(seed = 1)]

[["e", "c", "b", "d", "a"], ["a", "c", "e", "b", "d"]]

One call site with one seed gives one result each time it is reached. A seeded draw inside a map repeats; a seed that varies with the element varies the draw:

import random
deck = ["a", "b", "c", "d"]
{same: range(0, 3) | map(_ => deck | shuffle(seed = 1)), varied: range(0, 3) | map(i => deck | shuffle(seed = i))}

{same: [["c", "b", "d", "a"], ["c", "b", "d", "a"], ["c", "b", "d", "a"]], varied: [["d", "c", "b", "a"], ["c", "a", "d", "b"], ["d", "c", "a", "b"]]}

Moving a seeded call to another place in the program text changes its result; running the same program again does not.

docs.title: The evaluation seed
docs.text:
An unseeded draw reads the evaluation seed. --seed <int> fixes it; without --seed, the seed comes from the host's entropy. Each unseeded call site draws from a stream derived from the evaluation seed and its position in the program, so two call sites draw independently, and a program run twice with one --seed writes the same values:

import random
xs = range(1, 11)
{sample: xs | sample(3), shuffled: xs | shuffle, picked: xs | choice}

{picked: 9, sample: [1, 2, 4], shuffled: [10, 2, 1, 4, 9, 5, 6, 8, 7, 3]}

An evaluation that takes its seed from the host reports it at info, with the --seed that repeats it:

$ hql --report-level info eval 'import random
range(1, 11) | shuffle | size'
10
execute info[effect]: the evaluation seed is -7270767200120302920; `--seed -7270767200120302920` repeats this evaluation
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | import random
  | ^

Without --seed, a block's values differ from run to run, but what holds of every draw holds of each: a sample of n has n elements, and a shuffle holds every element once:

import random
[range(0, 1000) | sample(3) | size, (range(0, 29) | shuffle | sort) == range(0, 29)]

[3, true]

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
random_int(low, high) is an Int drawn uniformly from low to high, both included, and random_float() a Float from 0.0 included to 1.0 excluded. Both are effectful and have no seeded form, so --seed is what makes them repeatable:

import random
{dice: range(0, 5) | map(_ => random_int(1, 6)), fraction: random_float()}

{dice: [4, 6, 4, 1, 6], fraction: 0.5037399186078297}

high below low is an evaluation error:

import random
random_int(6, 1)

execute failure[invalid-argument]: `random_int` needs `high` at or above `low`, and 1 is below 6
 --> <expression>:2:1
  |
2 | random_int(6, 1)
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: UUIDs
docs.text:
A UUID is written as lowercase hyphenated text. uuid(name, namespace) is the version 5 UUID of a name in a namespace: a function of the two, with no draw. The namespace is a UUID's text, or one of the standard namespaces "dns", "url", "oid" and "x500":

import random
uuid("www.example.com", "dns")

"2ed6657d-e927-568b-95e1-2665a8aea6a2"

uuid() is a version 7 UUID. Its first 48 bits are the evaluation instant's Unix milliseconds and the next 42 a counter, so the UUIDs of one evaluation are distinct and sort in the order they were drawn:

import random
ids = range(0, 20) | map(_ => uuid())
[ids == sort(ids), size(Set(ids)) == 20]

[true, true]

Its remaining bits come from the evaluation seed. --now fixes the evaluation instant (the evaluation clock) and --seed the seed, and the two together make uuid() repeatable:

import random
[uuid(), uuid()]

["01a16cd1-04c0-706c-9aa2-de28777558c7", "01a16cd1-04c0-706c-9aa2-de29b51d9000"]

docs.title: A stream
docs.text: sample(n) also takes a stream, by reservoir sampling: the step holds n elements, never the stream, and gives its sample when the stream ends. A stream that does not end gives no sample. The stream form is effectful only.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 30 is about the modules that turn values into bytes and back: digests and encodings.

docs.title: 30. Digests and encodings
docs.text: A digest is the fixed-size output of a cryptographic hash function over a sequence of octets: equal input gives an equal digest, and a change to any octet changes it. An encoding writes octets as text-safe characters and reads them back. This chapter covers the two modules that provide them, crypto.digest and encoding, over a String, a Bytes value and a Data tree.

docs.title: The digest module
docs.text:
crypto.digest is not in the prelude. A program writes import crypto.digest and reaches the module as digest; without the import, the name is a check error:

"abc".digest(Sha256)

check error[unknown-name]: `digest` is provided by the `crypto.digest` extension: write `import crypto.digest`
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | "abc".digest(Sha256)
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

An algorithm is named by a type, as a format is: Md5, Sha1, Sha256, Sha512 and Blake3. s.digest(A) is the digest of a text's UTF-8 octets under A, written as lowercase hexadecimal, two digits per octet:

import crypto.digest
s = "abc"
[s.digest(Md5), s.digest(Sha1), s.digest(Sha256), s.digest(Blake3)]

["900150983cd24fb0d6963f7d28e17f72", "a9993e364706816aba3e25717850c26c9cd0d89d", "ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad", "6437b3ac38465133ffb63b75273a8db548c558465d79db03fd359c6cd5bd9d85"]

The length of the text follows from the algorithm: 32 hex digits for Md5, 40 for Sha1, 64 for Sha256 and Blake3, 128 for Sha512. Md5 and Sha1 are broken for collision resistance: two different inputs with one digest can be constructed. They serve to compare with digests other tools wrote, not to protect anything new.

b.digest(A) takes a Bytes value, the form for octets that are not text. The two forms agree: the digest of Bytes(s) is the digest of s:

import crypto.digest
import encoding
Bytes("68656c6c6f", Hex).digest(Sha256) == "hello".digest(Sha256)

true

docs.title: Fingerprints of data
docs.text:
fingerprint(x) is the SHA-256 digest of a Data tree's canonical JSON, the text canonical(x) gives. Canonical JSON follows RFC 8785: keys sorted, no whitespace, a number as its digits without trailing zeros, a time value as its ISO 8601 text and a Bytes leaf as its base64 text:

import crypto.digest
canonical({title: "Dune", pages: 412, price: 9.50, on: Date("2026-10-24")})

"{\"on\":\"2026-10-24\",\"pages\":412,\"price\":9.5,\"title\":\"Dune\"}"

Two trees equal under HQL equality have one canonical text, so one fingerprint. Key order, whitespace and 1.10 against 1.1 in the source text change neither:

import crypto.digest
a = Data("{\"b\": 1, \"a\": [1.10, \"x\"]}", Json)
b = Data("{ \"a\" : [1.1, \"x\"],\n  \"b\": 1.0 }", Json)
[fingerprint(a), fingerprint(b)]

["5b07d3c10bbccec19fd995c80fb3393b8fd39691dbcc412ac55c0d08262ed5af", "5b07d3c10bbccec19fd995c80fb3393b8fd39691dbcc412ac55c0d08262ed5af"]

A value's type does count: the number 9.50 and the text "9.50" are different leaves, with different fingerprints:

import crypto.digest
[fingerprint({price: 9.50}) == fingerprint({price: 9.5}), fingerprint({price: 9.50}) == fingerprint({price: "9.50"})]

[true, false]

fingerprint(x) is canonical(x).digest(Sha256), so a program in another language reproduces it with any RFC 8785 implementation and SHA-256.

docs.title: The encoding module
docs.text:
encoding is not in the prelude either: a program writes import encoding. An encoding is named by a type:

Encoding Writes octets as Hex two hexadecimal digits each, lowercase; either case reads Base64 RFC 4648 base64, standard alphabet, padded Base64Url RFC 4648 base64, URL-safe alphabet, unpadded; padding optional on reading Percent RFC 3986 percent-encoding: A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~ as they are, every other octet as %XX

s.encode(E) writes a text's UTF-8 octets in E:

import encoding
