["hé".encode(Hex), "??>".encode(Base64), "??>".encode(Base64Url), "a b/é~".encode(Percent)]

["68c3a9", "Pz8+", "Pz8-", "a%20b%2F%C3%A9~"]

s.decode(E) reads the text back as an Option<String>. It is none where the input is not valid in E, and also where the octets it holds are not UTF-8, as /w== in base64 is the single octet 0xff:

import encoding
["68C3A9".decode(Hex), "aGk/".decode(Base64), "6g".decode(Hex), "/w==".decode(Base64)]

["hé", "hi?", none, none]

Percent-decoding reads %20 as a space and leaves + as it is:

import encoding
"a+b%20%C3%A9".decode(Percent)

"a+b é"

docs.title: Between text and Bytes
docs.text:
Where the octets are not text, Bytes holds them. b.encode(E) writes a Bytes value in E, and s.to_bytes(E) reads it back as an Option<Bytes>, with no UTF-8 requirement; Bytes(s, E) reads it as a value and fails on invalid text. The page Bytes shows each:

import encoding
b = Bytes("ff00", Hex)
[b.encode(Hex), b.encode(Base64), b.encode(Base64Url)]

["ff00", "/wA=", "_wA"]

import encoding
["/w==".decode(Base64), "/w==".to_bytes(Base64)]

[none, 0xff]

docs.title: A record already seen
docs.text:
A fingerprint is a key that holds outside the program: in a column, a file name, a cache. Records that arrive with their keys in another order, or as another program wrote them, still match the keys of an earlier load. Here loaded holds a 12-digit prefix of each fingerprint an earlier run stored, and only the new record passes:

import crypto.digest
loaded = {"106815777291"}
incoming = [{to: "ada", id: 1}, {id: 2, to: "bo"}]
incoming | filter(r => not loaded.contains(fingerprint(r)[0:12]))

[{id: 2, to: "bo"}]

Within one program, distinct already removes records equal under HQL equality, and Deduplication covers duplicates by key. The fingerprint is for the comparison that crosses a run.

docs.title: A file's digest
docs.text:
source(file(p), Text) reads a file whole as one String, as Source shows. Its digest is the one shasum -a 256 prints for the file, so a program checks a download against a published digest:

import crypto.digest
expected = "ade391083e197c4575f5ccb436b35c499665e77202518e6873a02fa6b54cc8e3"
source(file("examples/io/counts.csv"), Text) | map(t => t.digest(Sha256) == expected)

[true]

The reference states every function of the two modules with its signature: crypto.digest and encoding.

docs.title: 31. Keys and cryptography
docs.text: The module crypto holds keys: the algorithms they belong to, the types that hold them, the text formats other tools write them in, and the rules that keep a private key out of every output. This chapter reads, writes and generates keys, signs and verifies with them, computes MACs and hashes passwords, and then describes the operations that are not in the current release: encryption and the key vault. Digests and text encodings, which need no key, are chapter 30, and the octets a key is made of are the Bytes type of chapter 2.

docs.title: Algorithms and key types
docs.text:
crypto is not in the prelude: a program writes import crypto. An algorithm is named by a type, as a format is, and a key's type carries its algorithm:

Algorithm Kind What it is Ed25519 signing RFC 8032, pure Ed25519 P256 signing ECDSA over NIST P-256 with SHA-256 Rsa signing RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 with SHA-256, 2048 to 8192 bits X25519 agreement RFC 7748; the key of an age recipient Aes256Gcm, ChaCha20Poly1305 cipher a 256-bit shared key HmacSha256, HmacSha512 MAC a shared key of any length

The first four are asymmetric, each key a pair of a public and a private half. The last four are symmetric, one shared key. Four types hold them:

Type What it holds PublicKey<A> the public half of a key of algorithm A PrivateKey<A> the private half KeyPair<A> both halves, as the fields public and private SecretKey<A> a symmetric key of a cipher or a MAC

PrivateKey, KeyPair and SecretKey are secret types, the subject of the section Private keys below.

docs.title: Reading a public key
docs.text:
read_public_key(file, format, algorithm) reads the key a file holds. The key here is the published test key 1 of RFC 8032, kept in the repository's examples:

import crypto

key = read_public_key(file("examples/crypto/keys/rfc8032-test-1.pub.pem"), Pem, Ed25519)
key

PublicKey<Ed25519>(kPrK_qmxVWaYVA9wwBF6Iuo3vVzz7TxHCTwXBygrS4k)

A public key prints as its type and its thumbprint: the RFC 7638 JWK thumbprint, the base64url SHA-256 of the key's canonical JWK. thumbprint() gives it as a String. It names a key in one short line, and is the same whichever format the key was read from.

A key format is named by a type:

Format Text Pem RFC 7468 text around DER: SPKI for a public key, PKCS #8 for a private one Jwk the RFC 7517 JSON text of one key OpenSsh an authorized_keys line, or an OpenSSH private key file Age age's Bech32 recipient and identity text, for X25519 only

PublicKey(text, format, algorithm) reads a key from a String. A public key is not a secret, so its text may be written in a program. The same key as an OpenSSH line and as a JWK is one value:

import crypto

line = "ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAINdamAGCsQq31Uv+08lkBzoO4XLz2qYjJa8CGmj3B1Ea"
jwk = "{\"kty\": \"OKP\", \"crv\": \"Ed25519\", \"x\": \"11qYAYKxCrfVS_7TyWQHOg7hcvPapiMlrwIaaPcHURo\"}"
a = PublicKey(line, OpenSsh, Ed25519)
b = PublicKey(jwk, Jwk, Ed25519)
[a == b, a.thumbprint()]

[true, "kPrK_qmxVWaYVA9wwBF6Iuo3vVzz7TxHCTwXBygrS4k"]

Public keys compare by their octets, so == holds across formats.

Text that is not a key of the format and the algorithm is an evaluation error. to_public_key gives none instead, for text whose validity is not known in advance:

import crypto

"ssh-ed25519 AAAA" | to_public_key(OpenSsh, Ed25519)

none

A key of one algorithm read as another is an evaluation error naming both:

import crypto

read_public_key(file("examples/crypto/keys/rfc8032-test-1.pub.pem"), Pem, P256)

execute failure[invalid-argument]: examples/crypto/keys/rfc8032-test-1.pub.pem: the DER text holds an Ed25519 key, and it is read as P256
 --> <expression>:3:1
  |
3 | read_public_key(file("examples/crypto/keys/rfc8032-test-1.pub.pem"), Pem, P256)
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A format that holds no key of the algorithm at all is a check error, found before anything is read. Age holds X25519 keys alone, and X25519 has no OpenSsh text:

import crypto

PublicKey("age1qyqszqgpqyqszqgpqyqszqgp", Age, Ed25519)

check error[type-mismatch]: Age text holds no Ed25519 key: `Age` holds `X25519` keys alone
 --> <expression>:3:1
  |
3 | PublicKey("age1qyqszqgpqyqszqgpqyqszqgp", Age, Ed25519)
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Writing a public key
docs.text:
to_text(format) writes a public key in a format another tool reads. OpenSsh is an authorized_keys line with no comment, Jwk the canonical JSON of the required members, and Pem 64-column lines with a final line break:

import crypto

key = read_public_key(file("examples/crypto/keys/rfc8032-test-1.pub.pem"), Pem, Ed25519)
[key.to_text(OpenSsh), key.to_text(Jwk)]

["ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAINdamAGCsQq31Uv+08lkBzoO4XLz2qYjJa8CGmj3B1Ea", "{\"crv\":\"Ed25519\",\"kty\":\"OKP\",\"x\":\"11qYAYKxCrfVS_7TyWQHOg7hcvPapiMlrwIaaPcHURo\"}"]

to_der() gives the key's SPKI DER as Bytes, and PublicKey(der, algorithm) reads it back:

import crypto

key = read_public_key(file("examples/crypto/keys/rfc8032-test-1.pub.pem"), Pem, Ed25519)
der = key.to_der()
[str(der.size()), str(der), str(PublicKey(der, Ed25519) == key)]

["44", "0x302a300506032b6570032100d75a980182b10ab7d54bfed3c964073a0ee172f3daa62325af021a68f707511a", "true"]

The last 32 octets are the Ed25519 key itself; the 12 before them name the algorithm.

docs.title: Private keys
docs.text:
A secret type is a type whose values hold private key material: PrivateKey, KeyPair and SecretKey. Four rules hold for every value of one:

  • it prints redacted;
  • no format writes it;
  • == does not compare it;
  • its text does not appear in a program's source.

read_private_key(file, format, algorithm) reads a private key. It prints as its type and its public key's thumbprint, which names the key and discloses nothing of it:

import crypto

key = read_private_key(file("examples/crypto/keys/rfc8032-test-1.pem"), Pem, Ed25519)
[str(key), key.public().thumbprint()]

["PrivateKey<Ed25519>(kPrK_qmxVWaYVA9wwBF6Iuo3vVzz7TxHCTwXBygrS4k)", "kPrK_qmxVWaYVA9wwBF6Iuo3vVzz7TxHCTwXBygrS4k"]

public() gives a private key's public key. On a Unix host, a private key file that its group or others may read gives a warning naming the path and its mode; chmod 600 the file to clear it. The warning is a diagnostic, and the result is unchanged.

A secret reaches no format. Writing one is a check error that names the operation that turns a private key into text:

import crypto

pair = generate_key_pair(Ed25519)
pair.private | format(Json)

check error[type-mismatch]: PrivateKey<Ed25519> holds private key material, which no format writes; `export_private` turns a private key into text where a program means to
 --> <expression>:4:16
  |
4 | pair.private | format(Json)
  |                ^^^^^^^^^^^^

A secret type implements no Eq. Two private keys are the same key when their public keys are equal, and that is the comparison to write:

import crypto

pair = generate_key_pair(Ed25519)
pair.private == pair.private

check error[type-mismatch]: PrivateKey<Ed25519> is a secret and implements no `Eq`: `==` does not compare key material; compare public keys, or a MAC with `verify_mac`
 --> <expression>:4:1
  |
4 | pair.private == pair.private
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A string literal that holds private key material is a check error. A private key is read from a file, the environment or a key vault, or generated:

import crypto

text = "-----BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY-----"
text

check error[type-mismatch]: this literal holds a PEM private key: private key material never lives in a program's source; read it from a file (`read_private_key`), the environment (`env.var`), a key vault (`keyvault.key`), or generate it
 --> <expression>:3:8
  |
3 | text = "-----BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY-----"
  |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Exporting a private key
docs.text:
export_private(format) writes a private key's material as a String, the one operation that does. The result is no longer a secret type: it prints, and a format writes it. With passphrase, the text is encrypted: PKCS #8 under scrypt and AES-256-CBC for Pem, bcrypt-pbkdf and AES-256-CTR for OpenSsh. PrivateKey(text, format, algorithm, passphrase = …) reads it back, and to_private_key gives none for a wrong passphrase:

import crypto

pair = generate_key_pair(Ed25519)
sealed = pair.private.export_private(OpenSsh, passphrase = "correct horse")
[PrivateKey(sealed, OpenSsh, Ed25519, passphrase = "correct horse").public() == pair.public,
 sealed | to_private_key(OpenSsh, Ed25519, passphrase = "wrong") | is_none]

[true, true]

PrivateKey with a wrong passphrase is an evaluation error that says so:

import crypto

pair = generate_key_pair(Ed25519)
sealed = pair.private.export_private(OpenSsh, passphrase = "correct horse")
PrivateKey(sealed, OpenSsh, Ed25519, passphrase = "wrong")

execute failure[invalid-argument]: the passphrase does not decrypt the OpenSsh private key
 --> <expression>:5:1
  |
5 | PrivateKey(sealed, OpenSsh, Ed25519, passphrase = "wrong")
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Generating keys
docs.text:
generate_key_pair(algorithm) gives a new KeyPair from the host's cryptographically secure generator, and is effectful. bits sets the size of an Rsa key, 2048 to 8192 and 3072 by default. A generated key differs on every evaluation, so the programs here show what holds of every one:

import crypto

pair = generate_key_pair(X25519)
[pair.public == pair.private.public(),
 pair.public.to_text(Age) | starts_with("age1"),
 str(pair) | starts_with("KeyPair<X25519>(")]

[true, true, true]

An X25519 public key in Age text is an age recipient, age1…, and its private key exported in Age is an age identity, the text the age command line reads with -i.

generate_secret_key(algorithm) gives a new symmetric key: 32 octets for a cipher and for HmacSha256, 64 for HmacSha512. SecretKey(bytes, algorithm) builds one from octets the program already holds. A secret key prints with no thumbprint, since it has no public half:

import crypto

[str(generate_secret_key(Aes256Gcm)), str(SecretKey(Bytes("Jefe"), HmacSha256))]

["SecretKey<Aes256Gcm>(redacted)", "SecretKey<HmacSha256>(redacted)"]

A cipher's key is exactly 32 octets, and a MAC's at least one. Another length is an evaluation error naming it:

import crypto

SecretKey(Bytes("short"), Aes256Gcm)

execute failure[invalid-argument]: a Aes256Gcm key is 32 octets, and this one is 5
 --> <expression>:3:1
  |
3 | SecretKey(Bytes("short"), Aes256Gcm)
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Signatures
docs.text:
A signature is Bytes, detached from what it signs. sign(key) signs a String's UTF-8 octets or a Bytes value with a private key of a signing algorithm. Every scheme signs deterministically: one key and one message give one signature. The Ed25519 test key signs the empty message as RFC 8032 says:

import crypto
import encoding

key = read_private_key(file("examples/crypto/keys/rfc8032-test-1.pem"), Pem, Ed25519)
"" | sign(key) | encode(Hex)

"e5564300c360ac729086e2cc806e828a84877f1eb8e5d974d873e065224901555fb8821590a33bacc61e39701cf9b46bd25bf5f0595bbe24655141438e7a100b"
Algorithm Signature Ed25519 64 octets, R and S P256 64 octets, r and s, as JWS ES256 Rsa the modulus length, PKCS #1 v1.5 over SHA-256, as JWS RS256

verify(signature, key) checks a signature with the public key. A signature of another message, of another key, of the wrong length or malformed gives false, never an error:

import crypto

pair = generate_key_pair(Ed25519)
signature = "ship order 1042" | sign(pair.private)
["ship order 1042".verify(signature, pair.public),
 "ship order 1043".verify(signature, pair.public),
 "ship order 1042".verify(signature[0:63], pair.public)]

[true, false, false]

OpenSSL writes a P-256 signature as ASN.1 DER. p256_signature_from_der converts one to the 64 octets verify reads, and gives none for octets that are not one.

docs.title: Signing a tree
docs.text:
sign_data(key) signs a Data tree over its canonical JSON, the RFC 8785 text chapter 30 fingerprints, and verify_data(signature, key) checks one. Two trees equal under HQL equality have one signature, whatever their key order:

import crypto

pair = generate_key_pair(Ed25519)
a = Data("{\"name\": \"hql\", \"version\": \"0.4.0\"}", Json)
b = Data("{\"version\": \"0.4.0\", \"name\": \"hql\"}", Json)
a.sign_data(pair.private) == b.sign_data(pair.private)

true

A verifier in another language checks the signature with any RFC 8785 implementation. The examples hold two releases, each a manifest and a base64 signature by the test key. The second manifest has its version changed, and its signature fails:

import crypto
import encoding

type Release {
    manifest  : Data
    signature : String
}

public = read_public_key(file("examples/crypto/keys/rfc8032-test-1.pub.pem"), Pem, Ed25519)
releases : Seq<Release> = source(file("examples/crypto/releases.jsonl"))
releases
| map(r => r.manifest.verify_data(r.signature.to_bytes(Base64) | unwrap_or(Bytes("")), public))

[true, false]

A String and a Data tree are signed by different names: sign signs a text's octets, and sign_data a tree's canonical JSON, in which a string is written with its quotes.

docs.title: MACs
docs.text:
A MAC is a tag computed under a shared SecretKey of HmacSha256 or HmacSha512: 32 octets for the first, 64 for the second. mac(key) gives the tag. A webhook's secret is the length its sender chose, and a MAC key takes any length from one octet. RFC 4231's test case 2:

import crypto
import encoding

key = SecretKey(Bytes("Jefe"), HmacSha256)
"what do ya want for nothing?" | mac(key) | encode(Hex)

"5bdcc146bf60754e6a042426089575c75a003f089d2739839dec58b964ec3843"

verify_mac(tag, key) checks a tag, comparing it in time independent of where it first differs. == over two Bytes is not constant-time, and a received tag is checked with verify_mac:

import crypto
import encoding

key = SecretKey(Bytes("Jefe"), HmacSha256)
tag = Bytes("5bdcc146bf60754e6a042426089575c75a003f089d2739839dec58b964ec3843", Hex)
["what do ya want for nothing?".verify_mac(tag, key),
 "what do ya want for something?".verify_mac(tag, key)]

[true, false]

docs.title: Password hashes
docs.text:
A password hash is an Argon2id PHC string: $argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$, then the salt and the hash. hash_password draws a new 16-octet salt on every call, so it is effectful and two hashes of one password differ. verify_password(hash) gives whether a password is the one the hash was made from, under the parameters the hash names:

import crypto

stored = "correct horse battery staple" | hash_password
["correct horse battery staple".verify_password(stored),
 "Tr0ub4dor&3".verify_password(stored),
 stored.starts_with("$argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$")]

[true, false, true]

memory_kib, iterations and parallelism raise the cost. A cost below OWASP's minimum is an evaluation error naming the parameter:

import crypto

"correct horse battery staple" | hash_password(memory_kib = 4096)

execute failure[invalid-argument]: `memory_kib` is 19456 to 1048576, and 4096 is outside: a cost below OWASP's minimum is refused
 --> <expression>:3:34
  |
3 | "correct horse battery staple" | hash_password(memory_kib = 4096)
  |                                  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

verify_password reads Argon2id, Argon2i and Argon2d hashes. A stored hash of another scheme, such as bcrypt's $2b$, is an evaluation error naming the scheme, not a wrong password.

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text:
Design only

This section describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: these programs do not run against the current binary, and names, types and outputs may change before they ship.

Shared-key encryption is authenticated: encrypt(key) under a SecretKey of Aes256Gcm or ChaCha20Poly1305 gives a new 12-octet nonce, the ciphertext and a 16-octet tag, as one Bytes. decrypt(key) gives the plaintext, or none for octets that are not an encryption of anything under that key:

import crypto

key = generate_secret_key(ChaCha20Poly1305)
sealed = "meet at the north gate" | encrypt(key)
[(sealed.decrypt(key) | and_then(to_text)) == some("meet at the north gate"),
 sealed[:-1].decrypt(key) | is_none]

[true, true]

Encryption to a recipient writes an age v1 message to one or more X25519 public keys, and any of their private keys decrypts it. The age command line reads and writes the same octets:

import crypto

pair = generate_key_pair(X25519)
sealed = "J45.909" | encrypt_to([pair.public])
sealed | decrypt_with(pair.private) | and_then(to_text)

"J45.909"

An encrypted endpoint encrypts what a format writes. encrypted_to wraps an endpoint that target writes, and decrypted_with one that source reads; orders.jsonl.age is JSON Lines, encrypted:

import crypto

pair = generate_key_pair(X25519)
orders = [{id: 1, total: 12.50}, {id: 2, total: 7.25}]
orders | target(encrypted_to(file("orders.jsonl.age"), [pair.public]))
source(decrypted_with(file("orders.jsonl.age"), pair.private)) | map(o => o.id)

[1, 2]

docs.title: The key vault
docs.text:
Design only

This section describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: these programs do not run against the current binary, and names, keys, types and outputs may change before they ship.

A key vault is a store of named keys that hql.toml configures, as it configures an endpoint. Its secrets are named by *_env keys and never written:

[keyvault.team]
kind = "file"
path = "keys.age"
passphrase_env = "HQL_TEAM_VAULT_PASSPHRASE"

The module crypto.keyvault, imported with import crypto.keyvault and reached as keyvault, names a key by the vault's id and the key's name. keyvault.key gives a KeyRef, which holds the two names and no key material. A stored private key signs and decrypts inside the vault and is never a value of the program:

import crypto
import crypto.keyvault

signer = keyvault.key("team", "release-2026", Ed25519)
manifest = {name: "hql", version: "0.4.0"}
signature = keyvault.sign_data(manifest, signer)
manifest.verify_data(signature, keyvault.public_key(signer))

true

keyvault.keys lists a vault's keys by name, algorithm and what each one does:

import crypto.keyvault

keyvault.keys("team") | map(k => {name: k.name, algorithm: k.algorithm, decrypts: k.decrypts})

[{algorithm: "X25519", decrypts: true, name: "backup-2026"}, {algorithm: "Ed25519", decrypts: false, name: "release-2026"}]

A vault is a file store encrypted with age, the operating system's keychain, an ssh_agent, or aws_kms. In an ssh_agent or aws_kms vault the private key never enters the hql process. hql keyvault generates, imports, lists and deletes the keys of a store; a program does none of these.

docs.title: 2. Data types
docs.text: Every value in HQL has a type, and the type of every expression is inferred and checked before the program is evaluated. This chapter meets the types values are built from: the scalars Int, Float, Decimal, String, Bool and Bytes, the time types Date, DateTime, Instant and Duration, and Data, the tree JSON and YAML are made of. Each has a page of its own; this one tries them in the REPL first.

docs.title: Trying values in the REPL
docs.text:
hql repl reads one input at a time, evaluates it and prints the value. A binding is kept for the inputs after it, and :type asks for a type without evaluating anything:

$ hql repl
hql 0.5.0. `:help` for commands, `:quit` to leave.
hql> pages = 412
()
hql> pages / 3
137
hql> pages % 3
1
hql> :type pages
Int
hql> title = "Dune"
()
hql> title.upper()
"DUNE"
hql> :type title
String
hql> fmt("{} has {} pages", title, pages)
"Dune has 412 pages"
hql> :quit

412 is an Int, so / divides whole numbers and drops the remainder, and % gives the remainder. "Dune" is a String, and title.upper() calls a function of String on it. fmt writes values into text, one {} each.

The same programs run with hql eval, as every program in this book does:

pages = 412
title = "Dune"
fmt("{} has {} pages", title, pages)

"Dune has 412 pages"

docs.title: Type checking
docs.text:
Each operation says which types it takes. An Int and a String do not add, and the checker rejects the program before it runs:

412 + "pages"

check error[type-mismatch]: addition requires two Int, two Float or two Decimal operands
 --> <expression>:1:7
  |
1 | 412 + "pages"
  |       ^^^^^^^

There is no implicit conversion between types: a function that takes a Decimal does not accept an Int. Arithmetic and comparison take an Int and a Decimal together, and arithmetic on them gives a Decimal; that is a rule of those operators, not a conversion. A conversion is written: str writes a value as text, and float turns an Int into a Float:

412.str()

"412"

hql check prints a program's type without evaluating it:

$ hql check - <<< '412 / 3'
Int

docs.title: The types, one page each
docs.text:
Type What it holds Page Int a whole number, 64 bits Int Float a binary floating-point number, written 2.5f Float Decimal an exact decimal number, written 2.50 Decimal String text String Bool true or false Bool Bytes a sequence of octets Bytes Date, DateTime, Instant, Duration a date, a wall-clock reading, a point in time, a length of time Date and time Data a tree of records, lists and scalars Data Option<T> a T, or nothing Option

Braces write three different things — a set, a Data record and, where one is declared, a map — and sets, Data and maps tells them apart. Lists, sets and maps as collections, and the steps they share, are chapter 3.

docs.title: Bool
docs.text:
A Bool is true or false. Comparisons give one, and and, or and not combine them:

3 < 4 and not (1 > 2)

true

and and or are connectives of the language, so the right side is evaluated only when the left side does not decide the answer.

A Bool is not a number, and compares only with another Bool:

true == 1

check error[type-mismatch]: `Eq` for Bool compares with Bool, not Int
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | true == 1
  | ^^^^^^^^^

A condition must be a Bool. a given condition otherwise b chooses a value by one:

pages = 412
"long" given pages > 300 otherwise "short"

"long"

A Bool is a Scalar but not Orderable: true < false means nothing.

docs.title: Bytes
docs.text:
A Bytes value is a finite sequence of octets: a key, a signature, a digest's raw form, the body of a binary file. A String cannot hold one, since a String is UTF-8 text. Bytes has no literal. Bytes(text) is the UTF-8 encoding of a text, and a value is written as 0x followed by its octets in lowercase hexadecimal, two digits each:

[Bytes("hé"), Bytes("")]

[0x68c3a9, 0x]

The 0x text is how a value is printed by the REPL, str and fmt; it is not a literal a program can write. é is two octets in UTF-8, so size counts three where a String's size counts two characters:

b = Bytes("hé")
[b.size(), "hé".size()]

[3, 2]

docs.title: From hex and base64
docs.text:
Bytes(text, Encoding) reads octets written in an encoding of the module encoding: Hex, Base64, Base64Url or Percent. The module is not in the prelude, so a program writes import encoding:

import encoding
[Bytes("68c3a9", Hex), Bytes("aMOp", Base64)]

[0x68c3a9, 0x68c3a9]

Text that is not valid in the encoding is an evaluation error naming the encoding and the first invalid position, counted from 0:

import encoding
Bytes("68g3", Hex)

execute failure[invalid-argument]: the text is not valid Hex: the first invalid character is at position 2
 --> <expression>:2:1
  |
2 | Bytes("68g3", Hex)
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

to_bytes reads the same text as an Option: the octets where the text is valid, and none where it is not. It is the form for text a program did not write itself:

import encoding
["68c3a9".to_bytes(Hex), "zz".to_bytes(Hex)]

[0x68c3a9, none]

docs.title: Positions and slices
docs.text:
Bytes implements Index<Int> and Slice, through the bytes module's at and slice. b[i] is the octet at i as an Int in 0..255, or none past the end, and a negative position counts from the end. b[a:b] is a Bytes, clamped to the value's size. + on two Bytes is concatenation:

b = Bytes("hé")
[b[0], b[-1], b[3]]

[104, 169, none]

b = Bytes("hé")
[b[0:2], b[1:], b + Bytes("!")]

[0x68c3, 0xc3a9, 0x68c3a921]

The bytes module is in the prelude, like string, and is a receiver module: b.size(), bytes.size(b) and b | size call one function.

docs.title: Back to text
docs.text:
to_text reads the octets as UTF-8, and gives none where they are not valid UTF-8. encode writes them in an encoding, which every octet has:

import encoding
[Bytes("hé").to_text(), Bytes("ff", Hex).to_text()]

["hé", none]

import encoding
b = Bytes("hé")
[b.encode(Hex), b.encode(Base64)]

["68c3a9", "aMOp"]

For every value b and every encoding E, b.encode(E).to_bytes(E) is some(b).

docs.title: Order and equality
docs.text:
Bytes is Orderable. Two values compare octet by octet as unsigned numbers, and a value that is a prefix of another comes first:

import encoding
[Bytes("ff", Hex), Bytes("0000", Hex), Bytes("01", Hex), Bytes("00", Hex)] | sort

[0x00, 0x0000, 0x01, 0xff]

Two values are equal when they hold the same octets, however each was built:

import encoding
Bytes("hé") == Bytes("68c3a9", Hex)

true

docs.title: Bytes in data
docs.text:
Every text format, JSON, JSON Lines, YAML and CSV, writes a Bytes value as its base64 text, padded, in the standard alphabet:

import encoding
{name: "key", body: Bytes("ff00", Hex)}

{
  "body": "/wA=",
  "name": "key"
}

Reading is the other way round only where a type says so. A base64 string read as Data stays a String; a field declared Bytes reads its text as base64, and text that is not base64 fails the read:

type Blob {
    name : String
    body : Bytes
}
Data("{\"name\": \"key\", \"body\": \"aGk=\"}", Json) | Blob

Blob(name = "key", body = 0x6869)

The digest of a Bytes value, and the other text encodings, are in Digests and encodings. The reference states each function of the bytes module.

docs.title: Data: records and lists
docs.text: The values JSON and YAML are made of — records of named fields, lists, and scalar leaves — are one type in HQL, Data. This page does with Data what jq does with JSON: build it, read into it, reshape it, and write it back out.

docs.title: A tree of values
docs.text:
A data literal is written in braces, with a key, a colon and a value per field. Values may be scalars, lists, or other records:

{title: "Dune", author: {name: "Frank Herbert", born: 1920}, tags: ["desert", "spice"]}

{author: {born: 1920, name: "Frank Herbert"}, tags: ["desert", "spice"], title: "Dune"}

A key that is not an identifier is quoted: {"first name": "Ada"}. The record prints with its keys in order, so the same tree always prints the same way.

The colon is what makes braces a record. The empty record is {:}; {} without a colon is the empty set, as {1, 2} is a set of two. So d : Data = {:} holds an empty record, and d : Data = {} is a type error: {} is a Set<Never>, which a Set<Int> binding accepts and a Data one does not.

docs.title: Reading a field
docs.text:
A path reads into the tree, one key per step:

book = {title: "Dune", author: {name: "Frank Herbert", born: 1920}}
book.author.name

"Frank Herbert"

A key the tree does not have is not an error. The key belonged to whoever wrote the record, so nothing promised it, and reading it gives absence:

book = {title: "Dune"}
book.year

none

The type says so. Reading a key of a Data record gives an Option<Data>: a some holding a tree, or none. HQL has no null; a value that may be missing is an Option, and the program says what absence means where it matters.

year = {title: "Dune"}.year
match year {
    some(_) => "dated",
    none => "undated",
}

"undated"

docs.title: Asking what a leaf is
docs.text:
A leaf of a tree could be any scalar; the record did not say. Equality compares through that, so book.title == "Dune" is an ordinary question:

{title: "Dune"}.title == "Dune"

true

Arithmetic and ordering need to know the type. is(T) asks whether a value is a T, and a match arm with a type, some(Int n), both tests and reads it:

pages = {title: "Dune", pages: 412}.pages
match pages {
    some(Int n) => n * 2,
    _ => 0,
}

824

docs.title: Lists of records
docs.text:
A list of records is a List<Data>. map applies a function to every element, and x => x.title is a function written in place, a lambda:

books = [{title: "Dune", pages: 412}, {title: "The Hobbit", pages: 310}, {title: "Leaves of Grass"}]
books | map(b => b.title)

["Dune", "The Hobbit", "Leaves of Grass"]

| is a pipe: the value on its left is the input of the step on its right. filter keeps the elements a predicate accepts:

books = [{title: "Dune", pages: 412}, {title: "The Hobbit", pages: 310}, {title: "Leaves of Grass"}]
books
| filter(b => match b.pages { some(Int n) => n > 300, _ => false })
| map(b => b.title)

["Dune", "The Hobbit"]

To add up the page counts, the leaves become numbers first. somes drops the absent ones, of_type(Int) keeps the leaves that are integers and reads each as the Int it holds, and sum adds them:

books = [{title: "Dune", pages: 412}, {title: "The Hobbit", pages: 310}, {title: "Leaves of Grass"}]
books
| map(b => b.pages)
| somes
| of_type(Int)
| sum

722

Each step is checked against the type the step before it produced. After of_type(Int) the list is a list of Int, which is what sum takes; without it the checker rejects sum over trees, before anything runs.

docs.title: Reshaping
docs.text:
A data literal can hold any expression, so map builds a new record from each old one:

books = [{title: "Dune", author: "Frank Herbert"}, {title: "Emma", author: "Jane Austen"}]
books | map(b => {book: b.title, by: b.author})

[{book: "Dune", by: "Frank Herbert"}, {book: "Emma", by: "Jane Austen"}]

merge combines two records. Every key of either is kept, and a key in both takes the value from the right:

merge({title: "Dune", pages: 412}, {pages: 896, edition: "illustrated"})

{edition: "illustrated", pages: 896, title: "Dune"}

docs.title: Writing it back out
docs.text:
A value is written in a presentation format by a step named for it. The result is text of that format — Json, Yaml, Csv, Markdown — and hql writes it as it is:

[{title: "Dune", pages: 412}, {title: "The Hobbit", pages: 310}] | json

[
  {
    "pages": 412,
    "title": "Dune"
  },
  {
    "pages": 310,
    "title": "The Hobbit"
  }
]

{title: "Dune", pages: 412, tags: ["desert", "spice"]} | yaml

pages: 412
tags:
- desert
- spice
title: Dune

[{title: "Dune", pages: 412}, {title: "The Hobbit", pages: 310}] | csv

pages,title
412,Dune
310,The Hobbit

A list of records becomes a table when it is built into one. Table takes the records as rows and columns names their fields in the order the table writes them; each format then writes the table in its own syntax, here a pipe table:

[{title: "Dune", pages: 412}, {title: "The Hobbit", pages: 310}]
| Table(columns = ["title", "pages"])
| markdown

| title      | pages |
| ---------- | ----- |
| Dune       | 412   |
| The Hobbit | 310   |

Chapter 8 is about formats in full.

A program writes its data as literals, reads it from a vault's documents, as chapter 21 does, or reads a JSON, YAML or CSV file with source, as chapter 9 does.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: How Data differs from a set and from a map, all three written in braces, is the next page. A Data list is one kind of collection. Chapter 3 meets the others — lists, sets and maps of typed values — and the steps that work on all of them.

docs.title: Decimal
docs.text:
A Decimal is an exact decimal number: an integer significand of up to 512 bits, about 154 digits, and a scale, the number of digits after the point, from 0 to 154. A number written with a decimal point is a Decimal, so arithmetic on it loses nothing to binary rounding:

0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3

true

The scale is kept for display. A sum or a difference has the larger scale of its operands, and a product the sum of their scales. Equality and order are by value, so 1.50 == 1.5 is true:

[1.50, 1.50 + 1.25, 1.50 * 1.5]

[1.50, 2.75, 2.250]

A literal keeps every digit it is written with, however many there are:

123456789012345678901234567890.123456789 + 0.000000001

123456789012345678901234567890.123456790

docs.title: Division and rounding
docs.text:
/ is exact where the quotient terminates, and otherwise rounded half to even to 100 significant digits. Division by zero is an evaluation error, as it is for an Int. round(x, places) rounds half to even to places digits after the point, and round(x) to a whole number:

[10 / 4.0, round(2 / 3.0, 4), round(2.345, 2), round(2.355, 2), round(2.5)]

[2.5, 0.6667, 2.34, 2.36, 2]

docs.title: Int, Float and Decimal
docs.text:
Arithmetic and comparison take an Int and a Decimal together. Arithmetic gives a Decimal, computed as if the Int were a Decimal of scale 0:

[12.50 * 3, 7 - 0.25]

[37.50, 6.75]

A Float does not mix with a Decimal: a binary float carries no exact decimal value, so the program says which conversion it means. decimal(x) reads an Int, or a Float by its shortest digits, as a Decimal; float(d) gives the nearest Float and int(d) the integer part:

1.5 + 2.0f

check error[type-mismatch]: a Decimal and a Float do not mix: write `decimal(x)` to read the Float as a Decimal, or `float(d)` to read the Decimal as a Float
 --> <expression>:1:7
  |
1 | 1.5 + 2.0f
  |       ^^^^

[decimal(0.1f) + 1.5, "12.50".to_decimal().unwrap_or(0.0)]

[1.6, 12.50]

JSON, YAML and CSV carry a Decimal without loss: a number read as a Decimal field keeps the digits it is written with, and a Decimal is written as a number with its digits and scale.

docs.title: Float
docs.text:
A Float is a 64-bit binary floating-point number, written with the suffix f: 0.5f, 6.02e23f, 2f. A number with a decimal point and no suffix is a Decimal. Arithmetic on two Float operands gives a Float:

7.0f / 2.0f

3.5

A binary fraction cannot hold most decimal fractions exactly, so a sum can be a little off:

0.1f + 0.2f

0.30000000000000004

That is why a Float is the wrong type for money; a Decimal holds an amount exactly as it is written.

An Int and a Float do not mix: 1 + 2.0f is a type error, and so is a Decimal beside a Float. float and int convert, the second truncating:

[1.float() + 2.0f, 3.9f.int().float()]

[3.0, 3.0]

docs.title: Int
docs.text:
An Int is a whole number: a signed 64-bit integer. Arithmetic on two Int operands gives an Int.

2 + 3 * 4

14

* and / bind tighter than + and -. Division truncates towards zero, and % is the remainder:

[7 / 2, -7 / 2, 7 % 3]

[3, -3, 1]

An Int that leaves the 64-bit range is an error, never a wrapped value:

9223372036854775807 + 1

execute failure[numeric-overflow]: numeric overflow
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | 9223372036854775807 + 1
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The math module adds what operators do not cover:

[2.pow(10), (-5).abs(), (-5).sign()]

[1024, 5, -1]

An Int is Orderable, so <, >, min, max and sort work on it, and it compares only with another Int. float turns it into a Float, and str into a String.

docs.title: Option: a value that may be missing
docs.text:
The reading club gives a book its rating when the book is done. A book still being read has no rating yet, so the club's notes have a field some records carry and others do not:

books = [
    {title: "Frankenstein", status: "done", rating: 5},
    {title: "Dune", status: "reading"},
    {title: "A Room of One's Own", status: "done", rating: 4},
]
books | map(b => b.rating)

[5, none, 4]

HQL has no null. A value that may be missing is an Option<T>: some(x), which holds an x, or none, which holds nothing. A present value prints as the value it holds, and an absent one as none.

docs.title: The type says so
docs.text:
Reading a field of a Data record gives an Option<Data>, whichever record it reads, because the type is known before any record is:

{title: "Dune"}.rating

Option<Data>

An Option is not the value it may hold. Adding to a rating that may be missing is a type error, reported before the program runs:

rating = {title: "Frankenstein", rating: 5}.rating
rating + 1

check error[type-mismatch]: addition requires two Int, two Float or two Decimal operands, or two values of a type implementing `Add`, not Option<Data>
 --> <expression>:2:1
  |
2 | rating + 1
  | ^^^^^^

The program says what a missing rating means, and the ways to say it follow.

docs.title: A value in place of none
docs.text:
unwrap_or(default) gives the value held, or default where there is none:

books | map(b => b.rating.unwrap_or(0))

[5, 0, 4]

There is no unwrap without a default. Every way out of an Option states what absence means.

docs.title: One answer for each case
docs.text:
match takes an Option apart. The some(r) arm binds the value held to r, the none arm covers the rest, and the checker rejects a match that leaves a case uncovered:

books | map(b => {
    book: b.title,
    verdict: match b.rating {
        some(r) => fmt("{} stars", r),
        none => "not rated yet",
    },
})

[{book: "Frankenstein", verdict: "5 stars"}, {book: "Dune", verdict: "not rated yet"}, {book: "A Room of One's Own", verdict: "4 stars"}]

is_some and is_none ask the question as a Bool, for a filter or a given:

books | filter(b => b.rating.is_none()) | map(b => b.title)

["Dune"]

docs.title: Only the values that are there
docs.text:
somes keeps the present values of a collection of options and drops the absent ones. The club's ratings so far are the ratings of the books it has finished:

books | map(b => b.rating) | somes

[5, 4]

docs.title: Comparing with a missing value
docs.text:
Equality compares through an Option: some(5) == 5 is true, and none is equal to no value. A book with no rating is not a five-star book:

books | filter(b => b.rating == 5) | map(b => b.title)

["Frankenstein"]

docs.title: Options from other places
docs.text:
A record field is one source of options; a step that may have no answer is another. to_int reads a String as an Int, and gives none where the text is not a number:

["412", "four", "310"] | map(s => s.to_int())

[412, none, 310]

A step applied to an Option is applied to the value held. map gives the result in a some, or none where there was nothing to apply it to; filter keeps a value that passes a test; and alternative gives a second option where the first is none:

[
    "412".to_int().map(n => n / 2),
    "four".to_int().map(n => n / 2),
    "1965".to_int().filter(y => y > 1900),
    "four".to_int().alternative("0".to_int()),
]

[206, none, 1965, 0]

max over an empty list, a position past the end of a string and a link to a card nobody has written are each an Option too, and each is handled the same way.

A missing value is not a failure. A computation that can fail gives a Result, ok or err, and chapter 10 meets it.

docs.title: Sets, Data and maps
docs.text:
Three kinds of value are written in braces, or hold keys and values, and they are easy to mix up. They are different types with different jobs:

Type What it is Written Set<T> distinct values of one type, with no positions {1, 2, 3} Data a tree of named fields of any types, the shape of JSON {title: "Dune", pages: 412} Map<K, V> keys of one type, each to a value of one type Map(["dune"], [412])

docs.title: The colon tells braces apart
docs.text:
Braces holding values are a set; braces holding key: value entries are Data. The colon is the only thing that tells them apart, and the empty forms keep it: {} is the empty set and {:} the empty Data.

{3, 1, 3, 2}

{3, 1, 2}

{title: "Dune", pages: 412}

{pages: 412, title: "Dune"}

{}

{}

{:}

{:}

A set keeps each value once. A Data record prints its keys in order, so the same tree always prints the same way.

{} has a definite meaning, the empty set, so it is not an empty record:

d : Data = {}
d

check error[type-mismatch]: `d` is declared Data but its value is Set<Never>
 --> <expression>:1:12
  |
1 | d : Data = {}
  |            ^^

{} is a Set<Never>: a set with no elements, and so no element type yet. A declared set type gives it one:

seen : Set<Int> = {}
seen | size

0

docs.title: Data is not a map
docs.text:
Data is the type of values whose shape is not known to the program: what a JSON or YAML document decodes to. A record's fields may hold different types, a number beside a text beside a list, and nesting goes as deep as the document does. It is not a hash map, and not a Map<String, Any>.

A Map<K, V> is a typed mapping: every key is a K and every value a V. The constructor pairs a list of keys with a list of values:

Map(["dune", "emma"], [412, 474])

Map {"dune": 412, "emma": 474}

Map(["dune", "emma"], [412, 474]).get("dune")

412

So the three answer different needs: a set, which values; a map, which value for each key, all of one type; Data, whatever structure arrived.

docs.title: {:} is Data, or a declared map
docs.text:
{:} has no type of its own. Where nothing says otherwise it is the empty Data; where a map type is declared for it, it is that empty map:

Written Type Value {:} with nothing around it Data the empty Data record, printed {:} d : Data = {:} Data the same m : Map<String, Int> = {:} Map<String, Int> an empty map, equal to Map<String, Int>([], []) m : SortedMap<String, Int> = {:}, or OrderedMap that map type an empty map of that kind f({:}) where f takes a Map<String, Int> Map<String, Int> an empty map 
counts : Map<String, Int> = {:}
counts == Map<String, Int>([], [])

true

Data is the default, and a declared Map, OrderedMap or SortedMap turns it into that empty map. An empty literal carries no information of its own, so the type around it decides: HQL infers a type while the literal says enough, and asks for an explicit one where it does not.

This holds for the empty literal only. A non-empty keyed literal is always Data, and binding it to a declared map type is a type error:

m : Map<String, Int> = {a: 1}
m

check error[type-mismatch]: `m` is declared Map<String, Int> but its value is Data
 --> <expression>:1:24
  |
1 | m : Map<String, Int> = {a: 1}
  |                        ^^^^^^

A non-empty map is built with the constructor, Map(["a"], [1]).

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 3 uses lists, sets and maps as collections, and the steps they share.

docs.title: String
docs.text:
A String is text, written in double quotes. Its functions are called on it with a dot:

"Ada Lovelace".upper()

"ADA LOVELACE"

Its size counts characters, not bytes:

"héllo".size()

5

A position reads one character. It may be past the end, so it gives an Option<String>, printed as the character when it is present:

"Dune"[0]

"D"

+ on two strings is concatenation. Both operands are strings: "a" + 1 is a type error. fmt writes values of any type into a template, one {} each, and join puts a list of strings together with a separator:

["Dune" + " (1965)", fmt("{} has {} pages", "Dune", 412), ["a", "b", "c"].join(", ")]

["Dune (1965)", "Dune has 412 pages", "a, b, c"]

split, trim, replace_all, starts_with, contains and the rest are in the string module, visible in every program:

"  Frankenstein  ".trim().starts_with("Frank")

true

A String is Orderable, in the order of its characters, so a list of them sorts. Any value becomes text with str.

docs.title: Date, DateTime, Instant and Duration
docs.text:
HQL has four time types. None of them has a literal: a value is built by the type's constructor from ISO 8601 text, the form SQL and JSON write it in.

Type What it holds Written as Date a calendar date 2026-10-24 DateTime a date and a time of day, with no zone 2026-10-24T09:30:00 Instant a point on the UTC timeline, to the nanosecond 2026-10-24T07:30:00Z Duration a signed length of time, to the nanosecond PT1H30M 
[Date("2026-10-24"), DateTime("2026-10-24T09:30:00"), Instant("2026-10-24T09:30:00+02:00"), Duration("PT1H30M")]

[2026-10-24, 2026-10-24T09:30:00, 2026-10-24T07:30:00Z, PT1H30M]

An Instant is read with its offset or Z and written in UTC, so 09:30+02:00 is 07:30Z. A DateTime names a wall-clock reading and carries no offset; it becomes an Instant only through a zone. A Duration counts days as 24 hours and has no months or years, whose length depends on the date they start from.

A constructor also takes named parts: Date(year =, month =, day =), DateTime(date, hour =, minute =), Instant(unix_seconds =) and Duration(hours =, minutes =, ...). Text that does not parse, or a part out of range, is an evaluation error naming it:

Date(year = 2026, month = 2, day = 30)

execute failure[invalid-argument]: year 2026, month 2, day 30 is not a date
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | Date(year = 2026, month = 2, day = 30)
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Order and equality
docs.text:
Each time type is Orderable: ==, <, sort, min and max compare two dates, two date-times or two instants by time, and two durations by length. Two instants written with different offsets are equal when they name one point:

[Date("2026-10-24"), Date("2025-12-31"), Date("2026-01-01")] | sort

[2025-12-31, 2026-01-01, 2026-10-24]

+ and - take two Durations, and no other time type. An instant or a date moves by a named operation of the time module:

Duration("PT1H") + Duration(minutes = 30) > Duration("PT1H15M")

true

abs, which the prelude's math module declares over numbers, also takes a Duration and gives its length without its sign, so the gap between two times reads the same whichever is subtracted from which:

[abs(Duration("PT1H") - Duration("PT90M")), Duration("PT2H").abs()]

[PT30M, PT2H]

docs.title: The time module
docs.text: Every operation over a time value is in the module time, which is not in the prelude: a program writes import time.

docs.title: Parts and calendar arithmetic
docs.text:
year, month, day, weekday (Monday is 1) and iso_week read a date's parts, and hour, minute and second a date-time's:

import time
d = Date("2026-10-24")
[d.year(), d.month(), d.day(), d.weekday(), d.iso_week()]

[2026, 10, 24, 6, 43]

add_days, add_months and add_years move a date by calendar units. A month added to January 31 lands on the last day of February. truncate gives the start of the Week, Month, Quarter or Year containing a date, the key a grouping by period uses:

import time
[Date("2026-01-31").add_months(1), Date("2026-10-24").add_days(10), Date("2026-11-12").truncate(Month)]

[2026-02-28, 2026-11-03, 2026-11-01]

days_since counts the days between two dates, since gives the Duration between two instants, and plus and minus move an instant by one:

import time
Instant("2026-10-24T07:30:00Z").since(Instant("2026-10-23T22:00:00Z"))

PT9H30M

docs.title: Zones
docs.text:
Zone(name) names a zone: an IANA name such as "Europe/Berlin", "UTC", or a fixed offset "+05:30". reading.in_zone(zone) gives the instant a wall-clock reading names there, and instant.at(zone) the reading an instant has there:

import time
berlin = Zone("Europe/Berlin")
meeting = DateTime("2026-11-02T10:00:00").in_zone(berlin)
[str(meeting), str(meeting.at(Zone("America/New_York")))]

["2026-11-02T09:00:00Z", "2026-11-02T04:00:00"]

When clocks move forward, a reading inside the skipped hour moves forward by the gap; when they move back, a reading that happens twice is the earlier instant. On 2026-03-29 Berlin skips 02:00 to 03:00, and on 2026-10-25 it repeats 02:00 to 03:00:

import time
[DateTime("2026-03-29T02:30:00").in_zone(Zone("Europe/Berlin")), DateTime("2026-10-25T02:30:00").in_zone(Zone("Europe/Berlin"))]

[2026-03-29T01:30:00Z, 2026-10-25T00:30:00Z]

A zone's rules come from a time-zone database: the host's where it has one, else the one compiled into hql. A reading in the future can move when that database changes its rules, so hql --version names the database on its second line: system for the host's, or the bundled database's release, 2026e, bundled:

$ hql --version
hql 0.6.0
time-zone database: system

docs.title: Text in other forms
docs.text:
fmt(pattern) writes a value through a strftime pattern, and parse_date, parse_datetime and parse_instant read text through one. The directives are %Y %m %d %H %M %S %f %z %Z %j %a %A %b %B %p %%:

import time
[Date("2026-10-24").fmt("%A, %d %B %Y"), str("24.10.2026".parse_date("%d.%m.%Y"))]

["Saturday, 24 October 2026", "2026-10-24"]

to_date, to_datetime, to_instant and to_duration read ISO 8601 text as an Option: the value where the text is one, and none where it is not. A parse function gives none the same way:

import time
["2026-10-24".to_date(), "24 Oct".to_date()]

[2026-10-24, none]

docs.title: The evaluation clock
docs.text:
now() gives the evaluation instant, today() the date it falls on in the evaluation zone, and local_zone() that zone. Each is read once per evaluation, so two calls in one program agree. --now and --zone fix them, which makes a program that reads the clock repeatable:

import time
[str(now()), str(today()), local_zone().name]

["2026-10-24T23:30:00Z", "2026-10-25", "Europe/Berlin"]

Without --zone, the zone is the one TZ names, else the host's.

docs.title: Time in data
docs.text:
Every format writes a time value as its ISO 8601 text, a JSON string:

{on: Date("2026-10-24"), took: Duration("PT1H30M")}

{
  "on": "2026-10-24",
  "took": "PT1H30M"
}

Reading is the other way round only where a type says so. A JSON or YAML string that looks like a date stays a String; a field declared Date, DateTime, Instant or Duration reads its text as one, and text that is not one fails the read:

type Event {
    name : String
    on   : Date
}
Data("{\"name\": \"launch\", \"on\": \"2026-10-24\"}", Json) | Event

Event(name = "launch", on = 2026-10-24)

SQL tables read the same way. A PostgreSQL DATE, TIMESTAMP and TIMESTAMPTZ column reads as a Date, a DateTime and an Instant, and Spark's DATE, TIMESTAMP_NTZ and TIMESTAMP likewise; a field of a time type written to SQLite, or to any text column, is its ISO 8601 text.

docs.title: 4. Functions
docs.text: A function is a value of a function type. It can be bound to a name, passed to a step, returned from another function, and written once for every type it works on. This page meets lambdas and function types; the pages after it declare functions with fn.

docs.title: Lambdas and their types
docs.text:
n => n * 2 is a lambda. Written as an argument, it takes its parameter's type from the step it is passed to. Written on its own, it states the type:

double = (n: Int) => n * 2
[412, 280] | map(double)

[824, 560]

A function's type is written with an arrow: Int -> Int, (Int, Int) -> Int.

double = (n: Int) => n * 2
double

Int -> Int

A lambda's body is one expression. A function whose value takes several steps is declared with fn, whose body may be a block of them.

docs.title: Calling a function
docs.text:
f(x) calls a function. Piping into one calls it too: x | f is f(x), and x | f(y) is f(x, y), the piped value filling the first parameter.

double = (n: Int) => n * 2
280 | double

560

docs.title: The pages of this chapter
docs.text: Page What it covers Declaring a function fn, typed parameters and a result, recursion, functions taken and returned, variadic parameters Function bodies the two body forms, = expr and the block { … }, and the rules a block follows Generic functions type parameters, and the bounds a call is checked against Aliases and holes := names a pipeline fragment, and _ leaves an argument open

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: A program's functions sit beside its expressions. Chapter 5 puts functions into modules of their own: files that a program imports, with public and private declarations.

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text:
Most small functions are a pipeline fragment with a name. := defines an alias, and the checker writes its type: the input is the most general one the fragment accepts, and each parameter takes the type of the step argument it fills.

top(n) := sort | take(n)
[412, 280, 310, 145] | top(2)

[145, 280]

hql check prints the signature it wrote:

top(n) := sort | take(n)
1

top : (Collection<T>, Int) -> List<T> where T : Orderable
Int

docs.title: Holes
docs.text:
A call with _ for an argument is a function of the arguments left open — a partial application:

fn add(a: Int, b: Int) : Int = a + b
[1, 2, 3] | map(add(10, _))

[11, 12, 13]

A hole is a whole argument. _ + 1 is not a hole, and a lambda, n => n + 1, writes that function.

docs.title: Function bodies
docs.text:
A function's body takes one of two forms: an expression after =, or a block in braces, written without =. The two forms are equally general: any function may take either, at any result type, and both declare the same function.

fn doubled_sum(xs: List<Int>) : Int = xs | map(x => x * 2) | sum

fn doubled_sum_block(xs: List<Int>) : Int {
    xs
    | map(x => x * 2)
    | sum
}

[doubled_sum([1, 2, 3]), doubled_sum_block([1, 2, 3])]

[12, 12]

A pipeline is an expression, so = xs | f | g binds the whole pipeline. In a block, a pipeline continues over several lines, each opening with |. A body longer than one line is written as a block.

docs.title: The value block
docs.text:
A value block is zero or more bindings, name = expr, one per line, followed by one final expression. The final expression is the function's value and has the declared result type:

fn label(pages: Int) : String {
    days = (pages + 39) / 40
    kind = "short" given pages < 200 otherwise "long"
    fmt("{} ({} days)", kind, days)
}

[145, 412] | map(label)

["short (4 days)", "long (11 days)"]

Each binding names one step of the computation. The steps may call other functions, and the final line combines them:

fn area(width: Float, height: Float) : Float {
    w = width
    h = height
    w * h
}

fn triangle(base: Float, height: Float) : Float {
    whole = area(base, height)
    whole / 2.0f
}

[area(2.0f, 3.0f), triangle(5.0f, 5.0f)]

[6.0, 12.5]

A value block takes any result type. A block returning Seq<Int> without yield is a value block, and its last line is the sequence it returns:

fn even_squares(xs: List<Int>) : Seq<Int> {
    evens = xs | filter(x => x % 2 == 0)
    evens | map(x => x * x)
}

List(even_squares([1, 2, 3, 4]))

[4, 16]

docs.title: A block's scope
docs.text:
A binding is in scope from the line after it to the end of its block, and nowhere else. A binding inside a block shadows a name outside it without changing that name. A lambda on the final line captures the block's bindings, and takes its parameter type from the declared result:

k = 100

fn adder(n: Int) : Int -> Int {
    k = n * 10
    x => x + k
}

add = adder(2)
[add(1), add(5), k]

[21, 25, 100]

A block's bindings are not visible after the function:

fn area(w: Float, h: Float) : Float {
    a = w * h
    a
}
a

check error[unknown-name]: `a` is not bound
 --> <expression>:5:1
  |
5 | a
  | ^
  = help: did you mean `at`?

docs.title: The iterating block
docs.text:
A block containing yield is an iterating block. It holds bindings, yield expr and for name in collection { … }, one per line, and produces its values in the order each yield is reached. Its result type is Seq<T>, which ends, or Stream<T>, which need not, and each yielded value is a T:

fn countdown(from: Int) : Seq<Int> {
    for n in range(0, from) {
        yield from - n
    }
}

List(countdown(3))

[3, 2, 1]

Chapter 7 is about iterating functions and the streams they produce.

docs.title: What a block may not be
docs.text:
A block ends either in a final expression or in yields, never in both and never in neither. The parser rejects each of these as a syntax failure.

A block of bindings alone has no value:

fn one() : Int {
    x = 1
}

one()

parse failure[unexpected-token]: a block ends in a value or yields; this one holds only bindings
 --> <expression>:1:16
  |
1 | fn one() : Int {
  |                ^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A block that yields holds no expression on a line of its own:

fn numbers() : Seq<Int> {
    yield 1
    2
}

List(numbers())

parse failure[unexpected-token]: a block that yields holds no expression on a line of its own
 --> <expression>:3:5
  |
3 |     2
  |     ^

for belongs to an iterating block:

fn total(xs: List<Int>) : Int {
    for x in xs {
        y = x
    }
    0
}

total([1, 2])

parse failure[unexpected-token]: `for` belongs to an iterating block; a value block is bindings and a final expression
 --> <expression>:2:5
  |
2 |     for x in xs {
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

= { begins a record or set literal, never a block, so a binding inside it does not parse:

fn one() : Int = {
    x = 1
    x
}

one()

parse failure[unexpected-token]: expected `}` after collection elements, found `=`
 --> <expression>:2:7
  |
2 |     x = 1
  |       ^

docs.title: Wherever a function is declared
docs.text:
A function has one shape wherever it is declared, and its body takes either form in each place: at the top level of a program, in a module (chapter 5), as a receiver function taking self (receiver modules), and as a trait's default body or an implementation's function (traits).

A lambda's body stays one expression; a function that needs a block is declared with fn.

docs.title: Declaring a function
docs.text:
fn declares a named function: a name, typed parameters, a result type and a body. fn days(pages: Int, per_day: Int) : Int gives days the type (Int, Int) -> Int.

fn days(pages: Int, per_day: Int) : Int = (pages + per_day - 1) / per_day
[days(412, 40), days(280, 40)]

[11, 7]

Every parameter has a type and the result type is written. Each call is checked against them before the program runs:

fn days(pages: Int, per_day: Int) : Int = (pages + per_day - 1) / per_day
days("412", 40)

check error[type-mismatch]: this argument is String, and parameter `pages` takes Int
 --> <expression>:2:6
  |
2 | days("412", 40)
  |      ^^^^^

The body after = is one expression. A body may also be a block of named steps, in braces; Function bodies covers both forms.

docs.title: A function by its name
docs.text:
Naming a declared function where a function is expected passes it as a value, xs | map(f). Its name is bound before its body is checked, so it may call itself:

fn factorial(n: Int) : Int = 1 given n <= 1 otherwise n * factorial(n - 1)
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5] | map(factorial)

[1, 2, 6, 24, 120]

docs.title: Functions taken and returned
docs.text:
A parameter may have a function type, and so may the result. A returned function keeps the values it captured:

fn adder(k: Int) : Int -> Int = n => n + k
fn twice(f: Int -> Int, x: Int) : Int = f(f(x))
twice(adder(3), 30)

36

docs.title: Every argument is passed
docs.text: A function with a body takes every argument it declares: its parameters have no default values. Write fn per_week(per_day: Int = 40) : Int = per_day * 7 and hql refuses the = 40. A default belongs to a declaration whose body the binary provides, as some standard library functions have: limit: Int = 0. Where a value is usually the same, bind it and pass it.

docs.title: Variadic parameters
docs.text:
A last parameter written ...T collects any number of trailing arguments into a list:

fn total(xs: ...Int) : Int = xs | sum
[total(), total(1, 2), total(1, 2, 3, 4)]

[0, 3, 10]

docs.title: A result that may be missing
docs.text:
Option<T> is the result type of a function whose value may be absent. some(x) and none build one, match takes one apart, and somes keeps the present values of a collection:

fn rating_of(r: Int) : Option<Int> = some(r) given r > 0 otherwise none
[5, 0, 4] | map(rating_of) | somes

[5, 4]

Option has the rest of Option's operations.

docs.title: Generic functions
docs.text:
A function written once for every type names a type parameter, one capital letter in angle brackets after its name. Each call fills it from its arguments:

fn first<T>(xs: List<T>) : Option<T> = xs | reduce((a, b) => a)
first(["Dune", "Emma"])

"Dune"

The same function over a list of numbers gives an Option<Int>:

fn first<T>(xs: List<T>) : Option<T> = xs | reduce((a, b) => a)
first([412, 280])

Option<Int>

docs.title: Bounds
docs.text:
Inside the body T is a type of its own: the body may rely only on what the parameter promises. A bound, T : Orderable, promises an order, so the body may sort or find a minimum, and each call is checked against the bound:

fn shortest<T : Orderable>(xs: List<T>) : Option<T> = xs | min
shortest([412, 280, 310])

280

fn shortest<T : Orderable>(xs: List<T>) : Option<T> = xs | min
shortest([{1}, {2}])

check error[type-mismatch]: `shortest` needs T : Orderable, and T is Set<Int> here
 --> <expression>:2:1
  |
2 | shortest([{1}, {2}])
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A bound is a type or a trait. Traits declares traits of a program's own and bounds by them.

docs.title: 5. Modules
docs.text: A module is a named unit of declarations — functions, types, traits and bindings — kept in a file of its own. A program reaches a module's declarations by importing it. This page writes a module and imports it; the pages after it cover receiver modules, visibility, and how a name resolves.

docs.title: A module is a file under a module root
docs.text:
A workspace module is an HQL file under a module root, named by its position under the root: lib/club/reading.hql is the module club.reading, and lib/club/mod.hql would be club. The roots come from hql.toml:

[modules]
roots = ["lib"]

or from --modules lib on the command line. The tutorial vault configures lib/ as its root, and keeps the book's modules there. Roots outside every workspace come from the user's ~/.hql/modules/, from [modules] roots in ~/.hql/config.toml, and from $HQL_PATH; the execution context lists them all. A module provided under two roots is an error, whichever layers the roots come from.

Every module file opens with its name, which is checked against the file's place under its root. This is lib/club/reading.hql:

/// Reading plans: how long a book takes at a number of pages a day.
module club.reading

private fn rounded_up(n: Int, d: Int) : Int = (n + d - 1) / d

/// Days to read `pages` at `per_day` pages a day; a part day counts as one.
fn days(pages: Int, per_day: Int) : Int = rounded_up(pages, per_day)

/// Days to read every book of `shelf`, one after another.
fn days_for_all(shelf: List<Int>, per_day: Int) : Int {
    each = shelf | map(pages => days(pages, per_day))
    each | sum
}

A /// line is a doc string: it documents the declaration after it, and hql help club.reading prints it. private keeps rounded_up inside the module, which visibility covers.

docs.title: Importing a module
docs.text:
import club.reading makes the module visible under its last segment, reading, and its functions are called through that name:

import club.reading

[reading.days(412, 40), reading.days(280, 40), reading.days_for_all([412, 280, 310], 40)]

[11, 7, 26]

import a.b as c makes it visible under c instead:

import club.reading as plan

plan.days(412, 40)

11

A module's function is a value like any other, and takes holes:

import club.reading

[412, 280] | map(reading.days(_, 40))

[11, 7]

Imports sit at the head of a source unit, before its declarations and expressions. Two imports may not share a local name:

import club.reading
import club.titles as reading
1

check error[unknown-name]: `reading` already names the module `club.reading` here; import `club.titles` under another name with `as`
 --> <expression>:2:1
  |
2 | import club.titles as reading
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A module that is not imported is not visible, however it is spelled:

reading.days(412, 40)

check error[unknown-name]: `reading` is not bound
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | reading.days(412, 40)
  | ^^^^^^^

docs.title: The standard modules
docs.text:
The standard library is modules of the same kind. The prelude is the list of modules every program imports without writing it: string, seq, math, option and result, among others. "a,b".split(",") calls the prelude's string.split. Other standard modules are imported by name:

import regex

regex.split("a1b22c", "[0-9]+")

["a", "b", "c"]

The reference has a page per standard module.

docs.title: The pages of this chapter
docs.text: Page What it covers Receiver modules module m for T, functions taking self, and value.f() calls Visibility public and private declarations, and a module's contract How names resolve import units, a unit's own names, ambiguity, and modules as closures

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: With functions and modules in hand, chapter 6 asks the questions SQL asks: where, order by, group by, and the aggregates.

docs.title: How names resolve
docs.text: Every module is an import unit: one scope in which its imports take effect and its names resolve. A program is an import unit of its own, the program module. An import makes a module visible in the importing unit and nowhere else.

docs.title: Imports are per unit
docs.text: A module's imports are its own. A module that imports math sees math, and a program that imports the module does not see math through it. The prelude, too, is the implicit import list of each unit separately.

docs.title: A unit's own names win
docs.text:
A declaration the unit writes itself wins over an imported declaration of the same name, in every spelling: an unqualified call, a pipeline step and a receiver call. The imported one stays reachable through its module. This program declares its own lower:

fn lower(s: String) : String = "mine"
[lower("ABC"), "ABC" | lower, string.lower("ABC")]

["mine", "mine", "abc"]

The program's lower takes no self, so the receiver spelling reaches nothing, and the prelude's lower is not reached in its place:

fn lower(s: String) : String = "mine"
"ABC".lower()

check error[unknown-name]: `lower` is this unit's own function, which takes no `self`, so `value.lower(…)` does not reach it and no import's `lower` over String is reached in its place; write `lower(value, …)`, or qualify the import's
 --> <expression>:2:1
  |
2 | "ABC".lower()
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A unit owns its own names, so a module that later gains a declaration of the same name cannot take one away from it. Which declaration wins does not depend on the order the declarations are written in.

docs.title: Two imports, one name
docs.text: Two imported declarations of one name, neither the unit's own, are an ambiguity, and the call naming them is a name error. Qualifying the call resolves it, titles.initials(s) or string.split(s, ","); the order of the imports never decides.

docs.title: A module is a closure
docs.text:
A free name in a module resolves through the module's own declarations and its own imports, and through nothing else. A module never sees the program module, and no module imports it. The bindings the host seeds into a program — vault, cards, stdin, stdout and the rest — are not bound in a module. What a module needs from a program reaches it as a parameter, a function argument or a trait bound:

module club.shelf

fn books(cards: Seq<Card>) : Seq<Card> = cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")

A program calls it with its own cards, shelf.books(cards). A module written this way checks once, and means the same in every program that imports it.

docs.title: Imports form no cycle
docs.text: The import graph is acyclic: an import that closes a cycle is a name error, and the diagnostic names the cycle. The module name tree is not a dependency graph — club and club.reading see nothing of each other unless one imports the other. A child may import its parent; a parent importing its child is warned at the import. Two modules that need each other are resolved by moving the shared part into a module both import.

docs.title: Receiver modules
docs.text:
A module that names a type pattern after for, module club.titles for String, is a receiver module. Its functions take self as their first parameter, at the module's pattern, and once the module is imported they resolve as receiver calls, value.f(args), on every value the pattern fits. This is lib/club/titles.hql:

/// Receiver functions over a book's title.
module club.titles for String

/// The first letter of each word, `"The Hobbit".initials()` is `"TH"`.
fn initials(self) : String = self.words().map(w => w.slice(0, 1)).join("")

/// A shelf mark: the initials and the year, `"TH-1937"`.
fn shelf_mark(self, year: Int) : String = fmt("{}-{}", self.initials(), year)

self is written untyped: its type is the module's pattern, String. Inside the module, self.initials() calls the module's own receiver function.

import club.titles

["The Hobbit".initials(), "Dune".shelf_mark(1965), titles.initials("Mrs Dalloway")]

["TH", "D-1965", "MD"]

value.f(args) is module.f(value, args): the value fills self, and titles.initials("Mrs Dalloway") is the same call written with its module. A function declared without self takes no receiver and is called only through its module.

docs.title: Receiver calls throughout the book
docs.text:
The prelude's modules are receiver modules too: string is module string for String, so "Dune".upper() calls string.upper, and [1, 2].size() calls the collection's size. A receiver call is resolved by the value's type among the modules in scope, so two modules may declare one name over different types: "abc".contains("b") is the string's and [1, 2].contains(2) the collection's.

c.title without parentheses is a field read, not a call.

docs.title: A receiver function's body
docs.text:
A receiver function is a function, and its body takes either form. A block over self names its steps as any block does:

module counting for Int

fn twice(self) : Int {
    doubled = self * 2
    doubled
}

A program declares no receiver functions: self belongs to a module's pattern, and a program has none.

fn initials(self: String) : String = "TH"
"The Hobbit".initials()

parse failure[unexpected-token]: a function with a body takes its receiver at the module's pattern: write `self` untyped
 --> <expression>:1:19
  |
1 | fn initials(self: String) : String = "TH"
  |                   ^^^^^^

docs.title: Visibility
docs.text: A declaration inside a module is public unless it is marked private. A module's contract is its public declarations: what an importer reaches, and what the module promises to keep.

docs.title: Public by default
docs.text:
club.reading declares days and days_for_all unmarked, so both are public, and rounded_up marked private:

module club.reading

private fn rounded_up(n: Int, d: Int) : Int = (n + d - 1) / d

fn days(pages: Int, per_day: Int) : Int = rounded_up(pages, per_day)

days calls rounded_up inside the module. An importer reaches days, and rounded_up is not part of the contract:

import club.reading

reading.rounded_up(412, 40)

check error[unknown-name]: the module `reading` has no function `rounded_up`
 --> <expression>:3:1
  |
3 | reading.rounded_up(412, 40)
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A private declaration is never exported: no importer reaches it qualified, unqualified, as a pipeline step, or — for a private receiver function — as value.f(). A helper marked private is free to change without changing the module's contract.

docs.title: What private marks
docs.text:
private may mark every declaration a module writes: a function, a receiver function, a type, a trait and a module-level binding.

  • A public declaration may not mention a private type or trait in its signature — a parameter, a result, a bound, a field or a supertype. The checker rejects such a declaration, since an importer would receive a value of a type it cannot name.
  • The parser rejects private on an impl. An implementation of a trait holds in every module that sees the type and the trait.

docs.title: A program is public
docs.text:
A program is read by no other unit, so every declaration in it is public, and the parser rejects private there:

private fn double(n: Int) : Int = n * 2

double(21)

parse failure[unexpected-token]: `private` belongs to a module: every declaration of a program is public, since no other unit reads it
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | private fn double(n: Int) : Int = n * 2
  | ^^^^^^^

docs.title: internal is reserved
docs.text:
internal is visibility across the modules of one package: wider than one module, narrower than every importer. It is reserved, and the parser rejects it wherever it is written:

internal fn double(n: Int) : Int = n * 2

double(21)

parse failure[unexpected-token]: `internal` is reserved: visibility across one package is admitted once every module records its package; mark the declaration `private`, or leave it public
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | internal fn double(n: Int) : Int = n * 2
  | ^^^^^^^^

docs.title: 9. I/O
docs.text: Every program so far read values written into the program itself. This chapter reads files, standard input and the network, writes files and standard output, passes values between parts of a program, and logs what a program does, all through one model: a program reads from a source and writes to a target.

docs.title: Sources and targets
docs.text:
source(endpoint, Format) reads every document an endpoint holds and gives them as values. A source is a value, and a pipeline starts from it the way it starts from a list:

source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"), Json)
| filter(s => s.seen == "morning")
| map(s => s.species)

["wren", "kingfisher"]

Three things meet in that first step, and each has a page. An endpoint, file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"), states where bytes are; constructing it performs no I/O. A format, Json, states how the bytes are documents, here one JSON document per line. source joins the two. Whether the documents end is carried by the type of what it gives: a file gives a Seq, standard input a Stream, and the checker reports which steps each one allows.

Writing is the mirror. target(endpoint, Format) writes one completed value as one document, and sink(endpoint, Format) writes one document per value as each arrives:

source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"))
| filter(s => s.seen == "morning")
| map(s => s.species)
| sink(stdout, Text)

wren
kingfisher

Both writing steps give Step, and a Step result prints nothing: the two lines above were written by sink while the program ran.

The io module is part of the prelude, so none of this needs an import. Logging and the network are modules of their own, import logging and import net.

docs.title: The pages
docs.text: Page What it covers Files and Standard Endpoints stdin, stdout, stderr, file(p) and file(p).end; Readable, Writable and Replayable; where a relative path resolves Reading with source documents as Data, the format from the extension, reading as a declared record, and the decode error Writing with target and sink one document or one document per value, replace or append, and branches that write Finite or live Seq from a file and Stream from a pipe, tap, and batches with collect(n) Formats and documents what one document reads as, how documents are separated, and which extension implies which format Endpoints by id [endpoint.<id>] in hql.toml, the kind that states the type, the schema boundary, and writing by id Subjects and lakehouse tables a core NATS subject, a JetStream subject and its durable consumer, io.msg.nats and io.msg.nats_jetstream, a Databricks or Spark table, and a pipeline from one to the other Channels Channel<T>(name), an endpoint of values held in memory Logging Logger, the five levels, --log-level, and logs kept as values The network http, websocket and tcp with import net Files and folders io.fs: a Path, walking a Folder, matching a Glob, and an Entry Environment and arguments io.env: environment variables and --arg arguments Effects and what a host allows effectful operations, and what hql eval, hql render and hql check grant hql on the command line hql '<program>', --to, --compact and --from

docs.title: Channels
docs.text:
An endpoint of bytes needs a format to make its bytes documents. A channel holds values instead. Channel<T>(name) is an endpoint of values of type T, held in memory for one evaluation. It keeps the values' type, so it takes no format. target writes one value to it, sink writes each value of a sequence, and source gives what it holds now:

c = Channel<Int>("nums")
1 | target(c)
[2, 3] | sink(c)
source(c)

[1, 2, 3]

Values are read in the order they were written. Reading does not consume: two reads give the same values.

c = Channel<Int>("n")
[1] | sink(c)
a = source(c)
b = source(c)
[size(a), size(b)]

[1, 1]

tap(c) gives only what is written after it, as a stream:

c = Channel<Int>("n")
[1] | sink(c)
t = tap(c)
[2] | sink(c)
t | take(5)

[2]

docs.title: The element type is checked
docs.text:
A channel's T is checked as any other type is, and a format beside a channel is a type error, since a channel holds values rather than bytes:

c = Channel<Int>("n")
"x" | target(c)

check error[type-mismatch]: Channel<Int> holds Int, not String
 --> <expression>:2:7
  |
2 | "x" | target(c)
  |       ^^^^^^^^^

c = Channel<Int>("n")
source(c, Json)

check error[type-mismatch]: a channel holds values, not bytes, so it takes no format
 --> <expression>:2:8
  |
2 | source(c, Json)
  |        ^

docs.title: One name, one channel
docs.text:
A channel lives for its execution scope: a program run, or one cell of a document. Within a scope one name is one channel, and constructing the same name with another element type is an evaluation failure naming both:

a = Channel<Int>("n")
b = Channel<String>("n")
1
