execute failure[invalid-argument]: the channel "n" holds Int, so it is not also a Channel<String>
 --> <expression>:2:5
  |
2 | b = Channel<String>("n")
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A cell of a document being rendered may write a channel, because a channel stays inside the evaluation (effects and what a host allows). A channel of LogEvent values is how a program keeps its own logs as values.

docs.title: hql on the command line
docs.text:
With source and sink, hql is a structured-data tool for the shell. A first argument that names no command is a program, so hql '<program>' is hql eval '<program>':

$ cat examples/io/sightings.jsonl | hql 'source(stdin, Json) | filter(s => s.seen == "morning") | map(s => s.species)'
"wren"
"kingfisher"

The result is a Stream<String>, so the host writes each value as it arrives, in HQL, the format a result is written in unless --to names another (writing results out).

docs.title: --to and --compact
docs.text:
--to json presents each document of the result pretty-printed, as jq . does, and --compact gives one line each, as jq -c does:

$ head -1 examples/io/sightings.jsonl | hql 'source(stdin, Json)' --to json
{
  "seen": "dusk",
  "site": "meadow",
  "species": "barn owl"
}

$ head -2 examples/io/sightings.jsonl | hql 'source(stdin, Json)' --to json --compact
{"seen":"dusk","site":"meadow","species":"barn owl"}
{"seen":"morning","site":"hedge","species":"wren"}

Concatenated JSON values are what source(…, Json) reads, so the output of one hql is the input of the next. sink(e, Json) writes one document per line whatever the flags: a program writing a file says what the file is, and --compact is about the terminal.

Converting between formats is a source and a --to:

$ hql 'source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")) | map(s => s.site)' --to yaml
- meadow
- hedge
- barn
- river

docs.title: --from
docs.text:
--from names the format of standard input once, on the command line, so the program reads stdin without naming one; a format the program names wins:

$ cat examples/io/sightings.jsonl | hql --from json 'source(stdin) | map(s => s.site)'
"meadow"
"hedge"
"barn"
"river"

docs.title: Input and output stay in the program
docs.text:
The command line names no input and no output of a program's own. Input is source or tap in the program, output is target or sink in the program, and --to only chooses how the host writes the final result. A program whose result is Step prints nothing:

$ cat examples/io/sightings.jsonl | hql 'source(stdin, Json) | filter(s => s.seen == "morning") | map(s => s.species) | sink(stdout, Text)'
wren
kingfisher

hql run - reads the program from standard input, so such a program cannot also read stdin as data, and source(stdin, …) in it is a type error. --log-level sets every logger's threshold (logging).

docs.title: Endpoints by id
docs.text:
A program that names a file path is tied to one machine's files. A vault declares its endpoints in hql.toml instead, each under an id, and a program names only the id. The field station of the endpoints examples is such a vault, and the programs on this page run with --vault examples/endpoints/station:

[endpoint.journal]
kind = "vault"
root = "journal"

[endpoint.counts]
kind = "csv"
path = "data/counts.csv"

[endpoint.sightings]
kind = "json"
path = "data/sightings.json"

journal = source("journal")
journal.cards | map(c => c.name)

["kite", "owl", "wren"]

A vault is a folder of documents, each a card with a name, the subject of chapter 21; journal.cards is the cards of that one. Here it is one endpoint among others, read by its id like the rest.

docs.title: The kind states the type
docs.text:
source("journal") is a Vault, with its own cards. source("counts") is a Seq<Data>, a row per element, and a json endpoint is the elements of its file's one array:

source("counts")

[{count: "2", species: "wren"}, {count: "1", species: "owl"}, {count: "1", species: "kite"}]

source("sightings") | map(s => s.species)

["wren", "owl", "kite"]

The kinds are vault, csv, json, json_lines, yaml, sqlite, one table of a database file, postgres, one table of a PostgreSQL database, kafka, one Kafka topic, nats, one core NATS subject, nats_jetstream, one subject of a NATS JetStream stream, and spark, one table of a lakehouse. postgres and kafka are the subject of topics and tables, and nats, nats_jetstream and spark of subjects and lakehouse tables. A path resolves against the directory of hql.toml. The type comes from the configuration, so checking a program reads hql.toml and opens nothing else.

An endpoint read as a declared record decodes each element as the record, as a file does, and tap("id") gives a finite endpoint one element at a time, as a Stream:

type Tally {
    species : String
    count   : Int
}

tallies : Seq<Tally> = source("counts")
tallies | map(t => t.count) | sum

4

docs.title: The id is a literal
docs.text:
The type an endpoint is read as is known only from its configuration, so the id is written in the program as a literal, and a connection string is not an id:

id = "counts"
source(id)

check error[type-mismatch]: `source` names a configured endpoint by a literal id, `source("field_notes")`: a computed id would leave its type unknown until evaluation
 --> <expression>:2:8
  |
2 | source(id)
  |        ^^

source("postgres://db/birds")

check error[type-mismatch]: "postgres://db/birds" is not an endpoint id: connection details belong in configuration, `[endpoint.<id>]` in hql.toml, and a program names the id
 --> <expression>:1:8
  |
1 | source("postgres://db/birds")
  |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

An id the configuration does not declare is a name error that names the nearest one:

source("count")

check error[unknown-name]: no endpoint `count` is configured; did you mean `counts`?
 --> <expression>:1:8
  |
1 | source("count")
  |        ^^^^^^^

docs.title: The schema boundary
docs.text:
The names and types an external system uses are facts about that system, not about the program's types, so they are configured beside the endpoint. The station's ledger is a CSV whose headers are Species Name, Total and Observer. [endpoint.<id>.fields.<field>] maps a field of the record a program reads to its external field, by name for a column or a key, and by a dotted path for a key below the top level of a JSON or YAML document:

[endpoint.ledger]
kind = "csv"
path = "data/ledger.csv"

[endpoint.ledger.fields.species]
name = "Species Name"

[endpoint.ledger.fields.count]
name = "Total"

[endpoint.profiles]
kind = "json"
path = "data/profiles.json"

[endpoint.profiles.fields.id]
name = "user_id"

[endpoint.profiles.fields.name]
path = "profile.display_name"

type Profile {
    id   : String
    name : String
}

profiles : Seq<Profile> = source("profiles")
profiles | map(p => p.name)

["Ada", "Grace"]

A field's table also takes type, the external type where the format's default is not it; absent, the external values read as an absent optional field, an empty cell in CSV unless written; and write = false for a field a write leaves out.

strictness says what a read does with an external field no field of the record reads. It is compatible unless written: the field is passed to the type, so a closed record does not decode a ledger with an Observer column. Under open the field is not read, under warn it is not read and is reported, and under strict it is an error:

type Tally {
    species : String
    count   : Int
}

tallies : Seq<Tally> = source("ledger")
tallies | map(t => t.count) | sum

execute failure[io-failure]: endpoint `ledger`: document 1 does not decode as Tally: field `Observer`: Tally declares no such field
 --> <expression>:6:24
  |
6 | tallies : Seq<Tally> = source("ledger")
  |                        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

[endpoint.ledger_open]
kind = "csv"
path = "data/ledger.csv"
strictness = "open"

[endpoint.ledger_open.fields.species]
name = "Species Name"

[endpoint.ledger_open.fields.count]
name = "Total"

type Tally {
    species : String
    count   : Int
}

tallies : Seq<Tally> = source("ledger_open")
tallies | map(t => t.count) | sum

4

hql boundary <file> <id> --as <Type> prints an endpoint's effective boundary, each property with the layer it comes from, the format's default or the configuration:

$ hql --vault examples/endpoints/station boundary tally.hql ledger --as Tally
endpoint ledger (csv), read as Tally; strictness compatible, mode replace
species : String
  external Species Name    configuration
  type     text            format
  position 1               format
  read     true            format
  write    true            format
  absent   empty, missing  format
count : Int
  external Total           configuration
  type     text            format
  position 2               format
  read     true            format
  write    true            format
  absent   empty, missing  format

docs.title: Writing by id
docs.text:
A configured endpoint is written by its id as well. xs | target("id") writes a Table<R>, or a List<R> or Seq<R>, of a declared record R through the same boundary: each field under its external name, in position order, a field with write = false left out. The kind fixes the format, so a format beside the id is a type error, and a vault is read and never written:

type Tally {
    species : String
    count   : Int
}

tallies : Seq<Tally> = source("counts")
tallies | filter(t => t.count > 1) | target("counts")

Step

source("counts") | target("counts")

check error[type-mismatch]: `target("counts")` writes rows of a declared record, and Data is not one
 --> <expression>:1:20
  |
1 | source("counts") | target("counts")
  |                    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

source("counts") | target("counts", Csv)

check error[type-mismatch]: a configured endpoint's format is its kind's, set in its configuration; name none
 --> <expression>:1:20
  |
1 | source("counts") | target("counts", Csv)
  |                    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The endpoint's table takes mode, how a write treats what the endpoint already holds. It is replace unless written:

mode A file A SQLite table create written where none exists; an existing file is an evaluation failure created where none exists; an existing table is an evaluation failure append the rows or documents added after the ones held; created where none exists rows inserted; the table created where none exists replace rewritten whole dropped and created again with the rows written

Reading an endpoint the same evaluation has replaced is an evaluation failure, as for a file, and a document being rendered writes nothing (effects and what a host allows).

docs.title: Topics and tables
docs.text:
A postgres endpoint is one table of a PostgreSQL database, and a kafka endpoint is one Kafka topic. The connection string of a database may hold a password, so the configuration names the environment variable that holds it, dsn_env; a topic's brokers are written as brokers or named the same way by brokers_env:

[endpoint.orders]
kind = "postgres"
dsn_env = "DEMO_DSN"
table = "orders"
order = ["id"]

[endpoint.events]
kind = "kafka"
brokers_env = "KAFKA_BROKERS"
topic = "events"
idle_ms = 2000

Checking a program reads this configuration and connects to neither system. The variables are read, and the connections made, when an endpoint is read or written.

A table ends. source("orders") is a Seq of rows, read through the schema boundary as a sqlite table is: the columns are compared with the record before any row is decoded, and only the columns the record reads are selected. A numeric column reads as a Decimal with its digits, a jsonb column as the tree it holds, and a NULL as an absent field:

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

events : Seq<Event> = source("orders")
events
| filter(e => e.kind == "order_placed")
| group(by = e => e.customer)
| map(g => {customer: g.key, total: g.items | map(e => e.amount) | sum})

{{customer: "ada", total: 135.75}, {customer: "grace", total: 42.00}, {customer: "linus", total: 7.99}}

target("orders") writes a Seq or a Table of a declared record in one transaction. A table that does not exist is created, a column per field: BIGINT for an Int, DOUBLE PRECISION for a Float, NUMERIC for a Decimal, BOOLEAN for a Bool, JSONB for a list or a record, and TEXT otherwise. Under mode = "replace" the rows the table holds are removed and its definition, indexes and grants are kept.

A topic does not end. tap("events") is a Stream, one JSON document per message, decoded as the element type. source("events") is a type error, since a Seq is a value that ends:

source("events")

check error[type-mismatch]: `events` is a `kafka` endpoint, read by `tap` as a `Stream`, not by `source` as a `Seq`
 --> <expression>:1:8
  |
1 | source("events")
  |        ^^^^^^^^

The stream starts at the earliest message the topic keeps, or at the next one under from = "latest". Without idle_ms it waits for messages without end; with it, the stream ends once no message has arrived for that many milliseconds.

sink writes as values arrive. sink("events") writes each value as one message, and sink("orders") each row as it arrives, committed one at a time. A stream has no last value for target to wait for, so moving a topic into a table is a tap and a sink:

events : Stream<Event> = tap("events")
events | sink("orders")

and moving a table into a topic is a source and a sink:

orders : Seq<Event> = source("orders")
orders | sink("events")

sink takes no format beside an id, and writes to a kafka, nats, nats_jetstream, postgres or spark endpoint only; a file or an SQLite table is written whole by target. A NATS subject and a lakehouse table take the places of the topic and the table on the next page.

docs.title: Files and Standard Endpoints
docs.text:
An endpoint states where bytes are. Constructing one performs no I/O: it opens, stats and resolves nothing, and prints as it was written:

file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")

file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")

Four endpoints are bound by the host, as vault is, and need no configuration: stdin, stdout, stderr and file(path).

docs.title: What an endpoint can do is its type
docs.text:
An endpoint's capabilities are its supertypes. A Readable endpoint is read by source and tap, a Writable one is written by target and sink, and a Replayable endpoint is a Readable one that gives the same bytes on every read within one evaluation. Stdin is Readable, Stdout and Stderr are Writable, and File is Replayable and Writable. Reading an endpoint that is not readable is a type error, reported before the program runs:

source(stdout, Json)

check error[type-mismatch]: `source` needs (Readable | String), not Stdout
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | source(stdout, Json)
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The String in the diagnostic is the other form of source, a configured endpoint named by its id (endpoints by id).

docs.title: A file and its end
docs.text:
file(p) is the whole file. file(p).end is a second endpoint, the end of the same file: Readable and Writable, and not Replayable, since what comes after the end is not there yet. Which endpoint a step names decides what the step does, so a file has no open mode:

file(p) file(p).end source every document in the file, as a Seq a type error naming tap tap the documents one at a time, then it ends the documents appended from now on, as tail -f gives them target, sink replace the file append to the file 
source(file("app.log").end, Lines)

check error[type-mismatch]: the end of a file holds nothing yet; follow what is appended there with `tap`
 --> <expression>:1:8
  |
1 | source(file("app.log").end, Lines)
  |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Where a relative path resolves
docs.text:
A relative path resolves against the directory of the source unit that names it: the document for hql render, the program file for hql run, and the working directory for hql eval and the REPL. A document or program reads the same file wherever it is run from. The programs in this chapter run from the repository root, so examples/io/sightings.jsonl is the file in the I/O examples.

A path with a scheme is a type error naming the network endpoint, since a URL is not a file:

file("https://example.com/x.json")

check error[type-mismatch]: "https://example.com/x.json" is a URL, not a file; a network resource is read with `http`
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | file("https://example.com/x.json")
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The network adds http, websocket and tcp with import net, and a channel is an endpoint of values rather than bytes.

docs.title: Environment and arguments
docs.text: The io.env module reads the invocation that runs a program: its environment variables and its arguments, the --arg name=value pairs of the command line. A program imports it, import io.env, and reaches it as env. Each operation reads a value fixed for the whole evaluation, so a program that reads the same name twice reads the same value.

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
env.arg(name) is the value of the invocation's --arg name=value, an Option<String>: some of the text, or none where no --arg names it. This program runs as hql --arg species=wren eval '…':

import io.env

[env.arg("species"), env.arg("limit")]

["wren", none]

env.args() is every pair of the invocation, a Map<String, String> by name:

import io.env

env.args()

Map {"limit": "20", "species": "wren"}

A name is a lowercase letter or _, then lowercase letters, digits and _; the value is the text after the first =, and may be empty. A malformed name and a name given twice are invocation errors, reported before evaluation starts:

$ hql --arg species=wren --arg species=owl eval '1'
error: --arg species is given twice: each argument is named once

Usage: hql [OPTIONS] <COMMAND>

For more information, try '--help'.

docs.title: Missing values and conversion
docs.text:
An argument the invocation does not pass is none, and the program supplies its default:

import io.env

env.arg("species") | unwrap_or("owl")

"owl"

An argument is text. A program converts it as it converts any text. to_int is none for text that is not an integer, and and_then passes that none on, so one default covers both a missing argument and a malformed one:

import io.env

limit = env.arg("limit") | and_then(s => s.to_int()) | unwrap_or(10)
limit * 2

40

import io.env

env.arg("limit") | and_then(s => s.to_int()) | unwrap_or(10)

10

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
env.var(name) is the value of the environment variable name, an Option<String>, and env.vars() is every variable the program may read, a Map<String, String> by name. A variable that is unset reads as none:

import io.env

env.var("HQL_BOOK_NEVER_SET") | unwrap_or("anonymous")

"anonymous"

env.vars() | get(name) is the same lookup in the map. A variable whose value is not UTF-8 reads as none too, and is absent from vars().

io.env is not in the prelude. Without the import, var is an unknown name, reported before the program runs:

var("HOME")

check error[unknown-name]: `var` is provided by the `io.env` extension: write `import io.env`
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | var("HOME")
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: What a host grants
docs.text:
Every operation of io.env is effectful, and hql check reports a function that uses one:

import io.env

fn limit() : Int = env.arg("limit") | and_then(s => s.to_int()) | unwrap_or(10)
limit()

limit is Effectful: it uses `arg`
Int

Arguments are always granted: the invocation wrote them. The environment is read through a grant the host fixes before evaluation:

Host Variables granted hql eval, hql run, hql repl every variable, or the names env = [...] lists in the workspace's hql.toml hql render none

In hql.toml, env is a list of names and PREFIX_* patterns, a * matching any suffix:

env = ["SHOP_*"]

A variable outside the grant reads as none. A withheld variable and an unset one are indistinguishable, so a program cannot tell which names exist beyond its grant. In that workspace, with SHOP_REGION set:

$ cat region.hql
import io.env

[env.var("SHOP_REGION"), env.var("HOME")]

$ SHOP_REGION=eu hql run region.hql
["eu", none]

A rendered document reads no variable, so its output depends on nothing in the renderer's environment and discloses nothing of it. It reads its arguments as any program does (effects and what a host allows):

# Notes

```hql
import io.env
[env.var("SHOP_REGION"), env.arg("who")]
```

$ SHOP_REGION=eu hql --arg who=owl render notes.hmd
# Notes

- none
- owl

The reference states each operation of io.env.

docs.title: Files and folders
docs.text:
A file(p) endpoint names one file by a path written in the program. The io.fs module lists what a folder holds, so a program finds its files first and then reads them. A program imports it, import io.fs, and reaches it as fs.

The programs on this page list a small tree in the file-system examples:

examples/fs/tree/
  assets/logo.txt        5 bytes
  assets/style.css      19 bytes
  data/2026/q1.csv      21 bytes
  data/2026-notes.md    17 bytes
  data/birds.csv        28 bytes

docs.title: A path
docs.text:
A Path is a place in a file system, written as text: segments separated by /. It is part of io, so it needs no import. Its operations read the text and never the file system, so they are pure:

p = Path("examples/fs/tree").join("data").join("birds.csv")
[p.text, p.name(), p.stem(), p.extension() | unwrap_or("?"), p.parent() | map(q => q.text) | unwrap_or("?")]

["examples/fs/tree/data/birds.csv", "birds.csv", "birds", "csv", "examples/fs/tree/data"]

parent() is none for a path of one segment, and extension() is none for a last segment with no .:

Path("data").parent()

none

Paths are ordered by their segments, compared in turn, each by its text. 2026/q1.csv sorts before 2026-notes.md, although - sorts before / as text, since the first segments 2026 and 2026-notes.md already differ:

[Path("data/2026-notes.md"), Path("data/2026/q1.csv")] | sort | map(p => p.text)

["data/2026/q1.csv", "data/2026-notes.md"]

This is the order of a sorted walk, and every listing below gives it.

docs.title: A folder
docs.text:
folder(path) is the Folder at a path, a String or a Path. A folder is an endpoint that holds files and folders, as a database holds tables. Constructing one opens, stats and resolves nothing, and a relative path resolves as a file's does (where a relative path resolves):

import io.fs

folder("examples/fs/tree")

Folder(path = Path(text = "examples/fs/tree"))

io.fs is not in the prelude. Without the import, folder is an unknown name, reported before the program runs:

folder("examples/fs/tree")

check error[unknown-name]: `folder` is provided by the `io.fs` extension: write `import io.fs`
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | folder("examples/fs/tree")
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A folder is not a Seq itself. Three effectful steps list it, each reading the file system once, where it is written, and each giving a Seq<Entry>. entries gives what is directly in the folder, sorted by name, an entry whose name opens with . included:

import io.fs

folder("examples/fs/tree/data") | entries | map(e => [e.name, e.kind])

[["2026", "folder"], ["2026-notes.md", "file"], ["birds.csv", "file"]]

walk gives every entry below the folder, the folder itself excluded: depth first, each folder's entries sorted by name, and each folder followed at once by what it holds:

import io.fs

folder("examples/fs/tree") | walk | map(e => e.path.text.trim_prefix("examples/fs/tree/"))

["assets", "assets/logo.txt", "assets/style.css", "data", "data/2026", "data/2026/q1.csv", "data/2026-notes.md", "data/birds.csv"]

The order is never the file system's: the same tree walks the same way on every machine. It is also the order a vault reads its cards in; the vault skips entries whose name opens with ., and walk lists them.

docs.title: An entry
docs.text:
An Entry is one thing a folder holds. It has five fields:

Field Type What it holds path Path the listed folder's path joined with the entry's path below it name String the last segment kind String "file", "folder" or "link" size Int, optional a file's length in bytes; absent for a folder or a link modified Instant, optional the time the entry was last modified, a link's own and not its target's; absent where the platform records none 
import io.fs

folder("examples/fs/tree")
| walk
| filter(e => e.name == "birds.csv")
| map(e => [e.path.text, e.kind, str(e.size)])

[["examples/fs/tree/data/birds.csv", "file", "28"]]

modified is an Instant, so it compares with an instant the program writes and sorts the entries by time. A listing reads it once, with the rest of the entry, so the files changed since a cut-off are a filter over it:

import io.fs

cutoff = Instant("2020-01-01T00:00:00Z")
folder("examples/fs/tree/data")
| entries
| filter(e => e.modified | map(t => t >= cutoff) | unwrap_or(false))
| map(e => e.name)

["2026", "2026-notes.md", "birds.csv"]

The times themselves are the file system's, so they differ from one checkout of a tree to the next; a program that must give the same answer on every machine does not read them.

size is optional, so a sum over it states what a folder counts as:

import io.fs

folder("examples/fs/tree")
| walk
| filter(e => e.kind == "file")
| map(e => e.size | unwrap_or(0))
| sum

90

A link is reported with the kind "link" and not followed.

docs.title: A glob
docs.text:
A Glob is a pattern over paths, matched against a path relative to the folder it is applied to. * matches within one segment, ** any number of whole segments, none included, ? one character other than /, [abc] one character of the set and [a-z] one of the range. matches reads the text and never the file system:

import io.fs

[
    Glob("data/*.csv").matches(Path("data/birds.csv")),
    Glob("data/*.csv").matches(Path("data/2026/q1.csv")),
    Glob("data/**/*.csv").matches(Path("data/2026/q1.csv")),
]

[true, false, true]

The glob step gives the entries of walk whose path below the folder matches, in walk order:

import io.fs

folder("examples/fs/tree") | glob(Glob("**/*.csv")) | map(e => e.path.text)

["examples/fs/tree/data/2026/q1.csv", "examples/fs/tree/data/birds.csv"]

A pattern that does not parse, an unclosed [ or a ** that is not a whole segment, is an evaluation error where Glob constructs it:

import io.fs

Glob("data/a**.csv")

execute failure[invalid-argument]: "data/a**.csv" is not a glob: `**` stands for whole segments, alone between `/`
 --> <expression>:3:1
  |
3 | Glob("data/a**.csv")
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Reading what was found
docs.text:
An entry's path is one file reads as written, so a listing feeds source (reading with source). Every row of every CSV file directly in data/:

import io.fs

folder("examples/fs/tree/data")
| glob(Glob("*.csv"))
| flat_map(e => source(file(e.path), Csv))

[{count: "2", species: "heron"}, {count: "1", species: "owl"}]

docs.title: A path that may not be there
docs.text:
Listing a folder that does not exist, or is not a folder, is an evaluation error naming its path:

import io.fs

folder("examples/fs/nowhere") | entries

execute failure[io-failure]: examples/fs/nowhere: no folder is there
 --> <expression>:3:33
  |
3 | folder("examples/fs/nowhere") | entries
  |                                 ^^^^^^^

exists and entry test a path without an error. exists is false where nothing is there, and entry is some(Entry) or none:

import io.fs

[
    str(Path("examples/fs/tree/data").exists()),
    str(Path("examples/fs/tree/missing").exists()),
    Path("examples/fs/tree/data").entry() | map(e => e.kind) | unwrap_or("?"),
    str(Path("examples/fs/tree/missing.csv").entry()),
]

["true", "false", "folder", "none"]

docs.title: What a host grants
docs.text:
entries, walk, glob, exists and entry are effectful, and hql check reports a function that uses one:

import io.fs

fn csv_files() : Seq<Entry> = folder("examples/fs/tree") | glob(Glob("**/*.csv"))
csv_files() | size

csv_files is Effectful: it uses `glob`
Int

A listing is granted exactly where reading a file at the same path is (effects and what a host allows): anywhere under hql eval, hql run and the REPL, and under hql render only below the document's own directory. The reference states each operation of io.fs.

docs.title: Finite or live
docs.text:
A file is replayable, so reading it gives a Seq: the documents end, and every step in the book applies. Standard input arrives once, as it is written, so reading it gives a Stream. hql check prints each type:

source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"))

Seq<Data>

source(stdin, Json)

Stream<Data>

That is the difference the streams chapter drew. map, filter and take run over standard input one document at a time, as it arrives. A step that needs the whole input is a type error until the stream is bounded with take(n) or batched with collect(n):

source(stdin, Json) | size

check error[type-mismatch]: `size` needs a finite input, and Stream<Data> may not end; bound it first with `take(n)`, or batch it with `collect(n)`
 --> <expression>:1:23
  |
1 | source(stdin, Json) | size
  |                       ^^^^

The same program checks over a file and over a pipe, and the checker reports which steps each one allows.

docs.title: One document at a time with tap
docs.text:
tap(endpoint, Format) reads any readable endpoint as a Stream, one document at a time, holding only the current one in memory. Over a file, source holds every document and gives a Seq; tap holds one and gives a Stream, so a file larger than memory is read with tap:

tap(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"))

Stream<Data>

tap(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")) | take(2) | map(s => s.species)

["barn owl", "wren"]

Over a live endpoint the two give the same stream: tap(stdin, Json) is source(stdin, Json). Over a file's end, tap gives each document appended after the tap began, as tail -F does, and waits for a file that does not exist yet:

tap(file("app.log").end, Lines) | take(1)

waits for the next line written to app.log, and gives it.

A format that is one whole document, such as Text, is not read one at a time:

tap(file("examples/io/counts.csv"), Text)

check error[type-mismatch]: Text is one document, so it is not read one at a time; read it whole with `source`
 --> <expression>:1:5
  |
1 | tap(file("examples/io/counts.csv"), Text)
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Batches
docs.text:
collect(n) gathers consecutive values into lists of n, and a list is finite, so a stream is answered in pieces:

tap(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")) | collect(2) | map(b => b | size) | take(2)

[2, 2]

Written by sink, each batch is one document:

tap(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")) | map(s => s.species) | collect(2) | sink(stdout, Json)

["barn owl","wren"]
["barn owl","kingfisher"]

Over standard input the same program writes each array as soon as its second value has arrived:

$ cat examples/io/sightings.jsonl | hql 'source(stdin, Json) | map(s => s.species) | collect(2) | sink(stdout, Json)'
["barn owl","wren"]
["barn owl","kingfisher"]

docs.title: What each shape allows
docs.text:
A Seq<T> is a Stream<T> that ends, so every rule for a stream holds for a sequence, and a sequence has more:

Seq<T> Stream<T> that is not a Seq source gives it over a Replayable endpoint or a channel over a live endpoint tap reads it one value at a time reads it as it is target writes one document a type error sink writes one document per element writes one document per value the result, by --to one whole text one piece per value, as it arrives size, sort, xs[i], contains accepted a type error filter, map, take, drop, tee accepted accepted, one value at a time collect(n) gives List<List<T>> gives Stream<List<T>>, in batches

emit keeps its meaning from the streams chapter: it gives the members of each list a stream carries. It is not needed to turn a Seq into a Stream, because a Seq already is one.

docs.title: Formats and documents
docs.text: A format states how bytes are documents: how one document is read from bytes and written to them, and how one document is separated from the next. The formats are the Format types of the writing results out chapter. source and tap decode with them, target and sink encode with them.

docs.title: What one document reads as
docs.text:
Format One document reads as Documents are separated by Json Data whitespace between top-level values Yaml Data a --- line Csv Data, one row keyed by the header a line; the header is read once Lines String, one line without its terminator a line terminator JsonLines Data, one JSON document per line a line terminator Text, Markdown, Hmd, Hql String, the whole text not separable: one document

Lines and JsonLines are framing formats, one document per line. The same file read as Lines gives its lines as strings, and read as Json or JsonLines the documents those lines hold:

source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"), Lines) | take(1)

["{\"species\": \"barn owl\", \"site\": \"meadow\", \"seen\": \"dusk\"}"]

A whole-text format reads one document, the whole file:

source(file("examples/io/counts.csv"), Text) | size

1

Bytes that do not decode in their format are an evaluation failure naming the endpoint, the line and the column.

D2 and Mermaid describe a whole, so they are written by target only:

source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"), Mermaid)

check error[type-mismatch]: Mermaid is written, not read
 --> <expression>:1:8
  |
1 | source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"), Mermaid)
  |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")) | sink(stdout, Mermaid)

check error[type-mismatch]: Mermaid describes a whole, so it is written by `target`, not `sink`
 --> <expression>:1:47
  |
1 | source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")) | sink(stdout, Mermaid)
  |                                               ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: The extension implies the format
docs.text:
When the format argument is left out, the extension of a literal file path implies it:

Extension Format .json Json .jsonl, .ndjson JsonLines .yaml, .yml Yaml .csv Csv .txt, .log Lines .md Markdown .hmd Hmd .hql Hql .d2 D2 .mmd Mermaid

A format that is given wins over the extension: source(file("notes.data"), Json) and target(file("result.txt"), Json) are both allowed. An extension outside the table implies none, and leaving the format out is then a type error naming the argument:

source(file("examples/io/notes.data"))

check error[type-mismatch]: the extension of "examples/io/notes.data" implies no format; name it: `source(…, Json)`
 --> <expression>:1:8
  |
1 | source(file("examples/io/notes.data"))
  |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: The format is not the shape
docs.text:
A format states the encoding, and the type states the shape. A Seq written by target in Json is one array; written by sink it is one document per line, which Json reads back, since whitespace separates top-level JSON values. sink(e, F) and source(e, F) are inverses: the documents one writes are the documents the other reads, in order.

Reading in one format and writing in another converts a file. A CSV cell is text, so the counts arrive in YAML as strings:

source(file("examples/io/counts.csv")) | target(stdout, Yaml)

- count: '2'
  species: barn owl
- count: '1'
  species: wren
- count: '1'
  species: kingfisher

Read as a declared record, the same cells are the Int the record declares (reading with source).

docs.title: Effects and what a host allows
docs.text:
Constructing an endpoint, a channel or a logger is pure: it names a place and touches nothing. source, tap, target, sink and every log call are effectful: they reach outside the program. A function whose body uses an effectful operation, or calls an effectful function, is effectful too, and hql check reports each one with what it uses, before the type of the program:

fn load() : Seq<Data> = source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"))
load() | size

load is Effectful: it uses `source`
Int

Every effect is known before evaluation, so the host checks each one against its policy and reports a use it does not grant as a type error naming the endpoint:

Host Reads Writes hql eval, hql run, hql repl any endpoint any endpoint hql render files under the document's directory, and channels channels hql check none none

hql check reads nothing but the program, so checking is offline: a program over a file that does not exist yet, or over the network, still checks.

docs.title: A document reads beside itself and writes only its channels
docs.text:
hql render evaluates the cells of a document (queries inside documents). A document someone else wrote changes no file and sends nothing: a cell may read files under the document's own directory and write channels, and nothing else. A cell that writes a file, standard output or standard error is reported when the document is checked, before any cell runs:

# Report

```hql
[1] | target(file("out.json"))
```

$ hql render report.hmd
type error: a document writes nothing outside itself, so `target` and `sink` are refused here
 --> report.hmd:4:7
  |
4 | [1] | target(file("out.json"))
  |       ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A network endpoint in a document is a type error in the same way, and a file read that leaves the document's directory, by .. or through a symbolic link, is an evaluation failure naming the path:

type error: a document reads and writes nothing on the network
 --> net.hmd:5:8
  |
5 | source(http("https://example.com/x"), Json)
  |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

evaluation failure: ../outside.json: a document reads only files under its own directory
 --> outside.hmd:4:1
  |
4 | source(file("../outside.json"))
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A logger is checked as the sink it is, so a cell logs to cell.logs, its own channel, and not to stderr (logging). The same program runs under different policies without changing its model: a terminal may write files, and a document being rendered may not.

docs.title: Bounds
docs.text: A source over a replayable endpoint holds every document, and the configuration's max_bytes bounds it; tap holds one document at a time and is bounded by what consumes it. A channel holds what its scope wrote, up to a million values; one more ends the evaluation, naming the channel.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
A program reports on itself through a logger, apart from its result. import logging provides one. Logger(endpoint, Format, name = …) names a producer and the destination it writes to:

import logging

log = Logger(stderr, Text, name = "club")
unread = ["The Hobbit", "Leaves of Grass", "The Common Reader"]
log | info("selected", {books: unread | size})
log | debug("not shown")
unread | size

INFO club selected {books: 3}
3

The event goes to standard error and the result to standard output. A logger has five operations, one per level, ordered from least to most severe: trace, debug, info, warn and error. Each takes a message and, optionally, structured data, and is called through a pipe or directly: info(log, "x") is log | info("x"). Each gives Step, so a log call never becomes part of a result.

docs.title: The threshold
docs.text:
A logger writes events at its threshold or above, Info unless level says otherwise, so the debug call above writes nothing. A level is a type, and the threshold is passed as one:

import logging

log = Logger(stdout, Text, name = "club", level = Warn)
log | info("quiet")
log | warn("loud")
1

WARN club loud
1

--log-level overrides every threshold without changing the program:

$ hql --log-level debug eval 'import logging
log = Logger(stderr, Text, name = "club")
log | debug("now shown")
1'
DEBUG club now shown
1

docs.title: The event and its format
docs.text:
A logger writes as sink would: one document per event, in the format given. In Text an event is one line: the level in capitals, the logger's name, the message, then the data unless it is empty. In Json each event is one document with four keys:

import logging

log = Logger(stdout, Json, name = "club")
log | warn("low stock", {title: "Dune"})
1

{"data":{"title":"Dune"},"level":"Warn","logger":"club","message":"low stock"}
1

A log file is appended to by naming its end, Logger(file("app.log").end, Text, name = "club"); a logger on file(p) replaces the file with this run's events, by the rules of sink.

docs.title: Logs as values
docs.text:
A logger whose destination is a Channel<LogEvent> takes no format and keeps its events as values, which the rest of the program can query. A level is a type, so it is tested with is:

import logging

events = Channel<LogEvent>("events")
log = Logger(events, name = "club", level = Debug)
log | debug("loaded")
log | warn("low stock", {title: "Dune"})
log | error("missing", {title: "Ulysses"})

source(events)
| filter(e => (e.level | is(Warn)) or (e.level | is(Error)))
| map(e => {level: e.level, message: e.message})

[{level: "Warn", message: "low stock"}, {level: "Error", message: "missing"}]

Inside a document, the host binds cell, the cell being rendered. Logger(cell.logs, name = …) writes to that cell's own channel, whose events an editor shows beside the cell's result. They are never saved into the document: the cell's result is its value, unchanged by anything it logged.

Constructing a logger is pure. What a logger writes to is checked by the host's policy as a sink to that endpoint, so logging grants nothing a program could not do with sink (effects and what a host allows).

docs.title: The network
docs.text:
import net adds endpoints that are transports. They are read and written by source, tap, target and sink like any other endpoint, and constructing one sends nothing. Naming the module in the program's first lines is how a program states that it may reach the network.

http(url) is Replayable: reading it sends one GET per evaluation and decodes the response body, so source gives a Seq:

import net
source(http("https://api.example.com/birds"), Json)

Seq<Data>

websocket(url) is live: each message is one document, read as it arrives, so reading it gives a Stream:

import net
tap(websocket("wss://events.example.com"), Json)

Stream<Data>

Writing an http endpoint sends one request per document, with the document as its body, by the method given, "GET" unless written. The response is read only for its status, and a status that is not a success is an evaluation failure naming the URL:

import net
source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"))
| target(http("https://api.example.com/report", method = "POST"), Json)

Step

tcp(host, port) is a TCP connection: its documents are separated as their format separates them, one JSON value after another or one line at a time.

docs.title: Network bounds
docs.text:
A network read or write ends. A connection that is not made within 10 seconds is an evaluation failure naming the URL, or the host and port of a tcp endpoint. An http response that sends nothing for 30 seconds is an evaluation failure naming the URL, and so is a websocket handshake the server answers nothing to for 30 seconds. timeout_ms sets the response bound of one http endpoint, in milliseconds above 0:

import net
source(http("https://api.example.com/birds", timeout_ms = 5000), Json)

Seq<Data>

Once a websocket or tcp connection is open, tap waits for the next document without limit, as any Stream does.

Without the import the endpoint constructors are not in scope:

source(http("https://api.example.com/birds"), Json)

check error[unknown-name]: `http` is provided by the `net` extension: write `import net`
 --> <expression>:1:8
  |
1 | source(http("https://api.example.com/birds"), Json)
  |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A header is ordinary data in the program's text, so a request that needs credentials belongs in configuration, as an endpoint by id, and not in a program (endpoints by id). A document being rendered reaches no network (effects and what a host allows).

docs.title: Reading with source
docs.text:
source(endpoint, Format) reads every document an endpoint holds, in a format, and gives them as values. examples/io/sightings.jsonl holds four JSON documents, one per line:

{"species": "barn owl", "site": "meadow", "seen": "dusk"}
{"species": "wren", "site": "hedge", "seen": "morning"}
{"species": "barn owl", "site": "barn", "seen": "night"}
{"species": "kingfisher", "site": "river", "seen": "morning"}

source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"), Json)
| filter(s => s.seen == "morning")
| map(s => s.species)

["wren", "kingfisher"]

docs.title: The format from the extension
docs.text:
A literal path whose extension names a format, .json, .jsonl, .yaml, .csv or .txt among them, implies it, so the format may be left out:

source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"))
| group(by = s => s.species)
| map(g => {species: g.key, sightings: g.items | size})

{{sightings: 2, species: "barn owl"}, {sightings: 1, species: "wren"}, {sightings: 1, species: "kingfisher"}}

The format may be left out only for file of a literal path, because the type of what is read depends on the format, and a path computed at run time has no extension the checker can read:

p = "examples/io/sightings.jsonl"
source(file(p))

check error[type-mismatch]: `source` needs a format, `source(…, Json)`: only a literal file path implies one
 --> <expression>:2:8
  |
2 | source(file(p))
  |        ^^^^^^^

Formats and documents has the table of formats and the extensions that imply them.

docs.title: Each document is Data
docs.text:
Each document is Data, the type of a dynamically structured value from the data types chapter. A CSV row is a record of strings, keyed by the header:

source(file("examples/io/counts.csv"))

[{count: "2", species: "barn owl"}, {count: "1", species: "wren"}, {count: "1", species: "kingfisher"}]

A JSON array is one document, a Data that is a list. A file whose whole content is one array holds one document, and its members are spread with of_type(List) | emit:

source(file("examples/endpoints/station/data/sightings.json")) | size

1

source(file("examples/endpoints/station/data/sightings.json"))
| of_type(List)
| emit
| map(s => s.species)

["wren", "owl", "kite"]

A configured json endpoint gives the members of its array without this step (endpoints by id).

docs.title: Reading as a declared record
docs.text:
A binding whose declared type names an element type decodes each document as that element; so does a function whose declared result is the read:

type Sighting {
    species : String
    site    : String
    seen    : String
}

sightings : Seq<Sighting> = source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"))
sightings | filter(s => s.seen == "morning") | map(s => s.species)

["wren", "kingfisher"]

The same reading is written as a step, source(file(p)) | Sighting:

type Sighting {
    species : String
    site    : String
    seen    : String
}

source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")) | Sighting | map(s => s.site)

["meadow", "hedge", "barn", "river"]

A CSV cell is text, so it is read as the Int, Float or Bool its field declares. A JSON or YAML leaf keeps the type it was written with: "3" is not an Int.

type Tally {
    species : String
    count   : Int
}

tallies : Seq<Tally> = source(file("examples/io/counts.csv"))
tallies | map(t => t.count) | sum

4

A document that does not decode is an evaluation failure naming the file, the document, counted from 1, and the field:

type Sighting {
    species : String
    site    : String
    seen    : Int
}

sightings : Seq<Sighting> = source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"))
sightings | size

execute failure[io-failure]: examples/io/sightings.jsonl: document 1 does not decode as Sighting: field `seen`: "dusk" is not Int
 --> <expression>:7:29
  |
7 | sightings : Seq<Sighting> = source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"))
  |                             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A plain record is closed: a document with an entry the record does not declare does not decode. A record narrowing Data, type Sighting : Data { … }, is an open view that keeps such entries beneath the fields it declares:

type Sighting : Data {
    species : String
}

sightings : Seq<Sighting> = source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"))
sightings | map(s => s.species)

["barn owl", "wren", "barn owl", "kingfisher"]

What each kind of record reads and what it does not is open and closed types in the advanced data typing chapter, and data contracts add rules the values must hold.

A source bound to a name is read once per evaluation, however many times the name is used.

docs.title: Subjects and lakehouse tables
docs.text:
A nats endpoint is one core NATS subject, a nats_jetstream endpoint is one subject of a NATS JetStream stream, and a spark endpoint is one table behind a Spark SQL endpoint: a Databricks SQL warehouse, or an open-source Spark Thrift Server over Delta Lake tables. They are configured as a topic and a table are, and they sit on the same two sides of the line source and tap draw: a subject is a log that does not end, and a table ends.

Kind What it is Read by Written by kafka one topic tap, as a Stream sink, target nats one core subject, kept by no one tap, as a Stream sink, target nats_jetstream one subject of a JetStream stream tap, as a Stream sink, target postgres one table source, as a Seq target, sink spark one table of a lakehouse source, as a Seq target, sink

The programs on this page need a server each, so none of them runs here. Each runs in the hql-demo repository, which starts NATS, MinIO and a Spark Thrift Server with Docker Compose and compares what the programs print with what this page shows.

docs.title: A core subject
docs.text:
NATS delivers a message to whoever is subscribed to its subject when it is published, and keeps nothing. A nats endpoint names the server and a subject:

[endpoint.orders]
kind = "nats"
url_env = "NATS_URL"
subject = "orders.>"
idle_ms = 3000

The address is written as url, or held by the environment variable url_env names. An address may hold a user and a password, and one that does is refused in hql.toml, so it is never written there.

tap("orders") subscribes when the stream is first traversed, and is given every message published from then on, in the order it arrives. A message published before is not there to be given, so a reader must be subscribed before the writer publishes; nothing is read from the earliest message, and the endpoint takes no from. A subject may hold the wildcards *, one token, and >, every token that follows, so orders.> reads every subject under orders.:

events : Stream<Event> = tap("orders")
events
| filter(e => e.kind == "order_placed")
| map(e => {id: e.id, customer: e.customer, amount: e.amount})

sink publishes each value as one message to one subject, so an endpoint with a wildcard is read only. Nothing confirms a core message: sink ends once the server has the messages, whether or not anyone was subscribed.

docs.title: A subject of a stream
docs.text:
JetStream is the part of the server that keeps messages: a stream stores every message published to the subjects it is configured with, in order. A nats_jetstream endpoint names the server, the stream, and one subject within it:

[endpoint.events]
kind = "nats_jetstream"
url_env = "NATS_URL"
stream = "EVENTS"
subject = "events.orders"
idle_ms = 2000

sink("events") publishes each value as one message, a JSON document. A message is written once the stream answers that it stored it, so a program that ends without a failure has lost nothing:

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

events : Seq<Event> = source("mock_events")
events | sink("events")

A subject that no stream stores is an evaluation failure, not a message that disappears. Creating the stream is the server's business, as creating a topic is a cluster's.

tap("events") reads the stream's messages under that subject in the order the stream holds them, from the earliest it keeps, or from the next one published under from = "latest". It is a Stream, and source("events") is a type error, as it is for a topic:

events : Stream<Event> = tap("events")
events
| filter(e => e.kind == "order_placed")
| map(e => {id: e.id, customer: e.customer, amount: e.amount})

{amount: 120.50, customer: "ada", id: 1}
{amount: 42.00, customer: "grace", id: 2}
{amount: 7.99, customer: "linus", id: 4}
{amount: 15.25, customer: "ada", id: 6}

The read leaves nothing on the server: no position is recorded, so reading a subject twice gives the same messages twice. Without idle_ms the stream waits for messages without end; with it, the stream ends once none has arrived for that many milliseconds.

A subject may hold the wildcards *, one token, and >, every token that follows. subject = "events.>" reads every subject of the stream under events.. Such an endpoint is read only: a message is published to one subject, and sink to a wildcard is an evaluation failure that says so.

docs.title: A position the server keeps
docs.text:
A stream stores messages. A consumer is the server's record of how far one reader has come in a stream, and a durable consumer is one the server keeps under a name. An endpoint that names one reads from where the read before it ended:

[endpoint.billing]
kind = "nats_jetstream"
url_env = "NATS_URL"
stream = "EVENTS"
subject = "events.orders"
consumer = "billing"
idle_ms = 2000

events : Stream<Event> = tap("billing")
events | map(e => e.id)

The first run reads every event the stream keeps:

1
2
3
4
5
6

A second run prints nothing, and a run after two more events are published prints those two. The first read under a name creates the consumer, starting where from says; every later read finds it, and from has no effect then. Two endpoints with different consumers each keep their own position over the same messages. A consumer keeps one position over one subject, so naming it with another subject is an evaluation failure.

A message is acknowledged once the program asks for the one after it, and the last one when the stream ends. A message is therefore delivered at least once: a program that fails while it holds a message, or that stops early as take(2) does, is given that message again by the next run.

tap("billing") | take(2) | map(e => e.id)

[1, 2]

The next run of the program above starts with 2.

docs.title: A subject without configuration
docs.text:
Each kind is also a transport type with a constructor, in a module of its own: Nats and nats(...) in io.msg.nats, NatsJetStream and nats_jetstream(...) in io.msg.nats_jetstream. A constructor's parameters are its kind's keys, so a program reaches a subject with no hql.toml:

import io.msg.nats_jetstream

orders = nats_jetstream("events.orders", stream = "EVENTS", url_env = "NATS_URL", idle_ms = 2000)

tap(orders) | filter(e => e.kind == "order_placed") | map(e => e.id)

1
2
4
6

A message is one document, so the format may be left out and is then Json. Both are transports on the network that carry messages, which is what their supertypes state:

import io.msg.nats

nats("orders.order_placed", url_env = "NATS_URL") | is(Network)

Bool

A module is imported by its full path, and naming it in the program's first lines is how a program states that it reaches NATS. Each module declares only its own transport: nats(...) takes no stream, and import io.msg.nats does not bring nats_jetstream into scope. The address is still url or the variable url_env names: a constructor takes no secret, and a url that holds credentials is refused.

A constructed transport has no schema boundary: fields, mode and strictness are stated only in configuration. A message is read as Data, or as the type an annotation names. The boundary of a configured endpoint writes a Decimal as JSON text so that its digits survive, and reads it back; to a constructed transport that field is text.

docs.title: A lakehouse table
docs.text:
A lakehouse keeps tables as files in object storage, with a transaction log beside them, and answers SQL over them. Databricks is one; Apache Spark with Delta Lake over an S3 bucket is another, built from open-source parts. Both answer the same protocol at an HTTP address, so one kind reaches either:

[endpoint.events]
kind = "spark"
url_env = "LAKEHOUSE_URL"
table = "default.events"
order = ["id"]
mode = "replace"

[endpoint.events.fields.amount]
type = "DECIMAL(12,2)"
Where LAKEHOUSE_URL token_env A Databricks SQL warehouse https://<workspace host>/sql/1.0/warehouses/<warehouse id> names the variable holding a personal access token A Spark Thrift Server in HTTP mode http://<host>:10001/cliservice left out

A table name holds its catalog and schema where it has them, main.sales.events. token is a secret key: written in hql.toml it refuses the vault, naming token_env.

target("events") writes a Seq or a Table of a declared record. A table that does not exist is created, a column per field: BIGINT for an Int, DOUBLE for a Float, DECIMAL(38,18) for a Decimal, BOOLEAN for a Bool, and STRING otherwise. A DECIMAL column states how many digits it holds, so the boundary above names the type amount is written as, and the amounts read back with two decimal places. A list or a record field has no column type and is a check error:

events : Seq<Event> = source("mock_events")
events | target("events")

Rows are written in statements of up to 500, and each statement is one commit to the table's log. A target of up to 500 rows is therefore atomic, and under mode = "replace" it puts its rows in place of the ones the table held in that same commit, so a reader never sees the table empty.

source("events") reads the table through the schema boundary, as a postgres table is read: the columns are compared with the record before any row is decoded, and only the columns the record reads are selected. A DECIMAL column reads as a Decimal with its digits and a NULL as an absent field:

events : Seq<Event> = source("events")
events
| filter(e => e.kind == "order_placed")
| group(by = e => e.customer)
| map(g => {customer: g.key, orders: g.items | size, total: g.items | map(e => e.amount) | sum})

{{customer: "ada", orders: 2, total: 135.75}, {customer: "grace", orders: 1, total: 42.00}, {customer: "linus", orders: 1, total: 7.99}}

The endpoint supplies the rows of one table; hql evaluates the filter and grouping locally. A future execution backend could translate supported pipeline steps to Spark SQL. Logical steps and physical plans explains that design direction and how engine planning fits into it.

docs.title: From a subject to a lakehouse
docs.text:
The two meet in the pipeline most platforms have: events arrive on a bus, the valid ones land in a table, the invalid ones go somewhere they can be repaired, and a second table holds what is reported.

producer ──▶ orders.raw ──▶ validate ──ok───▶ orders_silver ──▶ customer_revenue
             (subject)         │              (Delta table)     (Delta table)
                               └──err──▶ orders.rejected
                                         (subject)

One stream holds both subjects, and two tables hold the rest:

[endpoint.orders_raw]
kind = "nats_jetstream"
url_env = "NATS_URL"
stream = "ORDERS"
subject = "orders.raw"
idle_ms = 2000

[endpoint.orders_rejected]
kind = "nats_jetstream"
url_env = "NATS_URL"
stream = "ORDERS"
subject = "orders.rejected"
idle_ms = 2000

[endpoint.orders_silver]
kind = "spark"
url_env = "LAKEHOUSE_URL"
table = "default.orders_silver"
order = ["id"]
mode = "append"

[endpoint.customer_revenue]
kind = "spark"
url_env = "LAKEHOUSE_URL"
table = "default.customer_revenue"
order = ["customer"]

Streaming. The raw subject is read as Data, so no message fails to decode. validate gives one Result per message, and fork routes each to one of two sinks, in order, ending neither:

type EventData : DataContract = {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String

    require amount >= 0 as non_negative
    require ["order_placed", "order_shipped", "payment_failed"] | contains(kind) as known_kind
}

type Rejected {
    id      : Int
    message : Data
    rules   : List<String>
}

tap("orders_raw")
| validate(EventData)
| fork {
    silver =
        oks()
        | map(e => Event(id = e.id, kind = e.kind, customer = e.customer, amount = e.amount, at = e.at))
        | sink("orders_silver"),
    rejected =
        errs()
        | map(e => Rejected(
            id = match e.value.id { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 },
            message = e.value,
            rules = e.violations | map(v => v.rule)))
        | sink("orders_rejected"),
}

sink("orders_silver") appends the rows as they arrive, a commit each 500 rows and one at the end. sink("orders_rejected") publishes each rejected message as the producer sent it, with the rules it broke, so the dead-letter subject is itself a stream a later program taps:

rejected : Stream<Rejected> = tap("orders_rejected")
rejected | map(r => {id: r.id, rules: r.rules})

{id: 3, rules: ["EventData.amount.type"]}
{id: 5, rules: ["EventData.customer.missing"]}
{id: 7, rules: ["EventData.non_negative"]}
{id: 8, rules: ["EventData.known_kind"]}

Transformation. The silver table ends, so it is read whole, and the report is written whole over the one before it:

type Revenue {
    customer : String
    orders   : Int
    total    : Decimal
}

events : Seq<Event> = source("orders_silver")
events
| filter(e => e.kind == "order_placed")
| group(by = e => e.customer)
| map(g => Revenue(customer = g.key, orders = g.items | size, total = g.items | map(e => e.amount) | sum))
| target("customer_revenue")

The two programs share no state but the table between them. The first runs for as long as messages arrive; the second runs when a report is wanted, and reads whatever the first has committed by then.

docs.title: What is not here
docs.text: One reader reads through one consumer: several programs sharing a consumer to divide its messages is not supported. Credential files for NATS are not read. A lakehouse table holds no nested column and has no constructor yet, and a Databricks endpoint is reached with a personal access token only.

docs.title: Writing with target and sink
docs.text: Writing has two forms, chosen by the shape of the value. target(endpoint, Format) writes one completed value as one document. sink(endpoint, Format) writes one document per value, as each arrives. Both end a program with a Step, its final computation step. A Step carries no value; HQL has no void type, and Step stands in for one. A local engine runs the step at once; another engine may schedule it as part of an execution plan. A Step prints nothing, so what a program below prints is what was written.

docs.title: One document with target
docs.text:
source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"))
| map(s => {species: s.species, site: s.site})
| target(stdout, Csv)

site,species
meadow,barn owl
hedge,wren
barn,barn owl
river,kingfisher

A Seq written by target is one document: in Csv a header and a row per element, in Json one array:

source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")) | map(s => s.species) | target(stdout, Json)

[
  "barn owl",
  "wren",
  "barn owl",
  "kingfisher"
]

Over a file, target replaces the file atomically: the document is written beside the destination and renamed over it when complete, so a reader never sees a partial file, and a failed write leaves the old file in place. Run from a directory of your own:

source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"))
| map(s => {species: s.species, site: s.site})
| target(file("sites.csv"))

$ cat sites.csv
site,species
meadow,barn owl
hedge,wren
barn,barn owl
river,kingfisher

docs.title: One document per value with sink
docs.text:
source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")) | map(s => s.species) | sink(stdout, Json)

"barn owl"
"wren"
"barn owl"
"kingfisher"

A Seq written by sink in Json is one JSON document per line, which is what JsonLines and Json both read back. A stream may never complete, so sink is how a stream is written. target over a stream that is not a Seq is a type error, and the diagnostic gives the two ways out:

source(stdin, Json) | target(file("all.json"))

check error[type-mismatch]: `target` writes one completed value, and Stream<Data> may not end; write it piece by piece with `sink`, or bound it with `take(n)` first
 --> <expression>:1:23
  |
1 | source(stdin, Json) | target(file("all.json"))
  |                       ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

What each step accepts, by the shape of the values:

Seq<T> Stream<T> that is not a Seq target one document a type error: sink, or take(n) first sink one document per element one document per value

A batch is a list, so collect(2) | sink(stdout, Json) writes one JSON array per two values (finite or live).

docs.title: Replace or append
docs.text:
Writing file(p) replaces the file. Writing file(p).end appends to it, and creates it when it is missing. Run twice, once with each species:

[{species: "wren"}] | sink(file("log.jsonl").end)

$ cat log.jsonl
{"species":"wren"}
{"species":"kite"}

sink over file(p) truncates the file before its first document and writes each document as it arrives, since a stream that never ends cannot be renamed into place.

One evaluation replaces a file at most once, appends to its end any number of times, and never both. Reading a file the same evaluation has replaced is an evaluation failure too, as is a missing parent directory: neither step creates a directory.

1 | target(file("a.json"))
2 | target(file("a.json"))

evaluation failure: a.json: this evaluation has already replaced the file; append to `file(p).end`, or write it once
 --> <expression>:2:5
  |
2 | 2 | target(file("a.json"))
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Branches that write
docs.text:
A tee branch from the SQL-like queries chapter may end in target or sink. The branch receives each value before the trunk does and writes it, and the trunk goes on with every value:

source(stdin, Json)
| tee dusk =
    filter(s => s.seen == "dusk")
    | sink(file("dusk.jsonl").end, Json)
| map(s => s.species)
| sink(stdout, Text)

$ cat examples/io/sightings.jsonl | hql '…'
barn owl
wren
barn owl
kingfisher
$ cat dusk.jsonl
{"seen":"dusk","site":"meadow","species":"barn owl"}

One program reads sightings as they arrive, appends those seen at dusk to a file, and prints every species. A failed write on any branch ends the evaluation with that error.

docs.title: Standard output and the result
docs.text: target(stdout, F) and sink(stdout, F) write while the program runs. The result of a program is a different thing: the host presents it after evaluation, in the format --to names (hql on the command line). A program that ends in target or sink has the result Step, and prints nothing beyond what it wrote.

docs.title: 10. The type system
docs.text: The chapters so far query and transform data with the types HQL provides. This one is about the types a program declares for itself, and the mechanisms that relate one type to another: records and unions, results, subtypes, generics, receiver calls, operators and traits. The Mighty Types corpus has one program per topic.

docs.title: Strong typing
docs.text:
HQL is strongly typed. Every value has one type, and an operation accepts only the types it declares: 412 + "pages" is a type error. No value is converted to another type implicitly: a function that takes a Decimal does not accept an Int. Arithmetic on an Int and a Decimal gives a Decimal, 12.50 * 3 is 37.50, and that is a rule of the operators, not a conversion (Decimal). The checker type-checks the whole program before it is evaluated, and a program with a type error evaluates nothing.

Strong typing does not mean every value has a fixed shape. A program states as much about a value's structure as it needs to, from nothing to every field and rule:

Type What it states about a value Data A tree of records, lists and scalars, as JSON and YAML have it. The type is Data; which keys a record holds is read as the program runs. Open type, type B : Data = {…} The declared fields, each with its type. Whatever else the tree holds is kept. Closed type, type A = {…} Exactly the declared fields. A tree with any other field does not read as it. Contract, TypeContract or DataContract A closed or an open shape, plus rules its values must hold: an id not empty, an age in a range, an email that is one.

A value moves down the table only by a type boundary, tree | T, which reads a tree as a declared type and either succeeds or fails; nothing is guessed. After the boundary every declared field has its declared type, and the program is ordinary typed code. Chapter 11 is the whole of it.

docs.title: One relation symbol
docs.text:
Everything the type system says is said with :. Between a value and a type it states what the value is, pages : Int. Between two types under type it states that one narrows the other, type Card : Doc. Between a type parameter and a type or trait it is a bound, T : Orderable. The three readings are one relation: a value of the narrower type is usable wherever the wider one is expected, and a bound asks for exactly that.

type Named { name : String }
type Person : Named { born : Int }

fn greet(n: Named) : String = fmt("hello, {}", n.name)

greet(Person(name = "Ada", born = 1815))

"hello, Ada"

A Person is a Named, so greet takes one with no step and no check at run time.

docs.title: Three mechanisms
docs.text:
Three mechanisms end with a value used at a stronger type than it started with, and the chapter keeps them apart.

Mechanism Written The question it answers Subtyping type Card : Doc Which types stand in for which? Generics type Stack<T> What does this declaration leave unknown? Refinement d \| is(Point) What is known about this one value?

Subtyping relates whole types. Generics write a declaration once for a family of types, and a bound is where the two meet: T : Doc restricts an unknown by the subtype relation. Refinement is a statement about one value, established by a test that can fail, and the value itself is never changed. Chapter 11 is refinement at the boundary where data arrives.

docs.title: Capabilities are traits
docs.text:
What a type is and what can be done with it are two different statements. type Card : Doc says a card is a document. That + adds two values of a type, or that a generic function may call area on its parameter, is a capability, stated by implementing a trait for the type. A trait is not a type: nothing is held as a Shape, and a trait's name appears in a bound, an implementation and another trait's declaration, nowhere else.

type Vec2 { x : Int, y : Int }

impl Add for Vec2 {
    fn add(self, other: Vec2) : Vec2 = Vec2(x = self.x + other.x, y = self.y + other.y)
}

Vec2(x = 1, y = 2) + Vec2(x = 3, y = 4)

Vec2(x = 4, y = 6)

docs.title: Types in modules
docs.text: A module declares types, traits and implementations as it declares functions, and a public type is visible by its name to every unit that imports the module. Chapter 5 writes and imports modules, and visibility keeps a type or trait private to its module. An implementation belongs with its trait or with its type: a program implements its own trait for any type and any trait for its own type, and never a core trait for a built-in one.

docs.title: The pages
docs.text: Page What it covers Records fields, the constructor, optional and nested fields, generic records, constructors a program declares Unions and match a type that is one of several, match covering every case, guards, literal and type patterns Results Result<T, E>, ok and err, the ways out, and why there is no unwrap Subtypes and narrowing type A : B, supertype sets, abstract types, widening by annotation, narrowing by test, conversion by construction Generics type parameters, bounds, generic traits and the inference that fills them Receiver calls value.f(args), how the name resolves, and the three spellings of one call Operators the core traits behind +, ==, <, xs[i] and xs[a:b] Traits required functions and default bodies, bounds, a trait extending a trait, and how a trait differs from inheritance

docs.title: Generics
docs.text: A declaration written once for every type names a type parameter, a capital letter in angle brackets. Each use fills it: Stack<Int>, first([1, 2]). Within one use a parameter names one type in every position it occurs, and the declaration is checked once for all of them.

docs.title: Parameters and bounds
docs.text:
Generic functions introduced the parameter and its bound. Inside a body, T is a type of its own, and the body may rely only on what the parameter promises. T : Orderable promises an order, so the body may take a minimum, and each call is checked against the bound:

fn shortest<T : Orderable>(xs: List<T>) : Option<T> = xs | min
[shortest([3, 1, 2]), shortest(["b", "a"]) | map(s => s.size())]

[1, 1]

A bound is a type, as Orderable is, or a trait, as Shape is in traits. Both are written with :, since both restrict the unknown by the one relation the language has. A record's parameter takes a bound after its fields, type Box<T> { value : T } where T : Orderable, and a value that breaks it is a type error at construction.

docs.title: A generic trait
docs.text:
A trait names another type only through a parameter. Index<T> in the standard library is the capability behind xs[i], and T is the element type its at returns. An implementation gives the trait its argument, and takes parameters of its own to bind the implementing type's:

type Ring<T> { items : List<T> }

impl<T> Index<T> for Ring<T> {
    fn at(self, position: Int) : Option<T> = self.items[position % size(self.items)]
}

birds = Ring(items = ["raven", "robin", "wren"])
[birds[0], birds[4], birds.at(5)]

["raven", "robin", "wren"]

< after impl opens the implementation's parameters, and < after the trait's name its arguments. Each parameter of the implementation must appear in the implementing type or in the trait's arguments; one that appears in neither is a type error. A trait named with the wrong number of arguments is one too: impl Index for Box<Int> says Index takes one type argument, not none.

docs.title: Inference fills what a call leaves open
docs.text:
A bound may name a generic trait with the function's own parameters as its arguments, E : Index<T>. A call fills E from its argument, and T from the one implementation of Index that type has:

type Countdown { from : Int }

impl Index<Int> for Countdown {
    fn at(self, position: Int) : Option<Int> = match position {
        p given p >= 0 and p <= self.from => some(self.from - p),
        _ => none,
    }
}

fn first_of<T, E : Index<T>>(xs: E) : Option<T> = xs[0]

[first_of([10, 20]), first_of(Countdown(from = 3))]

[10, 3]

A List<Int> takes the standard library's implementation for sequences, which gives T = Int; a Countdown takes its own, Index<Int>. A type with no implementation is a type error at the call, and the message names the bound: first_of(1) says an Int does not implement Index<T>. There are no associated types. A type that the implementing type decides, as the element type is, is a trait parameter that inference fills.

docs.title: One trait at several arguments
docs.text:
A type may implement one trait at several arguments, and a call's argument types choose between them:

trait Scale<F> {
    fn scale(self, by: F) : Self
}

type Vec2 { x : Float, y : Float }

impl Scale<Float> for Vec2 {
    fn scale(self, by: Float) : Vec2 = Vec2(x = self.x * by, y = self.y * by)
}

impl Scale<Int> for Vec2 {
    fn scale(self, by: Int) : Vec2 = self.scale(float(by))
}

v = Vec2(x = 1.5f, y = 2.0f)
[v.scale(2).x, v.scale(0.5f).x]

[3.0, 0.75]

Self in the trait is the implementing type, Vec2 in both implementations. A generic body reaches an implementation through its receiver alone, so a bound over a trait with functions, T : Scale<F>, needs a type that implements the trait once; a type implementing it at several arguments is a type error there, since the body could not tell them apart.

docs.title: One implementation per trait and type
docs.text:
An implementation is identified by its trait, the trait's arguments and the implementing type, and two that could apply to one type at one argument list are a type error, whichever is generic:

type Box<T> { value : T }
impl<T> Index<T> for Box<T> {
    fn at(self, position: Int) : Option<T> = some(self.value)
}
impl Index<Int> for Box<Int> {
    fn at(self, position: Int) : Option<Int> = some(self.value)
}
Box(value = 1)[0]

check error[duplicate-implementation]: `impl Index<Int> for Box<Int>` overlaps `impl Index<T> for Box<T>`, in this program, at byte 26: one type at one set of arguments has one implementation of a trait
 --> <expression>:5:1
  |
5 | impl Index<Int> for Box<Int> {
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = note: the first implementation, at <expression>:2:1

The rule holds across the standard library, the imported modules and the program together, and import order never chooses. An implementation for a type applies to the types narrowing it, and where two apply the narrower type's is the one, so a List takes the implementation for Seq. No implementation specializes another.

docs.title: Variance
docs.text: Values are never changed in place, so a parameter a type only produces is covariant: a List<Person> is a List<Named>, and an Option<Person> an Option<Named>, as the previous page used. A parameter a type consumes is not: a Map is invariant in its keys, since lookup accepts them, and a function type T -> U is contravariant in T and covariant in U.

docs.title: Operators
docs.text:
The operators of the language resolve through the core traits, which are in scope in every program. + resolves Add for its operand type, == resolves Eq, < resolves Ord, xs[i] resolves Index and xs[a:b] resolves Slice. The built-in types implement the traits they have natively; a type of the program implements one to take the operator for its own values, and changes nothing else.

Operator Trait Function a + b Add add(self, other: Self) : Self a - b Sub sub(self, other: Self) : Self a * b Mul mul(self, other: Self) : Self a / b Div div(self, other: Self) : Self a % b Rem rem(self, other: Self) : Self a == b, a != b Eq eq(self, other: Self) : Bool a < b and the other comparisons, sort, min, max Ord compare(self, other: Self) : Ordering xs[i] Index<T> at(self, position: Int) : Option<T> xs[a:b] Slice slice(self, range: Range) : Self

and, or and not are language-defined and resolve through nothing, and so are |, = and :.

docs.title: Arithmetic
docs.text:
An arithmetic operator takes two values of one type. For Int, Float and Decimal that is built in, and the built-in operators also take an Int and a Decimal together, giving a Decimal; + over two strings is concatenation, since String implements Add. Any other type resolves the operator through its trait:

type Money { cents : Int }
impl Sub for Money {
    fn sub(self, other: Money) : Money = Money(cents = self.cents - other.cents)
}
impl Mul for Money {
    fn mul(self, other: Money) : Money = Money(cents = self.cents * other.cents)
}
[(Money(cents = 500) - Money(cents = 120)).cents, (Money(cents = 3) * Money(cents = 4)).cents]

[380, 12]

A type without the implementation does not take the operator, and the message names the trait:

type Vec2 { x : Int, y : Int }
Vec2(x = 1, y = 2) + Vec2(x = 3, y = 4)

check error[type-mismatch]: addition requires two Int, two Float or two Decimal operands, or two values of a type implementing `Add`, not Vec2
 --> <expression>:2:1
  |
2 | Vec2(x = 1, y = 2) + Vec2(x = 3, y = 4)
