  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

An operator is a function value where a function is expected, so reduce(0, +) sums a list and reduce("", +) joins strings:

[[1, 2, 3] | reduce(0, +), ["a", "b"] | reduce("", +)]

[6, "ab"]

docs.title: Equality
docs.text:
== over a type implementing Eq calls its eq. Without one, equality is the type's own rule: a record field by field, a list position by position, a set when each holds an equal of every element of the other, a map key by key. A type that wants another equality declares it:

type Email { address : String }
impl Eq for Email {
    fn eq(self, other: Email) : Bool = self.address.lower() == other.address.lower()
}
[Email(address = "Ada@Example.org") == Email(address = "ada@example.org"), Email(address = "a") != Email(address = "b")]

[true, true]

docs.title: Order
docs.text:
A type implementing Ord supplies compare, which gives an Ordering, Less, Equal or Greater, and with it the type is Orderable: < and the other comparisons, sort, min and max take it, and it may be a SortedMap key.

type Version { major : Int, minor : Int }

impl Ord for Version {
    fn compare(self, other: Version) : Ordering =
        compare(self.major * 100 + self.minor, other.major * 100 + other.minor)
}

versions = [Version(major = 1, minor = 10), Version(major = 1, minor = 2), Version(major = 0, minor = 9)]
[versions | sort | map(v => fmt("{}.{}", v.major, v.minor)), [Version(major = 1, minor = 2) < Version(major = 1, minor = 10)] | map(str)]

[["0.9", "1.2", "1.10"], ["true"]]

A record without Ord has no order of its own. sort over it is a type error, and the message says to sort with an explicit key, sort(by = v => v.minor), which needs only the key's order.

docs.title: Positions
docs.text:
xs[i] over a type implementing Index<T> is xs.at(i): the element at the position, or none past the end. The standard library implements it for sequences, so a List, a String and a Bytes value take it, and a program's type takes it with one implementation, as generics did for a Ring<T>.

[["a", "b", "c"][1], ["a", "b", "c"][5]]

["b", none]

A Set has no positions and a Map has keys, and neither implements Index, so the bracket over them is a type error.

docs.title: Parts
docs.text:
xs[a:b] over a type implementing Slice is a part of the value, of the value's own type. A bound left out is open, and a negative bound counts from the end:

["hello"[1:3], "hello"[-2:]]

["el", "lo"]

The bracket holds either an Int, a position, or a Range, a slice, and the type of what is inside decides which. Range(start = 1, end = 3) is the value a slice takes, and a type that says what a part of its values is implements Slice for them:

type Playlist { name : String, tracks : List<String> }

impl Slice for Playlist {
    fn slice(self, range: Range) : Playlist = Playlist(name = self.name, tracks = self.tracks[range])
}

mix = Playlist(name = "mix", tracks = ["first", "second", "third"])
mix[1:].tracks

["second", "third"]

docs.title: The core traits are owned by the language
docs.text: A program implements a core trait for its own types, and never for a built-in one: impl Add for Int is a type error, since Add is already implemented for Int in the standard library, natively. The implementations the built-in types have are declared there as bodyless headers, and a built-in type implements exactly what its headers name: Bool has Eq and no Add, so true + false is a type error. A program declares no new operator traits either; the operators of the grammar are the operators there are.

docs.title: Receiver calls
docs.text: value.f(args) is a receiver call: a call to a function declared with a receiver, self, where the value fills self and the rest are the arguments. It is how the book has written "Dune".upper(), xs.size() and o.unwrap_or(0) since chapter 2, and this page is about what the dot does.

docs.title: Three spellings of one call
docs.text:
A function of a module is called through the module, as a receiver, or as a pipeline step, and the three are one call:

[[3, 1, 2].sort(), [3, 1, 2] | sort, sort([3, 1, 2])]

[[1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3]]

xs.sort() is sort(xs), and xs | sort is sort(xs) too. They differ in what they say to a reader. The dot is local evaluation, a function applied to a value, and chains left to right. The pipe is dataflow, a step in a pipeline the planner sees, and stays distinct from expression evaluation. A program chains text functions with dots and pipes collections through steps, and may write either.

"  Hello, World  ".trim().lower().split(", ").map(w => w.upper()).join(" / ")

"HELLO / WORLD"

docs.title: How the name resolves
docs.text:
A receiver call is resolved by the value's type among the modules in scope. The prelude's modules, string, seq, math, option and result among them, are receiver modules, each declared for a type pattern: module string for String makes each of its self functions a function of every String. Two modules may declare one name over different types, and the value's type picks: "abc".contains("b") is the string's, [1, 2].contains(2) the collection's.

A module written import string is also reachable by name, so the one function has a third spelling, string.upper("hi"):

import string
[string.upper("hi"), "hi".upper(), upper("hi")]

["HI", "HI", "HI"]

A name no module in scope declares for the value's type is a name error, with the nearest name offered:

"hi".shout()

check error[unknown-name]: String has no function `shout`
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | "hi".shout()
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = help: did you mean `sort`?

Two imported modules that declare one name over one type make a call by that name ambiguous, a name error until it is written through its module. A declaration the unit writes itself wins over every import's. Receiver modules declares them, and how names resolve has the rules in full.

docs.title: A receiver module in a program
docs.text:
A program may open a receiver module for a type it declares, once the type is in scope. The functions after the module line take self at the pattern, and the type's values take them:

type Point { x : Int, y : Int }
module geometry for Point
fn norm(self) : Int = self.x * self.x
Point(x = 3, y = 4).norm()

9

self is written untyped, since its type is the module's pattern. A pattern may be generic, module seq for Seq<T>, and then every Seq takes the functions.

docs.title: A trait's functions are receiver calls
docs.text:
A function of a trait is called on a value as a receiver function is, and resolves to the implementation for the value's own type. Held at a wider type, a union of two implementing types, the value still takes its own:

trait Named {
    fn name(self) : String
}
type Dog { tag : String }
type Cat { tag : String }
impl Named for Dog {
    fn name(self) : String = fmt("dog {}", self.tag)
}
impl Named for Cat {
    fn name(self) : String = fmt("cat {}", self.tag)
}
type Pet = union { Dog, Cat }
pets : List<Pet> = [Dog(tag = "rex"), Cat(tag = "tom")]
pets | map(p => match p { Dog d => d.name(), Cat c => c.name() })

["dog rex", "cat tom"]

A trait's function has no module to call it through: name(dog) is a name error, and the receiver form is the one spelling. Traits is about when a function belongs to a trait and when to a receiver module.

docs.title: A field is not a call
docs.text: p.x without parentheses reads a field, and p.x() calls a function named x on the value. The two never collide: a record declares its fields, a module its functions, and the dot reads whichever the name is.

docs.title: Records
docs.text: A type with fields is a record. It declares a shape: which fields a value has, and the type of each. A record is a type of the program that declares it, and nothing else is a Point.

docs.title: Declaring and building
docs.text:
A record is declared with its fields in braces, each a name, a colon and a type, on one line separated by commas or one per line. Its constructor is its name, taking the fields by name, and a dot reads a field:

type Point { x : Int, y : Int }

p = Point(x = 1, y = 2)
[p.x, p.y]

[1, 2]

The fields may also be given in declaration order, Point(1, 2). A value prints as its constructor call, Point(x = 1, y = 2), so what the book shows is what builds it.

A record value is complete. Leaving a field out is a type error naming the field, and a field at the wrong type is one naming the type:

type Point { x : Int, y : Int }
Point(x = 1)

check error[type-mismatch]: `Point` needs `y`
 --> <expression>:2:1
  |
2 | Point(x = 1)
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^

Reading a field the record does not declare is a name error, before the program runs. A record has no hidden fields: what it declares is what a value has, and all of it is readable.

docs.title: Nested records
docs.text:
A field may be of a record type, and a path reads through it:

type Point { x : Int, y : Int }
type Rectangle { top_left : Point, bottom_right : Point }

fn area(r: Rectangle) : Int = (r.bottom_right.x - r.top_left.x) * (r.bottom_right.y - r.top_left.y)

area(Rectangle(top_left = Point(x = 0, y = 0), bottom_right = Point(x = 4, y = 3)))

12

docs.title: Optional fields
docs.text:
A field written email? : String may be absent. It reads as an Option<String>, none where nothing was given, and it may be left out at construction:

type Contact { name : String, email? : String }

[Contact(name = "Ada"), Contact(name = "Bob", email = "bob@example.com")] | map(c => c.email | unwrap_or("-"))

["-", "bob@example.com"]

Contact(name = "Ada") prints as Contact(name = "Ada", email = none). Absence is a value of the field, and chapter 2 has the ways out of an Option.

docs.title: Equality
docs.text:
Two records of one type are equal when their fields are, field by field. Nothing is declared for it:

type Point { x : Int, y : Int }
[Point(x = 1, y = 2) == Point(x = 1, y = 2), Point(x = 1, y = 2) == Point(x = 2, y = 1)]

[true, false]

A type that wants another equality implements Eq, as operators shows.

docs.title: Generic records
docs.text:
A record may take type parameters, and takes them from the values it is built from: Stack(items = [1, 2]) is a Stack<Int>, and Stack(items = ["a"]) a Stack<String>. A function over it names the same parameter:

type Stack<T> { items : List<T> }

fn push<T>(s: Stack<T>, x: T) : Stack<T> = Stack(items = concat(s.items, [x]))
fn peek<T>(s: Stack<T>) : Option<T> = s.items.last()

s = Stack(items = [1, 2]) | push(3)
peek(s)

3

Pushing "three" onto a Stack<Int> is a type error: within one use a parameter names one type in every position it occurs. The prelude's Pair<A, B> is a generic record, the element zip and enumerate produce, and Pair(first = p.second, second = p.first) swaps one.

A parameter may carry a bound, written after the fields: type Box<T> { value : T } where T : Orderable. A Box of a set is then a type error at construction, since a set has no order. Generics is about parameters and bounds in full.

docs.title: A record under another
docs.text: A record declared under another record, type Person : Named { born : Int }, has the fields of both. A Person is a Named, so it is taken wherever a Named is expected, as the chapter's first program showed, and a contract's rules are inherited the same way (type contracts).

docs.title: Constructors a program declares
docs.text:
Beside the constructor its fields give it, a type may declare constructors of its own: a function named after the type, in the unit that declares the type, returning it. Temp below is built from a temperature in Celsius as well as from its field:

type Temp { kelvin : Float }

fn Temp(celsius: Float) : Temp = Temp(kelvin = celsius + 273.0f)

[Temp(1.0f).kelvin, (2.0f | Temp).kelvin, Temp(kelvin = 5.0f).kelvin]

[274.0, 275.0, 5.0]

A constructor is an operation like any other, so it has two forms: called, Temp(1.0f), and as a pipeline step, 2.0f | Temp, where the piped value is its first argument. It is also a function value: xs | map(Temp) builds one per element. A type may have several constructors, told apart by the type of their first parameter.

A function in UpperCamelCase is a constructor and nothing else. One named after no declared type is a type error, and the message says to name it in snake_case. The standard constructors follow the same rule: List(xs), Set(xs) and Map(keys, values) are declared beside their types, and subtypes and narrowing uses them as the conversion between collections.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: Result<T, E> is a computation that may have failed: ok(v) holding a T, or err(e) holding an E that says how. The possibility of failure is in the type, so a caller cannot forget it, and the error is a value, so a program can say what it is.

docs.title: Building and matching
docs.text:
ok(v) and err(e) build a result, and ok(p) and err(p) match one. An error is any type, here a record the program declares for it:

type ParseError { input : String, reason : String }

fn parse_age(text: String) : Result<Int, ParseError> = match text.to_int() {
    some(n) given n >= 0 => ok(n),
    some(_) => err(ParseError(input = text, reason = "negative")),
    none => err(ParseError(input = text, reason = "not a number")),
}

["42", "-3", "forty"] | map(parse_age)

[ok(42), err(ParseError(input = "-3", reason = "negative")), err(ParseError(input = "forty", reason = "not a number"))]

A match over a result covers both cases, and a missing one is a type error, as over any union:

type ParseError { input : String, reason : String }

fn parse_age(text: String) : Result<Int, ParseError> = match text.to_int() {
    some(n) given n >= 0 => ok(n),
    some(_) => err(ParseError(input = text, reason = "negative")),
    none => err(ParseError(input = text, reason = "not a number")),
}

fn describe(r: Result<Int, ParseError>) : String = match r {
    ok(n) => fmt("age {}", n),
    err(e) => fmt("cannot read {}: {}", e.input, e.reason),
}

["42", "-3", "forty"] | map(parse_age) | map(describe)

["age 42", "cannot read -3: negative", "cannot read forty: not a number"]

docs.title: The ways out
docs.text:
The ways out of a Result mirror Option's. map transforms the value an ok holds and leaves an err as it is. and_then chains a second computation that may fail. unwrap_or leaves the result with a value for the error case:

fn parse(text: String) : Result<Int, String> = match text.to_int() {
    some(n) => ok(n),
    none => err(fmt("not a number: {}", text)),
}

[
    parse("7").map(n => n * 2).unwrap_or(0),
    parse("x").map(n => n * 2).unwrap_or(0),
    parse("7").and_then(n => parse("1").map(m => n + m)).unwrap_or(0)
]

[14, 0, 8]

map_err transforms the error and leaves an ok as it is. ok() and err() give either side as an Option, the other side being none:

fn parse(text: String) : Result<Int, String> = match text.to_int() {
    some(n) => ok(n),
    none => err("no"),
}
[parse("4").ok(), parse("x").ok(), parse("x").err()]

[4, none, "no"]

Over a collection of results, oks() keeps the values of the successes and errs() the errors of the failures, each at its own type:

fn parse(text: String) : Result<Int, String> = match text.to_int() {
    some(n) => ok(n),
    none => err(fmt("not a number: {}", text)),
}
rs = ["4", "x", "9"] | map(parse)
[rs | filter(r => r.is_ok()) | size, rs | oks(), rs | errs()]

[2, [4, 9], ["not a number: x"]]

docs.title: There is no unwrap
docs.text: Every way out of a Result says what the error case means: a match names it, unwrap_or replaces it, ok() makes it an absence. There is no operation that takes the value and stops the program otherwise. parse("4").unwrap() is a name error, since no such function exists. A failure the program cannot handle as a value is an evaluation failure, raised by the runtime and not caught by HQL code; the two are kept apart, and a Result is for the failures a program expects of its input.

docs.title: Where results come from
docs.text: Parsing, decoding and validation are the operations whose failure is an expected consequence of their input, and each has a Result form. validate(T) reads a tree as a contract and gives Result<T, Invalid>, with every reason for a failure inside the error; over a collection it is elementwise, and oks(), errs() and fork route the two sides. Validation as a value is that pattern in full.

docs.title: Subtypes and narrowing
docs.text: type A : B declares that A narrows B: every value of A is a value of B, with structure or constraints of its own. The relation reads from the specific toward the general. Nothing is extended or changed by writing it: B's declaration is unchanged, and the declaration is a claim about A alone.

docs.title: A subtype passes as its supertype
docs.text:
A value of the narrower type is usable wherever the wider one is expected, with no step and no check at run time. A Person : Named is a Named, and a list of persons is a list of named things, since a List of a subtype is a List of the supertype:

type Named { name : String }
type Person : Named { born : Int }

fn names(xs: List<Named>) : List<String> = xs | map(n => n.name)

names([Person(name = "Ada", born = 1815)])

["Ada"]

An annotation widens the same way. xs : Seq<Int> = [1, 2, 3] holds the list at the abstract type Seq, and xs : Collection<Int> = {1, 2, 3} a set at Collection. The value is the same value; the binding says less about it.

docs.title: An annotation never converts
docs.text:
An annotation to a type the value is not a subtype of is a type error. The message names what would build the value, since building is a cost the program writes where it is paid:

xs : Set<Int> = [1, 2, 2]
xs

check error[type-mismatch]: `xs` is declared Set<Int> but its value is List<Int>; a binding never converts, so construct it: `Set(…)`
 --> <expression>:1:17
  |
1 | xs : Set<Int> = [1, 2, 2]
  |                 ^^^^^^^^^

The same holds downward: n : Int = d over a Data value is a type error, because a Data is not known to be an Int. Going toward the subtype is a test, below.

docs.title: Several supertypes at once
docs.text:
A type may narrow several types, written as a set in braces: type Int : {Scalar, Orderable} in the standard library says an integer is a leaf and has an order. The set is a conjunction, every parent at once, and differs from a union, which is a choice. Two abstract types never exclude each other, since each is satisfied by other types. Two concrete types can share nothing, and the checker rejects such a set:

type Impossible : {Int, String}
1

check error[type-mismatch]: nothing is both Int and String, so this supertype set declares a type no value can have
 --> <expression>:1:25
  |
1 | type Impossible : {Int, String}
  |                         ^^^^^^

docs.title: Abstract types
docs.text:
An abstract type is defined by what holds of its values, not by a representation, and has no values of its own. Orderable is the type of values with a total order; Scalar of leaves; Seq<T> of finite, positioned collections, which List<T> narrows; Collection<T> of finite collections, which Set<T> narrows. An abstract type has no constructor, and a program declares one with abstract type:

abstract type Shape
type Circle : Shape { radius : Float }
fn describe(x: Shape) : String = "a shape"
describe(Circle(radius = 1.0f))

"a shape"

An abstract type is where a bound usually points. T : Orderable admits every type with an order: the built-in ordered types declare Orderable as a parent, and a program's type joins them by implementing Ord, as operators shows.

docs.title: Narrowing is a test
docs.text:
Toward the subtype a value goes only by a test, which can fail. is(U) asks whether a value is a U and gives a Bool. of_type(U) keeps the elements of a collection that are, at type U; it is filter with an is test, and the narrowing is the checker reading that predicate. A match arm written with a type does the same for one value:

[1, "owl", 2] | of_type(Int)

[1, 2]

Over a union, the test selects a member: shapes | of_type(Circle) from a List<Shape> is a List<Circle>. Over a Data tree, the test is by shape, and the value it binds is read at the type it passed, as chapter 11 describes. There is no assertion: a value that may not be a U is selected, matched or tested, never cast.

docs.title: Conversion is construction
docs.text:
Changing the container a value is in is building a new one, and the constructor of the target type does it. Set(xs) holds the distinct elements of a list, and xs | Set is the same call:

[1, 2, 2] | Set

{1, 2}

A constructor takes only what its type can honestly hold. List({1, 2}) is a type error, since a set has no order for a list to keep, and the message names sort, which orders a collection into a list. List over a stream that may not end is a type error naming take and collect. A constructor changes the container and keeps the elements; turning a String into an Int is parsing, text.to_int(), which gives an Option because it can fail.

docs.title: Side by side
docs.text:
is(U) of_type(U) a binding x : U List(xs), Set(xs) Does tests selects and narrows widens builds Direction none down up to another container Checked at run time at run time before running before running Can drop values no yes no Set drops duplicates Builds a value no yes, the selection no yes

There is no cast. Each of the four has its own name because each has its own properties, and the name written at the call states which check runs, and when.

docs.title: Traits
docs.text: A trait is a capability contract over a type: a named set of functions that an implementing type provides, each taking that type as self. A type satisfies a trait through one implementation, impl Trait for Type. The type checker verifies every implementation and every trait bound before the program runs. A function of a trait is either required, a signature with no body that every implementation supplies, or has a default body, which an implementation inherits unless it writes the function itself.

docs.title: In short
docs.text:
• A trait is not a type. No value, parameter or binding is typed by a trait. A function over every implementing type takes a bound, <T : Shape>(s: T), and a call through it runs the implementation of the value's own type. See A trait is not a type and Generic functions over a trait.
  • One construct, three uses. A capability trait is named in bounds. An operator trait is what an operator resolves through: Eq for ==, Ord for <, Index for xs[i]. A validator trait extends Validator and states a check that a value passes. See Operators are traits and Validators.
  • Two ways to implement. impl Shape for Rect { … }, or a trait list on a receiver module, module shapes.circle for Circle : Shape, whose self functions are the implementation. See A module that implements a trait.
  • One implementation per trait and type, whichever form declares it.
  • A trait may name a type. trait Shape as Figure declares Figure, the union of the types that implement Shape, so a List<Figure> holds a Rect and a Circle together. See A trait's type.
  • A validator field is a refinement. In a field email: Email, Email is a validator trait. The field's type is the one type that implements it, and the field's value is held to its check. See Validators.

docs.title: A trait and an implementation
docs.text:
Shape requires area and gives describe a default body. impl Shape for Rect writes area alone:

trait Shape {
    fn area(self) : Float
    fn describe(self) : String = fmt("area {}", self.area())
}

type Rect { width : Float, height : Float }

impl Shape for Rect {
    fn area(self) : Float = self.width * self.height
}

describe is a function of every Rect all the same, with the trait's body. The programs below run with these declarations before them:

Rect(width = 2.0f, height = 3.0f).describe()

"area 6.0"

docs.title: A default body calls the implementation
docs.text:
Inside a default body, self.area() resolves to the area of the type self has. The body is written once, against the required functions, and each type it runs over contributes its own:

type Circle { radius : Float }

impl Shape for Circle {
    fn area(self) : Float = 3.0f * self.radius * self.radius
}

[Rect(width = 2.0f, height = 3.0f).describe(), Circle(radius = 1.0f).describe()]

["area 6.0", "area 3.0"]

docs.title: Replacing a default
docs.text:
An implementation that writes a function the trait gives a default replaces the default for its type, and leaves it in place for every other type:

type Square { side : Float }

impl Shape for Square {
    fn area(self) : Float = self.side * self.side
    fn describe(self) : String = fmt("a square of side {}", self.side)
}

[Rect(width = 2.0f, height = 3.0f).describe(), Square(side = 2.0f).describe()]

["area 6.0", "a square of side 2.0"]

docs.title: What an implementation must supply
docs.text:
An implementation without one of the required functions is a type error at its impl line, and the diagnostic names the function:

trait Shape {
    fn area(self) : Float
    fn describe(self) : String = fmt("area {}", self.area())
}

type Circle { radius : Float }

impl Shape for Circle {
    fn describe(self) : String = "a circle"
}

Circle(radius = 1.0f).describe()

check error[missing-implementation]: `impl Shape for Circle` lacks `area`
 --> <expression>:8:1
  |
8 | impl Shape for Circle {
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A trait has one implementation per type in a program. The checker rejects a second:

trait Named {
    fn name(self) : String
}

type Dog { tag : String }

impl Named for Dog {
    fn name(self) : String = self.tag
}

impl Named for Dog {
    fn name(self) : String = "a dog"
}

Dog(tag = "rex").name()

check error[duplicate-implementation]: `Named` is already implemented for Dog: a trait has one implementation per type
  --> <expression>:11:1
   |
11 | impl Named for Dog {
   | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
   = note: the first implementation, at <expression>:7:1

docs.title: Generic functions over a trait
docs.text:
A bound, T : Shape, restricts a type parameter to the types that implement the trait. Inside the body x.area() resolves through the bound, and every call is checked against it:

type Circle { radius : Float }

impl Shape for Circle {
    fn area(self) : Float = 3.0f * self.radius * self.radius
}

fn total<T : Shape>(xs: List<T>) : Float = xs | map(x => x.area()) | sum

[total([Rect(width = 2.0f, height = 3.0f), Rect(width = 1.0f, height = 1.0f)]), total([Circle(radius = 1.0f)])]

[7.0, 3.0]

A call with a type that has no implementation is a type error:

trait Shape {
    fn area(self) : Float
}

type Line { length : Float }

fn total<T : Shape>(xs: List<T>) : Float = xs | map(x => x.area()) | sum

total([Line(length = 2.0f)])

check error[unsatisfied-bound]: `total` needs T : Shape, and Line does not implement `Shape`
 --> <expression>:9:1
  |
9 | total([Line(length = 2.0f)])
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: A trait is not a type
docs.text:
A trait's name appears only where a contract is meant: in a bound, in an impl, in another trait's declaration, in a receiver module's trait list and, for a validator trait, in a contract. It is not a type, so no parameter, binding or list is typed by one, and the refusal names the bound to write instead:

trait Shape {
    fn area(self) : Float
}

fn doubled(s: Shape) : Float = s.area() * 2.0f

1

check error[unknown-name]: `Shape` is a trait, not a type: a value of a type implementing it is written with a bound, `<T : Shape>(x: T)`
 --> <expression>:5:15
  |
5 | fn doubled(s: Shape) : Float = s.area() * 2.0f
  |               ^^^^^

A list that holds a Rect and a Circle together is typed by a union of the two, and a match reaches each member at its own type, where its implementation applies:

type Figure = union { Rect, Circle }

figures : List<Figure> = [Rect(width = 2.0f, height = 3.0f), Circle(radius = 1.0f)]

figures | map(f => match f {
    Rect r => r.describe(),
    Circle c => c.describe(),
})

["area 6.0", "area 3.0"]

docs.title: A trait's type
docs.text:
A trait's declaration may name the union of the types implementing it: trait Shape as Figure declares the trait Shape and the type Figure. Figure's members are the types with an implementation of Shape, so List<Figure> holds a Rect and a Circle, and f.describe() calls the implementation of the value's own type:

trait Shape as Figure {
    fn area(self) : Float
    fn describe(self) : String = fmt("area {}", self.area())
}

type Rect { width : Float, height : Float }
type Circle { radius : Float }

impl Shape for Rect {
    fn area(self) : Float = self.width * self.height
}

impl Shape for Circle {
    fn area(self) : Float = 3.0f * self.radius * self.radius
}

figures : List<Figure> = [Rect(width = 2.0f, height = 3.0f), Circle(radius = 1.0f)]

figures | map(f => f.describe())

["area 6.0", "area 3.0"]

Figure is a union and is checked as one: a match over it covers every member. It implements Shape, so it satisfies a bound T : Shape. Two values of Figure may be of two members, so a trait naming its type writes Self only as the receiver, never as a parameter or a result; and a trait with type parameters, or a validator trait, names no type.

docs.title: A trait extending a trait
docs.text:
A trait may extend others, trait Greeter : Named. The functions of the traits it extends are its own, so its default bodies may call them, and an implementation of it supplies them:

trait Named {
    fn name(self) : String
}

trait Greeter : Named {
    fn greet(self) : String = fmt("hello, {}", self.name())
}

type Dog { tag : String }

impl Greeter for Dog {
    fn name(self) : String = self.tag
}

Dog(tag = "rex").greet()

"hello, rex"

Implementing Greeter does not implement Named. A bound T : Named takes only the types with an impl Named of their own:

trait Named {
    fn name(self) : String
}

trait Greeter : Named { }

type Dog { tag : String }

impl Greeter for Dog {
    fn name(self) : String = self.tag
}

fn names<T : Named>(xs: List<T>) : List<String> = xs | map(x => x.name())

names([Dog(tag = "rex")])

check error[unsatisfied-bound]: `names` needs T : Named, and Dog does not implement `Named`
  --> <expression>:15:1
   |
15 | names([Dog(tag = "rex")])
   | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Operators are traits
docs.text: The operators resolve through the core traits, which are in scope everywhere: + through Add, == through Eq, < and sort through Ord, xs[i] through Index and xs[a:b] through Slice. Implementing one gives a type its operator, and operators has each.

docs.title: Traits and inheritance
docs.text:
A default body is the part of class inheritance a trait has: code written once against functions each type defines. The rest is absent.

Class inheritance A trait a subclass inherits method bodies an implementation inherits default bodies a subclass inherits fields a trait declares no fields a subclass is a subtype of its parent a trait is not a type; no value is held as a Shape a method overrides along a chain of parents, reaching up with super an implementation replaces a default, one level, with no super a class extends one parent or several a trait extends traits; a type implements each trait it needs, once

Where one value is genuinely another, as a Card is a Doc, HQL says so with an ordinary : between types, not with a trait.

docs.title: A receiver function without a trait
docs.text:
A receiver module adds functions to a type with no trait at all. module counting for Int makes each self function after it a function of every Int:

module counting for Int

fn twice(self) : Int = self * 2

[3.twice(), 21.twice()]

[6, 42]

The functions reach only the source unit that declares the module or imports it. Elsewhere the call is a name error, as "hi".shout() is without import mighty.text (receiver modules):

"hi".shout()

check error[unknown-name]: String has no function `shout`
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | "hi".shout()
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = help: did you mean `sort`?

Two imported modules that declare one name over one type make a call by that name ambiguous, and the call is a name error until it is qualified. A declaration the unit writes itself wins over every import's.

A trait is the form for a function that generic code quantifies over or an operator resolves through. A receiver module is the form for a function a type gains that nothing quantifies over.

docs.title: A module that implements a trait
docs.text:
A receiver module may list traits after its pattern, and its self functions are then the implementation of those traits for the pattern's type. The module shapes of examples/traits/lib declares Shape, with a default describe, and shapes/circle.hql implements it:

module shapes.circle for Circle : Shape

import shapes

type Circle { radius : Float }

fn area(self) : Float = 3.0f * self.radius * self.radius
fn name(self) : String = "circle"
fn diameter(self) : Float = 2.0f * self.radius

module shapes.circle for Circle : Shape declares the one implementation of Shape for Circle, as impl Shape for Circle would, with the module's area and name as its functions and the trait's default describe. diameter, which Shape does not require, stays a receiver function:

import shapes
import shapes.circle

c = Circle(radius = 1.0f)

[c.describe(), str(shapes.total([c, c])), str(c.diameter())]

["circle with area 3.0", "6.0", "2.0"]

A module that lists a trait and lacks a function the trait requires, and gives no default body for, is refused at its module line, and so is a module listing two traits that require one function name. The standard library states the brackets this way: module string for String : Index<String>, Slice makes s[1] the module's s.at(1), and s[1:3] its s.slice(Range(start = 1, end = 3)).

docs.title: Unions and match
docs.text: A union is a type whose value is exactly one of several alternatives. match is how a value of one is taken apart, one arm per alternative, and the checker requires every alternative to be covered.

docs.title: A union lists alternatives
docs.text:
type Shape = union { Circle, Square } declares that a Shape is a Circle or a Square. A match over it binds each member at its own type, and the arm sees that type's fields:

type Circle { radius : Float }
type Square { side : Float }
type Shape = union { Circle, Square }

fn area(s: Shape) : Float = match s {
    Circle c => 3.0f * c.radius * c.radius,
    Square q => q.side * q.side,
}

shapes : List<Shape> = [Circle(radius = 1.0f), Square(side = 2.0f)]
shapes | map(area)

[3.0, 4.0]

The annotation on shapes holds the literal at the union. Without it, a list of a Circle and a Square is a type error: the two meet nowhere on their own, and the message says the elements have no common type. A union is written with = and union, and that is the only way a type is one of several; type Id = Int is not a declaration.

A Circle passes where a Shape is expected with no step, since it is a member. Going the other way, from the union to a member, is a match, or is(Circle) and of_type(Circle) over a collection, as subtypes and narrowing describes.

docs.title: A match covers every case
docs.text:
A match is checked for coverage. Leaving a member out is a type error, and the message says how to complete it:

type Circle { radius : Float }
type Square { side : Float }
type Shape = union { Circle, Square }

fn area(s: Shape) : Float = match s {
    Circle c => 3.0f * c.radius * c.radius,
}

area(Circle(radius = 1.0f))

check error[non-exhaustive-match]: this match does not cover every Shape: cover every member of the union with a type pattern, or add `_`
 --> <expression>:5:29
  |
5 | fn area(s: Shape) : Float = match s {
  |                             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

_ fits anything. A match over an Int or a String has more values than arms can name, so it needs one; a match over an Option needs some and none, and one over a Result needs ok and err. This is what makes a case safe to consume: a forgotten alternative is a type error, not a silent default.

docs.title: Literal patterns and guards
docs.text:
A pattern may be a literal, a name that binds the value, or _. A guard, given after the pattern, narrows an arm with a condition. The first arm whose pattern fits and whose guard holds produces the result:

fn sign(n: Int) : String = match n {
    0 => "zero",
    k given k < 0 => "negative",
    _ => "positive",
}
[sign(-5), sign(0), sign(3)]

["negative", "zero", "positive"]

A guarded arm does not count toward coverage, since its condition may fail. Two guarded arms over an Int with no _ are a type error, even where their conditions together cover every number: the checker reads the patterns, not the arithmetic.

docs.title: Type patterns over a tree
docs.text:
Over a Data value, whose leaf could hold any scalar, an arm written with a type both tests and reads: Int n fits a leaf holding an integer and binds it as an Int.

fn classify(x: Data) : String = match x {
    Int n => fmt("int {}", n),
    String s => fmt("text {}", s),
    _ => "other",
}
[classify(1), classify("hi"), classify(true)]

["int 1", "text hi", "other"]

The same arm reads a tree as a declared record, Book b, when the tree has the record's fields at their types, as chapter 11 describes. Data is itself a union, declared in the standard library as a scalar leaf, a sequence of trees or a string-keyed map of trees, which is why whatever handles a Data may rely on there being three cases.

docs.title: Nested patterns
docs.text:
A pattern nests: some(1) fits a present value equal to one, some(_) any present value.

match [1, 2, 3].first() {
    some(1) => "starts with one",
    some(_) => "starts otherwise",
    none => "empty",
}

"starts with one"

docs.title: The short form
docs.text:
given … otherwise is a two-arm match on a Bool, read as a sentence: this value, given a condition, otherwise that one.

[17, 42] | map(age => "adult" given age >= 18 otherwise "minor")

["minor", "adult"]

Without otherwise the result is an Option: a value given a condition, and nothing otherwise, is a value that may be absent. "adult" given age >= 18 over the same two ages is [none, "adult"], and otherwise is the same step as unwrap_or on that Option.

docs.title: 11. Advanced data typing
docs.text: Chapter 2 read JSON-shaped trees as Data, and chapter 10 declared records of the program's own. This chapter is about the step between them: how a tree that arrived from outside becomes a value the program has a type for, and how a program states what it requires of that value beyond its shape. The structural examples have one program per case.

docs.title: The type boundary
docs.text:
Data from outside a program has no declared type when the program is checked. A JSON file, a message, a document's frontmatter or an API response decodes to Data, a tree whose leaves could hold anything. A program may carry the tree as it is and test each leaf where it is used, as the match arms of chapter 2 do. That works, and it spreads one decision over every place the data is read.

HQL's answer is a type boundary: one step, written tree | T, that reads the tree as a declared type T and either succeeds, giving a value of type T whose every field has a declared type, or fails when it runs. After the boundary the program is ordinary typed code. Before it, the data is Data, and nothing is assumed about it.

type Point = {
    x: Int
    y: Int
}

d : Data = {x: 1, y: 2}
p = d | Point
p.x + p.y

3

The rule the chapter rests on is this: a type is inferred while the information to infer it is present, and where structure is dynamic or absent, the program writes an explicit boundary rather than leaving a type to be assumed. The boundary is where a decision about the data is made, once, instead of being postponed to every reader of the value.

docs.title: Four kinds of structural type
docs.text:
A record type declared with fields reads a tree in one of four ways, depending on two independent choices. The first is whether the type is closed, admitting exactly its declared fields, or open, requiring its declared fields and keeping whatever else the tree holds. The second is whether it is a plain type, which states a shape, or a contract, which states a shape and rules the values must hold.

Plain Contract Closed type A = {…} type C : TypeContract = {…} Open type B : Data = {…} type D : DataContract = {…}

Whether a field is optional, email?: String, is a third choice, made per field, and has no bearing on the other two: a closed type with optional fields is still closed.

docs.title: Typing is not mapping
docs.text: Reading a tree as a type changes the type the value is checked as. It does not change the value. An open view over a tree with twelve fields still holds twelve fields beneath the three it declares, and the same tree read as another view exposes the others. Changing the value, renaming a field, trimming a string or dropping what a consumer does not need, is a map, written where the change is paid for. The two are kept apart on purpose: a reader of raw | UserData knows nothing was altered, and a reader of map(…) knows nothing was checked.

docs.title: Contracts are more than schemas
docs.text: A schema says what a value looks like: field names, types, optionality, nesting. A contract says that and what the value must mean: that an id is not empty, that an account that is closed says when, that an age lies in a range, that an email is one. The rules are written in the type, beside the fields they constrain, and hold wherever a value of the type is made. A schema can be exported from a contract; the rules are what the export loses.

docs.title: The pages
docs.text: Page What it covers Open and closed types type A = {…} against type B : Data = {…}, what each reads, what each refuses, and optional fields Type contracts TypeContract: a closed type with rules, for the program's canonical values Data contracts DataContract: an open contract for data from outside, defaults, presence and implication Validators a check with a name, validate f with Email, and the standard validators Validation as a value validate(T), Result<T, Invalid>, every violation at once, and routing the rejected Contracts and schemas what a schema states, what a contract adds, and where each lives

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: A value that does not read as its type is one of two kinds of failure. Chapter 12 is the whole error model: failures kept as data, and the diagnostics a phase writes when it cannot do what the program asked.

docs.title: Contracts and schemas
docs.text: Data arriving from outside passes three distinct things on its way to a typed value, and HQL keeps them apart. A format says how bytes are read. A schema says what a value looks like. A contract says what a value means, and whether it is acceptable.

docs.title: What a schema states
docs.text: A schema, a JSON Schema, an Avro record, a table's DDL, states field names, field types, which fields may be absent or null, and how records nest. It is a statement about representation: enough for a producer and a consumer to agree on the bytes. The structural half of an HQL type is a schema in this sense, and the four kinds of type on the first page add one thing a schema is usually silent on: whether fields the type does not name are admitted.

docs.title: What a contract adds
docs.text:
A contract has a schema and more. Every item below is written in the type, is checked wherever a value of the type is made, and is lost when the contract is exported to a schema language:

  • Rules over values. require id != "", require age? <= 150. A schema can say age is an integer; it cannot say which integers.
  • Rules across fields. require low <= high, require status == "closed" => closed_at?. A schema sees one field at a time.
  • Presence as a condition. require email? or phone?: at least one of two, which no optionality marker on either field can state.
  • Named checks. validate country with is_country_code, or a field declared email: Email. The check is a function or a type with a name, not a pattern string.
  • Defaults. country: String = "CH", filled before the rules run, so an older producer that never sent the field still satisfies a newer consumer.
  • Severity. warn against require: a rule the value may break and remain valid.
  • A stable identity per rule, UserData.id_present, and a structured record per failure, so a program and not only a reader can act on what went wrong.
  • Inheritance. A record declared under a contract has its rules.

And one thing a contract does not do. It does not reshape a value. A default fills what is absent; everything else that changes a value is a map, and the boundary between the two stays visible in the program.

docs.title: Where each lives
docs.text:
The three things have three homes.

The format is named at the source: source(file(p), Json) decodes bytes to Data, and the format is never a step of the pipeline. Formats and documents in the I/O chapter reads and writes through formats.

The mapping between an external system's own schema and an HQL type, its column names, physical types, nullable columns and CSV headers, is the schema boundary of a configured endpoint. It belongs to the configuration of that source, beside its connection, since it is a fact about the external system and not about the program's types. It is described with endpoints by id; a program declares HQL types only, and the boundary states what they meet.

The contract is declared in the program, where the values are used. It is the consumer's statement of what it requires, written once and held by every reading:

type Sighting : DataContract = {
    species: String
    seen: String

    require seen == "morning" or seen == "dusk" or seen == "night"
}

source(file("examples/structural/sightings.jsonl"), Json)
| validate(Sighting)
| oks()
| map(s => fmt("{} at {}", s.species, s.seen))

["barn owl at dusk", "wren at morning", "barn owl at night", "kingfisher at morning"]

The file's site field is not declared, and the open contract keeps it. The rule over seen is something no schema of the file could state. Were a fifth sighting to arrive seen at "noon", it would be an err in the results with the rule named, and the other four would read.

docs.title: Open contracts and change
docs.text:
Upstream data changes. A DataContract admits a field the producer adds, so the consumer's program is untouched by additions it does not read. A TypeContract refuses the same addition, which is the right answer for a value the program itself defines: an undeclared field there is a mistake, not an evolution. Choosing the open form for what is received and the closed form for what is owned is most of what makes a pipeline survive its inputs changing.

A contract's rules can change too, and a rule made stricter is a change in what the contract admits even when no field changes type. Reading the rules beside the fields, in the program, is what makes that visible.

docs.title: Data contracts
docs.text: type UserData : DataContract = {…} is an open contract: a tree reads as it when the declared fields are present at their types and the rules hold, and whatever else the tree holds is kept beneath the view. It is the form for data the program does not produce: a payload, an event, a document's frontmatter, a row from a system with fields of its own.

docs.title: A consumer's statement
docs.text:
A data contract says what a consumer requires and leaves the producer free beyond it. The tree below carries a signup_source the contract never mentions, and reads:

fn is_country_code(code: String) : Bool = code.size() == 2 and code.upper() == code

type UserData : DataContract = {
    id: String
    name: String
    age?: Int
    country: String

    require id != ""
    require name != ""
    validate country with is_country_code
    require age? >= 0
    require age? <= 150
}

d : Data = {id: "u-42", name: "Alice", country: "CH", signup_source: "campaign-7"}
d | UserData

UserData(id = "u-42", name = "Alice", age = none, country = "CH")

validate country with is_country_code is a rule that hands the field to a function: it is require is_country_code(country), with the check named once and reused. A check with a name of its own, a validator trait, is the next page.

An upstream system that adds a field breaks nothing here. That is the practical difference between the two contract forms: a TypeContract would refuse the same tree for its signup_source.

docs.title: Presence and implication
docs.text:
In a rule, an optional field written as a condition, email?, is true where the field is present. a => b is implication, not a or b; it binds loosest and groups to the right. The two together state the rules that a schema cannot: that one of two fields is given, or that one field's value calls for another's presence:

type Account : DataContract = {
    status: String
    closed_at?: String
    email?: String
    phone?: String

    require email? or phone?
    require status == "closed" => closed_at?
}

xs : List<Data> = [
    {status: "open", email: "a@example.com"},
    {status: "closed", phone: "+41", closed_at: "2026-10-01"}
]
xs | Account | map(a => a.status)

["open", "closed"]

A tree {status: "closed"} breaks both rules, and the failure names each as written. The connectives are and, or and not, and a rule reads any expression over the fields.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text:
A field written country: String = "CH" takes that value where the tree has no entry. Defaults are applied before the rules run, so a rule over a defaulted field always has a value to read:

type UserData : DataContract = {
    id: String
    age: Int = 18
    country: String = "CH"

    require age >= 0
}

xs : List<Data> = [{id: "u-1"}, {id: "u-2", age: 34, country: "DE"}]
xs | UserData

[UserData(id = "u-1", age = 18, country = "CH"), UserData(id = "u-2", age = 34, country = "DE")]

A default is the one normalization a contract performs. It fills in what is missing with a declared literal; it does not rename, trim, parse or restructure. Those change the value, and a map does them.

docs.title: Warnings and named rules
docs.text:
warn P is a rule whose violation leaves the value valid. It is written as require P is, and read as it is, and a tree that breaks it still reads. as name after a rule gives it a stable identity, Person.plausible_age, which a diagnostic shows and a program can match on:

type Person : DataContract = {
    name: String
    age?: Int

    require age? >= 0 as non_negative_age
    warn age? < 120 as plausible_age
}

xs : List<Data> = [{name: "Ana", age: 34}, {name: "Old", age: 130}]
xs | Person | map(p => p.age)

[34, 130]

A rule without a name is identified by its position, Person.2. The broken warning is reported alongside the errors when the value fails for another reason; on its own it does not fail the value.

docs.title: From the outside in
docs.text:
The two contract forms are used together. An open contract reads the data as it arrives and holds it to the consumer's rules. A map reshapes the view into the fields the program wants, and nothing else. A closed contract then establishes the canonical value:

type UserData : DataContract = {
    id: String
    name: String
    email?: String
    age: Int = 18
    country: String = "CH"

    require id != ""
    require age >= 0
}

type User : TypeContract = {
    id: String
    name: String
    email?: String
    age: Int
    country: String

    require id != ""
    require age >= 0
}

raw : List<Data> = [
    {id: "u-42", name: " Alice ", country: "ch", tracking_id: "abc123"},
    {id: "u-7", name: "Bob", email: "bob@example.com", age: 51}
]
raw
| UserData
| map(u => {id: u.id, name: u.name.trim(), email: u.email, age: u.age, country: u.country.upper()})
| User

[User(id = "u-42", name = "Alice", email = none, age = 18, country = "CH"), User(id = "u-7", name = "Bob", email = "bob@example.com", age = 51, country = "CH")]

Each step has one job. UserData validates the structural surface and the rules, keeping tracking_id beneath the view. map trims, uppercases and projects. User establishes the exact shape and checks the rules again over the value as it now is. Written raw | UserData | User, with no map between, the pipeline fails: the open view still holds tracking_id, and the closed type declares no such field.

When the source has names of its own, the open view is where the program declares them, and the map is where they are translated. The checker needs the view: x.full_name.trim() over a bare Data is a type error, since a leaf of a tree is not known to be a String until a type says so.

type Raw : Data = {
    user_id: String
    full_name: String
    age: String
    enabled: Int
}

type User : TypeContract = {
    id: String
    name: String
    age: Int
    active: Bool

    require id != ""
    require age >= 0
}

raw : List<Data> = [{user_id: "u-42", full_name: " Alice ", age: "34", enabled: 1}]
raw
| Raw
| map(x => {id: x.user_id, name: x.full_name.trim(), age: x.age.to_int() | unwrap_or(0), active: x.enabled == 1})
| User

[User(id = "u-42", name = "Alice", age = 34, active = true)]

A value that breaks a rule anywhere along this pipeline stops the program with the failure named. Validation as a value is the form that keeps going.

docs.title: Open and closed types
docs.text: A record type reads a Data tree through tree | T. Whether the type is closed or open decides what the tree may hold besides the fields the type declares.

docs.title: A plain type is closed
docs.text:
type Point = {…} admits exactly its fields. A tree with each of them, at the declared types, reads as a Point:

type Point = {
    x: Int
    y: Int
}

d : Data = {x: 1, y: 2}
d | Point

Point(x = 1, y = 2)

A tree with a field the type does not declare does not read. The refusal is an evaluation failure, since the shape of a Data value is known only when the program runs, and it names the field:

type Point = {
    x: Int
    y: Int
}

d : Data = {x: 1, y: 2, z: 3}
d | Point

execute error[contract-violation]: this does not read as Point: field `z`: Point declares no such field
 --> <expression>:7:1
  |
7 | d | Point
  | ^^^^^^^^^
  = expected: Point

A tree missing a field fails the same way, naming the field that is missing. A closed type is the right one for a value the program owns: the program wrote every field, so a field it did not write is a mistake.

docs.title: A type narrowing Data is open
docs.text:
type User : Data = {…} declares the part of a tree the program relies on. A tree reads as a User when it has those fields; the rest of the tree is kept beneath the view, neither checked nor dropped:

type User : Data = {
    id: String
    name: String
}

d : Data = {id: "u-42", name: "Alice", phone: "+41", country: "CH"}
user = d | User
user.name

"Alice"

The view is static. user.phone is a name error, since User declares no phone, even though the tree holds one. Another view over the same value sees it:

type User : Data = {
    id: String
    name: String
}

type Contact : Data = {
    phone: String
}

d : Data = {id: "u-42", name: "Alice", phone: "+41", country: "CH"}
user = d | User
(user | Contact).phone

"+41"

Typing changed what was known of the value and changed nothing in it. An open type is the right one for data someone else produces: a consumer requires at least these fields, and the producer is free to add others.

docs.title: Optional fields are a separate choice
docs.text:
email?: String is a field that may be absent. It reads as an Option<String>, none where the tree has no entry. It does not make the type open:

type User = {
    name: String
    email?: String
}

xs : List<Data> = [{name: "Alice"}, {name: "Bob", email: "bob@example.com"}]
xs | User | map(u => u.email) | List

[none, "bob@example.com"]

A tree {name: "Alice", phone: "+41"} still does not read as this User: phone is undeclared, and the type is closed. Required against optional is about one field; open against closed is about every field the type does not name.

docs.title: Reading a collection
docs.text:
A step | T over a List<Data>, a Seq<Data> or a Stream<Data> reads each element, and the result is a collection of T. A decoded file is read the same way, one document at a time:

type Sighting : Data = {
    species: String
}

source(file("examples/structural/sightings.jsonl"), Json)
| Sighting
| map(s => s.species)

["barn owl", "wren", "barn owl", "kingfisher"]

Json is the format, and decodes bytes to Data at the source. Sighting is the type, and reads each tree in the pipeline. The format is not a step of its own: | Json | Sighting is not written, because a format is how bytes are read, not a type a value has.

docs.title: Testing before reading
docs.text:
is(T) asks whether a tree reads as T, and of_type(T) keeps the elements that do, at type T, as of_type(Int) kept the integer leaves in chapter 2. Over a Data tree the test is by shape: the declared fields present at their types, and no undeclared one where T is closed.

type Point = {
    x: Int
    y: Int
}

xs : List<Data> = [{x: 1, y: 2}, {x: 1}, {x: 3, y: 4, z: 5}]
[xs | map(d => d | is(Point)), xs | of_type(Point) | map(p => p.x)]

[[true, false, false], [1]]

The second tree lacks y, and the third has a z the closed Point does not declare. is tests structure only; the rules a contract adds are the next two pages, and a contract's rules are held by | T, by its constructor and by validate(T), not by is.

docs.title: Type contracts
docs.text: A contract is a record type with rules. type User : TypeContract = {…} is a closed one: it admits exactly its declared fields, as a plain type does, and every value of it holds every rule written in its body.

docs.title: Rules beside the fields
docs.text:
A rule is written require P, where P is a Bool expression over the contract's fields. A tree reads as the contract when its shape fits and every rule holds:

type User : TypeContract = {
    id: String
    name: String
    age?: Int

    require id != ""
    require name != ""
    require age? >= 0
}

d : Data = {id: "u-42", name: "Alice", age: 34}
d | User

User(id = "u-42", name = "Alice", age = 34)

An optional field is read in a rule as age?, and the rule applies only where the field is present: a tree without age holds require age? >= 0.

A value that breaks a rule does not read, and every broken rule is named as written, in one failure:

type User : TypeContract = {
    id: String
    name: String
    age?: Int

    require id != ""
    require name != ""
    require age? >= 0
}

d : Data = {id: "", name: "Alice", age: -3}
d | User

execute error[contract-violation]: this does not read as User: `require id != ""` does not hold; `require age? >= 0` does not hold
  --> <expression>:12:1
   |
12 | d | User
   | ^^^^^^^^
   = expected: User

Structure comes first: a tree missing a field or holding one at the wrong type fails for that, and no rule runs over it. The rules see a value whose fields all read.

Only a contract has rules. require in a plain type is a type error, and the message names both contract forms.

docs.title: The constructor is held to the rules
docs.text:
A contract built in the program, User(id = …), is checked as a read tree is. A field written age: Int = 18 has a default: where neither the constructor nor the tree gives the field, the default stands, and the rules see it:

type User : TypeContract = {
    id: String
    age: Int = 18

    require id != ""
    require age >= 0
}

[User(id = "u-1"), User(id = "u-2", age = 34)]

[User(id = "u-1", age = 18), User(id = "u-2", age = 34)]

User(id = "", age = -1) fails as d | User fails over the same values, naming both rules. There is no way of making a User that skips its rules, which is what makes the type worth having: a function taking a User needs no check of its own.

A default is a literal of the field's type, a scalar or a list, set or record of literals. It is never a call, and it is written on a required field; an optional field has no default, since absence is its value.

docs.title: Rules a subtype inherits
docs.text:
A record declared under a contract, type Interval : Span = {…}, has the fields and the rules of Span and its own, and a rule of Interval reads both sets of fields:

type Span : DataContract = {
    low: Int
    high: Int

    require low <= high
}

type Interval : Span = {
    width: Int

    require width == high - low
}

d : Data = {low: 1, high: 10, width: 9}
d | Interval

Interval(low = 1, high = 10, width = 9)

A tree {low: 10, high: 1, width: 9} breaks both: Span's rule and Interval's are named together, Span's first.

docs.title: Where a type contract belongs
docs.text: A TypeContract is closed, so it is for values the program is the author of: a canonical record after the data from outside has been read and reshaped, a message the program sends, a value it stores. Every field is accounted for, and every rule is a fact about the value that holds wherever the value goes. The open form, for data the program receives, is the next page.

docs.title: Validation as a value
docs.text: tree | T stops the program at the first value that does not read. A pipeline over many values wants the other answer too: which ones failed, why, and what to do with them. validate(T) gives that as a value.

docs.title: One result per value
docs.text:
d | validate(T) is a Result<T, Invalid>: ok of the value read, or err of one Invalid that holds the original tree and every reason it did not read. A match covers both, and nothing is thrown:

type UserData : DataContract = {
    id: String
    require id != ""
}

d : Data = {id: ""}
match d | validate(UserData) {
    ok(user) => user.id,
    err(e) => fmt("{} violation of {}", e.violations.size(), e.contract),
}

"1 violation of UserData"

Over a List<Data>, a Seq<Data> or a Stream<Data>, validate(T) is elementwise and keeps the shape: a List<Result<T, Invalid>>, a stream of results. An invalid element is a value in the collection, not an exception out of it. oks() keeps the successes at type T, and errs() keeps the failures at type Invalid:

type UserData : DataContract = {
    id: String
    age?: Int

    require id != "" as id_present
    require age? >= 0
    warn age? < 120
}

xs : List<Data> = [{id: "u-1", age: 34}, {id: "", age: -3}, {age: "x"}, {id: "u-4", age: 130}]
results = xs | validate(UserData)
[
    results | oks() | map(u => u.id),
    results | errs() | flat_map(e => e.violations) | map(v => v.rule)
]

[["u-1", "u-4"], ["UserData.id_present", "UserData.2", "UserData.id.missing", "UserData.age.type"]]

Four things to see. The second value breaks two rules and both are reported. The third is missing id and has a text age: both structural faults are reported, and no rule ran over it. The fourth breaks only the warning and is among the successes. And every reason has a stable name: a named rule by its name, an unnamed one by its position, a structural fault by its field and kind.

docs.title: What a violation holds
docs.text:
A Violation is a record, not a message. Its contract and path say where, its kind says what sort of fault, missing, type, undeclared or rule, its rule is the stable identity and text the rule as written. For a structural fault, expected holds the declared type and actual the tree the field held:

type UserData : DataContract = {
    id: String
    age: Int
}

d : Data = {age: "forty-two"}
match d | validate(UserData) {
    ok(_) => [],
    err(e) => e.violations | map(v => [v.rule, v.kind, v.expected | unwrap_or("-"), fmt("{}", v.actual)]),
}

[["UserData.id.missing", "missing", "String", "none"], ["UserData.age.type", "type", "Int", "\"forty-two\""]]

A message is there for display, and a program reads the structured fields instead. Violation and Invalid are themselves open contracts declared in the standard library, so a producer may attach a source or a position, and a failure written to a file reads back with | Invalid.

docs.title: The original value
docs.text:
Invalid.value is the tree as it was validated, before any default was applied. A rejected value carries what is needed to repair it or to replay it later, without a lookup elsewhere:

type UserData : DataContract = {
    id: String
    age: Int = 18
    require id != "" as id_present
}

xs : List<Data> = [{id: "u-1"}, {id: ""}, {id: "u-3"}, {id: "", age: 3}]
xs | validate(UserData) | errs() | map(e => e.value)

[{id: ""}, {age: 3, id: ""}]

docs.title: Both sides at once
docs.text:
A pipeline that keeps the accepted values and does something else with the rejected ones is a fork: one input broadcast to named branches, each a pipeline of its own. Each result lands on one side, in source order, and each side is an ordinary collection to continue with or to write out:

type UserData : DataContract = {
    id: String
    require id != "" as id_present
}

xs : List<Data> = [{id: "u-1"}, {id: ""}, {id: "u-3"}]
{ accepted, rejected } = xs | validate(UserData) | fork { accepted = oks(), rejected = errs() }
[accepted | map(u => u.id) | json, rejected | map(e => e.violations | map(v => v.rule)) | json]

[[
  "u-1",
  "u-3"
], [
  [
    "UserData.id_present"
  ]
]]

The rejected side written to a sink is a dead letter: the full rejected tree and its violations, as data, where another program reads it back.

docs.title: The policy is the pipeline
docs.text:
The contract says what is valid. What happens to an invalid value is not a setting of the contract; it is the shape of the pipeline around it, and the same contract serves each:

To Write stop at the first invalid value xs \| T keep every result and decide xs \| validate(T) skip the invalid xs \| validate(T) \| oks() keep the accepted, route the rejected xs \| validate(T) \| fork { accepted = oks(), rejected = errs() } accept with a note a rule written warn

Over a stream that does not end the same words hold, and the stream continues past an invalid element as it continues past any other:

type Reading : DataContract = {
    value: Int
    require value >= 0
}

fn readings() : Stream<Data> {
    yield {value: 1}
    yield {value: -1}
    yield {value: 2}
    for r in readings() {
        yield r
    }
}

readings() | validate(Reading) | oks() | map(r => r.value) | take(5)

[1, 2, 1, 2, 1]

validate(T) reads a Data tree or an open view. A value that is already a closed record was checked when it was made, and validate(Point) over a Point is a type error saying so: there is nothing left to find out.

docs.title: Validators
docs.text: A check that several contracts share gets a name. A validator trait is a trait whose supertype is Validator, implemented for the type of value it checks with one function, validate(self) : Bool. A contract names it in a rule, or declares a field with it.

docs.title: Declaring one
docs.text:
Email below is implemented for String. The field work_email: Email is a String held to the check as it is read; the rule validate contact? with Email holds the optional contact to the same check, where it is present:

trait Email : Validator { }

impl Email for String {
    fn validate(self) : Bool = self.contains("@") and not self.starts_with("@")
}

type Signup : DataContract = {
    contact?: String
    work_email: Email

    validate contact? with Email
}

d : Data = {work_email: "ada@lovelace.org"}
d | Signup

Signup(contact = none, work_email = "ada@lovelace.org")

Signup.work_email is a String: a field declared with a validator trait has the type that implements it. The validator adds a check, not a type of value.

A tree {work_email: "@lovelace.org", contact: "nobody"} breaks both. The failure names the field's check as work_email: Email and the rule as written, validate contact? with Email.

docs.title: A function or a type
docs.text: validate f with V takes either. A function of the field's type to Bool, as is_country_code was on the previous page, is the check written once in the program. A validator trait is the check with a name in the type system: a field can be declared with it, a library can export it, and a diagnostic can name it. A validator named in a rule must be implemented for the field's type; validate age with Email over an Int field is a type error naming the missing implementation.

docs.title: The standard validators
docs.text:
import validators brings the standard ones. Email is implemented for String. NonEmpty is implemented for String, text that is more than whitespace, and for List<T>, a list with an element:

import validators

type Signup : DataContract = {
    email: Email
    name: String
    tags: List<String>

    validate name with NonEmpty
    validate tags with NonEmpty as tagged
}

xs : List<Data> = [
    {email: "ada@lovelace.org", name: "Ada", tags: ["math"]},
    {email: "ada@", name: "  ", tags: []}
]
xs | validate(Signup) | map(r => match r {
    ok(s) => s.email,
    err(e) => e.violations | map(v => v.rule) | join(" "),
})

["ada@lovelace.org", "Signup.email Signup.1 Signup.tagged"]

The second signup breaks three checks, and all three are named: the field declared with a validator as Signup.email, the unnamed rule by its position, and the named rule by its name. validate(Signup) is the form that gives these back as a value instead of stopping, and is the next page.

A validator implemented for more than one type, as NonEmpty is, is named in a rule, where the field's type selects the implementation. It cannot be a field's type, since there would be two types to read the field as.

The module is imported by name and never by the prelude, so a program's own Email is its own. It is written in HQL, in lib/std/validators/mod.hql, and a validator of the program's is declared the same way.

docs.title: 12. Errors
docs.text:
A failure is an operation that did not produce the value its signature promises. HQL has two kinds of failure, and each has its own mechanism:

  • A data failure is a value. err(e) of a Result<T, E>, and an Invalid with its Violations, are ordinary values of the program: map, match, errs() and sink act on them as on any other value.
  • A diagnostic is an event. A phase of the run — the loader, the parser, the checker, the planner, the evaluator or the renderer — writes one when it cannot do what the program asked. The program never constructs a diagnostic and never reads one.

The call site determines which of the two a data failure is. x | validate(User) gives Result<User, Invalid>, a value; x | User requires x to read as a User, and a value that does not is a diagnostic of the execute phase. No operation moves a failure from one side to the other.

Term Meaning failure an operation did not produce the value its signature promises data failure a failure the program keeps as a value: err(e), Invalid, Violation diagnostic a structured event describing a failure, written by a phase phase when the diagnostic occurred: load, parse, check, plan, execute, render kind what the problem is, by a stable kebab-case name: type-mismatch, division-by-zero severity how serious it is: debug, info, warning, error, failure disposition what the phase did next: warning, recoverable, fatal diagnostic channel the one Channel<Diagnostic> of a run, which every phase writes into format a rendering of a diagnostic: DiagnosticText, Json target where a rendered diagnostic is delivered: standard error by default

The two pages of this chapter take the sides in turn:

  • Failures as data: Result, validate, Invalid and Violation, and the operations over them.
  • Diagnostics: the four axes, the diagnostic channel, the formats, strict and collect, and the exit status.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Diagnostics are what hql says back. Chapter 13 is the rest of the conversation: the commands, the REPL, the reports and the settings.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text: A diagnostic is a structured event a phase of the run writes when it cannot do what the program asked, or has a fact about the program worth stating. It is not a value of the program.

docs.title: The four axes
docs.text:
Every diagnostic has four independent fields, each set by the phase that wrote it:

Axis Values Says phase load, parse, check, plan, execute, render when it occurred kind unexpected-token, unknown-name, type-mismatch, division-by-zero, … what the problem is severity debug, info, warning, error, failure how serious it is disposition warning, recoverable, fatal what the phase did next

The text form is headed by three of them, phase severity[kind]. A parse failure leaves no syntax tree:

[1, 2

parse failure[unexpected-token]: expected `]` after collection elements, found end of input
 --> <expression>:1:6
  |
1 | [1, 2
  |      ^

A check error is found before anything runs:

"total: " + 3

check error[type-mismatch]: `Add` for String takes String, not Int
 --> <expression>:1:13
  |
1 | "total: " + 3
  |             ^

An execute failure depends on a value, so hql check accepts the program and the run fails:

[6, 0, 3] | map(n => 6 / n)

execute failure[division-by-zero]: division by zero
 --> <expression>:1:22
  |
1 | [6, 0, 3] | map(n => 6 / n)
  |                      ^^^^^
  = element: 0, position 2 of 3 in `map`
  = bindings: n = 0

No axis is derived from another. A contract read x | T and a division by zero both fail in the execute phase; the first is an error, a wrong value read, and the second a failure, an operation with no result. An integer literal outside the Int range is a numeric-overflow of the parse phase, and the same kind in the execute phase is an addition whose sum left the range.

docs.title: Fields beyond the axes
docs.text:
What a field carries is not repeated in the message. Under the caret, the text form shows one = line per field that applies:

  • cell: the cell of a document the diagnostic is about;
  • note: a second place in the source, with what is there;
  • help: what to write instead, a nearest name or a conventional spelling;
  • expected and found: the type a step needed, and what was there;
  • element: the element a step was applying its function to;
  • source: the document a card the failure was about was read from;
  • bindings: the parameters in scope where it failed;
  • trace: the functions it was reached through, outermost first.
[1, 2] | mapp(n => n)

check error[unknown-step]: `mapp` is not a pipeline step
 --> <expression>:1:10
  |
1 | [1, 2] | mapp(n => n)
  |          ^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = help: did you mean `map`?

trait Shape { fn area(self) : Float }
type Circle { radius : Float }
impl Shape for Circle { fn area(self) : Float = 3.0f }
impl Shape for Circle { fn area(self) : Float = 4.0f }
1

check error[duplicate-implementation]: `Shape` is already implemented for Circle: a trait has one implementation per type
 --> <expression>:4:1
  |
4 | impl Shape for Circle { fn area(self) : Float = 4.0f }
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = note: the first implementation, at <expression>:3:1

A failure inside called functions names each call that reached it, and the parameters of the function it is in:

fn ratio(total: Int, parts: Int) : Int = total / parts

fn share(xs: List<Int>) : Int = ratio(xs | sum, size(xs) - 3)

share([4, 5, 6])

execute failure[division-by-zero]: division by zero
 --> <expression>:1:42
  |
1 | fn ratio(total: Int, parts: Int) : Int = total / parts
  |                                          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = bindings: parts = 0, total = 15
  = trace: share (call) → ratio (call)

A failure over a card's value names the document the card was read from. Here the divisor is zero for the book of 112 pages:

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
| map(c => match c.metadata.pages { some(Int n) => 1000 / (n - 112), _ => 0 })

execute failure[division-by-zero]: division by zero
 --> <expression>:3:52
  |
3 | | map(c => match c.metadata.pages { some(Int n) => 1000 / (n - 112), _ => 0 })
  |                                                    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = element: "a-room-of-ones-own", position 1 of 7 in `map`
  = source: books/a-room-of-ones-own.hmd

docs.title: The diagnostic channel
docs.text:
A run owns one diagnostic channel, Channel<Diagnostic>. It is a channel as the channels page of chapter 9 describes one: typed, in memory, its values in the order they were committed. Two properties set it apart. Its scope is the run, not one evaluation: it is opened before the loader reads the vault and closed after the last phase, so a parse failure or a type error, written before any HQL is evaluated, has a channel to go to. And the program holds no name for it: no operation reads the channel of the run it is in.

Every phase writes into it in order. A check warning and an execute failure of one run arrive in that order, and the failure leaves the warning intact:

fn totalOf(xs : List<Int>) : Int = xs | sum

totalOf([1, 2, 3]) / 0

check warning[naming-convention]: `totalOf` is a function, written in snake_case
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | fn totalOf(xs : List<Int>) : Int = xs | sum
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = help: write it `total_of`

execute failure[division-by-zero]: division by zero
 --> <expression>:3:1
  |
3 | totalOf([1, 2, 3]) / 0
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

2 diagnostics: 1 failure, 0 error, 1 warning

The loader writes into the same channel. A document whose header does not parse is skipped with a load warning[skipped-document], and the rest of the vault is read. A warning never changes the exit status.

docs.title: Formats and targets
docs.text:
What the channel holds reaches a person or a tool through a format and a target. The default is DiagnosticText on standard error, with the value on standard output. The host's options change that wiring, not the program:

Option Effect --diagnostics-format json each diagnostic is one JSON document per line on standard error, every field that applies present --envelope json one JSON document on standard output: the type, the value, and the channel's contents under diagnostics --report-level LEVEL the lowest severity shown; a hidden diagnostic is still in the channel and in the envelope 
"total: " + 3

{"disposition":"fatal","kind":"type-mismatch","message":"`Add` for String takes String, not Int","origin":"<expression>","phase":"check","severity":"error","span":{"end":13,"start":12}}

A report is the channel's contents rendered in a format, followed by a count per severity when there is more than one. It names a presentation, not an object of the run.

docs.title: Diagnostics as data in a later run
docs.text:
A run never reads its own channel, and a later run reads what an earlier one delivered as it reads any data. Diagnostic is a record of the standard library, so a file written with --diagnostics-format json reads back with | Diagnostic, and DiagnosticText writes such records as the report a run prints, without the source line:

source(file("run.jsonl"), JsonLines)
| Diagnostic
| filter(d => d.severity == "error" or d.severity == "failure")
| format(DiagnosticText)

execute failure[division-by-zero]: division by zero
 --> examples/error-handling/diagnostics/warning-then-failure.hql

docs.title: Continuation: strict and collect
docs.text:
Whether a phase continues after a diagnostic is the phase's. --report collect asks every phase for as much continuation as it can give; strict, the default, declines optional continuation after the first error.
