Phase After an error Under collect load skips the document and continues the same parse stops: nothing after an unparseable source has a structure the same check stops at the first checks every statement; a failed one still binds its name plan stops: a refused pipeline has no plan the same execute stops at the first map steps past an element whose function failed; an overflow or an I/O failure stops under both render stops at the failing cell renders every cell, each reported against its own fault

Under collect, the element map stepped past is lost, the value stands without it, and the diagnostic says disposition: recoverable:

$ hql --report collect '[6, 0, 3] | map(n => 6 / n)'
[1, 2]
execute failure[division-by-zero]: division by zero
 --> <expression>:1:22
  |
1 | [6, 0, 3] | map(n => 6 / n)
  |                      ^^^^^
  = element: 0, position 2 of 3 in `map`
  = bindings: n = 0

The value is on standard output and the diagnostic on standard error. In --diagnostics-format json the same diagnostic carries "disposition": "recoverable"; under strict it is fatal and there is no value.

The exit status is 1 when the channel holds a diagnostic at or above error, and 0 otherwise. The run above produced a value and still exits 1: a failure was written.

docs.title: The lifecycle of a fatal diagnostic
docs.text:
A fatal diagnostic ends its phase, and later phases do not start. What was written before it stays in the channel, and the run ends only after the channel's delivery consumers have delivered everything written:

Delivering a diagnostic never resumes the computation. Handling a failure is done with data, on the other side of the model.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: This is the last chapter. The examples page lists the runnable programs in the repository, the error-handling cases among them.

docs.title: Failures as data
docs.text: A data failure is a value of the program. Its type says it may be a failure, the checker holds every use of it to that type, and the run writes no diagnostic for it.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
Result<T, E> is ok(v) or err(e). A function that may fail declares it in its result type, and a match covers both cases:

fn parse(text: String) : Result<Int, String> = match text.to_int() {
    some(n) => ok(n),
    none => err(fmt("not a number: {}", text)),
}

["4", "x", "15"] | map(parse)

[ok(4), err("not a number: x"), ok(15)]

A Result is not its value. parse("4") + 1 is a type error, found before anything runs:

parse("4") + 1

check error[type-mismatch]: addition requires two Int, two Float or two Decimal operands, or two values of a type implementing `Add`, not Result<Int, String>
 --> <expression>:7:1
  |
7 | parse("4") + 1
  | ^^^^^^^^^^

unwrap_or gives the value or a default, map_err changes the error, and oks() and errs() keep one side of a sequence of results:

results = ["4", "x", "15"] | map(parse)
{
    total: results | oks() | sum,
    rejected: results | errs(),
    fallback: parse("x").unwrap_or(0),
}

{fallback: 0, rejected: ["not a number: x"], total: 19}

docs.title: validate: a contract read as a value
docs.text:
x | validate(T) reads x as the declared type T and gives Result<T, Invalid>. An Invalid carries the contract, the value and one Violation per broken rule, each with its path, kind, expected and actual:

type User { name : String, age : Int }

{name: "bob", age: "forty"} | validate(User)

err(Invalid(contract = "User", value = {age: "forty", name: "bob"}, violations = [Violation(contract = "User", path = ["age"], kind = "type", rule = "User.age.type", text = "\"forty\" is not Int", expected = "Int", actual = "forty", severity = "error", message = "field `age`: \"forty\" is not Int")]))

Over many rows, errs() keeps the rejected ones as data the program can count, sort or write out:

type User { name : String, age : Int }

rows = [{name: "ada", age: 36}, {name: "bob", age: "forty"}]
rows
| map(row => row | validate(User))
| errs()
| map(invalid => invalid.violations | map(v => v.message))

[["field `age`: \"forty\" is not Int"]]

The run above writes no diagnostic, and its exit status is 0. A Violation with severity = "warning" is data in the same way.

docs.title: x | T: a contract read as a requirement
docs.text:
Without validate, x | T requires x to read as T. A value that does not is a failure of the execute phase, written as a diagnostic, and the run ends:

type User { name : String, age : Int }

Data("{\"name\": \"bob\", \"age\": \"forty\"}", Json) | User

execute error[contract-violation]: this does not read as User: field `age`: "forty" is not Int
 --> <expression>:3:1
  |
3 | Data("{\"name\": \"bob\", \"age\": \"forty\"}", Json) | User
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = expected: User

The diagnostic carries the same Violations validate would have given, as its context. They remain the diagnostic's: no operation reads them back into the program. Which of the two forms to write is the program's decision, at the call site: validate where a rejected value is part of the result, | T where it ends the run.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Diagnostics describes the other side: what a diagnostic carries, where it goes, and when a run stops.

docs.title: 19. OLTP
docs.text:
The shop's systems so far are its OLTP side: online transaction processing, the side where things happen. An order is placed and a row is committed; a payment fails and a message is published; the warehouse reads the next shipment and acknowledges it. Each fact is one row or one message, written once as it occurs, and what the system holds is the current state of the business: these orders, these customers, this stock. The PostgreSQL table, the Kafka topic and the JetStream subject of chapters 16 and 17 are all of this kind, and so is the first lakehouse table the raw orders land in.

The pipelines of this side share a shape. They read one value at a time, tap, and write one value at a time, sink, as each arrives; they decide each value on its own, validate, filter, map, and keep nothing between two values; and they run for as long as values arrive. The guarantees they rest on are the ones of chapter 16 and chapter 17: a row committed as it is written, a message stored before the write ends, a message delivered at least once and so written so that twice does no harm.

This chapter is the shop's whole transactional day as one file, and what follows from its being a file. The other side, the history those transactions leave and the questions a report asks of it, is chapter 20.

docs.title: The pages
docs.text: Page What it covers The shop's day in one file one pipeline from the raw subject to an archive, a silver table, an alert subject and a dead-letter subject, checked against the configuration with nothing connected When a mistake is found the phase each broken binding is found in, and what is said A replay is the same file the pipeline as a function of its input: a test over a file, a replay over the archive, production over the subject, and a stream bounded into a batch Streams against tables enrichment of a stream by a lookup table, and windows, as design A transfer is one transaction insert, update and delete changing rows in place, and with transaction making several of them one transaction, with its rollback, its retries and its failure as data

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 20 turns from the transactions to what they leave behind: bronze, silver and gold tables, the grain of a row, duplicates and how they are removed, and a table kept up to date by key.

docs.title: When a mistake is found
docs.text:
A binding can break, and it breaks at the earliest phase that can see it. Checking sees the configuration; evaluation sees the systems:

What is wrong Found What is said tap("order_event") checking check error[unknown-name]: no endpoint order_event is configured; did you mean order_events? source("order_events") checking check error[type-mismatch]: order_events is a kafka endpoint, read by tap as a Stream, not by source as a Seq a stream written by target("orders") checking check error[type-mismatch]: target("orders") writes a Table or a sequence of a declared record, not Stream<Event> sink("ledger") checking check error[type-mismatch]: endpoint ledger is a sqlite endpoint, which sink does not write; write it whole with target a password in hql.toml loading the vault url holds credentials; name the environment variable that holds the address, url_env = "VARIABLE" SHOP_DSN not set evaluation, before the first row execute failure[io-failure]: endpoint orders: the environment variable SHOP_DSN, which dsn_env names, is not set a raw order read as Event evaluation, at that order execute failure[io-failure]: endpoint raw_events, field amount: "free" is not a decimal number a write to a wildcard subject evaluation, at the write execute failure[io-failure]: subject orders.> holds a wildcard, which reads many subjects and writes none; a message is published to one subject

A secret is named by the variable that holds it and never printed. A failure at evaluation names the endpoint by its id and the value by its field; what it never does is continue past a value it could not read and count it later as missing. A pipeline that must continue says so in its shape, as day.hql does with validate and fork: the order that would have stopped it is a row in the dead-letter subject instead.

docs.title: A replay is the same file
docs.text:
The pipeline names one input. Bound to a function, it takes any stream of Data, and the input is chosen where it is called:

type EventData : DataContract = {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String

    require amount >= 0 as non_negative
    require ["order_placed", "order_shipped", "payment_failed"] | contains(kind) as known_kind
}

route = (raw: Stream<Data>) => raw
| validate(EventData)
| fork {
    clean    = oks()  | map(e => fmt("ok   {}", e.id)) | sink(stdout, Text),
    rejected = errs() | map(e => fmt("err  {} {}", e.value.id, e.violations | map(v => v.rule))) | sink(stdout, Text),
}

tap("raw_events") | route

ok   1
ok   2
ok   4
ok   6
err  3 ["EventData.amount.type"]
err  5 ["EventData.customer.missing"]
err  7 ["EventData.non_negative"]
err  8 ["EventData.known_kind"]
{clean: (), rejected: ()}

tap over a file is a Stream that ends after the file's last order, so the routing written for a subject runs over a file of recorded messages, with no broker at all. That is a test. The archive day.hql writes is such a file, so the same call over tap(file("archive/orders.jsonl")) is a replay: last week's orders through this week's rules. And the call over tap("orders_raw") is production. The platform words, test, replay, backfill, name three inputs to one pipeline, not three pipelines.

The other direction is as short. A stream becomes something finite by bounding it: take(n) for a count, collect(n) for batches of a size, each batch a List every whole-input step of chapter 6 applies to:

tap("orders_raw") | take(100) | size

Int

A snapshot is the first hundred, or the first day, of a stream written whole by target; a micro-batch is collect(n) and one write per batch.

docs.title: Streams against tables
docs.text:
Design only

This section describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: these programs do not run, and names and types may change before they ship.

The commonest enrichment is a stream against a lookup: each order joined to its customer's record in a table. The finite side is read whole; the live side passes through one value at a time, and no value waits for another, so join takes a Stream on the left and a Seq on the right:

type Customer { customer : String, region : String, vip : Bool }

customers : Seq<Customer> = source("customers")

tap("orders_raw")
| Event
| join(customers, left = o => o.customer, right = c => c.customer,
       into = (o, c) => {id: o.id, region: c.region, vip: c.vip, amount: o.amount})
| filter(x => x.vip)
| sink("vip_orders")

Two streams joined would wait for each other without end, and the checker says so: join over two Streams is refused until one of them is bounded. A window is collect by time instead of by count, a Stream<List<T>> whose batches close when the span does:

tap("orders_silver_changes")
| window(1d, by = e => e.at)
| map(day => day
    | group(by = e => e.customer)
    | map(g => Revenue(customer = g.key, orders = g.items | size, total = g.items | map(e => e.amount) | sum)))
| emit
| sink("daily_revenue")

Inside a window every whole-input step applies, which is how a daily total is a group and a sum over an input that never ends.

docs.title: The shop's day in one file
docs.text:
Orders arrive on the JetStream subject orders.raw. Each is appended to an archive file as it arrived. Each is validated: the valid ones land in the silver Delta table, and a placed order of 100 or more is also published as an alert to a core NATS subject; the invalid ones go to the dead-letter subject with the rules they broke. The configuration is the shop's hql.toml; the pipeline, day.hql, is this:

type EventData : DataContract = {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String

    require amount >= 0 as non_negative
    require ["order_placed", "order_shipped", "payment_failed"] | contains(kind) as known_kind
}

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

type Rejected {
    id      : Int
    message : Data
    rules   : List<String>
}

tap("orders_raw")
| tee archived = sink(file("archive/orders.jsonl").end, Json)
| validate(EventData)
| fork {
    silver =
        oks()
        | map(e => Event(id = e.id, kind = e.kind, customer = e.customer, amount = e.amount, at = e.at))
        | tee large =
            filter(e => e.kind == "order_placed" and e.amount >= 100)
            | map(e => {customer: e.customer, amount: e.amount, text: fmt("large order from {}", e.customer)})
            | sink("alerts")
        | sink("orders_silver"),
    rejected =
        errs()
        | map(e => Rejected(
            id = match e.value.id { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 },
            message = e.value,
            rules = e.violations | map(v => v.rule)))
        | sink("orders_rejected"),
}

{silver: Step, rejected: Step}

Read top to bottom, it is the dataflow diagram a platform would draw:

orders.raw ──┬──▶ archive/orders.jsonl
             │
             └──▶ validate ──ok──┬──▶ orders_silver
                     │           └──▶ alerts.orders   (≥ 100, placed)
                     └──err─────────▶ orders.rejected

One input, three kinds of fan-out, four outputs. tee branches a pipeline without ending it: the archive receives every order before validation, and the alert branch receives each valid order before the silver table does. fork sends every value to every branch, and oks() and errs() keep one side each. A branch of either is typed like the trunk, so a branch that ended in target over this stream would be refused, as any target of a stream is.

There is no orchestration around the file: no activity names, no cluster, no connection strings. hql check day.hql reads hql.toml, resolves every id to its kind and every kind to a type, checks the whole file, and opens no connection; the result above is what it prints. Every system in the file is in the current release, and the nats-lakehouse case of hql-demo runs the same shape against NATS and a lakehouse.

The gold report of chapter 17 is the second file, and the subject of chapter 20: it reads the silver table whole when a report is wanted, and replaces the gold table in one commit. The two share no state but the silver table.

docs.title: A transfer is one transaction
docs.text:
The shop pays its suppliers from a ledger: an accounts table and a transfers table in the one PostgreSQL database of chapter 16. A transfer of 100 from one account to another changes two rows and adds one, and the three changes hold together or not at all. target cannot say that: it rewrites a table whole, and three writes are three commits. This page is the statements that change rows in place, and the scope that makes several of them one transaction (HQL-0051).

Every program here is checked, not run: the book's tests connect to nothing. The two records are declared once:

type Account { id : Int, owner : String, balance : Decimal }

type Transfer { id : Int, from_id : Int, to_id : Int, amount : Decimal }

The configuration names each table's record, element = "Account", beside its connection:

[endpoint.accounts]
kind = "postgres"
dsn_env = "SHOP_DSN"
table = "accounts"
order = ["id"]
element = "Account"

[endpoint.transfers]
kind = "postgres"
dsn_env = "SHOP_DSN"
table = "transfers"
order = ["id"]
element = "Transfer"

docs.title: Changing rows in place
docs.text:
configured("accounts") is the table itself as a value, where source("accounts") is its rows. Three statements change what a table holds. update selects rows with the filter of every pipeline and set gives the fields that change; its value is the number of rows changed:

accounts = configured("accounts")

update accounts
| filter(a => a.id == 1)
| set(a => {balance: a.balance - 100.00})

Int

The lambdas are not run row by row. The statement runs on the database as one UPDATE … SET … WHERE …, so a lambda holds only what translates: a field of the row, a literal, a value bound outside the lambda, comparisons, and, or, not, arithmetic, contains of a bound collection, and is_none or is_some of a field. Anything else is a check error that says to compute it in HQL and bind it. insert adds a row or a collection of them, and delete removes the rows it selects:

transfers = configured("transfers")

added = insert transfers Transfer(id = 1, from_id = 1, to_id = 2, amount = 100.00)
gone  = delete transfers | filter(t => t.amount == 0.00)

[added, gone]

List<Int>

A filter that matches no row is no failure: the statement changes nothing and its value is 0. A program that needs the row to exist reads the count. A statement outside a transaction is its own transaction, committed when it ends, as target of a table is. The checker refuses a statement over an endpoint that cannot take it: a Kafka topic is not Updatable, a CSV file is not Deletable. A sqlite or postgres table is all three, and a spark table too, where the table's format allows it.

docs.title: Two updates and an insert, or none
docs.text:
A transaction scope runs its block as one unit over its participants, a set of endpoints in one database, and commits when the block ends:

accounts = configured("accounts")
transfers = configured("transfers")
ledger = {accounts, transfers}

with transaction(isolation = Serializable) tx on ledger {
    sender = source(accounts) | filter(a => a.id == 1) | one
    tx.rollback("insufficient balance") given sender.balance < 100.00

    debited = update accounts | filter(a => a.id == 1) | set(a => {balance: a.balance - 100.00})
    credited = update accounts | filter(a => a.id == 2) | set(a => {balance: a.balance + 100.00})
    tx.rollback("no such account") given debited != 1 or credited != 1

    insert transfers Transfer(id = 1, from_id = 1, to_id = 2, amount = 100.00)
}

Result<Int, TransactionFailure>

Inside the block every read and write of a participant runs on the scope's own connection: a source after an update sees the update, and a sink commits no row of its own. one gives the one element of a sequence of exactly one, and fails otherwise. Each update is bound so that its count is read: a credit to an account that does not exist changes no row, and without the check the scope would commit the debit alone.

isolation = Serializable is what keeps the balance check true when two transfers run at once. Under it, two scopes that both read a balance of 150 and both debit 100 cannot both commit: the database refuses one of them as a conflict. PostgreSQL's default level, ReadCommitted, does not refuse it: the second debit waits for the first, then subtracts from the committed 50, and the balance ends at -50. SQLite has no other level.

The handle tx ends the attempt early: tx.rollback(reason) undoes it and gives the reason back, tx.commit(value) commits before the end, and tx.retry() runs the block again. Each is written as a statement of the block or as an arm of a given … otherwise or a match that is one, and tx goes nowhere else: not into a lambda, not into a function.

The scope's value is a Result: ok with the block's final value, here the rows the insert added, and err with a TransactionFailure saying why the scope did not commit. A rollback by the program's own rule, a constraint the database enforced and a conflict that outlasted the attempts are all data, matched like any other:

accounts = configured("accounts")
transfers = configured("transfers")

outcome =
    with transaction(attempts = 3, isolation = Serializable) tx on {accounts, transfers} {
        sender = source(accounts) | filter(a => a.id == 1) | one
        tx.rollback("insufficient balance") given sender.balance < 100.00
        debited = update accounts | filter(a => a.id == 1) | set(a => {balance: a.balance - 100.00})
        credited = update accounts | filter(a => a.id == 2) | set(a => {balance: a.balance + 100.00})
        tx.rollback("no such account") given debited != 1 or credited != 1
        insert transfers Transfer(id = 1, from_id = 1, to_id = 2, amount = 100.00)
    }

match outcome {
    ok(n) => "transferred",
    err(f) => f.kind + ": " + f.reason,
}

String

A scope is observed when it is bound, as outcome is here, or when it is the program's last statement, whose value is the program's result. A scope written as a statement before the last one has a value nothing reads, and the checker warns, kind effect: this transaction's `Result` is neither bound, nor the program's result, nor matched: its failure would be observed by nothing. The program still runs; a rollback in that scope goes unnoticed.

attempts = 3 runs the block again, on a fresh transaction, when the database refuses an attempt because of a concurrent one: in PostgreSQL a serialization failure under isolation = Serializable or a deadlock, in SQLite a database file another transaction is writing. The attempt is retried with no delay, whether a statement or the commit was refused, and after the last one the scope is err with kind = "conflict". A retried attempt reads the balance again, so a transfer that lost the race to another one meets the balance that one left, and rolls back by its own rule where it no longer holds. HQL's own tests run that race over SQLite: two of these transfers of 100 start together from a balance of 150, both pass the balance check, one commits, and the other rolls back on the balance after a retry or ends conflict, with no half of it left. A constraint violation is never retried, since the same rows would be refused again.

A retried attempt undoes what it wrote to a participant and nothing else. A write to an endpoint outside the set, a target or sink to a file, a channel or a topic, or a log call, runs on every attempt and is rolled back by none. Where attempts is written as a number above 1, the checker warns of each such write, kind effect, naming the endpoint: `sink` to `audit` runs on every attempt of the scope and is not rolled back. A write wanted once per outcome is written after the scope, from its value; a log line per attempt is often what is wanted, and the warning says what it is.

Any other failure inside the block, a division by zero, a lost connection, rolls the attempt back before it is reported, so a program that stops leaves no half-made transfer.

The ledger case of hql-demo runs this transfer against PostgreSQL 17: twice it commits, and the third time it rolls back on the sender's balance.

docs.title: What the kind promises
docs.text:
The statements read the same over every table; what a scope guarantees is the kind's.

Kind One scope holds insert, update, delete postgres every table of one database, at ReadCommitted unless the scope names RepeatableRead or Serializable all three, as one statement each sqlite every table of one database file, at Serializable, the one level it offers all three; a Decimal computed on the server is a float spark, a Delta table one table, and at most one statement that changes it: a Delta table commits one statement of itself all three where the table's format allows it

A set of two kinds, or two databases, is refused where the program is checked: no scope spans them, and nothing runs weaker than it was asked to. Two Delta tables that must change together are two commits, and the scope has no form for it; coordinating them is a later record.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 20 turns from the transactions to what they leave behind, and its merge page is the analytical counterpart of update: a table kept up to date by key, whole.

docs.title: 20. OLAP
docs.text:
Chapter 19 was the shop's transactions as they happen. This chapter is what they leave behind. The owner does not ask the order topic a question; the owner asks how much each customer spent this month, which day of the week sells most, and whether refunds are rising. Those are questions over history, over every order rather than the next one, and the tables they are asked of are the shop's OLAP side: online analytical processing, the warehouse, the lakehouse, the place a report reads.

The two sides differ in almost every way that matters to a pipeline, and a platform that serves both, as Databricks does, keeps them apart on purpose:

OLTP OLAP What a row is one fact as it happened: an order, a payment one fact at a chosen grain: an order, a customer-day, a customer What the table holds the current state the history How it is written one row at a time, as the fact occurs in batches, by a load that runs on a schedule or as a stream lands How it is read one row, by key many rows, by scan, aggregated The shape of its pipeline tap, decide each value, sink source whole, group and sum, target What goes wrong a row that does not decode a row that arrives twice, late, or corrected

The last line is the subject of most of this chapter. A transactional pipeline delivers each message at least once, and a message delivered twice into a transactional table is a duplicate row to be found later. In an analytical table a duplicate is a wrong total in a report, and the pipeline that loads the table is where it is removed. Every load of an analytical table therefore answers three questions: what a row stands for, which rows are the same row, and which of the same rows is the one to keep.

In the terms of chapter 14, an analytical load is usually a batch: a source that ends, whole-input steps over it, a target that replaces or appends. It need not be. The silver table of chapter 17 is an analytical table filled by a stream, and the pages here show the same deduplication over a batch and over micro-batches. The side a table is on says what its rows mean; whether it is loaded by a batch or by a stream is the type of the input.

docs.title: The pages
docs.text:
Page What it covers Bronze, silver and gold the three layers of a lakehouse, what each promises, and the load rule of each Grain and keys what one row stands for, the key that names it, and a duplicate at each grain Deduplication exact duplicates with distinct, duplicates by key with group and max_by, and a replayed stream as their source Windows one value per row from its place in its partition: over, ranks, neighbours and frames, and a total order with then Merge a table kept up to date by key: insert or update, today as a pipeline and as design as a write mode Incremental loads loading only what is new: a watermark the table holds, and a position the server keeps

The pages run against the shop's vault, --vault examples/pipelines/shop. A program that writes to the lakehouse is shown checked, with the type hql check prints; a pipeline that ends in target or sink is Step, the type of a program whose result is what it wrote. The file silver_replayed is the shop's six valid events as a replay delivered them: two delivered twice, one corrected after the fact, and one delivered late.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Part III reads a different kind of data. Chapter 21 opens a folder of documents and asks it the questions chapter 6 asked a table.

docs.title: Bronze, silver and gold
docs.text:
A lakehouse keeps tables as files in object storage, with a transaction log beside them, and answers SQL over them. Databricks is one; Apache Spark with Delta Lake over an S3 bucket is another, built from open-source parts, and the spark kind of chapter 17 reaches either. What a lakehouse holds is the shop's analytical side, and data platforms name its layers by their metals.

Bronze is what arrived, as it arrived. Silver is what passed the checks, typed, one row per fact. Gold is what a report reads, already aggregated at the grain the report asks. Each layer has a load rule, and the rule is what the layer promises:

Layer Holds Load Promise bronze every message, raw append only, never changed nothing is lost; a silver load can be run again from here silver every valid fact, typed, once append the new, deduplicated by key one row per fact; a sum over it is right gold one row per report grain replaced whole by each run what a reader sees is one run's answer

In the shop, bronze is the JetStream subject itself, kept by the stream; silver and gold are Delta tables:

checkout ──▶ orders.raw ──▶ validate ──ok──▶ orders_silver ──▶ customer_revenue
             (bronze)          │             (silver)          (gold)
                               └──err──▶ orders.rejected
                                         (dead letters)

[endpoint.orders_silver]
kind = "spark"
url_env = "LAKEHOUSE_URL"
table = "default.orders_silver"
order = ["id"]
mode = "append"

[endpoint.orders_silver.fields.amount]
type = "DECIMAL(12,2)"

[endpoint.customer_revenue]
kind = "spark"
url_env = "LAKEHOUSE_URL"
table = "default.customer_revenue"
order = ["customer"]
mode = "replace"

[endpoint.customer_revenue.fields.total]
type = "DECIMAL(12,2)"

A DECIMAL column states how many digits it holds, so the boundary names the type each amount is written as, and the amounts read back with two decimal places.

docs.title: Bronze to silver
docs.text:
The load is the quarantine of chapter 16 with four ids changed: the subject in place of the topic, a Delta table in place of the clean table, and a dead-letter subject in place of the quarantine table.

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

type EventData : DataContract = {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String

    require amount >= 0 as non_negative
    require ["order_placed", "order_shipped", "payment_failed"] | contains(kind) as known_kind
}

type Rejected {
    id      : Int
    message : Data
    rules   : List<String>
}

tap("orders_raw")
| validate(EventData)
| fork {
    silver =
        oks()
        | map(e => Event(id = e.id, kind = e.kind, customer = e.customer, amount = e.amount, at = e.at))
        | sink("orders_silver"),
    rejected =
        errs()
        | map(e => Rejected(
            id = match e.value.id { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 },
            message = e.value,
            rules = e.violations | map(v => v.rule)))
        | sink("orders_rejected"),
}

{silver: Step, rejected: Step}

sink("orders_silver") appends rows as they arrive, in statements of up to 500, each one commit to the table's log. The dead letters are a subject a stream keeps, so they are themselves a source another program reads, to repair or to count:

rejected : Stream<Rejected> = tap("orders_rejected")
rejected | map(r => {id: r.id, rules: r.rules})

{id: 3, rules: ["EventData.amount.type"]}
{id: 5, rules: ["EventData.customer.missing"]}
{id: 7, rules: ["EventData.non_negative"]}
{id: 8, rules: ["EventData.known_kind"]}

This load keeps the first half of silver's promise, every valid fact and only those, and not the second: a message the subject delivers twice is appended twice. The next three pages are the second half.

docs.title: Silver to gold
docs.text:
The report reads a table that ends, so it reads it whole, and writes the gold table over the one before it:

type Revenue {
    customer : String
    orders   : Int
    total    : Decimal
}

events : Seq<Event> = source("orders_silver")
events
| filter(e => e.kind == "order_placed")
| group(by = e => e.customer)
| map(g => Revenue(customer = g.key, orders = g.items | size, total = g.items | map(e => e.amount) | sum))
| target("customer_revenue")

Step

Under mode = "replace" the new rows take the place of the old ones in one commit, so a reader of the gold table never sees it empty:

revenue : Seq<Revenue> = source("customer_revenue")
revenue

[{customer: "ada", orders: 1, total: 120.50}, {customer: "grace", orders: 1, total: 42.00}]

Of the eight raw orders, four passed; of those, ada's first and grace's are the placed ones, and linus's only placed order was the one sent as "free".

The two programs share no state but the silver table. The first runs for as long as messages arrive; the second runs when a report is wanted and reads whatever the first has committed by then. Gold is cheap to throw away and rebuild, which is why it is replaced; silver is the one copy of each fact, which is why it is appended to and never replaced; bronze is the record of what was received, which is why it is never touched at all.

docs.title: Deduplication
docs.text:
A sum over the replay is wrong, and the amount it is wrong by is the whole motivation for this page:

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

rows : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")
rows | filter(r => r.kind == "order_placed") | map(r => r.amount) | sum

253.73

The right answer is 188.49: orders 2 and 4 are counted twice, and order 6 is counted at both its amounts. Three kinds of duplicate are in those nine rows, and each has its own step.

docs.title: Exact duplicates
docs.text:
A row delivered twice, identical in every field, is removed by distinct, which keeps each value once at its first position:

rows : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")
rows | distinct | map(r => r.id)

[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 6]

That is what at-least-once delivery produces: the subject of chapter 17 delivers a message again when a reader stopped before acknowledging it, and the message is the same bytes both times. distinct is the whole answer where every copy is exact. It is not the answer for order 6, whose two copies differ.

docs.title: Duplicates by key
docs.text:
Two rows with one key are the same fact, and one of them is the one to keep. Which one is a rule the pipeline states. For a correction, the latest by at:

rows : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")
rows
| group(by = r => r.id)
| map(g => g.items | max_by(r => r.at))
| somes
| sort(by = r => r.id)
| map(r => {id: r.id, amount: r.amount, at: r.at})

[{amount: 120.50, at: "2026-11-01T09:15:00Z", id: 1}, {amount: 42.00, at: "2026-11-01T09:20:00Z", id: 2}, {amount: 42.00, at: "2026-11-01T09:21:00Z", id: 3}, {amount: 7.99, at: "2026-11-01T10:02:00Z", id: 4}, {amount: 120.50, at: "2026-11-02T08:00:00Z", id: 5}, {amount: 18.00, at: "2026-11-02T11:50:00Z", id: 6}]

Read step by step: group(by = r => r.id) is one group per key, each holding every row with that key in input order; max_by(r => r.at) picks the row with the latest timestamp out of each group, an Option since a group could be empty; somes unwraps; sort puts the keys in order, since a set of groups has none. Six rows, order 6 at its corrected amount.

In SQL this is the pattern every warehouse carries:

select * from (
  select *, row_number() over (partition by id order by at desc) as n
  from silver_replayed
) where n = 1

partition by id is group(by = r => r.id), order by at desc with n = 1 is max_by(r => r.at), and nothing is numbered, because the row wanted is named by what makes it the one to keep rather than by its position after a sort. Keeping the first version instead, the fact as first reported, is min_by:

rows : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")
rows
| group(by = r => r.id)
| map(g => g.items | min_by(r => r.at))
| somes
| filter(r => r.id == 6)
| map(r => r.amount)

{15.25}

max_by and min_by take any Orderable key, so the rule may be a timestamp, a version number, or a comparison of two rows written out. Of two copies equal under the rule, the one earlier in the input is kept. Where they are the same row, as the exact duplicates are, that is no choice at all; where they differ, a rule that ends in a key no two rows share decides between them, and Windows writes one with then. row_number itself is there too, as the step over.

The sum, over the deduplicated rows:

rows : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")
rows
| group(by = r => r.id)
| map(g => g.items | max_by(r => r.at))
| somes
| filter(r => r.kind == "order_placed")
| map(r => r.amount)
| sum

188.49

docs.title: Duplicates with no key
docs.text:
A row with no key is identified by its content. Two deliveries of one webhook body carry the same fields, written in another key order or with 42.00 for 42, and differ in when each arrived, so distinct keeps both. The fingerprint of a Data tree is the SHA-256 of its canonical JSON, and two trees equal under HQL equality have one fingerprint. It is the key the rows do not have:

import crypto.digest

type Delivery {
    received : String
    body     : Data
}

deliveries = [
    Delivery(received = "2026-11-01T09:15:02Z", body = Data("{\"customer\": \"c-17\", \"sku\": \"tea\", \"amount\": 42.00}", Json)),
    Delivery(received = "2026-11-01T09:15:09Z", body = Data("{\"amount\": 42, \"sku\": \"tea\", \"customer\": \"c-17\"}", Json)),
    Delivery(received = "2026-11-01T09:16:40Z", body = Data("{\"customer\": \"c-21\", \"sku\": \"jam\", \"amount\": 6.50}", Json))
]
deliveries
| group(by = d => fingerprint(d.body))
| map(g => g.items | min_by(d => d.received))
| somes
| sort(by = d => d.received)
| map(d => d.body)

[{amount: 42.00, customer: "c-17", sku: "tea"}, {amount: 6.50, customer: "c-21", sku: "jam"}]

The step is the one of Duplicates by key, with fingerprint(d.body) as the key and the first delivery as the one to keep. A fingerprint is a String, so a load may write it as a column and the merge page match on it as on any key. crypto.digest and canonical JSON are chapter 30.

docs.title: In the load
docs.text:
Deduplication belongs in the load that writes silver, once, at the grain of a fact. A batch load reads the replay whole, deduplicates and writes. It writes to the lakehouse, so it is shown checked: Step is what hql check prints for a pipeline that ends in target, a program whose result is what it wrote:

rows : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")
rows
| group(by = r => r.id)
| map(g => g.items | max_by(r => r.at))
| somes
| sort(by = r => r.id)
| target("orders_silver")

Step

A streaming load cannot group a stream that never ends, and the checker refuses it, as chapter 14 showed for a sum. It deduplicates within each micro-batch instead, and sort makes each batch a List of the declared record, which is what sink writes as rows:

events : Stream<Event> = tap("orders_raw")
events
| collect(500)
| map(batch => batch
    | group(by = r => r.id)
    | map(g => g.items | max_by(r => r.at))
    | somes
    | sort(by = r => r.id))
| emit
| sink("orders_silver")

Step

Two copies that land in different batches are not caught by this program, and that is a limit of what a bounded window can know. The merge page is the complement: deduplication against what the table already holds.

docs.title: Grain and keys
docs.text:
Before a row can be a duplicate, it has to be clear what one row stands for. That is the table's grain: the thing in the business that one row describes. The shop's silver table has one row per event; its gold table has one row per customer. A row is a duplicate when the table already holds a row for the same thing, and "the same thing" is decided by the grain, not by the row's contents.

The key is the field, or fields, that name the thing at the table's grain. Two kinds of key are told apart:

  • a primary key names a row and is given by whoever produced it: the event's id, which the checkout assigned. It is unique by construction and means nothing to the business.
  • a business key names the thing in the business's own terms: the customer's name, the order's number on the invoice, the pair of a customer and a day. It is what two systems that never shared an id agree on.

The silver table's key is the primary key id. The gold table's key is the business key customer. A table at the grain of a customer-day has the composite business key of the two.

docs.title: The replay
docs.text:
silver_replayed is the shop's six valid events as a replay of the subject delivered them. Reading it as Events, the rows, the distinct rows, and the distinct ids are three different counts:

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

rows : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")
[rows | size, rows | distinct | size, rows | map(r => r.id) | distinct | size]

[9, 7, 6]

Nine rows arrived. Seven are distinct as values: two events were delivered twice, identical to the byte. Six ids are distinct: one event was delivered twice with different contents, a correction. At the grain of an event, the table should hold six rows, and which six is the question of the next page.

The ids that occur more than once, with how often and with which amounts:

rows : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")
rows
| group(by = r => r.id)
| filter(g => (g.items | size) > 1)
| map(g => {id: g.key, copies: g.items | size, amounts: g.items | map(r => r.amount) | distinct})

{{amounts: [42.00], copies: 2, id: 2}, {amounts: [7.99], copies: 2, id: 4}, {amounts: [15.25, 18.00], copies: 2, id: 6}}

Order 6 is the one whose copies disagree: placed for 15.25, then corrected to 18.00 five minutes later.

docs.title: Another grain
docs.text:
The same rows at another grain are a different table with a different key. One row per customer per day, keyed by both:

rows : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")
rows
| group(by = r => {customer: r.customer, day: r.at.slice(0, 10)})
| map(g => {customer: g.key.customer, day: g.key.day, events: g.items | size})

{{customer: "ada", day: "2026-11-01", events: 1}, {customer: "grace", day: "2026-11-01", events: 3}, {customer: "linus", day: "2026-11-01", events: 2}, {customer: "ada", day: "2026-11-02", events: 3}}

The counts are wrong, because they were taken over the replay and not over the deduplicated events: grace has two events on the first day, not three. A gold table is only as right as the silver table it is built from, which is why deduplication is silver's job and is done once, at the grain of a fact, before any report is built at any other grain.

docs.title: What a key is to the checker
docs.text: A declared record has no field marked as its key, and the configuration of a table has none yet either. The key is stated where it is used: in the by of a group, in the left and right of a join, in the key of a to_map, which refuses two values under one key as an evaluation error, and, as design, in the key of a write mode on the merge page.

docs.title: Incremental loads
docs.text: A load that reads everything every time is simple and, past a certain size, impossible. An incremental load reads only what is new since the last one. There are two places the pipeline can learn where "new" starts: from the table it writes, or from the system it reads.

docs.title: A watermark the table holds
docs.text:
If every fact carries a timestamp, the latest one in the table is the watermark: everything after it is new. The load reads the watermark, filters the incoming rows by it, and appends:

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

current  : Seq<Event> = source("ledger")
incoming : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")

watermark = current | map(o => o.at) | max

incoming
| filter(o => o.at > watermark.unwrap_or(""))
| map(o => {id: o.id, at: o.at})

[{at: "2026-11-02T11:50:00Z", id: 6}]

The ledger holds the six orders as first reported, so its watermark is order 6's first timestamp, and the only row after it is the correction. max over an empty table is none, and unwrap_or("") makes the first load a full one.

A watermark is only as good as the timestamp: a row that arrives late, with an at before the watermark, is never loaded. The replay has one, the second copy of order 4, which here is harmless because it is an exact duplicate of a row the table holds, and in general is the reason a watermark load is paired with the merge of the previous page, or replaced by a position the reading side keeps.

docs.title: A position the server keeps
docs.text:
The durable consumer of chapter 17 is an incremental load with no watermark in the program at all. The server records how far the consumer has read, so each run of the load is given only what was published since the run before, and the program is the plain append:

events : Stream<Event> = tap("billing")
events | sink("orders_silver")

Step

A message is acknowledged once the program asks for the next one, so a run that fails is given its last message again, and the silver table it appends to needs the deduplication of this chapter exactly once: at that message. A late message is no problem, because the position is in the stream's order, not the message's timestamp.

The two mechanisms suit the two sides. A watermark is what an analytical table can offer a batch load over another table, where no server keeps a position for it. A consumer is what a transactional system offers a streaming load, and it is the better of the two whenever it is there.

docs.title: The three loads together
docs.text:
Load Reads Writes Guards against full the whole source replace nothing; it starts over incremental by watermark rows after the table's latest timestamp append reading what is already held incremental by consumer messages after the server's position append or sink reading what is already held, and late arrival

None of them guards against a duplicate on its own; that is the deduplication in the load, or the merge mode of the table. Bronze is loaded in full and never again; silver is loaded incrementally and merged; gold is rebuilt in full from silver. The layers of the first page are the three loads, one each.

docs.title: Merge
docs.text: The write modes of chapter 16 are create, append and replace, and each is about the table as a whole. An analytical table that is kept up to date needs a fourth, about rows: a row whose key the table does not hold is inserted, and a row whose key it does hold is updated. Warehouses call it upsert or merge, and Delta Lake calls the statement MERGE INTO.

docs.title: Merge as a pipeline
docs.text:
Merge is deduplication by key over the union of what the table holds and what arrives. The current rows and the incoming rows are read, concatenated, and deduplicated with the same rule as the previous page, and the result replaces the table:

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

current  : Seq<Event> = source("ledger")
incoming : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")

current
| concat(incoming)
| group(by = r => r.id)
| map(g => g.items | max_by(r => r.at))
| somes
| sort(by = r => r.id)
| map(r => {id: r.id, amount: r.amount})

[{amount: 120.50, id: 1}, {amount: 42.00, id: 2}, {amount: 42.00, id: 3}, {amount: 7.99, id: 4}, {amount: 120.50, id: 5}, {amount: 18.00, id: 6}]

The ledger held six orders; the replay brought nine rows; the result is six rows, with order 6 updated to its corrected amount and the other five unchanged. An incoming row with a new id would be inserted by the same steps, since a group of one keeps its one row. Written back under mode = "replace", the table is the merge, in one transaction:

current  : Seq<Event> = source("orders_silver")
incoming : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")

current
| concat(incoming)
| group(by = r => r.id)
| map(g => g.items | max_by(r => r.at))
| somes
| sort(by = r => r.id)
| target("orders_silver")

Step

The merge rule, which copy wins, is the max_by and nothing else. A rule that prefers the row already held is min_by over the same key; a rule that prefers the incoming row whatever its timestamp is last over each group, since concat put the current rows first.

This reads and rewrites the whole table, which is right for a table of thousands of rows and wrong for one of billions. The cost is the point of having a write mode for it. A row changed in place, one at a time as a transaction does it, is update of the transfer page; a merge is the whole table kept up to date by key.

docs.title: Merge as a write mode
docs.text:
Design only

This section describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: names and keys may change before it ships.

A table's key is a fact about the table, so it is configured beside it, and mode = "merge" makes the key the rule of every write:

[endpoint.orders_silver]
kind = "spark"
url_env = "LAKEHOUSE_URL"
table = "default.orders_silver"
order = ["id"]
mode = "merge"
key = ["id"]

rows : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")
rows
| group(by = r => r.id)
| map(g => g.items | max_by(r => r.at))
| somes
| sort(by = r => r.id)
| target("orders_silver")

target sends only the deduplicated rows, and the system does the rest: a row whose key the table holds replaces that row, and a row whose key it does not hold is inserted, in one commit. A lakehouse runs it as MERGE INTO, a PostgreSQL table as INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, a SQLite table as INSERT OR REPLACE. The program is the one above, and which statement the kind runs is the kind's business, as a transaction is today.

Two rules follow. A write under mode = "merge" to an endpoint with no key is a check error naming the key. And the rows a target sends must themselves be unique by the key, so the deduplication stays in the program: a merge is told which row to keep among the incoming ones by the pipeline, and which to keep between an incoming row and a held one by the mode.

sink under mode = "merge" writes each row as it arrives, inserting or updating one at a time, which is the streaming load of the previous page without its blind spot: a copy that lands in a later batch updates the row the earlier one inserted.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text: group makes one group of the rows with one key, and a step after it reduces each group to one value. Some questions keep every row and add a value that depends on the row's neighbours: the position of an order among its customer's orders, the balance after each ledger entry, the change from the previous revision. In SQL those are window functions, written OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...). In HQL they are the step over.

docs.title: One value per row
docs.text:
over(by, order, into) partitions a sequence by the key by gives each row, orders each partition by order, and calls into once per row, with the row and its Window: the row's place in its ordered partition. The result is a List holding what into gave for each row, at the row's input position. No row is merged or dropped.

row_number is the row's position in its partition, from 1. Ranking the replay's rows within each id, latest first, and keeping the first of each is the deduplication of the previous page in its SQL form, row_number() over (partition by id order by at desc) = 1:

type Event {
    id       : Int
    kind     : String
    customer : String
    amount   : Decimal
    at       : String
}

rows : Seq<Event> = source("silver_replayed")
rows
| over(by = r => r.id, order = (a, b) => compare(b.at, a.at),
       into = (r, w) => {row: r, n: w | row_number})
| filter(x => x.n == 1)
| map(x => {id: x.row.id, amount: x.row.amount})

[{amount: 120.50, id: 1}, {amount: 42.00, id: 2}, {amount: 42.00, id: 3}, {amount: 7.99, id: 4}, {amount: 120.50, id: 5}, {amount: 18.00, id: 6}]

order = (a, b) => compare(b.at, a.at) is a comparison of two rows, here reversed for latest first; order may also be a key, r => r.at, for ascending order. The kept rows are in input order, each at its own row's position. Without by, every row is in one partition.

group with max_by gives the same six rows, and is the shorter program when one row per key is all a step wants. over is the step when a row's position is itself the value, or when every row stays.

docs.title: Ranks
docs.text:
Rows equal under order keep their input order, so row_number never gives two rows one position. rank gives rows equal under the order one rank and skips the positions they share; dense_rank does not skip:

type Score {
    name  : String
    score : Int
}

scores = [
    Score(name = "a", score = 9),
    Score(name = "b", score = 7),
    Score(name = "c", score = 9),
    Score(name = "d", score = 5),
]
scores
| over(order = (x, y) => compare(y.score, x.score),
       into = (s, w) => [w | row_number, w | rank, w | dense_rank])

[[1, 1, 1], [3, 3, 2], [2, 1, 1], [4, 4, 3]]

a and c tie at 9. a is first in the input, so its row_number is 1 and c's is 2; both have rank 1. b has rank 3 and dense rank 2.

docs.title: A total order
docs.text:
A row kept by its position among equals is kept by where it happened to arrive. Two revisions of one order written in the same second are equal by at, and max_by, like row_number, keeps the earlier in the input:

type Revision {
    id     : Int
    at     : String
    seq    : Int
    amount : Int
}

rows = [
    Revision(id = 6, at = "2026-11-02T11:50:00Z", seq = 1, amount = 15),
    Revision(id = 6, at = "2026-11-02T11:50:00Z", seq = 2, amount = 18),
]
rows
| group(by = r => r.id)
| map(g => g.items | max_by(r => r.at))
| somes
| map(r => r.amount)

{15}

With the rows in the other order the result is 18. then composes two comparisons, the second deciding where the first is Equal; a comparison that ends in a key no two rows share, here the change sequence seq, is a total order, and the row kept no longer depends on input order:

rows = [
    Revision(id = 6, at = "2026-11-02T11:50:00Z", seq = 1, amount = 15),
    Revision(id = 6, at = "2026-11-02T11:50:00Z", seq = 2, amount = 18),
]
rows
| group(by = r => r.id)
| map(g => g.items | max_by((a, b) => compare(a.at, b.at) | then(compare(a.seq, b.seq))))
| somes
| map(r => r.amount)

{18}

docs.title: Neighbours
docs.text:
lag is the row before in the partition and lead the row after, each an Option, none past either end. lag(n) and lead(n) reach n rows:

[1, 4, 9]
| over(order = x => x,
       into = (x, w) => [w | lag | unwrap_or(0), w | lead | unwrap_or(0)])

[[0, 4], [1, 9], [4, 0]]

docs.title: Frames
docs.text:
A frame is a list of rows of the partition, in order. running is the rows from the first up to and including the row, rows(before, after) the rows from before positions before to after after, clipped at the ends, and whole the partition. An aggregate over a frame is an ordinary step over a list. The balance after each ledger entry, per account:

type Posting {
    account : String
    seq     : Int
    amount  : Int
}

ledger = [
    Posting(account = "a", seq = 1, amount = 100),
    Posting(account = "b", seq = 1, amount = 50),
    Posting(account = "a", seq = 2, amount = -30),
    Posting(account = "b", seq = 2, amount = 20),
    Posting(account = "a", seq = 3, amount = 10),
]
ledger
| over(by = t => t.account, order = t => t.seq,
       into = (t, w) => w | running | map(x => x.amount) | sum)

[100, 50, 70, 70, 80]

running counts rows, as SQL's ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW does. SQL's default frame with an ORDER BY also takes in the rows equal to the current one; running does not. A moving sum, and the partition's first, last and size:

[1, 2, 3, 4]
| over(order = x => x,
       into = (x, w) => [w | rows(1, 1) | sum, w | first, w | last, w | size, w | whole | sum])

[[3, 1, 4, 4, 10], [6, 1, 4, 4, 10], [9, 1, 4, 4, 10], [7, 1, 4, 4, 10]]

docs.title: The first n of each key
docs.text:
Keeping the two latest orders of each customer is row_number and a filter. A record literal is Data, whose fields are Option<Data> and not ordered, so into builds a declared record to compare n with <=:

type Order {
    id       : Int
    customer : String
    at       : Int
}

type Ranked {
    id : Int
    n  : Int
}

orders = [
    Order(id = 1, customer = "ada", at = 1),
    Order(id = 2, customer = "ada", at = 3),
    Order(id = 3, customer = "bob", at = 2),
    Order(id = 4, customer = "ada", at = 2),
    Order(id = 5, customer = "bob", at = 1),
    Order(id = 6, customer = "ada", at = 4),
]
orders
| over(by = o => o.customer, order = (a, b) => compare(b.at, a.at),
       into = (o, w) => Ranked(id = o.id, n = w | row_number))
| filter(x => x.n <= 2)
| map(x => x.id)

[2, 3, 5, 6]

docs.title: What over refuses
docs.text: A window is a view of its partition while into runs. into may not give one back, in any type: the checker refuses into = (x, w) => [w]. And over takes a Seq: a partition of a stream is never complete, since a stream may not end, so over of a Stream is refused like group of one. Inside collect(n), over ranks each batch, and a row in one batch is not compared with a row in another.

docs.title: Commands at a glance
docs.text:
Command What it does hql eval <program> check and evaluate an argument hql check <file> print the type without evaluating hql run <file> check and evaluate a file hql repl read, evaluate and print, keeping bindings hql render <file> run the HQL cells in a document and build the Markdown document they yield hql help <name> the declarations of a function, type, trait or module, with their doc strings hql builtins list the steps hql config the reporting mode and shown level in force, and where each came from hql doctor check the semantic-search chain and name the first missing part hql ai list the model requests waiting under --ai host, and answer one (next release)

hql '<program>' is hql eval '<program>'. - reads standard input wherever a file is taken. Success is exit 0, a language or I/O failure 1, a usage error 2.

docs.title: Doc strings
docs.text: A block of /// lines opened after an empty line is the doc string of the declarations below it, up to the next empty line. hql help <name> and :help <name> in hql repl print each declaration of a name with its module and doc string; :type <name> prints the first sentence. The pages below are the standard library's doc strings, one page per function, type and trait.

docs.title: The standard library
docs.text:
• std/core — The types every other module is written in: the scalars, the collection types, the open tree Data, absence, failure, value order, the format category and the core traits.
  • std/doc — Documents: a header of everything known about one and a body someone wrote, and the card, a document a vault holds.
  • std/retrieval — Retrieval: a corpus ranked against a query.
  • std/graph — Graphs: nodes and the edges among them, structural only; what a node or an edge means is the knowledge module's.
  • std/knowledge — Knowledge: the semantic domain, where everything is a claim.
  • std/collections — The operations over the collection types core declares: membership, filtering, mapping, order, grouping, joins and reductions.
  • std/string — The functions of a String, in the prelude.
  • std/seq — The sequence, set and map operations beyond the core's membership, order and lookup, in the prelude.
  • std/math — Numbers, in the prelude.
  • std/stats — Descriptive statistics over a collection of numbers: the mean, the sample and population variance and standard deviation, the median, quantiles, the mode, covariance and correlation.
  • std/time — Time: zones, the units a value truncates to, and the operations over the time scalars of core: conversion from text, parts, arithmetic, truncation, rendering, and the evaluation clock.
  • std/random — Randomness: samples, shuffles, choices, numbers and UUIDs.
  • std/option — The ways out of an Option<T>, in the prelude, each stating what absence gives.
  • std/result — The ways out of a Result<T, E>, in the prelude, each stating what a failure gives.
  • std/regex — Text matched against a regular expression.
  • std/format — The formats, how bytes are read as values and how values are written as text, and the codec contracts over them.
  • std/io — Input and output: endpoints, the data sources read from them, and the data targets written to them.
  • std/io/fs — The file system as data: folders, globs over paths, and the entries a folder holds, with their kinds, sizes and modification times.
  • std/io/env — What a program reads from the invocation that runs it: environment variables and named arguments.
  • std/io/net — Network endpoints: transports, read and written by source, tap, target and sink like any other endpoint (module io).
  • std/io/logging — Logging: structured events written to a destination, apart from the result.
  • std/io/db/sqlite — SQLite: one table of a database file, as a transport read by source and tap and written by target like any other endpoint (module io).
  • std/io/db/postgres — PostgreSQL: one table of a database, as a transport read by source and tap and written by target like any other endpoint (module io).
  • std/io/db/spark — Spark SQL: one table behind a Spark SQL endpoint, a Databricks SQL warehouse or a Spark Thrift Server, as a transport read by source and tap and written by target like any other endpoint (module io).
  • std/io/transaction — The control calls of a transaction scope's handle, tx, bound by with transaction tx on participants { … } (module io): each ends the attempt and gives no value, so it stands where any type is expected and nothing after it runs.
  • std/io/msg/nats — Core NATS: one subject, as a transport read by tap and written by sink and target like any other endpoint (module io).
  • std/io/msg/nats_jetstream — NATS JetStream: one subject of a stream, as a transport read by tap and written by sink and target like any other endpoint (module io).
  • std/vault — The current vault: the source a program runs against.
  • std/crypto/digest — Cryptographic digests of text and of Data trees.
  • std/encoding — Text-safe encodings of a text's UTF-8 octets.
  • std/bytes — The functions of a Bytes value, in the prelude.
  • std/crypto — Keys, signatures, MACs, password hashes and encryption.
  • search/lexical — Lexical retrieval: a corpus ranked by the words it shares with a query, a hashed bag of words compared by cosine.
  • search/semantic — Semantic retrieval: a corpus ranked against a query by vectors a language model made ahead of time, read from the index that [semantics] index in hql.toml names.
  • std/validators — Validators: the standard validator traits, imported where they are used, import validators, and never by the prelude, so a program's own Email is its own.

docs.title: search/lexical
docs.text:
module lexical

Lexical retrieval: a corpus ranked by the words it shares with a query, a hashed bag of words compared by cosine. Offline, deterministic and exact; it models no meaning, so a query and a document that share no word score zero. Imported where it is used: import lexical.

  • lexical — Lexical retrieval: a corpus ranked by the words it shares with a query, a hashed bag of words compared by cosine.

docs.title: lexical
docs.text:
In search/lexical.

fn lexical<T : Doc>(self: Collection<T>, query: String) : Ranking<Card>

The cards of self ranked by the words their text shares with query, as a Ranking<Card>. The text of each, and query, is a hashed bag of its words of two or more letters or digits, lowercased, and the two are compared by cosine. A card that shares no word with query scores zero and is not a hit; the rest are in descending order of score. The retrieval names the model hql.hashbag.v1 and the metric cosine, and is not approximate.

docs.title: search/semantic
docs.text:
module semantic

Semantic retrieval: a corpus ranked against a query by vectors a language model made ahead of time, read from the index that [semantics] index in hql.toml names. The query is looked up in the index too; one the index does not hold is an evaluation failure. Imported where it is used: import semantic.

  • semantic — Semantic retrieval: a corpus ranked against a query by vectors a language model made ahead of time, read from the index that [semantics] index in hql.toml names.

docs.title: semantic
docs.text:
In search/semantic.

fn semantic<T : Doc>(self: Collection<T>, query: String) : Ranking<Card>

The cards of self ranked against query by the cosine of their vectors in the vault's index, as a Ranking<Card> in descending order of score; a card scoring zero or less is not a hit. query must be in the index. A card the index holds no vector for is left out of the ranking, with a warning; one changed since the index was built is scored, with a warning that its score is stale.

docs.title: std/bytes
docs.text:
module bytes for Bytes : Index<Int>, Slice

The functions of a Bytes value, in the prelude. A receiver module: b.size(), bytes.size(b) and b | size are one declaration. Bytes implements Index<Int> and Slice through at and slice: b[0] is b.at(0), the octet as an Int in 0..255, and b[0:12] is a Bytes.

  • at — The octet of self at position, as an Int in 0..255, or none outside it; a negative position counts from the end: Bytes("hi").at(0) and Bytes("hi")[0] are 104.
  • slice — The octets of self from start to end, clamped to its size; a negative bound counts from the end.
  • size — How many octets self holds: Bytes("hé").size() is 3.
  • to_text — self read as UTF-8 text, or none where it is not valid UTF-8: Bytes("hé").to_text() is some("hé").

docs.title: at
docs.text:
In std/bytes.

fn at(self, position: Int) : Option<Int>

The octet of self at position, as an Int in 0..255, or none outside it; a negative position counts from the end: Bytes("hi").at(0) and Bytes("hi")[0] are 104.

docs.text:
In std/bytes.

fn size(self) : Int

How many octets self holds: Bytes("hé").size() is 3.

docs.title: slice
docs.text:
In std/bytes.

fn slice(self, start: Int, end: Int) : Bytes
fn slice(self, range: Range) : Bytes

The octets of self from start to end, clamped to its size; a negative bound counts from the end. With one argument, a Range, it is Slice's: b[0:12] is b.slice(Range(start = 0, end = 12)).

docs.title: std/collections
docs.text:
module collections

The operations over the collection types core declares: membership, filtering, mapping, order, grouping, joins and reductions. Each one is callable directly or as a pipeline step, and carries the shape a planner splits it by.

  • Group — One partition of a group: its key, and the occurrences with that key in input order, as items.
  • size — The number of element occurrences in self, an Int: [1, 2, 2, 3] | size is 4, and Set([1, 2, 2]) | size is 2.
  • count — The number of element occurrences in self, as size gives it: count is the kept alias of size.
  • contains — true when value occurs in self, and false otherwise: [1, 2, 3] | contains(2) is true.
  • get — The value a map holds for key, or none when the key is missing: {"a": 1} | get("a") is 1, and {"a": 1} | get("b") is none.
  • filter — The elements for which a type test holds, each at the tested type.
  • of_type — The elements whose runtime type is type or one of its subtypes, each at that type, in an F<U>: filter(x => x | is(U)).
  • is — true when the runtime type of self is type or one of its subtypes.
  • somes — The present values of a collection of options, in an F<T>; the absent ones are dropped: [some(1), none, some(3)] | somes is [1, 3].
  • oks — The success values of a collection of results, in an F<T>; the failures are dropped: [ok(1), err("x"), ok(3)] | oks is [1, 3].
  • errs — The error values of a collection of results, in an F<E>; the successes are dropped: [ok(1), err("x"), ok(3)] | errs is ["x"].
  • map — Each element through by, in a collection of the input's constructor: [1, 2, 3] | map(x => x * 10) is [10, 20, 30].
  • retry — Each element through the fallible operation, invoked again while it fails with an error when accepts (every error, without when) and fewer than attempts invocations have run.
  • take — The first n elements.
  • drop — The elements after the first n, in the input's order and type: [5, 3, 4] | drop(1) is [3, 4].
  • collect — Consecutive elements in batches of n, in order; the last batch may be shorter: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] | collect(2) is [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]].
  • emit — Every member of every sequence, in order, the inverse of collect: [[1, 2], [3]] | emit is [1, 2, 3].
  • flat_map — Each element through by to a sequence, and the members of those sequences in order: map(by) | emit.
  • sort — The elements in ascending order: by their own value order, by the key by gives each, or by a comparison by of two elements; elements that compare equal keep their input order.
  • then — self where it is Less or Greater, and next where it is Equal: a comparison that a second one decides on a tie.
  • group — The occurrences partitioned by the key by gives each, as a set of Groups, each a key and its occurrences in input order.
  • join — The pairs of an element of the input and an element of other that match, each built by into, ordered by the input element's position, then other's.
  • left_join — A join that keeps every element of the input: one with no match in other is built by into with none on the right.
  • right_join — A join that keeps every element of other: one with no match in the input is built by into with none on the left.
  • full_join — A join that keeps every element of both sides, with none for the missing side; the unmatched elements of other come after the matched results.
  • cross_join — Every pair of an element of the input and an element of other, built by into, in order, with no condition: [1, 2] | cross_join(["a", "b"], into = (x, y) => [x, y]) is [[1, "a"], [1, "b"], [2, "a"], [2, "b"]].
  • semi_join — The elements of the input that match some element of other, by keys, a predicate on, or both; each is kept at most once, in its position.
  • anti_join — The elements of the input that match no element of other, by keys, a predicate on, or both, in their positions.
  • reduce — The elements folded from the left by by, from initial, or without it from the first element, the result then none over []: [1, 2, 3] | reduce(0, (a, x) => a + x) is 6.
  • sum — The sum of the occurrences, reduce(0, +); [] | sum is 0.
  • product — The product of the occurrences, reduce(1, *); [] | product is 1.
  • average — The mean of the occurrences, or none over []: [1, 2] | average is 1.5.
  • merge_all — Every map merged in order, a later key winning: reduce({:}, merge).
  • union_all — Every member of every set: reduce(Set([]), union).
  • concat_all — Every member of every sequence, in order: reduce([], concat).
  • min — The least occurrence by value order, reduce(min), or none over [].
  • max — The greatest occurrence by value order, reduce(max), or none over [].
  • variance — The population variance of the occurrences, as a Float, or none over []: [1, 2, 3, 4] | variance is 1.25.
  • count_by — The number of occurrences with each key by gives, as a map from key to count; empty over [].
  • histogram — The number of occurrences in each bucket of width, keyed by the bucket's lower bound, the greatest multiple of width not above the value, in key order: [1, 5, 12, -3] | histogram(5) is SortedMap {-5: 1, 0: 1, 5: 1, 10: 1}.
  • top_k — The k greatest occurrences, by value order or by the key by gives, greatest first, equal keys in input order: [3, 1, 4, 1, 5] | top_k(2) is [5, 4].
  • approx_distinct — An estimate of the number of distinct occurrences, size(Set(xs)); 0 over [].

docs.title: std/core
docs.text:
module core

The types every other module is written in: the scalars, the collection types, the open tree Data, absence, failure, value order, the format category and the core traits. A type sits here when a module below it would otherwise import a module above it: Data is a tree of sequences and maps, so the collection types are core types, and the operations over them are the collections module's.

  • Orderable — A type whose values have a total order: of any two values of the type, one comes first or the two are equal.
  • Scalar — A leaf: a value with no parts of its own.
  • Bool — The truth values true and false: a Scalar with equality and no order.
  • Int — A 64-bit whole number, ordered by value: 7 / 2 is 3, and 7 % 2 is 1.
  • Float — A 64-bit binary floating-point number, written with the suffix f (2.5f), ordered by value.
  • Decimal — An exact decimal number, written with a decimal point and no suffix (2.50), ordered by value: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is true.
  • String — Text, ordered character by character: "ab" + "cd" is "abcd", and "hello"[1] is "e".
  • Date — A proleptic Gregorian calendar date, ordered by time: Date("2026-10-24").
  • DateTime — A date and a time of day with no zone or offset, ordered by time: DateTime("2026-10-24T09:30:00").
  • Instant — A point on the UTC timeline with nanosecond precision, ordered by time: Instant("2026-10-24T07:30:00Z").
  • Duration — A signed length of time in nanoseconds, ordered by length: Duration("PT1H30M").
  • Bytes — A finite sequence of octets, ordered octet by octet as unsigned numbers, a shorter prefix first (HQL-0053 part 1).
  • Iterable — A value whose elements can each be visited: the bound an operation states when it only visits each value.
  • Collection — A finite multiset of occurrences, unordered, with no runtime representation.
  • Stream — An ordered, possibly unending run of values x0, x1, x2, ....
  • Seq — A finite stream: a collection in which every occurrence has exactly one position in 0 .. size(c) - 1.
  • List — A sequence of materialized occurrences; repeated traversal preserves positions.
  • Set — Materialized distinct values under HQL equality: count(s, x) <= 1.
  • Map — Materialized associations from distinct keys of K to values of V; not a Collection.
  • OrderedMap — A Map whose keys keep their construction positions: its keys are a Seq<K>.
  • SortedMap — An OrderedMap whose key positions follow the intrinsic total order of K.
  • Data — An open tree whose keys belong to whoever wrote them: what a YAML or JSON document is.
  • TypeContract — The supertype of a closed contract: a structural type declared type C : TypeContract = {…} has exactly its declared fields, and is validated as a contract.
  • DataContract — The supertype of an open contract: a structural type declared type D : DataContract = {…} is a view over Data with at least its declared fields, and is validated as a contract.
  • Option — An optional value of T: present, holding one T, or absent.
  • Result — A computation that may have failed: ok(value) with a T, or err(error) with an E.
  • Ordering — The result of compare(a, b): Less, Equal or Greater.
  • Window — One row's place in its ordered partition under over: the rows with its key, in the order over gives them, and its position among them.
  • Type — A type written as an argument: is(Card), of_type(Card).
  • Format — The category of formats: how bytes are documents.
  • Is — What a predicate that tests its parameter's type, x => x | is(U), gives: a Bool that, where true, holds the parameter at U.
  • Eq — Equality: a == b and a != b over a type implementing Eq call its eq.
  • Ord — Order: a < b and the other comparisons over a type implementing Ord call its compare.
  • Add — Addition: a + b over a type implementing Add is a.add(b).
  • Sub — Subtraction: a - b over a type implementing Sub is a.sub(b).
  • Mul — Multiplication: a * b over a type implementing Mul is a.mul(b).
  • Div — Division: a / b over a type implementing Div is a.div(b).
  • Rem — Remainder: a % b over a type implementing Rem is a.rem(b).
  • Range — A window of positions, what a slice takes: xs[a:b] is xs[Range(start = a, end = b)], and a bound left out is absent.
  • Index — A position: xs[i] over a type implementing Index is xs.at(i), the element there or its absence.
  • Slice — A part: xs[a:b] over a type implementing Slice is xs.slice(Range(start = a, end = b)), a value of the type itself.
  • Validator — A check a value passes: a trait extending Validator is a validator trait.
  • Operation — A function from I to O that also carries its shape: what an executor may assume about splitting the step.
  • Elementwise — An Operation whose result for each element depends on that element alone, so it may run over any split of its input: map and filter are elementwise.
  • Partition — An Operation that regroups its input by a key, each group running independently and completing in any order: group is one.
  • Reduction — An Operation that collapses its whole input to one value through a combiner the runtime holds, so each split may be reduced and the results combined: size combines by addition, contains by disjunction.
  • Barrier — An Operation that needs its whole input before any output, so it is not split: sort, take and reduce are barriers.
  • Pair — Two values held together, each at its own type: what zip, enumerate, entries and join produce, and what Pair(first = a, second = b) builds.
  • Violation — One reason a value does not read as a contract, as validate(T) reports it.
  • Invalid — A value that did not read as a contract, and every reason why: its contract, the value, and the violations.
  • Diagnostic — A diagnostic a run delivered, read back as data: its phase, kind, severity and disposition, its message, and where it points, origin and span, a {start, end} byte range.

Addition: a + b over a type implementing Add is a.add(b).
